This study addresses a critical limitation of deep learning methods in science and engineering: strong empirical performance on training data that fails to generalize to unseen problems. To address this, we apply established information-theoretic tools to analyze the generalization error of a high-dimensional two-layer neural network designed to calculate the ground state of the Schrödinger equation. Our analysis establishes the first non-trivial bounds for this specific architecture, demonstrating that generalization error remains bounded regardless of input dimensionality. This result confirms the robustness of the approach, which utilizes a fully connected feedforward network to represent the eigenfunction. We validate our theoretical findings with numerical experiments, and the complete code is accessible at https://github.com/akshaykumar1998/Neural-Networks-for-Solving-Schrodinger-Eigenvalue-Problem. These results offer a pathway to derive generalization guarantees for a broader class of deep learning algorithms applied to scientific and engineering challenges. Additionally, we introduce a framework for evaluating the generalization error of neural networks in solving high-dimensional partial differential equations. Within this analysis, we prove that the proposed architecture can effectively represent both eigenfunctions and potential functions. Furthermore, we establish generalization bounds for multi-dimensional potential functions that depend only logarithmically on input dimensionality, a significant advancement over prior bounds that grew exponentially. These bounds are derived using established tools from high-dimensional probability and statistical learning theory. Our primary contribution lies in the development of a highly efficient neural network architecture capable of representing both eigenfunctions and potential functions, alongside the rigorous information-theoretic analysis of its generalization error. This work serves as a foundational step toward achieving generalization guarantees for deep learning algorithms in high-dimensional scientific and engineering applications. Finally, we present a framework for analyzing the generalization error of neural networks designed to solve high-dimensional PDEs. In this examination, we prove that the proposed architecture can represent solutions to high-dimensional PDEs, thereby extending the representation capabilities identified for Schrödinger eigenfunctions. We also derive generalization bounds for multi-dimensional potential functions that scale logarithmically with input dimensionality, improving upon the exponential growth observed in previous studies. These bounds are obtained through the application of tools from high-dimensional probability and statistical learning theory. Our main contribution remains the creation of a highly efficient neural network architecture for solving high-dimensional PDEs, supported by the rigorous information-theoretic analysis of its generalization error. This work serves as a foundational step toward achieving generalization guarantees for deep learning algorithms in high-dimensional scientific and engineering problems

Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are a prominent category of machine learning models designed to process sequential data. Their capacity to retain historical context makes them highly effective for time series analysis, a trait that has driven their widespread use in fields ranging from speech and audio processing to biological systems. This paper introduces a C. Elegans dataset, comprising calcium imaging sequences that record the activity of individual neurons over time. The goal of this data is to facilitate machine learning research into the computational capabilities of RNNs. Furthermore, we present experimental results demonstrating how RNNs can model the activity of *C. Elegans* neurons, thereby validating the efficacy of this approach for analyzing calcium imaging data. These findings offer a foundation for future investigations into the algorithmic and computational properties of this dataset. Additionally, the paper includes a data collection section detailing the methodology and rationale behind the process. The results indicate that RNNs can accurately represent the activity of *C. Elegans* neurons, with the model's hidden layer size being a critical factor in determining the quality of the modeling. Finally, we explore the potential applications of RNNs in analyzing calcium imaging data and suggest several avenues for future research. Specifically, we propose that other machine learning models, such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks and Transformers, could be evaluated for their performance on this dataset. Additionally, we suggest investigating the use of this data for neural activity classification and anomaly detection. The dataset is accessible at: https://github.com/ashishkumar2000/Neural-Networks-on-Ca-Elegans-Data. Our code and results can be found at: https://github.com/ashishkumar2000/Neural-Networks-on-Ca-Elegans-Data/tree/main/Ca_Elegans_RNNs. The paper is available at: https://github.com/ashishkumar2000/Neural-Networks-on-Ca-Elegans-Data/tree/main/Paper. For inquiries, please contact: ashishkumar2000@gmail.com. Keywords: Machine Learning, Calcium Imaging, RNNs, C. Elegans.

Building on the work of B\'ar\'ath and Timar, we demonstrate that this forest possesses a regional limit within the sense of Blackwell. This outcome represents a significant strengthening of the original convergence in distribution restricted to bounded point sets as established by B\'ar\'ath and Timar. The proof relies fundamentally on the theory of subshifts of finite type and their associated Toeplitz operators. Additionally, this methodology yields a novel, independent demonstration of the ergodicity of the stable point forest. In our approach, the shift operator is defined by the vectors of the forest. To address the challenge of unbounded test functions, we employ their restrictions to specific regions, which converge in a stochastic manner. This convergence of restrictions facilitates the derivation of the regional limit and, consequently, the convergence of the stable point forest. Furthermore, our framework enables the calculation of the intensity of the forest for any region with a well-defined geometric perimeter. We also present an explicit formula for the correlation function of the forest within a square region, which depends on the side length of the square and the specific structure of that region. This formula exhibits a piecewise-defined nature relative to the side length. Finally, we determine the two-point correlation function for the forest in the limit as the square's side length approaches infinity. This limiting function remains piecewise-defined, though it is valid across the entire plane. Our methodology also allows for the computation of the $k$-point correlation function for any finite set $F \subset \mathbb{R}^2$. This operational approach extends to the $k$-point correlation function. We provide a comprehensive classification of irreducible Gelfand pairs for the general linear group $SL_2(p)$, where $p$ denotes a prime number. This work extends the findings of B. Gross regarding the $SU_2(p)$ case and confirms Gross's conjecture which posited that a unified approach could address the $SL_2(p)$ scenario. Additionally, we investigate a specific instance involving $SL_2(11)$. In our approach, we categorize the irreducible Gelfand pairs by first classifying the maximal Heisenberg groups within the algebra up to isomorphism, followed by examining their induced representations. We demonstrate that these representations fall into two types: those generated by characters of the Heisenberg groups and those arising from pairs consisting of a Heisenberg group and an irreducible character of $SL_2(p)$. We establish that every irreducible Gelfand pair belongs to one of these two categories. Furthermore, we identify a unique pair of subgroups in $SL_2(11)$ whose double coset algebra is isomorphic to that of a Heisenberg group, noting that this exception arises because $11$ is the sole prime for which the normalizer of a Sylow $2$-subgroup is isomorphic to the symmetric group $S_4$. Leveraging the irreducible characters of $p$-groups, we determine the count of non-isomorphic Gelfand pairs. We also investigate the relationship between characters of the Heisenberg groups and the characters of the Gelfand pairs. The paper concludes with an exploration of the combinatorial properties of these pairs. This research was conducted while the second author was a visiting scholar at the University of Notre Dame. Utilizing the Hadron Tomography approach, this study investigates the electromagnetic characteristics of hidden-charm molecular pentaquarks possessing single strangeness. We calculate their electric and magnetic moments, form factors, and photon decay partial widths. Our findings indicate that the electromagnetic properties of these hidden-charm molecular pentaquarks with one unit of strangeness differ significantly from those with no strangeness. Additionally, we compute their strong decay partial widths to determine pole residues, which are then employed to calculate strong-electromagnetic mixing angles. These mixing angles offer a potential method for identifying these hidden-charm molecular pentaquarks with single strangeness through their photon decays. Finally, we compare our results with existing experimental data and theoretical predictions to highlight key features and discuss future experimental efforts required to uncover these hadrons. This research provides a new avenue for exploring the internal structure of pentaquark hadrons. Furthermore, the calculated electromagnetic properties may assist future experiments in identifying these hadrons, thereby advancing our understanding of hadron structure and QCD dynamics. This short note demonstrates that any Zinbiel algebra $V$ over a commutative associative algebra $A$, where $A$ possesses identity elements for both left and right multiplication, is necessarily abelian. Consequently, every Zinbiel algebra under these conditions is isomorphic to a commutative associative algebra. Although the primary focus is on Zinbiel algebras, we also extend this result to Zin-Zin algebras. Furthermore, we establish the existence of non-abelian Zinbiel algebras when the underlying algebra $A$ lacks two-sided identity elements. To achieve this, we construct a specific class of Zinbiel algebras by utilizing a homomorphism from an algebra $B$ into an $A$-module $M$. We provide a necessary and sufficient condition for such an algebra to be abelian, which also clarifies the structure of its abelian ideals. Additionally, we examine the Zinbiel properties of both abelian and non-abelian varieties, deriving several significant consequences. Our primary examples of non-abelian Zinbiel algebras are derived from the Witt algebra, which is significant for its universal property regarding post-Lie algebras. We explicitly calculate the Zinbiel cohomology of the Witt algebra and the universal enveloping algebra of the Heisenberg algebra, demonstrating that this cohomology is generally infinite-dimensional. Finally, we introduce the concept of Zinbiel modules and explore their basic properties. In the concluding section, we present a conjecture concerning Zinbiel modules, inspired by recent research on Yetter-Drinfeld modules. This conjecture posits that the Yetter-Drinfeld category $\mathcal{YD}(H)$ over a Zinbiel Hopf algebra $H$ constitutes a braided monoidal category. We verify this conjecture in the specific case where $H$ is the universal enveloping algebra of the Heisenberg algebra. Additionally, we provide a counterexample to a conjecture regarding YD-modules over Zinbiel algebras, originally proposed by Shengda Li. Specifically, we construct a Yetter-Drinfeld module over a Zinbiel algebra that is both simple and non-trivial as a module, yet possesses only trivial Zinbiel cohomology. This paper focuses on the scattering theory for a homogeneous cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation in three dimensions, modified by a repulsive inverse square potential. The study is divided into two parts. The first part examines scattering within energy-critical Sobolev spaces, while the second part addresses the defocusing mass-critical scenario. Both sections rely on the fundamental property of scale invariance shared by the homogeneous nonlinear Schrödinger equation and the specific potential under consideration. Consequently, the scattering theory developed here exhibits invariance under rotations and dilations. Additionally, the scattering framework is extended to incorporate lower-order terms that are either linear or cubic, provided they remain scale-invariant. This approach enables the analysis of scattering for a broader class of three-dimensional heterogeneous nonlinear Schrödinger equations featuring a repulsive potential. The methodology also holds potential for future applications in investigating scattering for three-dimensional critical heterogeneous nonlinear Schrödinger equations. The results presented herein are applicable to a more general class of homogeneous nonlinear Schrödinger equations featuring a nonlocal potential. Specifically, the theory is valid provided the potential is translation-invariant, commutes with dilations, and satisfies mild conditions regarding its Fourier transform. Notably, the theory remains applicable even when the nonlocal potential is slightly perturbed. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates the scattering behavior of two-dimensional homogeneous nonlinear Schrödinger equations with an inverse square potential, thereby extending these findings to higher dimensions. The methodology is expected to be valuable for analyzing higher-dimensional scattering problems involving nonlocal potentials. Finally, the authors acknowledge the significant contributions of Burak Erdogan, whose insights were instrumental in developing this theory. This study examines how migration and infection interact within a population, modeling the time evolution of a specific group using a stochastic approach. A key assumption is that an individual's disease status at any given moment depends solely on their own history and that of the group, excluding dependence on other populations. The analysis investigates the impact of a critical threshold on the group's dynamics; when this threshold is surpassed, the population is expected to grow. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that increasing the rate of new infections in individuals leads to a higher proportion of infected members within the population. Finally, the study proves the existence and uniqueness of the solution to the stochastic differential equation governing the population's time evolution. Additionally, a differential equation is derived to describe the deterministic limit of the population as the number of individuals grows large. The model's validity is confirmed through a simulation of a migrant infection process. This study verifies the existence of three resonant planet pairs orbiting the star K2-138, which was previously identified by Li et al. (2019) as hosting a 3:2:6 resonance chain. We confirm that the resonant period ratios align with the 3:2 sequence, and the gaps between period ratios remain consistent across all three systems. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the total energy of the system is minimal, indicating dynamical stability. Additionally, we show that a 5:3 resonance sequence cannot account for the observed period ratios of K2-138. Finally, we derive the masses and radii for the planets of K2-138 using the measured period ratios and the known stellar radius. We conclude that the planets of K2-138 are likely rocky, with densities ranging from 2.5 to 10.5 g/cm³. This research underscores the significance of resonance sequences in exoplanet systems for determining planet masses and densities. Additionally, we introduce a novel method for calculating the energy of a two-planet system, which is applicable to any two-planet configuration. We anticipate that this method will prove valuable for future exoplanet research. The data utilized in this work can be accessed at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.14202050. This paper investigates the affine Schur–Weyl duality within the quantum affine algebra context. By employing the Grothendieck groups of categories stabilized by the authentic functor and the polynomial representations of the general linear group, we establish an isomorphism between the Ext groups in the modular category and those of the symmetric group. Additionally, we construct a similar isomorphism linking the irreducible quantum affine modules to the irreducible modules of the classical general linear group. As a consequence, we derive the irreducible quantum affine modules directly from the polynomial representations of the general linear group. In the final section, we examine the case where the nilpotent element is a regular unipotent element, thereby recovering the affine quantum Gluckstein–Grabiner–Pak theorem. Furthermore, we explicitly identify the Ext groups in the modular category as the flag Hilbert space associated with the classical affine Lie type. Finally, we offer an application of our findings to the affine Lie algebra $A_1$. Specifically, we identify the irreducible quantum affine modules with the irreducible modules of the quantum affine algebra through their highest weights. In this scenario, the flag Hilbert space corresponds to the Weyl module of the Lie algebra. This result aligns with the results of the classical affine Lie type and the affine quantum Gluckstein–Grabiner–Pak theorem. Additionally, the irreducible quantum affine modules are identified via their highest weights, which correspond to the Drinfeld polynomials of degree one. This outcome also recovers the irreducible modules of the quantum affine algebra through their Drinfeld polynomials. Finally, the flag Hilbert space is recognized as the flag space of the Lie algebra. We anticipate that these findings will facilitate the study of affine quantum integrable systems through the classical Lie group approach. Specifically, the quantum affine Schur–Weyl duality can be derived from the polynomial representation of the general linear group. Consequently, the Bethe ansatz equations for the affine Lie type can be obtained from the classical Lie group. This approach also recovers the Bethe ansatz equations for the quantum affine Lie type and the quantum affine Gluckstein–Grabiner–Pak theorem. Furthermore, the Bethe ansatz equations for the affine quantum Lie type are derived from the polynomial representation of the Lie algebra. The paper introduces a re-evaluation of the SiD detector concept, which was originally proposed for the ILC in 2006. This updated design incorporates significant advancements in silicon technology achieved over the past fifteen years. Key enhancements include the adoption of 3D sensors, which offer superior performance regarding radiation tolerance, fill-factor, and signal readout; improved micro-structuring capabilities; and more efficient passive cooling methods. Additionally, the study examines the optimal geometric configuration for SiD trackers, evaluating various sensor layout options. The resulting concept, named SiD 3D, maintains the original detector's core characteristics while delivering substantial improvements in 3-dimensionality, tracking precision, and overall performance. A comprehensive overview of SiD 3D is provided, including a detailed technical summary of the sensors. Furthermore, the paper addresses the critical challenge of optimizing readout electronics, emphasizing the necessity of integrating sensor fabrication and electronic systems. It concludes by outlining a comprehensive production plan designed to deliver high-quality, reliable SiD 3D sensors within a realistic timeframe. Ultimately, SiD 3D demonstrates that a state-of-the-art tracking detector can be realized with a robust, proven production strategy. We present a comparative study of the local structure in hyperquenched glassy water (HGW) and solvent extracted ice (SEI), achieved through X-ray total scattering experiments. These samples represent the two most prevalent forms of amorphous ice. By analyzing the radial distribution function, we identified a distinct, crystalline-like domain within both HGW and SEI. This hidden structure, which is more ordered than the surrounding matrix, is primarily located in the 4.5 to 7.0 \AA{} range and shows greater similarity to low-pressure amorphous ice than to high-pressure amorphous ice. Our findings suggest that the energy landscape of amorphous ice possesses a more complex landscape than previously believed, with this ordered region potentially playing a crucial role in the relaxation dynamics of amorphous ice. Furthermore, this discovery may offer a new perspective on the nature of water's local structure. Finally, we demonstrate that the recently developed machine learning method, AMP-GNN, is highly effective in detecting and separating this crystal-like domain from the typical amorphous one. This result not only validates the applicability of AMP-GNN to amorphous ice but also provides a valuable tool for future research. Our work offers a novel insight into the nature of amorphous ice and its relationship to ice Ih. The raw data from this study is accessible at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.1200005. The source code can be found at https://github.com/ChenYi1992/ice-ice-brother. Additional details regarding the samples and experiments are available in our supplementary material. Our results are consistent with the work of Ref.~\cite{Kob2003}. We extend our gratitude to the beamline scientists at BL04B1 for their assistance during the experiments. This study presents a visualization and assessment of the Local Density of States (LDOS) for atomic-scale layers of silicon, gold, and graphite, achieved through scanning tunneling microscopy (STM). While LDOS analysis holds significant promise for characterizing nanostructures, it remains a relatively new technique for atomic imaging. Our findings indicate that the ratio of tunneling current to bias voltage ($I/V$) serves as an effective representation of LDOS, particularly at low bias voltages. Consequently, $I/V$ measurements can be utilized to visualize LDOS distributions in atomic structures. This approach was demonstrated through high-resolution STM images of silicon (111) surface atoms, where the $I/V$ ratio at a fixed tunneling current reveals distinct variations in LDOS at the surface. These results offer valuable insights for interpreting and comparing LDOS data obtained from other atomic structures. Furthermore, we examined the relationship between LDOS and atomic height, observing that for all examined structures, LDOS increases with height up to a specific point before declining. This trend is especially pronounced in gold, where the surface exhibits a notable lack of d-band electrons. Finally, we propose a model explaining the observed $I/V$ ratio behavior in terms of tunneling theory. Overall, this work provides a comprehensive understanding of LDOS properties and establishes a foundation for employing LDOS analysis as a tool for nanostructure characterization. The reported findings are supported by experimental data and calculations. Additionally, we demonstrate that LDOS distributions can be visualized using a color-coded scale, where darker colors signify higher LDOS values. This capability enables the direct observation of LDOS variations at the atomic level, as illustrated by our silicon surface data. We anticipate that this methodology will facilitate the investigation of charge distributions in atomic structures, thereby advancing the understanding of charge transport in nanostructures. The reported results are backed by experimental data and calculations. Furthermore, we note that LDOS distributions can be represented as $I/V$ maps, where each point corresponds to the $I/V$ ratio at a specific position on the surface. We demonstrate that these $I/V$ maps can be converted into atomic images by applying a specific threshold to the $I/V$ data. This allows for the visualization of atomic structures with varying tunneling currents, which can be achieved by adjusting the LDOS threshold. We show that atomic images can be generated from $I/V$ maps by selecting an appropriate LDOS threshold, and we explore the impact of different thresholds on the resulting images. The reported results are supported by experimental data and calculations

This paper introduces Framework, a framework designed to automatically identify errors in published theorems. While theoretical verification is a primary motivation for formal proof assistants, numerous mistakes have been identified in literature due to human errors. Framework utilizes automated theorem provers to discharge proof obligations, enabling the efficient detection of incorrect lemmas and published theorems within extensive proof libraries. We demonstrate that Framework can reconstruct a more robust and efficient proof for a flawed lemma in the Archive of Formal Proofs (AFP). Furthermore, we present a novel approach to mitigate false positives by leveraging IsarTactics and oracles, which filters uninformative proofs to improve the precision of our failure analysis. This enhancement allows Framework to successfully verify 90% of theorems in selected AFP proofs that were previously unverified. The tool is available at https://github.com/andrew-p/IsarTactics. Additionally, we have developed a user-friendly web interface for theorems and proofs, which can be accessed at https://framework.isa-afp.org. We conclude that Framework offers a valuable method for identifying potential errors in published theorems and for optimizing proofs within formal proof libraries. Our findings indicate that theorems in the AFP library are difficult to verify using conventional methods, but the IsarTactics approach effectively mitigates this challenge. Ultimately, we believe that theorems in the AFP library are now more trustworthy than before, thanks to the contributions of Framework. This research was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 61972025). The authors' website is located at https://www.cs.ucas.ac.cn/~apliu/. Keywords: Theorem Verification, Formal Proof Verification, Automated Theorem Proving, Archive of Formal Proofs, Computer Science.

Ultra-low frequency (ULF) waves are a prevalent phenomenon in Earth's magnetosphere, where they are believed to be both generated and influenced by various plasma processes. These waves, typically occurring in the 0.001 to 10 Hz range, are difficult to detect with the human ear. This study proposes a method for converting the frequency of magnetospheric plasma waves into the audible spectrum (0.001 to 20 kHz) for human perception. By applying a constant time delay, we demonstrate that the most effective strategy involves sampling data at 1 Hz, shifting it by 1 second, and playing it back at 1 Hz. We validate this approach by showing that it accurately represents the fundamental temporal variations of simulated and observed waves within the human audible range. Furthermore, this simple shift operation enables the clear visualization of simultaneous wave activity across multiple observation points. The findings indicate that the variations in both simulated and observed waves fall within the limits of human hearing. Consequently, this work introduces a novel method for making ULF waves perceptible to the human ear. The resulting ULF-audio could serve as a valuable educational tool in magnetospheric physics education and research. Additionally, it offers a new means for scientists to perceive simultaneous wave activity recorded by different observatories, potentially aiding in the identification of waves with a global nature. Finally, this technique could assist in the detection of magnetospheric wave events by the general public. The ULF-audio website (http://ulfaudio.org) will facilitate the visualization of multi-point wave data and provide access to real-time data for public engagement. The ULF-audio method is implemented in the open-source MAGNETOSPHERE VISUALIZATION TOOL (MVT) (https://github.com/ulfaudio/MVT). This tool is freely available for researchers and educators to generate ULF-audio from their own data. The paper also outlines how users can create ULF-audio using MVT. The ULF-audio method is also applicable to other plasma wave data, such as those from the Van Allen Probes. The paper includes examples of ULF-audio generated from these observations. The ULF-audio website will also provide access to ULF-audio derived from the Van Allen Probes observations. The paper also describes how users can create ULF-audio from the provided ULF-audio data using MVT. This would enable users to hear the waves recorded by the Van Allen Probes and compare them with the waves recorded by other observatories

This study investigates the impact of logarithmic nonlinear electrodynamics on ionized dilaton black membranes that are coupled to this framework and capable of rotation. The analysis examines how the nonlinear nature of the electromagnetic field alters the thermodynamic properties of these rotating, charged black membranes. Furthermore, the conditions required for the ionization of these systems are explored. The findings indicate that the nonlinear characteristics of the electromagnetic field influence the behavior of both charged and rotating black membranes. Additionally, it is determined that the rotational motion of these ionized dilated systems can induce a phase transition, resulting in the black membrane shifting from a nonconducting to a conducting state. Finally, the impact of the dilaton field is analyzed, revealing that it can generate exotic solutions, including both charged and neutral black membranes exhibiting conducting and nonconducting behaviors. These results suggest that such exotic black membranes could serve as effective models for studying the interaction between black holes and electromagnetic fields. The paper concludes with several suggestions for future research directions. This work is relevant to the fields of black hole physics, nonlinear electrodynamics, and condensed matter physics. Keywords: dilaton black membranes; nonlinear electrodynamics; thermodynamics; exotic solutions. PACS: 04.50.Kd; 04.70.Bp; 04.20.Jb; 12.60.Jv.

Natural Language Processing (NLP) has seen significant recent advancements, driven by the widespread adoption of deep learning. However, these approaches depend heavily on extensive datasets and substantial computational resources. This paper introduces a method for encoding textual data that enables its application in scenarios lacking both data and computing power. The text is encoded into a sequence of declarative statements grounded in recall, which are subsequently represented as a sequential pattern. To validate this approach, the paper applies the algorithm for mining sequential patterns with numerical constraints—specifically, the Growth Constraint-based Recall (GCR) algorithm—to the well-known Iris dataset. The results demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method. Furthermore, the text can be reconstructed from these declarative statements, and experimental findings indicate that this reconstruction yields more accurate results than the original input text. Finally, the proposed approach is designed to be easily extensible for text mining applications. The CCR algebras, also referred to as Weyl algebras, and the CCR algebras involving anti-periodic functions can be connected through a continuous sequence of Cuntz-Toeplitz algebras. This intermediary sequence is parameterized by the shift operator $Q$, which possesses no eigenvalues on the circle and serves as the bridge between the CCR and CAR algebras. Notably, the CCR algebra itself corresponds to the case where $Q$ is the identity operator. The text also examines the specific subalgebra of the CCR algebra generated by exponentials of smeared field operators with test functions exhibiting anti-periodic behavior. Furthermore, it demonstrates that the quasi-equivalence of states on the CCR algebra is contingent upon the properties of the symplectic form. Finally, the discussion explores the implications of these findings for the construction of the Fermion Fock space. GP 2 is a small-step operational semantics for the lambda calculus extended with explicit garbage collection. Although it enables garbage collection, GP 2 is not a true small-step semantics because values and non-value terms can reduce directly to final results, bypassing intermediate steps. This paper introduces Mini-GP 2, a small-step semantics that is true to its name and shares several properties with GP 2. These include a large set of structural lemmas, a large set of normalisation lemmas, and the ability to model lazy evaluation. Additionally, this paper provides a small set of syntactic structural lemmas and a small set of syntactic normalisation lemmas, which are more concise and concise, respectively, than their semantic counterparts. The paper also presents a small set of semantic normalisation lemmas that are more concise than the syntactic version. Finally, this work demonstrates that Mini-GP 2 is equivalent to the small-step semantics from [1]. The authors intend to extend GP 2 with beta-reduction and eta-expansion, then compare the resulting mini-step semantics with the small-step semantics from [1]. The authors believe that comparing the small and large step semantics of lambda calculi with explicit garbage collection is an interesting research area. The authors hope that this paper will contribute to that field.

The photoevaporation model predicts that stellar XUV radiation strips material from the inner regions of protoplanetary disks, creating a pressure-driven wind from the disk surface to the outer edge. Conversely, MHD models suggest that magnetocentrifugal forces within global disk winds can drive material outward from the disk surface to the outer edge. Both mechanisms forecast a density structure characterized by a disk surface, a wind cavity, and a disk outer edge. This study aims to determine which model better explains the observed density structure of the TW Hydrae disk. We employ a hydrodynamic code to simulate the photoevaporation model and an MHD code to simulate the MHD model, generating synthetic visibility data for a future observation with a 100-meter baseline. We analyze the visibility data to identify which model aligns with observations. Results indicate that the photoevaporation model fails to match the visibility data, whereas the global disk wind model successfully reproduces it. The paper concludes that the global disk wind model is the most accurate description of TW Hydrae's density structure, while also discussing the limitations of the study and proposing future research directions. This study examines multiple factorization variants of Chebyshev polynomials by analyzing the minimal equations involving powers of $\cos(\frac{2\pi}{d})$ over $\mathbb{Q}$. The analysis reveals that determining these minimal equations for a given $d$ is equivalent to identifying the prime factors of the corresponding $d$. We establish that the degree of the field extension $\mathbb{Q}(\cos(\frac{2\pi}{d}))$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ equals $\phi(d)/2$, where $\phi$ denotes Euler's totient function. Furthermore, we explore the prime factors of $d$ and their influence on the degree of the minimal polynomial, ultimately deriving a formula for this degree based on the prime factorization of $d$. This approach facilitates the identification of the degrees of minimal polynomials for any $d$ and enables the classification of the factorization variants of Chebyshev polynomials under consideration. Additionally, we present several theorems and examples to illustrate how to apply these findings in practice. Our work provides a foundation for future research into Chebyshev polynomials and related trigonometric functions. We conclude by proposing several open problems for further investigation. This study presents a straightforward and effective method for safeguarding and managing transients arising from switching operations in devices that utilize electromagnetic induction between windings. Specifically, the research focuses on load transients occurring within two-core symmetrical phase-angle-regulating transformers, which are commonly used in high-voltage power distribution. The proposed approach involves installing surge arresters on specific windings to safely dissipate energy released during transients. By applying this technique, the voltage stresses experienced by all windings can be significantly reduced. The paper details the methodology for arresters and categorizes the transients based on their duration and the energy they contain. Furthermore, it outlines the procedure for calculating the necessary surge arrester ratings and provides experimental validation using windings modeled with a lumped-parameter approach. The results confirm that this technique effectively mitigates transient stresses in symmetrical phase-angle-regulating transformers. Additionally, the findings demonstrate that transients in these devices can be divided into two distinct categories based on their duration and energy levels. This classification is crucial for accurately determining the appropriate surge arrester ratings. The study concludes that the proposed method offers a practical and efficient solution for safeguarding transformer windings against transients. It also underscores the significance of the transient categorization for future research and development endeavors. Finally, the paper suggests that this approach can be extended to safeguard other types of transformers against transients. Furthermore, the work highlights the need for more accurate mathematical models of transients in symmetrical phase-angle-regulating transformers, as well as the development of suitable measurement techniques to enable precise recording of these transients. This enhanced understanding will facilitate the creation of more effective safeguarding strategies. Overall, the research contributes to the advancement of safer and more reliable electrical systems. Future work will explore the application of this technique to other types of transformers and the development of more sophisticated transients models. Additionally, the authors intend to investigate the impact of various factors, such as winding configuration and core material, on the performance of the proposed method. Finally, the study will examine the potential for using this technique in conjunction with other safeguarding methods to further improve system reliability. In conclusion, this work represents a significant step toward the development of more robust and resilient electrical systems, with far-reaching implications for the electrical engineering field. The authors are committed to continuing their research in this area and collaborating with other researchers to advance the field of electrical system safeguarding. The findings of this study have the potential to influence the design and operation of electrical systems, leading to more efficient and cost-effective solutions for safeguarding electrical systems

This paper investigates hybrid encoding schemes designed for multi-group broadcasting within millimeter-wave (mmWave) systems. The primary objective of these schemes is to facilitate efficient group communication by leveraging multi-beam capabilities inherent to mmWave technology. Specifically, the study examines two distinct approaches: one that selects a single beam per mmWave transceiver to serve all user groups, and another that allocates multiple beams to specific groups. We demonstrate that, for a given set of user group locations, the optimal beam configuration can be identified by solving a finite search problem. Furthermore, we establish that the search space for beam selection is significantly reduced when considering only group locations on the Cartesian grid. Leveraging this search space compression, we develop two hybrid encoding schemes: a greedy algorithm and a dynamic programming approach. Finally, numerical simulations are presented to evaluate the performance of these proposed methods. Simulation results indicate that the dynamic programming scheme outperforms the greedy approach, achieving a 20% improvement in decoding success probability. Additionally, the proposed hybrid encoding methods are shown to yield substantial improvements over conventional single-beam encoding schemes. In terms of search complexity, both proposed schemes exhibit linear complexity relative to the number of user groups, while their computational complexity is independent of the number of users within each group. Consequently, these schemes are particularly well-suited for mmWave multi-group broadcasting scenarios involving a large number of user groups. However, it is important to note that the optimal beam configuration requires prior knowledge of user group locations, which may not be feasible in practical deployments. A finitely generated group $G$ exhibits $n$-th level $\kappa$ expansion if its ball of radius $n$, denoted $B_n(G)$, contains at least $\kappa$ elements when quotiented by any finite normal subgroup $N$. We term such groups "highly finitely generated." This paper demonstrates the existence of families of groups that are highly finitely generated with an exponent approaching 1, utilizing p-rank arguments within finite simple groups. Furthermore, we construct groups where the exponent of expansion is at least $\frac{\log_2(3)}{2} \approx 0.71$. However, we also establish that no group with a symmetric generating set of size 2 can have an $(n+\frac{1}{2})$-th level expansion exceeding $3^n$. Finally, we address a question posed by Lubotzky and Mirzakhani by constructing groups where the $n$-th level expansion grows nearly as $e^{n\log n}$. The methodology involves analyzing the power structure of matrix groups over finite fields, a topic of independent significance. This study addresses the stability of an elongated Euler-Bernoulli beam modeled as a function on the interval $[-1,1]$, linked via the $\tanh$-projection to a beam defined on $\mathbb{R}$. The elongated beam system is represented by a fourth-order differential operator featuring a potential derived from the $\tanh$-projection of the constant $1/2$ from $\mathbb{R}$. We demonstrate that this potential decays rapidly at infinity, enabling the identification of a positive constant $C$ such that the operator is equivalent to the Laplacian plus a constant potential $C$. Furthermore, we establish that the spectrum of the Laplacian shifted by $C$ lies within $[0, \infty)$, ensuring no bound states exist. Additionally, we prove that all discrete eigenvalues of the model are negative and provide an estimate for the ground state energy. These findings are applied to analyze the stability of the model as a perturbation of the Airy operator and a self-adjoint differential expression on a star graph with a negative vertex self-adjoint extension parameter. We show that this perturbation yields a stable system by deriving an upper bound for the negative eigenvalue associated with the Airy operator on a star graph and a lower bound for the eigenvalue of the vertex operator corresponding to $C$. Finally, we examine the case of a periodic beam on $\mathbb{R}$ connected to the model at the interval endpoints, demonstrating that this configuration also constitutes a stable system. This conclusion is supported by an estimate estimating from below the positive eigenvalues of the periodic model and a lower bound estimate for a specific self-adjoint differential expression on a star graph. The proofs of these estimates rely on variational methods and spectral theory for ordinary differential equations. The paper concludes with an analysis of the eigenvalues of the model using Weyl's Titchmarsh theory for singular second-order differential operators. Specifically, we show that the positive eigenvalues of the periodic model serve as asymptotic upper and lower bounds for the eigenvalues of the model on the star graph. Consequently, we derive an asymptotic formula for the eigenvalues of the model on the star graph. The stability of the model on the star graph is then deduced from the asymptotic behavior of these eigenvalues. The final section outlines several open problems regarding the spectral properties of the model on the star graph. The $r$-process, responsible for creating the majority of heavy elements in the universe, relies on a deep understanding of nuclear properties. However, experimental data are restricted to a narrow range of isotopes, necessitating theoretical models to predict properties for unmeasured nuclei. This study employs machine learning to forecast nuclear masses using extensive theoretical datasets. We utilize various algorithms, including random forests, support vector machines, and neural networks, and assess their performance against experimental data. Our results indicate that a neural network, trained on a comprehensive set of energy minimization theory calculations, achieves root mean square deviations of 0.5–0.6 MeV when compared to experimental masses. This level of accuracy is essential for modeling the $r$-process, as it enables the calculation of beta-decay half-lives with sufficient precision to determine the production rates of heavy elements. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these precise mass predictions can facilitate the optimization of future beta-decay experiments. By identifying nuclei with the highest predicted uncertainties, we can guide experimental efforts to achieve precision necessary for $r$-process modeling. This approach has already informed the targets of the upcoming JYFLTRAP campaign. Additionally, we show that these accurate mass predictions can support the discovery of new nuclei in future experiments. Optimizing the search for neutron-rich nuclei, which are critical for $r$-process modeling, will enhance the scientific return of future facilities. The precise measurement of dielectric loss in quantum materials is essential for the advancement of quantum technologies. This study presents a high-precision measurement method for the microwave dielectric attenuation of sapphire, designed to serve as a proof-of-concept for future quantum regime applications. By utilizing a microwave resonator and employing a fitting technique to analyze single-shot transmission data, we demonstrated the measurement of sapphire's dielectric attenuation at 5 GHz down to 200 MHz with parts-per-billion sensitivity. We also examined how fitting parameters are influenced by variations in the dielectric attenuation under test. Furthermore, we demonstrated the detection of minute changes in sapphire's dielectric attenuation caused by shifts in its temperature. These findings provide a reliable approach for measuring the dielectric properties of sapphire within the quantum regime. Additionally, our results indicate that sapphire's dielectric quality factor remains stable between 200 and 500 MHz, suggesting its potential utility in superconducting quantum circuits operating at gigahertz frequencies. This work establishes a foundation for investigating the dielectric loss mechanisms of sapphire within the quantum frequency range. The developed methodology is applicable to measuring the dielectric attenuation of other materials at microwave frequencies. The experimental setup is anticipated to be valuable for quantum material research and material characterization. This paper addresses a two-stage minimax problem where the distribution of second-stage uncertainties is constrained by a finite set of scenarios, with each scenario's probability determined by binary variables. Since this formulation is generally non-convex and computationally intractable, we introduce a robust counterpart that relaxes the problem to a convex one. We then provide sufficient conditions to guarantee that this relaxation yields an optimal solution for the original problem. Furthermore, we develop a novel solution method that leverages a specific property of the relaxed problem to significantly reduce the number of variables and constraints. Finally, we apply this approach to a two-stage robust economic dispatch problem and validate its effectiveness through numerical experiments. These results demonstrate that the proposed approach is both efficient and effective, achieving a solution in under a second for instances involving hundreds of generators. Additionally, the method consistently finds globally optimal solutions for all tested instances, even those with the highest complexity. Numerical comparisons also indicate that our approach is more efficient than a standard branch-and-bound method. This paper introduces H4M, a large-scale, diverse, multi-source, multi-modal, multi-dimensional, multi-distributional, and multi-view dataset designed for socioeconomic analytics in the context of Beijing. The H4M dataset comprises four distinct data sources: (1) POI data capturing Beijing's POI types, locations, and popularity; (2) Trajectory data reflecting Beijing residents' movement patterns; (3) Image data depicting Beijing's landscapes; and (4) Text data representing Beijing residents' opinions on various topics. Additionally, the dataset includes four types of ground truth: (1) population size, (2) population density, (3) urbanization rate, and (4) crime rate. This work demonstrates four applications utilizing the H4M dataset: (1) population size estimation, (2) population density estimation, (3) urbanization rate estimation, and (4) crime rate prediction. Furthermore, the study evaluates four baseline methods and introduces five proposed methods for these four tasks. The results indicate that the proposed methods outperform the baselines, achieving improvements of 1.1% to 10.6% for population size estimation, 1.1% to 11.1% for population density estimation, 1.1% to 10.6% for urbanization rate estimation, and 1.1% to 10.6% for crime rate prediction. Finally, the paper discusses the potential of H4M for Beijing socioeconomic analytics and its applicability to other cities. The dataset is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/H4M. Graph Neural Architectures (GNAs) have recently emerged as a significant area of research, extending the principles of deep neural networks to operate on graphs. GNAs enable the processing of both node and graph-level data, making them ideal for applications in social network analysis, gene expression analysis, and traffic prediction. However, existing GNAs often suffer from overfitting and are prone to adversarial attacks. Transfer learning offers a solution to these challenges by allowing pre-trained models to be adapted for new tasks, thereby reducing overfitting and increasing robustness against adversaries. This study investigates the application of transfer learning within GNAs. We evaluated various transfer learning strategies—including fine-tuning, feature extraction, multi-task learning, and model ensembling—across six graph datasets using three standard GNAs. Our findings indicate that transfer learning enhances both the accuracy and generalization capabilities of these architectures. Furthermore, we demonstrated that transfer learning improves the robustness of GNAs against adversarial attacks. Finally, we introduced a novel method for generating adversarial node labels, which attacks node classification tasks. Our results show that this new attack method reduces classification accuracy more severely than previous approaches. We evaluated this model against two baseline approaches: one relying on collaborative filtering and the other on content-based filtering. This work investigates data stream algorithms for the Set Disjointness problem, defined as determining whether two $n$-element sets $A$ and $B$ share any common elements. In the data stream model, the sets are presented via a sequence of $2n$ updates, where each update adds an element to one set. We introduce a straightforward algorithm that solves this problem with $\tilde{O}(n)$ space, achieving a time complexity per update of $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n})$. This approach relies on a straightforward application of polynomial rolling hashing. Our method represents the first straightforward algorithm to achieve space usage below $n \log n$ bits. Furthermore, we extend this algorithm to the dynamic graph problem of identifying triangles in an $m$-edge graph using $\tilde{O(m))}$ space, marking the first dynamic algorithm to do so. We also address the related problem of identifying $K$-cliques for $K > 3$, though we note that dynamic algorithms for this latter case currently require space exceeding $\Omega(m)$. We demonstrate that our triangle detection algorithm is nearly optimal by proving that a data stream algorithm capable of identifying triangles in a stream of updates would require space greater than $\tilde{\Omega}(\frac{m^{1.5}}{n})$. These results are complemented by a randomized reduction from the Online Indexing problem to Set Disjointness, which holds significant independent value. We anticipate that this reduction will be a valuable tool for future research in data streams. We derive the real part of the wave function for a two-magnon bound state within the paramagnetic phase of the Heisenberg antiferromagnet, demonstrating that it depends non-analytically on momentum. This characteristic is shown to be universal for all quantum antiferromagnets in the paramagnetic phase. Furthermore, we establish that the spin-spin correlation function, static spin susceptibility, and magnon-magnon scattering cross section all exhibit a non-analytic reliance on momentum through their connection to the two-magnon bound state wave function. Finally, utilizing a high-temperature expansion of the partition function, we calculate the critical exponents for the paramagnetic phase of the Heisenberg model in three and four spatial dimensions, revealing that these exponents are non-renormalizable. Our findings for the Heisenberg model in three and four dimensions are consistent with the critical exponents predicted by the $O(N)$ model. Additionally, we provide the first analytical proof of the non-analytic momentum dependence of the static spin susceptibility in the paramagnetic phase of the Heisenberg model, a feature that was previously absent from numerical studies. This non-analytic dependence is also confirmed in the classical limit. We further demonstrate that the non-analytic momentum dependence of the static spin susceptibility in the Heisenberg model is linked to the non-renormalizability of the critical exponents in both the Heisenberg and $O(N)$ models. Finally, we discuss the implications of our results regarding the existence of a two-magnon bound state in the Heisenberg model. Our conclusions are supported by the classical limit, where the non-analytic momentum dependence of the static spin susceptibility in the Heisenberg model is directly derived from the classical equations of motion. We also examine the implications of these findings for the two-magnon bound state in the Heisenberg model. In conclusion, the non-analytic momentum dependence of the static spin susceptibility in the Heisenberg model is a robust feature that persists across various theoretical frameworks, including the classical limit, high-temperature expansion, and the non-renormalizable nature of the critical exponents. This result is also consistent with the two-magnon bound state in the Heisenberg model. Readout constitutes a critical component of quantum information processing, yet current approaches often neglect the interplay between atomic states and optical fields. This study introduces a single-atom interface designed to integrate the modulation and readout phases of quantum memory. By employing a multi-diffraction architecture, we demonstrate that a quantum memory atom can be read out through multiple output ports while undergoing diffraction-induced modulation. Furthermore, the readout process is shown to be governed by atomic parameters, enabling atomic-controlled readout. Finally, our proposed quantum memory architecture is demonstrated to achieve recordable, erasable, and modulable operations. These findings may hold significant promise for the development of integrated quantum devices. Additionally, the methodologies employed could offer valuable insights for engineering quantum systems that harness atomic-induced modifications in multi-diffraction setups. This study investigates the linear and nonlinear Hall conductance across weak and strong disorder regimes for a half-filled one-dimensional lattice of spin-1/2 fermions subject to spin-up channel disorder and electron-electron interactions. The analysis begins with the noninteracting case, where the lattice forms a gapped spin-liquid state characterized by dimerization. In this regime, the linear Hall conductance equals $e^2/h$, while the nonlinear Hall conductance is $-6e^3/h\Omega$. Subsequent examination of interaction effects reveals that the linear Hall conductance remains robust, whereas the nonlinear conductance exhibits a significant reduction. Finally, the influence of strong disorder is explored, demonstrating that the nonlinear Hall conductance experiences a substantial increase under strongly disordered conditions. Furthermore, the linear Hall conductance is verified to be invariant across both weak and strong disorder limits. These numerical findings align with analytical results derived from the renormalization group method for $U(1)$ symmetry-protected topological phases. Additionally, the study confirms that the nonlinear Hall conductance remains quantized even when interaction and disorder effects are strong. Ultimately, the quantization of the nonlinear Hall conductance is attributed to the presence of a bulk energy gap and the existence of a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ topological invariant. This work extends the understanding of the quantized nonlinear Hall effect to interacting fermion systems. Finally, the stability of the nonlinear Hall conductance against symmetry-breaking disorders is examined, showing that it is fragile in the presence of such disorders. Consequently, the preservation of quantization in interacting systems requires the absence of symmetry-breaking disorder. The research concludes by discussing the potential for experimental observation of these interacting effects and outlining future directions. Finally, the paper addresses the impact of finite-size scaling on the nonlinear Hall conductance and explores the possibility of deforming the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ topological invariant. Overall, the work underscores the stability of the nonlinear Hall conductance against interaction and non-symmetry-breaking disorder, as well as its sensitivity to symmetry-breaking disorders. The significance of these findings is underscored by the observation that the nonlinear Hall conductance is quantized in interacting systems, a result consistent with theoretical predictions. The authors also note that the quantization of the nonlinear Hall conductance is robust against interaction and non-symmetry-breaking disorder, but fragile in the presence of symmetry-breaking disorder. The COVID-19 pandemic has created an urgent demand for ventilator capacity, particularly for patients experiencing breathing failure. To address this, we introduce a framework designed to directly generate functional breathing devices from demand signals, thereby enhancing patient outcomes. This capability is realized through our Dynamic Enhancement (DE) framework, which utilizes the same neural network architecture as Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) but is retrained to model dynamic time-series data. We demonstrate the DE framework's efficacy by applying it to extract demand-enhanced breathing signals from two patients, resulting in significant improvements in tidal volume and peak inspiratory pressure. Furthermore, we show that DE can be trained in a multi-source manner to generalize across different sources, such as different individuals, thereby increasing device robustness. Finally, we provide a comprehensive tutorial on implementing the DE framework, including source-specific and multi-source training, to facilitate its adoption by the broader research community. The accompanying code repository offers a detailed walkthrough of all experiments, training procedures, and code modifications required to replicate our work. This framework holds broad potential for generating demand-enhanced signals in various applications, including multi-source training for diverse sources and demand signals. The source-specific and multi-source training experiments were conducted on a single NVIDIA RTX 2080 GPU. Additionally, the code repository includes a detailed walkthrough for replicating our work, and we welcome inquiries from the community interested in adopting our work for other applications. For more information, please visit our website at https://neural-gadgets.github.io/. The source code is available at https://github.com/neural-gadgets/Dynamic-Enhancement. We present a novel, intrinsic classification of the platform groups for iterates of bicritical rational functions based on quasi-Fibonacci sequences of platforms. This finding extends the established description of platform groups for polynomials to a broader context. Additionally, we offer detailed descriptions of all "potential" platform groups, defined as those not violating any known properties, highlighting that several nonrealizing potential candidates exist. Finally, we examine various realizing mechanisms for platforms and their images under iteration. Specifically, we identify distinct single and double families of simple first return maps, which account for the Fibonacci and all but one decagonal platform groups, respectively. We also detail mechanisms generating platforms within elliptic components, thereby explaining the quadratic, cubic, and all but one dodecagonal platform groups. Furthermore, we outline how to construct parabolic and elliptic components that contain platforms and those formed by the images of previous iterations. The proof of our primary result relies on a generalization of the decomposition theorem, which states that the platform group of an iterate is typically the free product of its constituent platforms. We demonstrate that this decomposition holds for all polynomials and rational functions and provide a comprehensive description of the amalgamation for "most" bicritical rational functions. The remaining case involves rational functions with parabolic components, where platforms may amalgamate across multiple components. We show that this scenario does not occur for bicritical rational functions, leaving only a single unresolved case. This case is resolved by a new proof based on parabolic component analysis, which also clarifies the amalgamation process. Consequently, our proof for bicritical rational functions is more direct than the current general description. The paper begins with an introduction to the problem and a review of relevant background. It then presents a general theory of parabolic components, followed by an analysis of their images under iteration. The final section addresses the amalgamation problem, followed by an appendix containing a computer-assisted verification of certain assertions. This appendix is essential for the completeness of our results, as it provides a proof for a bicritical family where the platform group of an iterate amalgamates three parabolic components, a situation where no other mechanism can produce platforms. We conclude with a discussion of open problems. This work is part of a series extending polynomial dynamics to bicritical rational functions. The series builds upon the methodology established in \cite{Kuchera-Petkovsek}, which was inspired by the polynomial case developed in \cite{Kuchera-Petkovsek2}. Mo and W transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) are recognized for their exceptional optical and electrical characteristics, making them ideal for flexible electronics and nanoelectronics. While bulk properties of these materials are well-documented, their thin-film behaviors remain largely unexplored. This study investigates the thickness dependence of work function, ionization potential, and electron affinity in Mo and W TMDs using density functional theory (DFT) and GW methods. Our findings indicate that GW calculations yield results comparable to those from the DFT+U approach. Specifically, GW-calculated work functions for Mo and W TMDs are 0.2–0.4 eV higher than DFT predictions, aligning closely with experimental data. Furthermore, GW calculations reveal a reduction in the band gap of Mo and W TMDs as thickness decreases, accompanied by an increase in the electron affinity of the chalcogen layer. These insights are anticipated to assist in the design of thin-film devices. Additionally, GW calculations suggest that the electron affinity of monolayer MoTe$_2$ is 3.1 eV, indicating its potential suitability as an efficient electron collector. Finally, the study examines the effects of lattice strain on work function, ionization potential, and electron affinity, demonstrating that strain can be utilized to tune the electronic properties of Mo and W TMDs. These conclusions are expected to aid in the development of flexible electron collectors. The work function of Mo and W TMDs is observed to be sensitive to the specific stacking sequence of the layers. Ultimately, GW calculations prove to be a highly effective tool for predicting the electronic properties of two-dimensional materials. This study introduces an adaptive multigrid method designed to efficiently solve the steady-state Boltzmann equation across multiple scales and rarefied conditions for two-dimensional rarefied gas flows. The approach begins by applying a multigrid technique to the original Boltzmann equation, which is reformulated using the running maximum relative deviation (RMRD) to mitigate the wide disparities in magnitude between collision source terms and convective terms. To further enhance the convergence speed of the multigrid solution, an implicit time-dependent sub-iteration is performed at each multigrid cycle. This sub-iteration utilizes a time-dependent equation with a carefully selected time scale to rapidly drive the solution toward a quasi-steady state. The proposed method is validated through two representative cases: 2D shock wave reflection over a flat plate at a Mach number of 3, and 2D shock wave impingement on a cylinder at a Mach number of 6. Results demonstrate that the method achieves the calculation of steady-state solutions within dozens of iterations, showing significant improvements in computational efficiency. Additionally, the study examines the effects of various parameters, such as the number of multigrid levels and time step sizes, on the method's efficiency. Ultimately, the research confirms that the proposed approach can substantially reduce computational time for multiscale and rarefied gas flows. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/Chenchen-chen123/AMG.

The Horizon-10T experiment, situated in the Antarctic ice sheet, functions as a wide-band neutrino telescope designed to detect Cherenkov light generated by relativistic charged particles. This paper introduces a novel method for identifying and classifying particle events, utilizing machine learning to analyze both charged particle tracks and showers. This methodology enables the reconstruction of event topology, facilitating the investigation of rare phenomena such as Axion Quark Nuggets (AQN). AQNs are hypothesized to form during the early universe via a strong first-order phase transition of the quark-gluon plasma and may still exist today. Distinct from standard neutrino interactions, AQNs are expected to produce multi-particle showers. We outline the development of this new AQN search technique and present initial results from the Horizon-10T data. Although the dataset is limited, the study successfully identified a small number of AQN candidates. These findings are consistent with the theoretical predictions of the most probable AQN model. Furthermore, the search yielded no events that would indicate the presence of high-density nuggets. Consequently, we establish an upper limit on the flux of AQNs with a radius of 10 fm, which is comparable to the constraints set by the IceCube collaboration. This work demonstrates that multi-particle events are detectable within the current data, and the proposed search method is applicable to other next-generation ice-cherenkov detectors. Ultimately, this approach will allow for the examination of a broader spectrum of exotic phenomena. Additionally, the event classification technique can be adapted for other rare particle searches, such as those involving dark matter. All event data utilized in this study are publicly accessible.

The term "Pauli crystal" refers to a state where fermions in the lowest Landau level form a crystalline arrangement. This study examines two distinct definitions of Pauli crystals: the Wigner crystal and the Wigner Pauli crystal. By applying statistical thermodynamics, we develop a framework to distinguish between these two phenomena. For both Wigner and Wigner Pauli crystals, we derive thermodynamic quantities, including internal energy, specific heat, and entropy, as functions of the filling factor. Furthermore, we investigate how thermodynamic phase transitions correspond to the emergence of Pauli crystals. This paper presents a survey of research on the development, implementation, and application of neural networks designed to address time-fluctuating matrix problems. It introduces the concept of Zeroing Neural Networks (ZNN) and examines various design methodologies, including error function selection, dynamic law formulation, and performance analysis. The study also outlines multiple computational approaches for real-time prediction using ZNN, with a specific focus on predicting time-fluctuating matrices. Finally, ZNN applications are explored across diverse fields, including robotics, control systems, and signal processing. The paper concludes by identifying current limitations and gaps in the literature and proposes potential future directions for ZNN research and development. X-ray optical systems are currently being explored as a solution to broaden the field of view for wide-area x-ray astronomy missions. However, these systems are typically limited by broad diffraction-based constraints, including diffraction by the aperture, diffraction from the x-ray mirror, and the evanescent field. This paper reviews existing methods to mitigate these restrictions and enhances their performance through a unified framework. Specifically, we demonstrate that both diffraction by the aperture and the evanescent field limitations can be resolved by employing a finite-size point source. Furthermore, we show that the diffraction-by-the-mirror constraint can be overcome by utilizing a hard-edge edge-illuminated geometry. These approaches are applicable to various techniques, such as micro- and nano-structuring, that convert diffraction into total external reflection. We provide a detailed analysis of these methods using a single-layered x-waveguide. Additionally, we illustrate how this concept can be implemented in a more complex system, namely a two-layered x-waveguide coupler. Our findings indicate that these proposed schemes can expand the field of view by several orders of magnitude. We also address the impact of source size on the field of view and discuss the associated trade-offs regarding spatial resolution and energy resolution. Finally, we present preliminary results concerning the potential for further enhancing the field of view. Overall, we conclude that this framework is applicable to any x-ray optical system, offering a pathway to achieve broad fields of view in x-ray waveguides and other nanostructures. Moreover, these concepts may extend to other configurations, such as multilayered x-waveguides and photonic crystals. Our proposed concepts can be validated through full-wave simulations and experiments utilizing nano-fabricated waveguides. We anticipate that this framework will facilitate the development of new x-ray optical devices capable of operating within broad fields of view. Additionally, these ideas may have applications in other areas, including wavefront shaping and x-ray quantum information. To our knowledge, this is the first instance where such a comprehensive approach has been presented. We believe this work will inspire further research into new x-ray optical devices functioning in wide fields of view. We anticipate that these developments will enable new applications in x-ray imaging, sensing, and communication. Furthermore, this work may contribute to new research in x-ray quantum information. We expect that these advancements will lead to new x-ray quantum devices operating in broad fields of view. Our work may also contribute to new x-ray imaging techniques, such as x-ray holography and computed tomography,

This study examines the quantum dynamics of a single charge carrier within a finite, arbitrary periodic potential under a perpendicular magnetic field using the time-dependent Schrödinger equation in twisted bilayer graphene. By employing the magnetic gauge transformation method, we derive analytical expressions for the magnetic Bloch wave functions and energy levels of a charge carrier in a moiré pattern when the flux through the unit cell reaches $2\pi$. We demonstrate that this flux value causes the magnetic Bloch wave functions to vanish, resulting in charge carrier localization and the reemergence of magnetic Bloch states. Furthermore, our numerical analysis of twisted bilayer graphene reveals that this reentrant phenomenon occurs at $2\pi$ flux and generates reentrant flat energy levels within the band gaps. These levels exhibit invariance to the magnetic field and are contingent upon the moiré lattice constant, the angle of twist, and the initial wave function characteristics. These flat bands facilitate the formation of many-body bound states, which manifest as zero-width peaks in the charge carrier's probability density function. Additionally, we show that the probability density function can be modulated by adjusting the initial wave function. These findings offer a novel approach to designing quantum devices in twisted bilayer graphene and provide a foundation for investigating quantum phase transitions in this system. Finally, we suggest that the zero-width peaks observed in recent experiments [J. H. Chan et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 122, 086803 (2019)] correspond to these theoretically predicted reentrant flat energy levels. This conclusion is supported by comparing our theoretical predictions with the experimental data. Our results indicate that the experimentally observed flat energy bands arise from the reentrant flux in the magnetic gauge transformation method. Furthermore, the experimentally measured unit cell dimensions align with the theoretical predictions for the moiré lattice constant in twisted bilayer graphene. These outcomes offer new insights into the quantum dynamics of twisted bilayer graphene. The methodology developed in this work can be applied to investigate the quantum dynamics of charge carriers in other two-dimensional materials exhibiting two-dimensional periodic potentials and moiré patterns. Additionally, the findings may contribute to the design of quantum devices utilizing these materials. Although steganography has been extensively researched for decades, recent studies indicate that traditional methods struggle when English constraints are stringent. This paper introduces a novel, Steganographic Pairwise Replacement Steganographic Channel (SPRCSC) designed for shallow water acoustic communications. Drawing inspiration from recent deep learning advancements in steganography, our approach utilizes Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks to enhance steganographic performance. We validate our method through simulations on a proprietary acoustic dataset, comparing our results against traditional steganographic techniques and recent deep learning solutions. Our steganographic channel achieves a secret bit rate of 0.05 bps and a BER of 0.10, surpassing traditional deep learning approaches that rely on convolutional networks and fail to leverage contextual information. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method outperforms previous acoustic steganographic schemes that achieved a bit rate of 0.02 bps with a BER of 0.10. These findings suggest that LSTM-based models are highly effective for shallow water acoustic steganography. The source code will be made available at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/SPRCSC. Unit commitment (UC) models are widely utilized in power system operations to economically schedule the on/off status and output levels of power plants. However, solving large-scale, high-resolution UC problems quickly remains difficult due to their nonconvex nature and the presence of complex constraints. This paper introduces a new machine learning-based expense model designed to enable rapid screening of UC problems with limited generation limits. The model is trained using data generated from the exact UC model and incorporates a novel loss function to ensure it accurately reflects the nonconvex, piecewise linear cost structure of generating units. By substituting this learned cost function into the UC model, we can assess the impact of limited generation constraints on total system costs without solving the full optimization problem. This approach allows for a rapid evaluation of the necessity for reserve allocation and the adequacy of the proposed limits. Numerical tests on a 69-bus system demonstrate that the learned cost function achieves high accuracy, and utilizing it for screening significantly reduces the computational time required to solve the UC problem. Furthermore, the study confirms that limiting generation can substantially increase total system costs and reduce the feasibility of solutions. The rapid screening method offers a practical tool for operators to analyze the effects of limited energy access on power systems. Additionally, this technique can be extended to evaluate the impact of other operational constraints, such as transmission line limits and spinning reserve requirements. The proposed method is implemented in Python and accessible at https://github.com/PowerSystemsML/LearningExpenseModel. The repository includes a tutorial that outlines the algorithm and provides a step-by-step guide for applying the rapid screening approach.
