Although classification tasks typically involve concepts within a shared semantic space, these concepts often exhibit hyperbolic geometric characteristics, such as hierarchical and compositional structures. Current Euclidean models struggle to accurately capture such geometry, resulting in a significant performance drop when applying pre-trained embeddings to classification. To address this, we introduce HyperExpan, a method that integrates hyperbolic representation learning with expansion learning. Specifically, we first embed concepts into a hyperbolic space and subsequently apply a projection layer to a lower-dimensional feature space optimized for the specific task. We demonstrate that HyperExpan surpasses state-of-the-art results on two classification datasets, offering compelling evidence for the efficacy of hyperbolic representation learning in classification. This study examines the impact of external electric fields on non-covalent interactions using the S66 benchmark dataset. The S66 collection comprises 616 molecular pairs featuring 13 distinct types, characterized by 1,122 interaction energies. To model these interactions, we employed the XTB method combined with the xDEC program, which calculates electrostatically decomposed exchange-repulsion energies. Our analysis reveals that the sensitivity of XTB and xDEC energies to external electric fields varies across different molecular pairs. Furthermore, we identified a strong correlation between the energy changes induced by external fields and the polarizability of the individual molecules. These findings offer valuable insights for applications involving molecular assemblies subjected to external electric fields. Additionally, the computed interaction and xDEC energies for S66 pairs are accessible via the web-based platform xTBServer. This resource enables the calculation of XTB and xDEC energies for any molecular structure, including custom inputs, by simply providing a SMILES string. The platform also facilitates the visualization of molecular orbitals and electron density, as well as the atomic charge distribution derived from the xDEC model. The URL for xTBServer is https://xtbserver.com. The method employed is detailed in our prior publication: "Electrostatically decomposed molecular orbital theory," published in *J. Chem. Phys.* 151, 124101 (2019). The xDEC program source code can be accessed at https://github.com/xtb/xDEC. Furthermore, the external electric field calculations were performed using the DEC program, with the source code available at https://github.com/DECprogram/DEC. The S66 benchmark dataset was originally compiled by Jurecka et al. in *Phys. Chem. Chem. Phys.* 8, 2914 (2006) and subsequently expanded by the current authors in *Phys. Chem. Chem. Phys.* 14, 1124 (2012). The correlation between xDEC energy changes and molecular polarizability was established through linear regression analysis. Finally, the visualization of structures, electron density, and polarizability was achieved using Avogadro, version 1.2.0.20200201.1. This study introduces a novel ambiguity model grounded in the theory of possibility theory, designed to capture the inherent non-determinism found in industrial environments. Unlike previous approaches that primarily focused on probabilistic models, this method is specifically tailored for applications where data is vague, imprecise, or ill-defined. The significance of this approach is demonstrated through its application to job shop scheduling. The paper provides a comprehensive review of ambiguity modeling techniques, outlines the characteristics of the proposed possibility-based model, and presents an exact algorithm for computing optimal schedules. A numerical study is included to validate the method and illustrate its effectiveness. Furthermore, the study confirms the model's ability to handle real-world data, as evidenced by a collaboration with an automotive component manufacturer. Finally, the paper discusses the method's limitations and suggests potential avenues for future research. Keywords: Ambiguity modeling, possibility theory, job shop scheduling, non-determinism.

This paper introduces a robustness formulation for Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) utilizing Signal Temporal Logic (STL). We begin by extending STL to create a new formalism that expresses time-dependent temporal constraints on the trajectories of continuous-time dynamical systems. Building upon this framework, we propose methods to quantify the robustness of a dynamical system's trajectory against model uncertainty. Our approach enables the design of controllers that optimize (both positively and negatively) this trajectory robustness, thereby enhancing robustness to model uncertainties. To demonstrate the practical utility of our proposed framework, we apply it to a multi-robot coverage control problem. Furthermore, we validate our theoretical findings through numerical simulations of both linear and nonlinear systems. The results indicate that our method outperforms existing approaches in terms of trajectory robustness. Additionally, the computational complexity of our proposed framework is comparable to that of related techniques. Finally, we illustrate the robustness improvements achieved by our method through simulations of a two-dimensional linear vehicle. (Cross-Referenced: 1706.09703)

This paper introduces a novel method for detecting gravitational wave signals from supermassive black hole (SMBH) inspirals by utilizing data from numerous small-scale, low-cost accelerometers. The study demonstrates that a network of these devices can surpass the sensitivity of a comparable LIGO-like interferometer network. The proposed detection framework combines Bayesian model selection with the matched filter technique. Furthermore, we establish that a dense deployment of these inexpensive sensors can identify inspirals across a broad frequency spectrum, ranging from the low frequencies associated with early inspiral stages to the high frequencies of merger and ringdown phases. We also illustrate that the signals from these early inspirals can be extracted from accelerometer output by applying a simple bandpass filter. Additionally, we show that the parameter estimation accuracy for SMBH inspirals using a LIGO-like network is on the order of 10%, whereas a dense network of small accelerometers achieves significantly superior precision, with estimates within the 1% range. Finally, we provide a detailed examination of the advantages and limitations of this new approach, including its potential to enable early warnings for mergers and to investigate the merger history of SMBH populations. We conclude that this new method is complementary to interferometers, as it can observe the early inspiral phase that interferometers generally cannot detect. This capability offers the opportunity to study the formation mechanisms of SMBH pairs and to issue early warnings for mergers. We also address the necessary conditions for implementing such a network, including the required number of sensors, their cost, and their operational lifespan. We anticipate that this new detection method will be feasible in the near future. The source code used in this study is available at https://github.com/AniruddhaSahu1998/Accelerometer-based-Gravitational-Wave-Detection. The simulations were performed using the open-source Python package PyCBC. PyCBC is a widely used open-source toolkit for gravitational wave data analysis, developed by the LIGO Scientific Collaboration and the Virgo Collaboration. PyCBC is freely accessible at https://www.ligo.org/science/PublicationPyCBC.html. The PyCBC package includes various detection methods, including matched filtering and Bayesian model selection, which are essential for identifying gravitational wave signals. We have utilized PyCBC to conduct the detection simulations presented in this paper. PyCBC can be accessed at https://www.ligo.org/science/PublicationPyCBC.html. The simulations were executed on the NASA Advanced Supercomputing Center, located at https://www.advanced.mpi-hd.mpg

This work examines a specific class of nonlinear diffusion equations featuring convex diffusion coefficients, which encompass the $p$-Laplace equation and the Laplace-Beltrami operator as end-members. The study explores gradient approximations for these equations, demonstrating their utility in establishing solution regularity on general Riemannian manifolds and providing discrete energy estimates through finite difference methods. These outcomes depend on technical assumptions regarding the manifold's Ricci curvature, specifically isopерimetric and curvature-dimension conditions. Additionally, the analysis addresses the existence and uniqueness of solutions by leveraging nonexistence results for dual problems, thereby extending previous findings from the Euclidean setting to curved complete manifolds. Finally, the existence and uniqueness of solutions are guaranteed under mild conditions on the diffusion coefficient, combined with isoperimetric and curvature-dimension assumptions, complete manifold regularity results, and discrete energy estimates. Furthermore, the gradient flow formulation of the equations is derived, accompanied by an analysis of the convergence rate of gradient schemes. These results are supported by numerical examples on a compact manifold.

The nature of compact radio sources remains a fundamental yet unresolved issue in radio astronomy. This study investigates the angular structure of the most compact and luminous radio sources, characterized by high surface brightness and low redshifts. By applying a stacking technique to 1.4 GHz VLBI images of 120 sources with a mean luminosity of $10^{26}$ W/Hz/sr, we analyzed their morphology and compared results with existing data. Our findings indicate that the average stacked image is dominated by jet material, with the core contributing less than 10% of the total flux. The mean radio core exhibits a Gaussian profile with a full width at half maximum of 0.0015 arcsec, and the mean radio jet displays a top-hat profile measuring 0.006 arcsec at half maximum. We estimate the mean jet opening angle to be approximately 0.001 arcsec. Furthermore, we determined that the mean radio jet has a linear size of roughly 100 AU, with a mean proper motion of 1000 km/s. These results suggest that the physical properties of the most compact and luminous radio sources are more uniform than previously believed. Additionally, the mean jet size is comparable to the Schwarzschild radius of a supermassive black hole with a mass of approximately $10^7$ solar masses. Finally, the mean proper motion of the jet is consistent with the expected velocity of a supermassive black hole accreting at the Eddington rate. These conclusions are supported by the observed angular sizes of individual sources. We propose that the majority of these sources are microquasars, and the remaining ones are likely young, low-luminosity active galactic nuclei. The latter may represent the initial phase of AGN activity, where jets are initially collimated by the surrounding medium. This research is part of the Compact Dim Radio Sources (CoDiRS) project. Information leakage from software systems is frequently modeled using probabilistic or quantitative information flow (QIF). This paper introduces a new system for representing information flow, drawing on category theory and quantitative reasoning. Our approach, the Concealed Markov Model (CMR), is an "abstract" variant of traditional probabilistic hidden Markov models (HMMs). While standard HMMs use explicit probability distributions, CMRs define these distributions through an "adjoint" observation process that extracts data from a software system. This method allows CMRs to capture information flow that goes beyond what simple probabilistic models can express. We demonstrate that CMRs can be understood as a monad within the category of endofunctors on Set. This structural insight enables the use of established category-theoretic tools to analyze information flow. Furthermore, we show that this monad encodes the concept of noninterference, a fundamental property in QIF. Finally, we outline a path toward developing a general theory of information flow based on CMRs. This work extends our findings presented at the 2019 IEEE Security and Privacy Data Science workshop. This report provides a more detailed exposition of that research. Specifically, it offers a more rigorous treatment of CMRs and their relationship to HMMs, and it expands the original monadic analysis using broader categorical concepts. Additionally, it presents a more comprehensive exploration of the proposed future research directions. These directions involve characterizing noninterference via the CMR monad and laying the groundwork for a general theory of information flow rooted in CMRs. This theory would integrate existing QIF methods with probabilistic methods, utilizing category theory to unify them. The extended discussion of these topics is supported by examples and connections to established work in the field. We present a framework for analyzing the statistical coherence of periodically driven quantum systems, extending concepts of quantum coherence and relative entropy to include temporal and Poincaré return dimensions. Applying this method to quantum kicked Ising models, we investigate the evolution of statistical coherence during quantum quenching from an ordered to a disordered phase, observing exponential growth that we link to dynamical patterns of spatial coherence. Specifically, we associate this behavior with a renormalization group flow toward strong coupling, which we characterize as statistical self-similarity. Furthermore, we connect the exponential growth rate of statistical coherence to the Poincaré return dimension, demonstrating that this rate diminishes as the system's complexity increases. These findings offer new insights into the relationship between complexity and statistical coherence in periodically driven quantum systems. Finally, we discuss the connection between statistical and quantum measures of nonlocality, showing that our states exhibit enhanced statistical nonlocality even when entanglement is absent. These results provide a foundation for future experimental work aimed at exploring the phase space of periodically driven quantum systems. We introduce a framework for investigating flexible scattering amplitudes across various theories of scalar fields, which exhibit dependence on kinematic invariants through arbitrary functions of them. Focusing on conformal scalar interactions and Lorentz invariant counterterms, we derive general constraints on these functions utilizing the bootstrap principles of unitarity, analyticity, and crossing symmetry. We uncover new nontrivial functions permitted by these constraints, which can be realized through effective actions featuring higher-derivative terms. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to include derivative interactions, thereby broadening the scope of applicable scalar theories. Our findings offer valuable insights for EFT and S-matrix approaches to quantum gravity. As a specific application, we examine the scattering of polarized photons in Lorentz covariant quantum gravity, deriving constraints on the functions of the Riemann tensor that appear in the four-point amplitude. This work serves as a precursor to a subsequent study [arXiv:2205.01581] that incorporates two-loop quantum corrections. Additionally, we explore the implications of our findings for holographic theories and string theory. Our results suggest that a broader range of scalar interactions than previously assumed can arise from string theory, specifically through the condensation of tachyon and higher excited states on the Lorentz invariant surface defined by on-shell conditions. This mechanism offers a potential explanation for the anomalous dimensionals identified in the AdS/CFT correspondence. Finally, we discuss how our findings relate to recent research on higher-derivative corrections in string theory. This paper functions as a comprehensive review of scalar scattering in quantum field theory, quantum gravity, and string theory. It provides a detailed outline of the "scattering amplitudes program," which aims to construct a UV complete quantum theory of gravity by building on the infrared amplitudes of general relativity. We demonstrate that this program encompasses a significantly wider landscape of possibilities than previously recognized. Our work offers a systematic methodology for analyzing and classifying the extensive space of data points accessible through the bootstrap program. We anticipate that these methods will prove valuable for exploring the structure of quantum gravity and string theory. Our findings underscore the necessity of developing a comprehensive and systematic approach to the bootstrap program to fully uncover the space of viable quantum gravity theories. This space is likely far richer than the narrow set of options suggested by a straightforward extension of the Einstein-Hilbert action. We believe that a thorough exploration of the space of quantum gravity amplitudes, grounded in the principles of the scattering amplitudes program, will be essential

Additionally, we show that the free energy of a blackbody radiation field is not altered by the system's temperature or volume. Finally, we provide a detailed analysis of these findings. This research addresses the privacy of location data shared with third parties, such as navigation services. It establishes novel theorems and offers algorithms to evaluate privacy under two distinct scenarios: when a third party possesses knowledge of the user's route planning strategy, and when they do not. The study introduces the concept of conditional privacy, which measures the loss of privacy resulting from the third party inferring the user's route planning process. We propose two specific privacy metrics: the Conditional Information Leakage (CIL) algorithm, which quantifies the average reduction in uncertainty regarding the user's locations, and the Maximum Location Leakage (MLL) algorithm, which determines the maximum potential for a third party to deduce the user's future locations. Additionally, we examine the impact of various route planning strategies on privacy levels. Finally, an experimental section compares our proposed privacy measures against traditional ones. The results indicate that CIL and MLL offer greater generality and flexibility, enabling users to balance privacy against travel efficiency. Furthermore, these algorithms are applicable to both homogeneous and heterogeneous location sequences. Finally, the experiments reveal that route planning strategies can compromise up to 50% of the user's location privacy. To mitigate this, we recommend that users either avoid using route planning tools or employ them only when necessary. This paper introduces NDT-Transformer, a new method for large-scale 3D point cloud localization that integrates the Normal Distribution Transform (NDT) optimization framework with Transformer-based attention mechanisms. NDT-Transformer leverages the NDT depiction, which models a map as a grid of anisotropic, multivariate Gaussian distributions. Each distribution's conditional probability density is estimated using multi-head self-attention within a Transformer encoder, which processes 3D point coordinates and their corresponding normal vectors. The NDT-Transformer architecture is designed to be differentiable, enabling the use of traditional NDT cost functions—such as the minimum distance constraint and anisotropy constraint—as loss functions for end-to-end training. We evaluate the method on both synthetic and real-world datasets, showing that it surpasses state-of-the-art point cloud registration techniques, including PointNetLK, D4, and NDT, in achieving accurate global localization. Furthermore, NDT-Transformer demonstrates robustness against noisy inputs and sparse sensor data, such as GPS points. The implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/ashishkumar123/NDT-Transformer. The reliability of statistical inference and estimated parameters is a critical issue in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) research. This study addresses reliability in the context of resting-state functional connectivity, which is typically assessed through correlation or mutual information between the time courses of distinct brain regions. We introduce a generalized framework for estimating the joint statistical dependence between multiple pairs of random variables, thereby extending the standard two-pair approach. This generalization enables the evaluation of both the precision of significance testing and the accuracy of parameter estimation for functional connectivity. Our methodology relies on the concept of the average reproducibility of a statistical test, which is estimated via test-train splits of empirical data. We demonstrate that the reproducibility of the significance test for the mean correlation coefficient between two fMRI time courses is highly sensitive to the number of time points. Furthermore, we show that this average reproducibility can be approximated using the variance of a bootstrap estimator for dependence measures, a technique that facilitates efficient assessment of reliability across multiple pairs of time course samples. We validate this approach through a case study involving a single subject from the Human Connectome Project. The findings indicate that the reproducibility of the significance test for the average correlation coefficient between two fMRI time courses is strongly dependent on the number of time points. Additionally, we observe that the reproducibility of the average correlation coefficient itself is only weakly influenced by the number of time points. Finally, we demonstrate that the reproducibility of the average correlation coefficient between two fMRI time courses can be effectively approximated by the reproducibility of the average Fisher z-transformed correlation coefficient. These results suggest that Fisher z-transformation serves as a valuable tool for enhancing the precision of functional connectivity estimates. Furthermore, we establish that the reproducibility of the average correlation coefficient can be reliably approximated by the reproducibility of the average correlation coefficient across a larger number of time points. These findings imply that reproducibility can be estimated using a significantly larger sample of time points. Ultimately, we conclude that reproducibility can be reliably approximated by leveraging the reproducibility of an expanded time point sample. This insight enables researchers to determine the necessary time point count required to achieve a target level of reproducibility. The findings presented herein are expected to advance the precision of statistical inference in resting-state fMRI connectivity research. Additionally, the reproducibility estimation approach developed in this work is applicable to other fMRI analyses. This study addresses single-hop communication within beeping networks, where nodes exchange brief one-bit messages without employing a scheduling protocol. The primary objective is to minimize total energy usage, defined as the sum of transmitting energy and listening energy, with each node's listening energy proportional to the fraction of time it spends listening. We establish that the optimal total transmitting energy amounts to $2E_t$, matching that of single-hop broadcast scenarios, and we propose a straightforward distributed algorithm achieving this energy efficiency. This approach demonstrates superior energy performance compared to existing methods. Furthermore, we prove a lower bound for the total listening energy and present a beeping single-hop algorithm that simultaneously optimizes both transmitting and listening energy components. Additionally, we explore communication between two nodes within a bounded time frame, presenting a beeping protocol that meets this deadline while optimizing total energy consumption. Finally, we extend our primary algorithm to handle multi-hop communication, showing results on energy usage and delay for specific topological cases. In this extended context, we derive lower bounds for total transmitting and listening energy, as well as latency, and present a beeping multi-hop algorithm that adheres to these limits. Topology-specific simulations indicate that our proposed algorithm outperforms current state-of-the-art solutions. To the best of our knowledge, this work represents the first application of beeping techniques to multi-hop communication. Our findings are supported by both theoretical analysis and simulations. This research was conducted during the authors' internship at the Fraunhofer Institute for Integrated Circuits (ICV) in Erlangen, Germany. This paper is derived from the authors' doctoral thesis. Keywords: Wireless Communications, Beeping, Energy-Efficient Communication, Distributed Algorithms.

Positional encoding is essential for processing sequences in Transformer-based neural network architectures. However, creating effective positional encodings for code-switched (Code-Mixed) languages is difficult because of their unique sequential structure. This work introduces PESTO, a novel Transformer-compatible positional encoding designed for Code-Mixed data. We observe that the sequential nature of Code-Mixed sentences allows for the identification of "transition points" where one language shifts to another. Leveraging these transition points, we developed a method to create positional encodings relative to them. Experimental results across three Code-Mixed languages demonstrate that PESTO surpasses standard encodings, such as those used in BERT and RoBERTA, for tasks involving Code-Mixed inputs. Additionally, we present a theoretical analysis of Transformer-based encodings and provide a guide for selecting the optimal positional encoding strategy. Our source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashwinb/PESTO.

This study employs first-principles calculations to investigate the pressure-dependent critical temperature ($T_c$) of H$_3$S hydride, utilizing the maximum-entropy (MaxEnt) approach to analyze electron-phonon coupling. By incorporating a pressure-induced pressureless optical phonon mode, we demonstrate that the $T_c$ of H$_3$S reaches approximately 208 K at 160 GBA. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the isotope effect coefficient ($\alpha$) varies with pressure, ranging from 0.20 to 0.25 across the 80–200 GBA pressure interval. Additionally, the calculated BCS gap ratio ($2\Delta_0/E_g$) exhibits a value near 4.3 at 200 GBA, signaling the presence of a van Hove singularity. These results provide compelling evidence for the existence of a van Hove singularity within H$_3$S. Additionally, we examine the impact of a pressureless phonon mode on the isotope effect coefficient. Finally, we explore the potential for enhancing the $T_c$ of H$_3$S through the implementation of this pressureless phonon mode. These conclusions are substantiated by the observation that the BCS gap ratio is highly sensitive to the frequency of this mode. Ultimately, our findings suggest that the van Hove singularity in H$_3$S is intrinsically linked to the high-temperature superconductivity of this material. Additionally, we note that the pressureless phonon mode significantly contributes to the isotope effect coefficient. Our analysis indicates that the pressureless phonon mode is essential for achieving the highest $T_c$ in H$_3$S. Furthermore, the pressureless phonon mode substantially amplifies the isotope effect coefficient, thereby facilitating the experimental verification of the van Hove singularity in H$_3$S. Finally, we demonstrate that the pressureless phonon mode can be engineered by adjusting the volume of the H$_3$S unit cell. This work offers a theoretical foundation for future experimental investigations into the van Hove singularity within H$_3$S. Additionally, our results suggest that the pressureless phonon mode is a critical factor in achieving the highest $T_c$ in H$_3$S. Moreover, the pressureless phonon mode significantly influences the isotope effect coefficient, which is essential for experimentally confirming the van Hove singularity in H$_3$S

This study addresses the challenge of planning collision-free trajectories for a single autonomous agent within a 2D environment containing multiple obstacles and a goal region that is in constant motion. The proposed method, named SLICEMAP, plans the vehicle's path in a grid-based gridworld by artificially imposing spatial limitations on the vehicle's movement. These constraints are established by constructing a cost map that assigns higher costs to states with a greater number of neighboring cells that are unreachable due to the dynamic nature of the system. The paper provides a detailed description of the algorithm, demonstrates its operation through a simulation, and evaluates its performance against other algorithms by comparing the quality of the generated paths. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/robinmuller1997/SLICEMAP. Furthermore, the authors intend to extend this approach to more complex, realistic settings in future research, such as planning routes for multiple vehicles in a 4D space or determining optimal routes for a fleet of delivery trucks in a city. This extension would involve learning a value function that estimates the potential cost of visiting a state, thereby creating spatial limits for the vehicle to reach a target. Such an extension would necessitate a learning algorithm, for instance, one based on Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS), to iteratively improve the value function. The authors will explore this direction in future work. Additionally, the authors would like to thank the reviewers for their valuable feedback and suggestions. We are currently revising our paper to incorporate their insights, with the aim of submitting the updated version to a suitable venue. Specifically, a reviewer noted that the source code is not included in the submission, which is a significant oversight. We are actively working to rectify this issue. Another reviewer suggested that the paper lacks a clear comparison with existing path planning algorithms. We are addressing this concern by providing a more comprehensive discussion on the advantages and disadvantages of the proposed algorithm relative to other methods. Finally, a reviewer pointed out that the experiments were conducted on a small grid, raising questions about the algorithm's performance in larger environments. We are expanding our experimental section to include results from a larger grid environment. In conclusion, we are diligently working to incorporate all these improvements into our revised submission. This paper presents a new visual relocalization approach that leverages both color and depth data from prior scans within a depth map. Traditional relocalization methods typically depend on point features, which can be sparse and unreliable in textureless or repetitive areas. In contrast, our technique utilizes supervoxels derived from a multi-level depth hierarchy to create robust local descriptors. Furthermore, we introduce a neural network that combines these depth-based features with learned visual features from image patches to achieve accurate relocalization. This method is particularly effective in environments where visual-only approaches often fail. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves a 30% higher success rate compared to state-of-the-art visual relocalization techniques. Additionally, we show that combining our approach with geometric optimization yields results comparable to those of visual-place localization methods. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar12345/3d-surfel-map-assisted-relocalization.

This study tackles the challenge of optimizing downlink precoding and user selection in multiuser MIMO networks. To achieve this, we formulate a joint optimization problem that simultaneously downlinks data to multiple users while maximizing the network's sum rate. We introduce a group LASSO-based algorithm capable of solving this problem to its global optimum. This approach handles the combinatorial nature of user selection by approximating it with an L1-norm regularization term, while sparsity is induced through a soft thresholding operation within the group LASSO framework. We demonstrate that the resulting algorithm converges to a global optimum and exhibits superior computational efficiency compared to existing methods. Furthermore, numerical results confirm that our method significantly outperforms state-of-the-art solutions in both sum rate and energy efficiency. Finally, we illustrate the algorithm's application to massive MIMO systems employing wideband code division multiple access. In this specific context, the algorithm demonstrates that the codebook can be selected based on channel characteristics, leading to a substantial increase in achievable sum rate. Additionally, the algorithm remains robust against interference from other cells. Finally, we show that the algorithm can be implemented in a distributed fashion, allowing it to solve the downlink problem jointly with its corresponding uplink counterpart. In this scenario, the algorithm successfully identifies the optimal downlink user set that matches the uplink set identified by a previously proposed uplink solution. This indicates that a single algorithm can be utilized to optimize the entire network, thereby reducing the computational burden on the base station. Such an approach is particularly advantageous for massive MIMO systems, where numerous base stations may be deployed. In this case, the algorithm enables the base station to downlink data to a larger number of users, resulting in a significant boost to the network's total capacity. We demonstrate that the rational function semifield associated with a tropical arc is finitely generated as a semifield over the tropical semifield $\Rbar \bar{+} \bar{-} \bar{+} \infty$. This result extends a theorem by Shih and Yu, which established the property for the rational function semifield of a log curve. Furthermore, we derive applications of this finding to the study of rank functions on tropical arcs and to characterizing such semifields through their finite rank arcs. A key innovation in our proof is the development of a new concept: semi-algebraic functions on tropical arcs, which are defined as rational functions on algebraic curves that map to $\Rbar \cup \{-\infty\}$. We prove that the rational function semifield of a tropical arc is generated as a semifield over $\Rbar \bar{+} \bar{-} \bar{+} \infty$ by rational semi-algebraic functions on the arc. Additionally, we provide a constructive method for finding a finite arc whose rational function semifield generates that of a given arc. Finally, we generalize our approach to rational function semifields of higher dimensional log schemes and rational functions on algebraic varieties. Specifically, for a quasi-projective variety $X$ defined by polynomial equations with coefficients in $\Rbar \times \{+\infty, -\infty\}$, we prove that the rational function semifield of $X$ is finitely generated as a semifield over the rational function semifield of $\Rbar ^{n-1} \times \{+\infty, -\infty\} \times \Rbar ^{m-1}$, where $n$ and $m$ represent the numbers of variables in the respective equations. The well-known consistent convergence of the empirical transition matrix toward the Q-process can be accelerated by employing a transition matrix derived from an occupation time that weights transitions based on a specific, potentially path-dependent criterion. This work presents a general framework for this technique, which is applied to a continuous-time Markov decision process to demonstrate how it achieves faster convergence. Additionally, the article includes a simulation study that validates this theoretical result.

This research investigates the relationship between the Vassiliev characteristic of order three and the Fox-Hatcher characteristic. The characteristic of order three is defined as the sum of the three signs associated with the knot complement in $S^3$, as determined by the cohomology class in $H^2(M_\kappa, \mathbb{C})$ resulting from the representation $\rho: \pi_1(M_\kappa) \to SL_2(\mathbb{C})$. We calculate this characteristic for the Fox-Hatcher knots and demonstrate that it corresponds to the knotting number. This finding provides an alternative derivation of a result established by Shonfeld. Furthermore, we present additional examples of Vassiliev characteristic computations for other representations. Finally, we outline an algorithm for computing the Vassiliev characteristic of order three given a braid representation. These methods are implemented in a Mathematica package available for download. The package also includes an algorithm to determine the knotting number of any knot given its braid representation. We illustrate this by computing the knotting numbers for the knots presented in [10]. Additionally, we introduce a conjecture regarding an algorithm to decide whether a braid representation yields a non-zero value for the Fox-Hatcher characteristic. Our analysis of 12,000 knots from the KnotInfo database suggests that the knotting number is frequently the Vassiliev characteristic for braids. We also provide a formula for this quantity in specific cases. As an application, we establish a formula for the Vassiliev characteristic of order three for torus knots represented as braids. We conjecture that this characteristic is zero for all torus knots, a claim supported by computations across a broad range of examples. We further demonstrate that the characteristic is non-zero for certain braids representing non-alternating knots, thereby addressing a question posed by the authors in [11]. Finally, we offer conjectures concerning the knotting number, including its equivalence to the Vassiliev characteristic of order three under braid representations and its relationship with the signature of the knot. The Nernst effect offers a valuable method for investigating quasi-two-dimensional (q2D) electronic systems, as it becomes significant near magnetic phase transitions and can signal the presence of a nematic phase. To detect this nematicity, we measured the Nernst coefficient across various temperatures and magnetic fields for LiFeAs both in its pristine state and after ion irradiation. Our results show that the Nernst effect in LiFeAs is substantial even at room temperature, a finding that contrasts sharply with other q2D q2D electron systems. This discrepancy suggests that the Nernst effect in LiFeAs stems from a non-degenerate carrier gas rather than nematic fluctuations. Furthermore, irradiation-induced disorder markedly amplified the Nernst effect, indicating that the sample contained a high concentration of pre-existing point defects. These findings imply that ion irradiation can be utilized to enhance the Nernst signal in LiFeAs. Additionally, we observed that applying a magnetic field induces a distinct peak in the Nernst coefficient at low temperatures, which we attribute to a magnetic field-driven phase transition. This interpretation is supported by the observation that ion-irradiated samples exhibit a more pronounced Nernst peak under the same magnetic field conditions. Our analysis indicates that this transition is first-order, with the additional disorder from irradiation causing a more evident manifestation of the transition in the Nernst signal. We propose that this transition represents a field-induced nematic phase, potentially arising from the interplay between nematic fluctuations and magnetic field effects. Our conclusions are reinforced by the fact that similar behavior was observed in a second batch of irradiated LiFeAs samples. Finally, we suggest that the magnetic field-induced peak in the Nernst coefficient may also be influenced by the anisotropy of the LiFeAs Fermi surface. Overall, our findings demonstrate that ion irradiation can enhance the Nernst signal in LiFeAs, and that the magnetic field-induced peak in this signal likely reflects the nematic properties of the material. These results provide a new perspective on the nematic phase in LiFeAs and open up new avenues for investigating this phase through the Nernst effect. The Two Higgs Doublet Model (2HDM) extends the Standard Model (SM) by incorporating a second Higgs doublet, resulting in five physical scalar states: a heavy CP-even ($H$), a light CP-even ($h$), a heavy CP-odd ($A$), and a light, pseudo-CP-odd pseudoscalar ($H^0$). While the light CP-even state $h$ aligns with SM predictions at the LHC, the additional scalars—$H$, $A$, and $H^0$—remain undetected. These particles may possess masses within the reach of current and near-future experiments, including the LHC, LHCb, ILC, and FCC-ee. This study examines the parameter space of 2HDM types I and II, constrained by direct searches at the LHC and LHCb, indirect limits from $g-2$ of the muon and electroweak precision tests, and current and upcoming flavor data. Furthermore, we investigate the branching ratios of $B_s \to f_0(K^*\to K\pi)\gamma$ and the branching ratio of $B_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$, which are sensitive to $H$, $A$, and $H^0$. Our analysis demonstrates that the $H$-mediated contribution to the $B_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ branching ratio can be approximately 10% larger than the SM value, whereas $A$- and $H^0$-mediated contributions are negligible. Additionally, we show that the $H$-mediated contribution to $B_s \to f_0(\to K\pi)\gamma$ can be up to 10% lower than the SM prediction. Finally, we present contours in the 2HDM parameter space representing the allowed regions based on current and future experimental data. Our findings indicate that future measurements of $B_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ and $B_s \to f_0(\to K\pi)\gamma$ will significantly constrain the 2HDM parameter space. Specifically, the future $B_s \to \mu^+\mu^-$ measurement will restrict the parameter space by a factor of 100, while the $B_s \to f_0(\to K\pi)\gamma$ measurement will reduce it by a factor of 10. This study explores neuroevolutionary training as a method for self-assembly, specifically addressing two core questions: whether training particles to form specific structures is viable, and if so, what parameters facilitate this. To validate the approach, we successfully demonstrated the formation of both linear and triangular configurations. Furthermore, we applied the method to create a more complex structure—a square of 3x3 particles—which required the optimization of multiple initial conditions, including mutation rates, selection strategies, particle interaction potentials, and the distribution of initial kinetic energies. Our findings indicate that lower mutation rates and mutation-biasing toward conservative alterations are critical for achieving complex self-assembly. Additionally, the selection strategy must be tailored to the specific target structure, while the choice of particle potential and initial kinetic energy distributions significantly impacts the success of the formation process. These results establish essential guidelines for designing self-assembly tasks within particle simulations. Finally, we outline how this methodology can be extended to more complex scenarios, such as creating hollow structures or assembling particles into functional machines. By employing mutation-biasing and implementing intermediate training goals, the approach is adaptable for training particles to build functional devices and optimize particle distributions for creating materials with desired properties. This marks the first time such a comprehensive set of design principles has been identified for self-assembly, providing a robust foundation for future research in this field. Our methodology is readily adaptable for self-assembly tasks in other domains, including molecular dynamics simulations and agent-based simulations of autonomous agents. Specifically, the agent-based model can be extended to design self-organizing swarms and flocks, as well as to assemble autonomous robots into functional structures. Moreover, the mutation-biasing technique can be utilized to synthesize new materials with target properties, such as band gaps. Ultimately, this work provides a foundational framework for self-assembly design and serves as a starting point for advancing the field. This study investigates the interaction between magnons and phonons in the antiferromagnetic insulator yttrium iron garnet (YIG) under high-intensity, low-frequency acoustic wave excitation. By employing both time-resolved magneto-optical Kerr effect (MOKE) and Brillouin light scattering (BLS) techniques, we detect a significant increase in acoustic wave amplitude and shifts in frequency. Our analysis demonstrates that these observations align with a Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert (LLG) model incorporating a magneto-elastic coupling term. This theoretical framework elucidates the mechanisms driving thermal compression and nonlinear spectral displacement of magnons driven by spin-elastic interactions. Furthermore, the model establishes a quantitative relationship among magnon, phonon, and magnon-phonon interactions, offering new insights into energy transfer dynamics within magnetic insulators. Consequently, this model serves as a foundation for designing magneto-acoustic devices capable of controlling spin-elastic interactions. The experimental methodology is also applicable to other magnetic materials. Finally, our findings underscore the potential of magneto-acoustic systems in advancing quantum information science. Specifically, the observed thermal compression of acoustic waves in YIG suggests a pathway for generating nonclassical phonon states. Additionally, the detected spectral displacement of yig magnons may facilitate the creation of squeezed states of light through magneto-optical processes. These outcomes are supported by comprehensive time-resolved spectroscopic measurements. Notably, the observed thermal compression of acoustic waves in yig marks the first demonstration of such an effect in a magnetic insulator. While the spectral displacement of yig magnons has been previously reported in metallic ferromagnets, this is the first time it has been demonstrated in a magnetic insulator. The study concludes by discussing the implications of these findings for quantum information science. Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem relies on the symmetric dual of Goppa codes as the secret key. This paper introduces two modifications to enhance the system's security. The first variant utilizes a full rank matrix with a specific structure to generate the Goppa code, while the second employs a structured Goppa vector. We present two algorithms for the first variant to reduce the storage requirements for matrices and vectors, and provide one algorithm for the second variant to minimize key size. Furthermore, we analyze the complexities of the proposed key extraction attacks for both versions and discuss the system's security performance. Finally, we compare our proposed system against original code-based cryptosystems, highlighting its advantages in terms of key size, storage needs, and security robustness. Experimental results confirm that the first variant offers significant improvements over existing code-based cryptosystems regarding key size, storage, and security. Additionally, we demonstrate that the second variant outperforms systems based on structured Goppa vectors regarding key size and security. Both variants are implemented in C++ and validated through comparative experiments with various code-based cryptosystems. The results indicate that both versions achieve better performance than their respective original counterparts. We have made the source code available for the first variant at \url{https://github.com/AlirezaKarami/QRGoppaImplementation}. Our findings suggest that the first variant is highly promising and warrants further investigation. This research was conducted while the first author was a visiting scholar at the University of Waterloo. The second author's work is detailed in his thesis, available at \url{https://www.researchgate.net/publication/341911001_Structured_Goppa_vector-based_cryptosystem}. Both authors' thesis documents include comprehensive comparisons with other code-based cryptosystems. This research received support from the Iran National Science Foundation (Grant No. 3101207). Language models (LMs) are now a cornerstone of numerous state-of-the-art machine learning applications. Self-supervised LMs are particularly effective at capturing intricate contextual information, yet their performance can be further enhanced by integrating external lexical knowledge. This paper presents Dict-BERT, a BERT-based model that leverages a lexical database to automatically enrich the pre-training process with word definitions. We begin by analyzing the pre-training objectives of BERT and subsequently modify them to incorporate lexical data. To validate our methodology, we applied Dict-BERT to two standard NLP benchmarks: the GLUE benchmark and text classification tasks. The experimental results demonstrate that Dict-BERT surpasses BERT in NLP task performance. Additionally, we fine-tuned the model for clinical text classification, achieving state-of-the-art results. Our source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-1998/DictBERT.

These discoveries are supported by a novel Hodge theory-based randomization technique for constructing persistence diagrams. The paper concludes by identifying intriguing open questions concerning the limiting behavior of these diagrams. This work represents the first instance of rigorously addressing the emergence of homology mass in high-dimensional Euclidean complexes derived from point processes. Additionally, it marks the first application of persistence diagrams to analyze random graphs beyond the limited scope of Euclidean distance-based point processes. This approach facilitates the analysis of limiting behavior for random complexes by reducing the problem to the study of random matrices. The resulting framework allows for the derivation of limiting persistence diagrams for various point processes, including the Poisson point process and the uniform point process on a Euclidean ball. We also address the limiting behavior of minimal spanning complexes and demonstrate that the distribution of their persistence diagrams converges to the same limit as that of general random complexes. Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) has recently emerged as a privacy-preserving framework for training machine learning models across multiple organizations. In this approach, organizations collaborate by contributing either horizontal (client data) features or vertical (various attribute) features to a specific task. VFL has been applied in diverse sectors, including healthcare, finance, and marketing. However, the inherent privacy risks associated with VFL have received insufficient attention. This study introduces three novel pragmatic privacy attacks on VFL, which are both effective and efficient. Our findings demonstrate that the proposed attack methods can successfully infer private information from target organizations with high precision and recall rates. Furthermore, we show that these attack techniques can be adapted to other federated learning frameworks. This research offers valuable insights for organizations considering participation in VFL, enabling them to better evaluate the potential privacy risks involved. Additionally, the code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1998/pragmatic-privacy-assault-VFL. Finally, the paper includes supplementary materials with detailed methodological explanations and experimental results. We also hope it will encourage organizations to more carefully assess the potential risks before joining federated learning initiatives. Utilizing QCD light-cone synthesis rules, the matrix element for $B\to p\bar{\rm Y}$ is derived from the $B\to{\rm Y}\bar{\rm Y}$ transition, which is calculated within the quantum chromodynamic potential model. This model incorporates the effective mass of the $\bar{\rm Y}\bar{\rm Y}$ pair, arising from their interaction with the $B$-meson, and the momentum distribution of the produced $\bar{\rm Y}\bar{\rm Y}$ pair, described by a normalized pair distribution function. The resulting decay width is subsequently used to determine the production cross section for dark antibaryons in cosmic ray interactions. Finally, the theoretical predictions are compared against experimental data regarding the production of antiprotons and their isotopes. The analysis indicates that the derived production cross sections align with experimental observations for antiprotons. Furthermore, the study establishes constraints on the mass and coupling constant of the dark scalar, contingent upon the mass of $\bar{\rm Y}$ and the specific $B$-meson decay under consideration. These findings suggest that this framework could facilitate the detection of dark antibaryons in cosmic rays. Intelligent cities are evolving into complex socio-cyber-physical systems that integrate advanced cyber capabilities with physical infrastructure. These systems rely on a vast array of interconnected devices and software, ranging from large-scale infrastructure to individual consumer units. While this digital transformation enhances urban quality of life, it simultaneously exposes city systems to diverse cyber threats. This paper introduces a new mathematical framework for analyzing the security of intelligent cities, conceptualizing the challenge as a two-player, two-sided defense game. In this scenario, two attackers target two distinct system components, each protected by a pool of defense resources. The core problem involves attackers selecting optimal attack strategies to maximize success, while system defenders deploy tactics to minimize losses. We model this situation using a two-sided defense game and a corresponding resource allocation game, where both players select strategies based on available resources to optimize their outcomes. This approach offers a novel method for assessing city security and paves the way for developing intelligent defense resource management systems. Furthermore, we explore the equilibrium solutions of this game, providing a practical approach to resource allocation for intelligent city defense. Finally, we validate the proposed model through a case study of a hypothetical city subjected to a cyber-physical attack. The results demonstrate that the game effectively identifies the most probable attack scenarios and suggests appropriate resource distributions for defenders. Additionally, we observe that the game's solutions are highly sensitive to resource allocation, indicating that intelligent management of defense resources is essential for maximizing system security. This research holds significant potential for enhancing city security and could serve as a foundation for future intelligent resource allocation systems. Our proposed game offers a novel analytical tool for city security analysis and resource management, with applications extending to other cyber-physical systems, including smart grids, industrial automation, and supply chains. We investigate the thermodynamics of a charged black hole within a finite chamber, demonstrating the existence of large and small phases alongside a Hawking--Page phase transition. Notably, our findings indicate that the transition point for the charged black hole shifts to lower temperatures as the size of the chamber decreases. Furthermore, we examine the thermodynamic behavior of this system as the boundary is adjusted. We also address the thermodynamics of a Schwarzschild black hole in a chamber, observing that the transition temperature increases with the chamber's size. Additionally, we show that the thermodynamic analysis of a Schwarzschild black hole in a chamber is mathematically equivalent to that of a charged black hole within a cosmological constant. Finally, we explore the relationship between the two isobaric phase diagrams. These results suggest that the thermodynamic properties of a charged black hole in a chamber are more complex than those of a Schwarzschild black hole in the same setting. In the domain of noisy web ranking, a significant challenge involves training a ranking model despite labeled data containing noise. This noise primarily manifests as label noise, where training samples are often incorrectly annotated. This paper introduces a straightforward and effective sampling technique designed to extract high-quality data subsets from noisy labeled collections. The method is adaptable to various downstream tasks, such as web search and universal document ranking. The core concept relies on the observation that web ranking labels follow a power-law distribution, meaning a few categories dominate the distribution while many others have very low support. By identifying the long-tail categories and randomly sampling from them, a representative subset can be extracted. To validate the effectiveness of this approach, the study constructs a noisy dataset for document ranking by randomly scrambling labels from a large-scale web ranking corpus. A simple downstream model is then trained on this corrupted dataset to demonstrate that the sampling method yields superior performance compared to models trained on the original noisy data. The paper also explores and compares multiple sampling strategies. Finally, to address the long-tail distribution issue, a novel loss function is proposed to further enhance the ranking model's performance on extracted samples. This cluster-wise loss function is also applicable to other scenarios featuring long-tail distributions. Finally, the paper discusses the implementation of this cluster-wise loss through a straightforward and efficient algorithm. Experimental results confirm that the cluster-wise loss can further improve the ranking model's performance. The paper concludes by outlining the method's advantages and suggesting potential future research directions. The code is available at: https://github.com/ChenYi1997/LabelNoiseDataRetrieval. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated significant potential for semi-supervised learning on graph structures, yet fully labeled nodes are often scarce in real-world applications, forcing models to rely heavily on a small subset of ground-truth labels. This label scarcity can hinder performance, particularly when the selected labels are uninformative. To address this, we introduce the concept of illuminating pseudo-labels, which are selected based on their ability to enhance the performance of a specific GNN model. Unlike prior methods that uniformly choose top-k labels, our approach identifies label nodes that best adapt to the unique requirements of the GNN. To achieve this, we propose the EnGNN framework, which employs an end-to-end trainable node selector within the GNN model. This framework optimizes both the graph model and the label selector simultaneously, ensuring that pseudo-labels contribute positively to learning. Experimental results across various real-world datasets confirm the effectiveness of EnGNN, demonstrating its superiority over state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we provide a detailed analysis of the framework's effectiveness and interpretability. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1990/EngNN.

This study examines the generation of betatron radiation during the proton-electron collision phase of the AWAKE Run 2 experiment, which operates at CERN's Large Hadron Collider. By employing the open-source Geant4 toolkit, we analyze the spectral and angular characteristics of this phenomenon. Our results indicate that electron beams with energies up to 10 GeV produce betatron radiation detectable by standard optical devices, offering a valuable tool for measuring final state variables. Furthermore, we explore potential applications of this radiation for probing the existence of dark matter mediators. These findings are critical for assessing the experiment's sensitivity to various dark matter scenarios. Additionally, we demonstrate that the observed radiation can be accurately modeled using an analytical approach, which significantly streamlines simulation workflows. Ultimately, this research underscores the potential of betatron radiation as both a diagnostic instrument and a means to enhance the dark matter search sensitivity of AWAKE Run 2. All simulation data and corresponding scripts are accessible at https://github.com/awakecollab/g4awakey.

This study introduces a suite of algorithms for distributed decision tree learning that adhere to differential privacy (DP). These methods are both scalable and provably private, offering rigorous guarantees for sensitive data. The research addresses two primary scenarios: secure multi-party computation (SMPC) and trusted execution environments (TEEs). We establish the first provably private SMPC algorithm for learning differentiable random forests, while also proposing a novel, provably private algorithm for the same purpose within a TEE setting. To enhance practicality, we develop multiple strategies to minimize the complexity and communication overhead of these private algorithms. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate that our proposed private algorithms are highly scalable, effectively supporting large datasets. Furthermore, they achieve performance comparable to their non-private counterparts. To the best of our knowledge, this work presents the first provably private algorithms for decision tree learning in distributed environments with provable guarantees. Additionally, we release the private versions of our algorithms as open-source software. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/PranavKumar1998/DP-DT. This paper introduces a regularized variant of the $f_\alpha$-divergence, also known as Rényi divergence, specifically designed for application with the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence. We demonstrate that minimizing the distance between two probability distributions on $\mathbb{R}^d$ under the discrete topology via regularized Rényi divergence is equivalent to minimizing the KL divergence subject to a constraint on the $\ell_\infty$ distance between the distributions. Furthermore, we establish the $\kappa$-strongly convex property of the regularized Rényi divergence and propose two iterative algorithms for its efficient computation. These methods are proven to achieve linear convergence when regularized Rényi divergence is employed as a proximal measure within the Bregman proximal gradient framework. Additionally, we extend these algorithms to handle infinite-dimensional spaces, maintaining convergence guarantees under specific conditions. Chain event graph models have recently been suggested for analyzing conditional probability data. While previous research has addressed the estimation of a single CEG from this data using the maximum likelihood estimator, this paper introduces a Bayesian framework for model selection among chain event graphs. We define a prior distribution over the space of CEG models and employ the mean squared error criterion to identify the posterior maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimator within that space. Furthermore, we provide an efficient dynamic programming algorithm to determine the Bayesian framework selection of the optimal CEG model. A practical example demonstrates the application of our proposed method. Additionally, we illustrate how CEG model selection can facilitate CEG estimation, and we argue that this approach is superior to the traditional method of estimating a single CEG via maximum likelihood. Our results indicate that the Bayesian framework selection method yields a more accurate CEG model. We also address the challenge of CEG model selection when data volume is insufficient to reliably select the true CEG, offering a potential solution through pooling. We apply a basic pooling method to a real-world case study, showing that it facilitates CEG model selection and enhances accuracy. Finally, we discuss the extension of this pooling approach to other model selection criteria. Throughout this work, we have implemented the CEG model selection method in the R package `cegbayes`. The package is available at https://github.com/cegbayes/cegbayes. This work was partially funded by the Swedish Research Council (grant no. 2016-03790). The authors thank the referees for their constructive comments, which significantly improved the manuscript. The corresponding author can be reached at firstname.lastname@example.org. Beyond deriving Poincare-Lyapunov type inequalities, we establish convergence results utilizing Lyapunov functions, specifically showing that for any critical value, all trajectories asymptotically approach the set of minimizers of the Tikhonov-regularized problem. We further demonstrate that this minimal norm solution is the unique asymptotic attractor, with trajectories converging strongly and uniformly. Additionally, we prove that trajectories originating from unbounded initial data converge asymptotically to the solution with the smallest norm. Finally, we present numerical experiments to corroborate these theoretical findings. This research extends our earlier work (arXiv:2005.03000) which established weak convergence. The primary innovation lies in the construction of a Lyapunov function that incorporates a time-dependent term to account for energy dissipation caused by damping. This novel approach enables us to demonstrate that all solutions converge asymptotically to the unique minimizer of the regularized problem, thereby exhibiting strong convergence. Specifically, our results indicate that any positive damping exponent ensures convergence to the minimal norm solution. This finding is particularly significant for hyperbolic problems, where the damping exponent is typically very small. This paper investigates the wall-following task, which involves a robot traversing a corridor while maintaining a fixed distance from a wall. This problem is significant for mobile robotics, particularly in narrow corridors where GPS is ineffective. We examine the dynamics of a simple wall-following controller, which can be expressed as a piecewise smooth function. Our analysis demonstrates that the dynamics near a switching manifold are conformally equivalent to those of the piecewise smooth system, allowing us to characterize the limit set of the dynamics using the concept of characteristic exponent. Furthermore, we establish the existence of chaotic dynamics in specific parameter regimes. Finally, we illustrate the application of these theoretical findings through various examples. The code used in this research is accessible at https://github.com/alexei-gorodetskiy/wall_following. Additionally, a preliminary version of these results was presented in [1].

Kinetic energy driven superconductors, including cuprates and iron-based compounds, are thought to consist of nanometer-sized regions of coherent superconductivity separated by barriers. This study investigates how conductivity behaves in the presence of power-dependent microwave fields and defects within such materials. We find that defect scattering can cause dc transport and microwave conductivity to diverge at temperatures above the superconducting transition. Furthermore, the coupling between the superconducting state and electromagnetic fields leads to a conductivity that exhibits an inverse power-law dependence on incident power. This effect is amplified by defects, resulting in a conductivity that varies with frequency and is ultimately power-dependent. These findings offer a potential explanation for the enigmatic microwave conductivity observed in cuprates. Additionally, we demonstrate that this power dependence can be mitigated by utilizing thin films thinner than the magnetic skin depth. Finally, our results indicate that the current power-law dependence of conductivity on frequency in cuprates may stem from the interaction between electromagnetic fields and the superconducting state. These insights could aid in interpreting microwave spectroscopy data for these materials. Our analysis relies on a model of superconductivity driven by kinetic energy, where charge carriers move through an electrostatic potential landscape. This framework is applicable to cuprates, iron-based superconductors, and other materials where superconductivity emerges from electronic correlations. The model incorporates superconducting fluctuations and the coupling between Cooper pairs and electromagnetic fields. We also examine the impact of superconducting vortices on microwave conductivity. Our results align with recent microwave conductivity measurements on YBCO thin films. Finally, we explore the potential for detecting the superconducting state in dc transport through weak localization measurements. These efforts could help clarify the debated nature of the superconducting state in kinetic energy-driven superconductors. Our analysis employs the Maxwell-Garnett effective medium theory to calculate the microwave conductivity of superconducting films. This approach is grounded in the optical properties of individual inclusions and their volume fraction within the film. We assume these inclusions are spherical and exhibit electromagnetic properties consistent with bulk bulk materials. While the inclusions are modeled as superconductors with electromagnetic properties independent of the presence of other inclusions, the electromagnetic properties of the matrix are treated as those of a normal metal. This assumption is justified by the observation that microwave conductivity in normal metals is largely independent of the specific arrangement of individual atoms. This paper introduces GrowSpace, a novel 3D interactive simulation designed to investigate plant growth dynamics and spatial planning. Our motivation stems from the rising interest in indoor gardening driven by the need for sustainable food production. GrowSpace offers a unique, engaging, and extensible platform for both scientific research and education. The platform features a science mode grounded in real-world principles and a game mode that encourages exploration. We have already deployed GrowSpace in two K-12 classrooms, where it successfully enhanced students' understanding of scientific concepts, including plant growth factors, environmental interactions, and spatial reasoning. Furthermore, teacher feedback indicates that GrowSpace is enjoyable, motivating, and effective for both learning and teaching. As a collaborative project between computer science and education teams, the platform is built to be extensible, supporting diverse applications ranging from entertainment to science education. To facilitate this, we provide an API and teacher tools for creating custom spaces and experiments. We invite researchers and educators to explore GrowSpace and contribute to its development. We derive the scaling limit of nested loops generated by the SLE loop fusion process, demonstrating that the resulting loop is described by a quantum disk. Specifically, we establish the scaling limit of nested boundaries for quantum disk instances arising from the Brownian disk and Liouville quantum gravity (LQG) converging to the quantum disk. We further prove that the scaling limit of nested boundaries for the quantum cone is conformally equivalent to the quantum disk. The proof relies on establishing that the scaling limit of nested loops from the SLE loop fusion process is equivalent to the scaling limit of nested boundaries of quantum disks. This equivalence holds for both the quantum disk and Liouville quantum gravity. Additionally, we provide a rigorous definition of conformal fusion for quantum disks and verify its invariance under conformal maps. Finally, we offer an alternative proof of the conformal invariance of the quantum cone. These findings are essential for understanding the scaling limit of the uniform spanning tree and the quantum gravity tree. The primary tools employed are the quantum gravity insertion operator and the quantum Markov property. We also present a novel approach to proving the conformal invariance of the quantum cone. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of conformal fusion for quantum disks and demonstrate its conformal invariance. Recent advancements in machine learning have driven significant progress in medical image analysis. Nevertheless, the widespread adoption of these methods into clinical practice remains uncertain. To address this, we propose a comprehensive strategy for the clinical integration of machine learning-based image biomarkers. This approach centers on a newly defined metric known as repeatability coefficient, which quantifies the consistency of quantitative image biomarkers during repeated scans of the same subject. We outline a systematic framework for validating machine learning pipelines using this metric. Furthermore, we introduce the Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative (IBSI), a global collaborative effort dedicated to establishing standardized protocols for training, testing, and reporting quantitative image biomarkers. The initiative aims to provide a unified nomenclature for image features, establish rigorous validation protocols, and ensure that image feature extraction methods are robust and reproducible. This paper details the initial stages of the IBSI, with subsequent volumes covering feature validation and nomenclature, as well as specific applications in CT and MR imaging. The ultimate goal is to foster trust in image-based quantitative methods within the clinical community. This paper details the image preparation utilizing the OpenCV toolkit for the MORPH-II face dataset. We propose a novel cosmological model featuring a curvaton-like field that decays into a dark matter candidate possessing a negative coupling to the Ricci scalar. The curvature perturbation $\zeta$ associated with the dark matter is driven by the expectation value of the curvaton, $\sigma$, which is influenced by the Ricci scalar $R$. This leads to the development of a dark hole within the $\sigma$-field, a phenomenon that has been rigorously examined. Consequently, the power spectrum of $\zeta$ is significantly amplified, offering a viable mechanism for generating the density fluctuations necessary for the observed cosmic microwave background anisotropies. Furthermore, the mass of the dark matter particle can be constrained based on the curvaton's lifetime and the dark matter's coupling strength to the curvaton field. This framework also provides a solution to the domain wall problem. Finally, we demonstrate that dark matter can be produced via freeze-in from the dark matter candidate, with the resulting relic density matching observational constraints. Finally, we explore a scenario where the dark matter candidate serves as dark radiation, consistent with the upper limits on extra relativistic degrees of freedom. This study investigates the connections between high school and college courses by analyzing a large-scale, multi-year dataset of high school students from a single school district. We introduce a new method for examining course links, which are modeled as latent variables within a generalized item response model. We validate the model's capacity to generate accurate posterior distributions of these connections using synthetic data. Subsequently, we apply the approach to real-world data to assess high school freshman course links and explore how these courses relate to college success. Our results indicate that while students in honors classes tend to select similar subsequent courses, this pattern does not hold for regular or advanced placement classes. Furthermore, we find that high school course selections are not always predictive of college performance. Finally, we demonstrate that the proposed method can be extended to evaluate the relevance of online courses. These findings have significant implications for the design of online learning programs and other initiatives aimed at enhancing academic achievement. The code required to replicate our results is accessible at https://github.com/andrewjgill/latent-variable-models-for-course-links. Additionally, we have made our R package for modeling item links publicly available on CRAN at https://cran.r-project.org/package=linkmodels. The package's vignette, titled "Modeling Item Linkages Using a Generalized Latent Variable Model," details the package's features and includes examples based on this study. The package is also available on GitHub at https://github.com/andrewjgill/linkmodels. This study introduces a novel vehicle platoon controller that integrates advantages from existing heuristic and optimal methods. The proposed Linked Automated Vehicle Platoon Arrangement (LAVPA) controller offers the simplicity of a heuristic approach while delivering optimal performance. By employing differential games, multiple vehicle platoon arrangements can be optimized simultaneously to minimize total fuel consumption, while individual vehicle costs remain bounded. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the LVPA controller outperforms both heuristic and optimal controllers in terms of fuel efficiency. Furthermore, sensitivity analysis reveals that the LVPA controller maintains robustness even when accounting for disturbances such as wind and initial conditions. Additionally, it is shown that the LVPA controller remains effective for reducing costs in scenarios involving both connected and unconnected vehicles. These findings indicate that the LVPA controller is well-suited for real-world deployment.
