It is a well-known phenomenon that including the product of two features in a logistic regression model can prevent them from interacting within the learned decision boundary. This note provides a more comprehensive understanding of this issue. Specifically, we demonstrate that if two features do not interact with every other feature in the decision boundary, their product will possess a significantly lower coefficient compared to individual features. Furthermore, we show that when one of the features is constant, its coefficient will be even lower than that of the product. These findings are supported by examples and simulations. Additionally, we present a theoretical result indicating that in linear regression, a similar phenomenon occurs with constant biases. Finally, we explore how this phenomenon applies to Lasso and Elastic-Net penalized regression. Our motivation for this research stems from a real-world application where interaction terms were inadvertently excluded from the decision boundary due to this effect. Consequently, we propose a method to identify interactions that can be incorporated into the decision boundary, which performs comparably to state-of-the-art techniques. We validate the effectiveness of our approach through simulations and various real-world datasets. Our code is available at: https://github.com/ashwinbhatia/avoiding_interaction.

This work introduces a task aimed at creating news headlines through a transformer-based model. We define "mechanically created" as those generated by algorithms, encompassing both natural-sounding results and oddly phrased ones. Our objective is to identify the former within a dataset containing both headline types. We provide a detailed examination of the dataset collection process and present a comparative analysis of various model types, ultimately demonstrating that a pre-trained transformer achieves the highest accuracy. Additionally, we evaluate the model's performance on the dataset and discuss its limitations. Finally, we explore potential applications of mechanically detecting headlines in news consumption and propose future research directions. The code is accessible at: https://github.com/robertas22/mh-transformer. The dataset can be found at: https://github.com/robertas22/mh-transformer/tree/master/data.

We present a comparative study of the spin-1/2 Kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnet conducted on geometrically frustrated samples featuring amorphous and polycrystalline structures. Through inelastic neutron scattering experiments, we analyze the magnetic excitation spectrum across both materials and contrast these empirical findings with results from classical and quantum Monte Carlo simulations. Our analysis indicates that polycrystalline disorder does not disrupt the emergence of a chiral spin liquid, a state characterized by long-range topological order, in the amorphous sample. Conversely, we demonstrate that both amorphous and polycrystalline geometrical frustrations are inadequate to prevent a quantum phase transition from this chiral spin liquid ground state to a topologically ordered valence-bond solid phase. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for future research into the magnetism of amorphous and polycrystalline systems. This work is based on research reported in [Phys. Rev. This paper introduces a suite of algorithms designed to calibrate data from a regular-grid array, specifically tailored for large-N radio interferometers. The methods encompass the standard $uv$-diagonal solution to the gain equation, as well as self-calibration and self-consistent calibration. A key advantage of these approaches is their computational efficiency, scaling as $\mathcal{O}(N\log{N})$ per iteration, where $N$ denotes the number of baselines. This performance is achieved by integrating a fast Fourier transform with a specialized data structure that represents redundant baselines. Additionally, we introduce a new algorithm for solving the gain equation that exhibits a favorable scaling behavior with respect to the number of iterations. We have implemented these methods in the CASA software package and have applied them to various datasets, demonstrating their utility in producing accurate and computationally efficient results. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/brayn/regular-grid-calibration.

This study introduces a novel deep learning approach for portfolio distribution diversification, utilizing an autoencoding conditional Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) to generate synthetic stock returns. By employing conditional GAN, the model produces return data for a specific stock while simultaneously training an autoencoder within the GAN framework. This dual-generation capability allows for the creation of synthetic returns for both individual stocks and market indices. Empirical results indicate that these synthetic returns achieve a high degree of correlation with actual returns and maintain statistical properties consistent with index returns. Leveraging this enhanced generalization, the proposed method demonstrates superior performance over benchmark models in terms of risk-adjusted returns and capital allocation stability. Furthermore, the approach proves robust against significant market fluctuations, including the 2008 financial crisis and the recent COVID-19 pandemic. Finally, the methodology is validated through a backtesting comparison against existing literature. Overall, this research seeks to enhance portfolio distribution diversification, offering a stable investment alternative to traditional market indices. Additionally, the approach holds potential for expanding the dimensionality of synthetic data generation, which could be valuable for training deep learning models in other financial applications. These findings indicate that Bayesian ANN serves as a robust tool for categorizing high-energy sources. Additionally, the research explores the potential for using Bayesian ANN to investigate a link between FR I and FR II blazar data and the presence of jets in their host galaxies. The results suggest that such a relationship exists for sources with flat spectra and is likely present in those with curved spectra. Finally, this work establishes a foundation for employing Bayesian ANN to classify the blazars featured in the upcoming Fermi-LAT fourth source catalog. This study investigates natural cubic splines for analyzing time-to-event data in clinical trials involving repeated measurements. We propose using the coefficient of the first spline term to identify the inflection point of the hazard ratio relative to time, thereby helping to detect shifts in a treatment effect's magnitude. Furthermore, we develop test statistics and corresponding hypothesis tests to assess the presence of such inflection points. Our approach is demonstrated through an example involving Alzheimer's disease patients. Additionally, simulation studies are conducted to evaluate the performance of the proposed tests. Finally, we illustrate the method's utility in both Alzheimer's disease and a hypothetical clinical trial context. We introduce a new technique for identifying and optimizing dominant transition routes between two states within stochastic dynamical systems. This approach is grounded in the variational principle of minimizing the action functional. Our method utilizes a novel geometric representation of these paths, enabling the efficient global optimization of the system's most probable transition route by directly optimizing the discrete approximation of the action functional. We demonstrate the application of this technique to identify the dominant escape paths of a stochastic dynamical system subject to colored noise. Furthermore, we apply it to investigate the switching dynamics of a bistable system where the two states are weakly coupled via a stochastic field. Finally, the method is employed to map the transition pathways of a well-known protein conformational change. These applications illustrate that our approach offers an efficient and straightforward means for global optimization in the search for the most probable transition paths of stochastic dynamical systems. This study investigates the connection between piecewise regular functions and typed lambda-calculi. Regular functions are defined as finite combinations of functions mapping regular languages to regular constants. We introduce a regular calculus, derived from the simply typed lambda-calculus, capable of exactly characterizing the class of regular functions. We demonstrate that applying specific type transformations to the regular calculus—constrained by normalizability—precisely delineates other significant function classes, including weakly regular, piecewise linear, and piecewise polynomial functions. Furthermore, we examine a hierarchical structure of lambda-calculi based on the functions they encode, analyzing the complexity of their encoding problems. Finally, we explore the complexity of beta-reduction within the regular calculus, proving that it is PSPACE-complete. This finding contrasts with higher-type lambda-calculus, where beta-reduction is known to be decidable. The paper concludes by outlining open questions regarding regular calculus, particularly concerning its potential extension to second-order functions. These second-order regular functions would consist of functions that map regular functions to regular constants. We posit that the second-order regular calculus can exactly characterize these second-order regular functions, and we present evidence supporting this conjecture. Additionally, we show that functions capable of encoding the second halting problem can be constructed using the second-order calculus, thereby providing a lower bound for this class. To our knowledge, this work represents the first investigation into the encoding of functions within the context of regular functions. The study also presents a novel characterization of functions encoding the second halting problem, which previously lacked a concise description. Finally, we establish that the complexity of beta-reduction in the regular calculus remains invariant under small perturbations. This result underscores the necessity of restricting regular functions to regular constants, as the complexity of beta-reduction for general functions is undecidable. The paper ends with several questions concerning the complexity of beta-reduction for functions of varying nature. This work is partially derived from the author's doctoral thesis. This study examines Itô integrals where the integrands are defined by functions representing conditional distributions within dynamical systems. The dynamics of these integrals are characterized by flow functions that depend on historical conditions. The primary objective is to establish the equivalence between the Itô integral and the Stratonovich integral in scenarios where functional integrands consist of conditional distributions. This equivalence holds when flow functions represent conditional distributions of variables at time $t$ given observations from times $t_1$ through $t_n$ (where $t_n < t_1 < \dots < t_n = 0$), or when they represent joint distributions of variables at times $t$ and $t_n$, conditioned on observations made at $t_1, \dots, t_{n-1}$. These findings are applicable to financial modeling, specifically for pricing financial derivatives and managing risk. Furthermore, the results address the existence and uniqueness of solutions to stochastic differential equations that utilize such functionals as integrands. A key advantage of this work is that the conditional distributions employed as integrands are derived from empirical data, eliminating the need for a priori assumptions about the underlying system's dynamics. Additionally, the derived conditions for existence and uniqueness are more general than those previously proposed in existing literature. Finally, this research contributes to the broader field of stochastic calculus with data. The asset price simulation utilizes a conditional distribution derived from historical data, with the intensity of the Poisson process modeled as a non-stationary, non-ergodic process. We present a framework of norm spaces for groups grounded in Banach spaces equipped with a multiplicative norm, beginning with a review of such spaces and their connections to non-archimedean local fields. We define a broad category of amenable groups known as Banach groups, which encompasses the non-compact units of local fields as a significant subset. For each Banach group, we associate a corresponding graph, demonstrating that specific graph families arise naturally from the groups themselves. Finally, we define the standard space linked to a graph and apply this concept to the standard spaces of Banach groups. Additionally, we investigate the geometric properties of these standard spaces and examine the relationships between the groups and their corresponding spaces. We specifically analyze the standard spaces of the groups GLₙ, SLₙ, and SUₙ across all n ≥ 2. Our findings indicate that the standard space of GLₙ is separable for every n ≥ 2, whereas the standard spaces of both SLₙ and SUₙ are separable if and only if the field is finite. We also establish that the unit sphere within the standard space of GLₙ is isometric to the group SLₙ. Furthermore, we explore the dual spaces of these groups and their corresponding duals, deriving several significant results. In particular, we demonstrate that the dual space of GLₙ possesses a finite basis for all n ≥ 2. Finally, we outline open questions regarding the spaces defined in this work. Notably, for any n ≥ 2, the space derived from the graph of GLₙ is separable, while the same holds true for SLₙ only when the underlying field is finite. This leads to a natural inquiry: can the separability issue of the standard space of SLₙ be resolved by refining the construction method? We address this question and provide a positive answer. We conclude by introducing a question concerning the relationship between the group of a graph and its associated space, which encompasses the standard space of a Banach group as a special instance. We propose a general approach to this problem and offer a partial resolution. Ultimately, this paper offers a systematic investigation into the interplay between groups and their corresponding spaces. The results herein may serve as a foundation for future research into the relationships between groups, their associated spaces, and dual spaces. Additionally, the techniques developed could be valuable for analyzing other graph families, such as those generated by buildings. We anticipate that the methods presented will facilitate further research into the relationships between groups and their corresponding structures.

Cross-domain Text-to-SQL has garnered significant interest due to its extensive practical utility. While most current approaches rely on auxiliary tasks to enhance performance, these often introduce additional computational costs. This study proposes a lightweight method that leverages auxiliary tasks to improve cross-domain Text-to-SQL models by incorporating O21L and blank-padding techniques as just auxiliary losses within an end-to-end architecture. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that these methods yield performance gains without increasing computational expenses. Furthermore, the research explores the impact of different blank-padding strategies, such as word-level and token-level approaches, on model effectiveness. The proposed methods achieve state-of-the-art results on the Spider benchmark, reaching an 86.5% accuracy rate. Additionally, the paper examines how auxiliary tasks influence various components of the generation process. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/End-to-End-Cross-Domain-SQL. Finally, the authors hope this work will inspire future developments in the field. Keywords: Cross-Domain, Text-to-SQL, Auxiliary Task.

This study addresses the safe navigation of multi-robot systems within uncertain environments by introducing a new Information-Focused Risk-Aware Model Predictive Control (IFF-A MPC) framework. The proposed method utilizes a Risk-Aware Nonlinear Program (RA-NP) that integrates a tailored cost function, probability bounds propagation, and a novel concept known as the information flow field. This information flow field quantifies the likelihood of collisions between robots and obstacles, accounting for uncertainties in robot dynamics and measurement noise. Simulation results demonstrate that IFF-A MPC successfully and safely guide multiple robots through unknown terrains, effectively mitigating collision risks. Furthermore, an experimental study validates the approach using real robots, confirming its practical applicability. The results indicate that IFF-A MPC achieves a 90% improvement in successful navigation trials compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, the method exhibits robustness against various noise levels, maintaining safe navigation even under high-noise conditions. Finally, the computational efficiency of the proposed approach is analyzed. IFF-A MPC achieves a 2.5x speedup in computation time relative to current state-of-the-art solutions. Overall, IFF-A MPC offers a highly effective solution for the safe navigation of multi-robot systems in uncertain settings. We report the discovery of Andromeda XXV (And XXV), a compact dwarf galaxy situated approximately 780 kiloparsecs from the Milky Way. This object was identified through a search for new Andromeda satellites using the Pan-STARRS1 survey, which revealed a new candidate within the Andromeda halo. We have confirmed its status as a galaxy by analyzing its spectrum, which exhibits strong emission lines and a red continuum indicative of an old stellar population. Furthermore, we identified a stellar stream extending about 10 arcminutes from the Andromeda nucleus, which we attribute to And XXV. By examining the And XXV stellar population, we determined that it is a dwarf galaxy with a stellar mass of roughly $1.5 \times 10^6$ solar masses. We also established an upper limit on its distance from Andromeda at 100 kiloparsecs and constrained its tangential velocity to less than 100 km/s. Additionally, we derived an upper limit for its dark matter density within the central region, finding it to be less than 100 solar masses per cubic parsec. This low central dark matter density suggests that And XXV resides in a dark matter-deficient environment, a characteristic also observed in other dwarf galaxies. We propose that And XXV is a member of the Andromeda group and that its presence in such a dark matter-poor setting may offer insights into the formation of dark matter-free galaxies. Finally, we discuss the implications of And XXV's existence for the Andromeda halo's dark matter density and the overall dark matter content of the Andromeda group. This study examines various approximations for dry air and water vapor used in humid air modeling, focusing on their equation of state, specific heats, and enthalpy formulations. The analysis evaluates each approach against thermodynamic principles and numerical assessments to identify limitations and the domains where they remain valid. Ultimately, the research proposes thermodynamically consistent adjustments for specific relations to enhance their applicability within broader ranges. These recommendations are pertinent to multiple disciplines, including atmospheric modeling, combustion, and refrigeration. The analysis is conducted using the molal framework. Although the thermodynamically consistent adjustments suggest utilizing a temperature-dependent gas constant for water vapor ($R_w$), the author acknowledges that the more prevalent and established formulation—employing a constant $R_w$—remains adequate for most applications. Furthermore, the discussion does not address the necessary numerical techniques for implementing these thermodynamically consistent relations. Finally, while the analysis is extensive, it is not exhaustive, and the author welcomes discussions on additional improvements. The author also thanks the reviewers for their insightful comments, which have significantly improved the quality of this work. Any remaining errors are the sole responsibility of the author. Additionally, the author thanks his family for their patience and support throughout this endeavor. This paper is dedicated to his wife, who has been his steadfast companion. Any shortcomings in this work are entirely his own.

This paper introduces a new method for dialogue state tracking that models speech recognition uncertainty using a Markov Logic Network (MLN) and Word Confusion Networks (WCN). By representing ASR uncertainty through WCNs, we can integrate lexical and semantic information from both the speaker and the assistant into a unified probabilistic framework. This approach enables the system to infer the most likely semantic states and quantify the confidence in those inferences. We evaluated the proposed method on a public Restaurant Domain dataset, comparing it against both a deterministic baseline and a state-of-the-art probabilistic model. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves performance comparable to the probabilistic model while being significantly more efficient in terms of both training and inference. Furthermore, we analyze the learned models to provide insights into the parameters and confidence levels of the inferred semantic states. Finally, we discuss how this method facilitates multi-domain dialogue management. The accompanying code and data are available at https://github.com/abhishekkumar1997/WCN-MLN. This work was presented at the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics. (2020).

Our findings indicate that the moduli space of stable rank-2 vector bundles on the Fermat quartic is one-dimensional, contrary to the previously conjectured four-dimensional space. Furthermore, we identify that both the surfaces and the moduli space of stable curves on the quartic possess canonical vector bundles, which are identified as weight 1 and weight 2 cusp forms, respectively. Finally, we provide a computational verification of the conjecture regarding the existence of a vector bundle on the Fermat quartic whose restriction to a plane section corresponds to a unique weight 3 weakly elliptic modular form. The introduction of novel frameworks for the universal quantum mechanical evolution of systems is examined through the lens of intricacy, a measure that quantifies the complexity of a state's description. A key finding is that the universal intricacy of universal entry is infinite. This conclusion stems from the necessity to manage an uncountably infinite set of possible initial conditions when computing the universal state, which requires addressing the concept of "the intricacy of a set of states." It is demonstrated that the total intricacy of a set of states is finite only if the set is countable. Consequently, the universal algorithm for entry must be formulated as a co-algorithm, consisting of two components: one that generates a countable set of initial conditions and another that manages the remainder. This duality implies that the co-algorithm is inherently distributed. Furthermore, the co-algorithm for entry is shown to be the logical complement of a co-algorithm for rejection. The impossibility of concentrating all initial conditions into a single trajectory indicates that the distribution of pre-images is a fundamental property of the universal map, rather than a specific characteristic of any single distribution. Finally, the co-algorithm for rejection is demonstrated to be equivalent to the universal rejection algorithm proposed by Alberti and Prandini. These outcomes suggest that the rejection principle is an intrinsic feature of the universal quantum mechanical evolution of systems. Additionally, it is established that the universal state describing rejection is independent of the initial condition. Finally, the rejection principle is linked to the non-contraction principle, which asserts that the intricacy of a system never decreases over time. The significance of these principles in the context of the universal quantum mechanical evolution of systems is also explored. (Univ. Access to Local Resources) (Univ. We introduce a general framework for calculating the fidelity relative to Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger (GHZ) or W states, applicable to any two-qubit projection onto these entangled configurations. For systems involving photons, we identify the specific polarizations of incoming light that maximize this fidelity and derive an explicit formula for it. These findings are validated through a table of optimal fidelities and corresponding optimal analysis light polarizations for various input states, which were generated using our numerical simulation method. We also present experimental data confirming these results for specific input polarizations. The reported fidelities align with theoretical predictions within experimental uncertainty, thereby demonstrating the efficacy of our approach. Ultimately, this framework is essential for establishing the necessary conditions to verify the entanglement nature of any two-qubit system. Furthermore, it is particularly valuable for optical quantum computing, as it enables the precise analysis of entangled states produced during gate operations. This facilitates the identification of optimal input analysis light polarizations, thereby enhancing the fidelity of the resulting entangled states. Consequently, our results provide a foundation for the development of future entangled optical quantum computers. *Keywords:* entanglement, quantum computing, GHZ states, W states, optical quantum computing, input analysis light polarization, quantum gates. *Abbreviated Title:* Optical entanglement assessment. *Corresponding author:* Dr. Alexander V. This study details the characteristics of 3/2 Palm Tree Modes (PTMs) observed in the JET tokamak, detailing their discovery and explaining their source and genesis. During the 2007/08 refill period, JET utilized a mixed deuterium/tritium (D/T) fuel mixture. PTMs emerged in edge plasma profiles characterized by significant D/T asymmetries, exhibiting both toroidal and poloidal mode numbers of n=3/2. These modes were detected via neutral particle imaging systems, which revealed a distinct toroidal asymmetry in neutral density. The analysis indicates that the PTM's toroidal mode number results from the superposition of two 1/2 modes with opposite poloidal rotation directions. The PTM's growth rate is primarily governed by the local deuterium concentration gradient, while its radial localization is dictated by the deuterium source position. Furthermore, PTMs can be interpreted as a form of neutral deuterium fueling, with the neutral density asymmetry representing the radial distribution of the deuterium fuel. This mechanism is particularly relevant for tokamaks employing neutral deuterium pellet fueling. Additionally, PTMs can be excited via neutral deuterium beam injection, where the growth rate is regulated by the beam's neutral deuterium concentration. This research establishes a framework for understanding PTM behavior and offers a potential method for controlling edge localized modes (ELMs). Ultimately, this study provides a foundational understanding of palm tree oscillations. (A video of the PTM is available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4222222222). Continual learning (CL) aims to master a sequence of tasks over time while retaining prior knowledge. Recently, CL has gained significant traction, with numerous studies exploring the use of pretrained models as effective strategies for mitigating catastrophic forgetting. These approaches yield state-of-the-art results, particularly when pretrained on ImageNet. However, we argue that their superior performance in many cases stems not from their CL techniques, but from their reliance on specific ImageNet-derived evaluation protocols. To investigate this, we introduce a straightforward baseline that challenges the necessity and universality of such pretrained models. Our method rivals or exceeds the performance of advanced CL approaches that utilize pretrained models. We attribute this success to two key factors: first, our baseline demonstrates robustness across both ImageNet-based and from-scratch evaluation protocols; second, our pretrained models are sourced from non-image domains, thereby questioning the generalizability of current trends in applying pretrained models to continual learning. This study addresses the challenge of identifying hate speech across multiple social media platforms by utilizing their textual content, images, and hashtags. This study examines how topological heterogeneity influences the synchronization of integrate-and-fire neurons connected via random directed and undirected topologies. We demonstrate that in degree-heterogeneous networks, the onset of global spiking activity is governed by the second largest eigenvalue of the interaction matrix, which can be approximated using the moment-closure method. Furthermore, we find that both the emergence and termination of spiking states are driven by bifurcations occurring at the average coupling strength, regardless of whether the network's degree distribution is heterogeneous. These theoretical predictions are supported by numerical simulations. These findings indicate that the theoretical frameworks developed for homogeneous networks remain applicable to topologically heterogeneous systems. Additionally, the results provide a basis for understanding how neuronal network topology affects the generation of collective oscillations. Finally, we outline how these conclusions can be extended to more complex networks. The code used in this study is available at: https://github.com/alejandro-garcia/degree-heterogeneous-networks. Automated Program Repair (APR) has garnered significant research interest in recent years. While existing APR tools predominantly rely on syntactic methods, they frequently fail to generate correct patches for bugs involving complex control flow. To address this, we introduce Antagonistic Patch Creation (APC), a novel technique that automatically generates antagonistic patches to fix control flow-dependent bugs. An antagonistic patch is defined as one that produces the opposite of a pre-existing patch for a given bug; for instance, if a pre patch causes the expression `a + b` to evaluate to 5, an antagonistic patch would cause it to evaluate to 7. We present a systematic approach for APC and have integrated it into a new tool named APCoRnER. Experimental results demonstrate that APCoRnER successfully fixes 18 bugs that were previously unresolved by existing APR techniques. Furthermore, we find that APCoRnER enhances the performance of all other APR methods tested. The APCoRnER tool and its dataset are accessible at https://github.com/abhishekkumar1234/APCORNER. A detailed description of the methodology and additional details can be found in our paper at ASE'21. Our source code is also available on GitHub at https://github.com/abhishekkumar1234/APCORNER. The ability to generate diverse quantum data spectra serves as a valuable tool for investigating data-dependent quantum information processing tasks. This paper demonstrates that the capability region—the set of achievable data spectra—of graphs states can be defined by the convex hull of elementary operations, specifically quantum rotations and quantum deletions. This finding offers a method for characterizing the capability region of any graph state, provided its maximum degree is known. Furthermore, this study establishes that the proposed operations are both necessary and sufficient for generating the entire capability region, thereby resolving an open question posed in our previous work. We also examine the entanglement structure of states arising from these elementary operations and their potential application in designing states with long-range multipartite entanglement. Additionally, we address the issue of target state alignment, showing that graphs can be aligned using an optimal number of deletions equal to the minimum graph cut size. Finally, we outline future research directions, including the development of data-driven quantum algorithms and the application of data spectrum theory to other graph states. This work is based on the research presented in [1].

We present a new 3-dimensional flow analysis technique designed to investigate the nuclear equation of state (EoS) and collision dynamics. This method utilizes the complete 3-dimensional flow field, derived from the initial and final positions of individual participants, to extract the bulk EoS coefficient, $c_s^2 = \partial P/\partial\epsilon$, and the shear EoS coefficient, $c_s^2_s = \epsilon(dP/d\epsilon)$. The collision dynamics are quantified by the dynamic viscosity, $\eta$, and the Prandtl number, $Pr = \eta/\kappa$, where $\kappa$ represents the thermal conductivity. These coefficients are determined by comparing the 3-dimensional flow fields generated by different hydrodynamic models. The collision dynamics extracted via this analysis have been benchmarked against experimental data from the ALICE and STAR collaborations. Furthermore, the 3-dimensional flow field is modeled using a machine learning approach based on the STAR experiment. This novel 3-dimensional flow analysis offers a fresh perspective on hydrodynamic modeling and serves as a valuable tool for interpreting experimental results. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have recently demonstrated exceptional performance in wireless transmission systems, offering a pathway to surpass the limitations of conventional methods. However, applying GNNs to massive wireless networks remains difficult due to their reliance on a centralized adjacency matrix. To address this challenge, this paper introduces a distributed inference architecture for GNNs within wireless transmission systems. In this proposed framework, nodes collaboratively process a subset of the network's adjacency information to individually construct and utilize sub-matrices of the global GNN weight matrix. Consequently, nodes can independently perform GNN-based signal processing without requiring communication from other nodes. Wireless transmission systems are designed to support GNN-based processing through the implementation of broadcast channels. Simulation results indicate that the proposed architecture achieves performance comparable to a centralized system while offering superior scalability. Furthermore, this approach reduces computational complexity by enabling nodes to perform GNN-based signal processing in parallel. Notably, a node's computational load is determined solely by the size of its sub-matrix rather than the entire global matrix. Finally, the architecture supports flexible configuration of sub-matrix parameters to meet specific application requirements. Overall, this work provides a promising solution for implementing distributed GNN-based wireless transmission systems. Homicide rates in Brazil have historically been high, with recent data indicating further increases. This study analyzes the spatio-temporal distribution of homicides across the Brazilian province of Goiás, covering the period from 2002 to 2014. The province was selected due to its significant economic and political relevance within the nation. We applied a novel methodological approach that integrates several techniques to achieve a comprehensive analysis of the data. Our methodology involved dividing the province into 20 municipalities, calculating annual homicide counts for each, and subsequently analyzing the results using spatial and temporal statistics. Key methods included calculating local indicators of spatial association (LISA) for each municipality, conducting a temporal Cluster-Change-Cluster analysis on the time series, and performing a spatial Cluster-Change-Cluster analysis on the data grid. These methodological choices were driven by the need to identify spatial and temporal correlations, as well as shifts in homicide rates over time. The study's primary objective is to provide a detailed understanding of homicide distribution in the province to inform future policy interventions. Results indicate that homicides in Goiás are not evenly distributed; instead, they concentrate in specific municipalities, with rates rising in some areas and falling in others. These findings offer valuable insights for policymakers, particularly those in the province's government, to design effective public policies aimed at reducing the high prevalence of homicide in Brazil. Ultimately, this work contributes to the broader goal of achieving a safer society. The code used for the analysis is accessible at: https://github.com/rafael-oliveira/Cluster-Examination-of-Homicide-Rates-in-Goias. Furthermore, the study includes a Python-based application that allows users to visualize the analysis results interactively by selecting a specific year. This tool is available at: https://rafael-oliveira.github.io/Cluster-Examination-of-Homicide-Rates-in-Goias/. This paper investigates various strategies for accelerating stochastic gradient descent (SGD) by incorporating domain knowledge regarding issue and sound audio data. Specifically, we examine (i) how to utilize the statistical properties of issue data to adjust learning rates and (ii) how to exploit the non-issues trajectory to enhance learning speed. We assess these approaches across diverse speech enhancement tasks, including single-channel denoising and multi-channel dereverberation. Our findings indicate that integrating issue statistics into SGD is highly effective for single-channel denoising. Furthermore, we demonstrate that combining these methods yields additional acceleration benefits for multi-channel dereverberation tasks. The proposed algorithms are straightforward to implement and require no extra computational cost. Additionally, we introduce a unified framework for evaluating the performance of accelerated SGD. This framework relies on a single metric that simultaneously assesses both the accuracy and acceleration of the method. We show that this metric is strongly correlated with the actual acceleration achieved on specific tasks. Finally, we recommend this metric as a preliminary step for selecting accelerated SGD, as it enables rapid performance estimation without requiring extensive SGD runs. The entire codebase is made available to facilitate reproducibility. This work serves as a foundation for further research into developing sound-adaptive and sound-issue methods. Our approach is easily extensible to other machine learning applications, such as speech recognition and speech synthesis. The paper is structured as follows: Section II reviews SGD fundamentals; Section III details our proposed sound-adaptive SGD algorithms; Section IV presents experimental results across multiple speech enhancement tasks; and Section V concludes with a discussion on the related research community. The Sun's core is a primary target for particle physics research, with neutrinos produced by the pp chain and potential axion-like particles (ALPs) generated in the nuclear reaction p+p->d+e+nu being its main signatures. While solar neutrinos have been detected by experiments like Homestake, GALLEX, GNO, and Borexino, the signal from p+p->d+e+nu has not yet been observed. A promising method for detecting these ALPs is the axion helioscope experiment IAXO, which converts solar ALPs into X-rays within a magnetic field and observes them using a large mirror and camera. This study presents a proof-of-principle analysis of IAXO's sensitivity to the p+p->d+e+nu signal, demonstrating that the next-generation camera, BabyIAXO, could detect this signal within a few years of operation. This represents a significant advancement over current solar neutrino experiments. Additionally, the analysis explores the potential for distinguishing between p+p->d+e+nu and axion-like particle signals. Although the BabyIAXO exposure required to achieve a 90% confidence level for the p+p->d+e+nu signal is substantial, it remains feasible for IAXO. Consequently, IAXO will be capable of investigating the Sun's core through both neutrino and ALP channels. However, a future analysis will be necessary to determine whether a specific ALP model can be identified with a given IAXO exposure. This investigation will require examining the ALP signal's spectral and temporal characteristics, as well as its correlations with solar activity. Furthermore, the p+p->d+e+nu signal is expected to be visible with a few IAXO years of exposure, whereas a 90% confidence level detection of the p+p->d+e+nu signal may necessitate several decades of IAXO operation. This timeline could be shortened if the solar neutrino flux is confirmed by other experiments, such as the upcoming JUNO reactor neutrino experiment. Finally, this work is part of the IAXO Science Assessment Phase, and the findings will be further developed in upcoming IAXO proposals. This paper specifically addresses the sensitivity of BabyIAXO to the p+p->d+e+nu signal. We introduce a new class of self-exciting systems, extending beyond traditional self-exciting maps and systems. We establish the existence of chaotic invariant sets and investigate the characteristics of their associated dynamics. Furthermore, we provide a method for generating infinite families of these chaotic systems, which can be directly applied to create novel chaotic self-exciting systems across various scientific and engineering disciplines. Finally, we examine practical applications, including the design of new random number generators and random circuits. Specifically, we propose a new random circuit based on a chaotic self-exciting system and analyze its performance in terms of randomness quality and energy efficiency. Additionally, we explore the potential for developing new ultra-high sensitivity sensors within this category of self-exciting systems. This work represents the inaugural study in a series dedicated to developing this novel class of systems and their applications. Subsequent papers will address their design, analysis, and implementation. The proposed random circuits are expected to offer significant advantages over existing designs regarding cost, size, and energy consumption. Additionally, the new random number generators are anticipated to achieve higher precision and operate at faster speeds than current generators. Ultimately, the novel random circuits introduced herein are expected to find extensive application in the fields of physics and engineering. Robot dexterous manipulation is a critical capability for future autonomous systems. To facilitate research in this domain, there is a growing need for large-scale, high-quality grasp datasets. While existing public datasets are primarily derived from real-world environments, they are limited by the time and labor required for data collection, resulting in insufficient data volume. This paper introduces DexGraspNet, a high-quality, large-scale robotic dexterous grasp dataset generated via a high-fidelity simulation environment. We demonstrate that a public object dataset can be automatically annotated with diverse and challenging grasps using a novel algorithm. Furthermore, we show that existing robotic grasp policies can achieve strong generalization performance on DexGraspNet without any fine-tuning. Our dataset comprises 1.2 million three-fingered and 1.2 million two-fingered grasps across 1,000 objects, with each grasp featuring 12 degrees of freedom. The source code and data are available at https://github.com/robinzhou/dexgraspnet. This work aims to provide a high-quality, large-scale, cost-effective, and scalable simulation-based grasp dataset to advance robotic dexterous manipulation. Additionally, we release a baseline model trained on DexGraspNet to support fair comparisons for subsequent research. Our experiments indicate that policies trained on DexGraspNet generalize effectively to unseen objects and real-world settings. The paper details the dataset's quality, scale, and generation process, while also exploring and comparing several robotic grasp policies. We hope DexGraspNet will significantly contribute to the advancement of robotic dexterous manipulation. Our website is located at https://dexgrasenet.github.io/. This study introduces a free-breathing, 4D (3D plus respiration) body MRI sequence utilizing a turbo spin-echo with variable echo time (TE) and trajectory (4D-TSETV) method. The process begins with a free-breathing 3D T2-weighted turbo spin-echo scan that samples each line of k-space at a distinct echo time. Following this, a breathing trace is recorded, and the 3D data is sorted into respiratory phases. For each phase, the k-space is reorganized into concentric rings to generate images. These 4D images are then used to reconstruct a time-resolved series of k-space trajectories. The resulting 4D-T2* sequence images are demonstrated to be free of flow artifacts and show superior tissue contrast compared to both the 3D and 4D-TSETV methods. Furthermore, the contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR) of the 4D-T2* sequence is comparable to that of a reference 2D turbo spin-echo with TE variation (2D-TSETV) sequence. Additionally, the 4D-T2* sequence achieves a scan time approximately 1.5 times shorter than the 3D-TSETV approach. In conclusion, the 4D-T2* sequence offers enhanced tissue contrast, reduced scan time, and the absence of flow artifacts, making it a promising technique for 4D body MRI. This is particularly advantageous for patients with high heart rates or arrhythmias, as it eliminates the need for breath-holding. Future research will explore the application of these 4D-T2* images in tumor segmentation and respiratory motion correction. (Image Reconogition in Medicine, 2019; 19: 100470). Model compression is essential for deploying deep neural networks on resource-constrained devices. While knowledge distillation has emerged as a leading compression strategy, it often disrupts the original data flow of student networks, resulting in a significant loss of information and performance. To address this, we introduce a data flow-preserving knowledge distillation method that maintains the student network's pre-distillation data flow, thereby retaining more information. Our approach involves three key contributions: first, we present a weight-preserving structure designed to retain the weights of specific layers during distillation; second, we propose a weight-mapping module that projects the distillation weights onto the original weights of certain layers; third, experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves superior accuracy compared to existing state-of-the-art distillation techniques across various datasets. The shift from static to adaptive data collection has significantly influenced learning theory, particularly regarding generalization bounds. A prevalent technique involves adaptively sampling points to maximize the empirical training loss. Previous research established a gap of $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ between the generalization errors of adaptive and non-adaptive learning, yet this result was limited to linear regression with squared loss. This study advances the state of the art by demonstrating that the gap can be reduced to $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ for linear regression and extended to $\Omega(\sqrt{n})$ for logistic regression. Furthermore, we introduce CountSketch as a new, efficient algorithm for both linear and logistic regression, matching the generalization performance of non-adaptive methods while reducing the dependence on dimensionality from $O(n)$ to $O(\text{poly}(\log n))$. These findings are supported by both information-theoretic lower bounds and high-probability upper bounds. Additionally, we illustrate the practical efficacy of CountSketch through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets. We present ipie, a Python-based auxiliary-field quantum Monte Carlo (AFQMC) software designed for many-electron systems. The project was initiated to develop a versatile, straightforward, and efficient code capable of running on both CPU and GPU architectures. This work outlines the principles behind ipie, emphasizing its flexibility, effectiveness, and performance. The core functionality is implemented in Python, while GPU-specific components are written in CUDA. To demonstrate its capabilities, we apply ipie to various electronic structure problems, including the helium atom, the uniform electron gas, and the hydrogen molecule. Our AFQMC approach utilizes a novel combination of the stochastic optimization method, the walk ratio estimator, and the fixed-node (FN) estimator. The stochastic optimization technique enables the direct calculation of accurate many-body wave functions for ground and low-lying excited states. By employing the walk ratio estimator, we achieve a linear scaling relationship between computational cost and electron count. Additionally, the FN estimator ensures that the cost per electron remains independent of the number of electrons. We have established a comprehensive suite of unit tests and established a standardized workflow for wave function optimization, FN estimation, and data analysis. Furthermore, we have implemented a variety of control mechanisms to monitor and regulate the optimization process. These features facilitate the rapid development of new capabilities and the deployment of high-performance AFQMC simulations. The ipie code is accessible at https://github.com/iee-group/ipie. Data distillation involves training a single model on a curated subset of data to replicate the performance of a much larger collection. While recent research has primarily focused on distilling generative models for specific tasks like summarization and translation, the goal of abstractive condensation remains to generate an equivalent model for the entire dataset. This study introduces a new algorithm, Active BEntity discovery for Abstractive Condensation (ABAC), which utilizes an acquired entity prompt discovery model to identify the most representative examples for the full dataset. Our proposed method was validated using summary data from the ColossalText corpus. The results demonstrate that our approach successfully distilled the entire corpus with state-of-the-art efficiency, achieving a distillation ratio of 1:100 while maintaining the same summary F1 score as a model trained on the full corpus. Furthermore, our generated models outperform strong baselines, such as Pegasus and T5, under the same memory constraints. Additionally, we present novel analyses that reveal the novel discovery capabilities of our model. Finally, we have made the code and models for ABAC publicly available. This paper investigates internal differentiability within nonstandard set theory and nonstandard analysis, employing a natural extension of the partial derivative concept for multivariate functions. Based on the nonstandard characterization of classical differentiable functions, we derive an higher-order differentiability criterion: if $f$ and $g$ are $n$ and $(n-1)$-dimensional internally partially differentiable functions respectively, and $f$ satisfies certain conditions, then $f$ is a differentiable function. Furthermore, we establish a classical equivalent for this higher-order differentiability, demonstrating that it constitutes a necessary and sufficient condition for differentiability. We also provide examples illustrating that this condition cannot be weakened. Additionally, we present illustrative examples of functions that are differentiable and partially differentiable, yet not continuously differentiable. These findings facilitate the design of efficient algorithms for computing higher-order partial derivatives. The proposed criterion may find applications in nonstandard analysis, the theory of fuzzy numbers, and stochastic processes. As an application, we demonstrate that the stochastic process derived from a $C^{\infty}$ function via the "different function deduced by the $n$-dimensional function" possesses a finite order of differentiability, which is lower than that of the original function. This result offers a new approach to calculating the Wiener integrals of the original function and the derived stochastic process. We anticipate that this work will contribute to the advancement of nonstandard stochastic analysis. This paper introduces a new performance metric designed to assess vocal entrainment within dialogic contexts. Entrainment refers to the alignment of behavior between interacting individuals, which can be observed in speech through the matching of vocal qualities like pitch and formant frequencies. While prior research has evaluated entrainment in dyadic interactions using statistical correlations, these methods often overlook the time-sensitive and context-dependent nature of vocal behaviors, rendering them less effective for understanding the dynamics of human-human communication. To address these limitations, we developed a novel computational approach based on phase-locking value (PLV), a technique originally developed for analyzing electroencephalogram (EEG) data in neuroscience. We applied this method to evaluate entrainment in simulated dialogic scenarios involving simulated humans. Our findings indicate that the PLV-based approach is both sensitive and reliable for detecting entrainment in dyadic communications, demonstrating superior performance compared to traditional statistical methods. This suggests that PLV-based evaluation is a robust solution for analyzing the dynamics of human communication. This study addresses a Stokes variational inequality arising in glaciology, characterized by a degenerate, semicoercive mobility function dependent on the solution. We establish sufficient conditions for the well-posedness of the problem and derive error estimates using finite element methods. Specifically, we demonstrate that the discrete solution converges to the continuous solution at a suboptimal rate within the energy norm. Furthermore, we propose a straightforward augmented Lagrangian approach, showing that this method yields optimal convergence rates for a discrete saddle point problem against the variational inequality. Finally, we present numerical results that validate our theoretical findings. Notably, these conclusions are derived without relying on any specific a priori assumptions regarding the solution. Additionally, we confirm that our error estimates remain valid for a broader class of mobility functions, including those with Lipschitz continuity. The proposed strategy is also applicable to general Stokes variational inequalities featuring degenerate mobility. The entire analysis is conducted in two dimensions, with direct extension to higher dimensions being straightforward. However, numerical experiments conducted in three dimensions suggest that our theoretical error estimates may not be sharp in that context. This discrepancy likely stems from regularity issues inherent in three-dimensional domains with corners, which are not accounted for in our current approach. To address this, we propose an alternative strategy for estimating errors in three-dimensional settings. This new approach requires no a priori regularity assumptions and is applicable to any domain. Nevertheless, it results in nonconforming finite elements, introducing a novel source of error that complicates the determination of convergence rates. Consequently, while we can prove well-posedness for the discrete saddle point problem, we are unable to derive any error estimates. We conclude by discussing potential avenues for future research. We report on DUVET (Dust and UV Emission from the Veil of an Outflow Trace), a 1.5-hour JWST observation of the nearby starburst galaxy Mrk 259. This observation targets the bright outflow identified in prior JWST NIRCam imaging, which exhibits a two-sided, collimated structure extending 1.5 kpc from the nuclear region. By analyzing Mrk 259's outflow, we aim to elucidate the mechanisms driving and containing star formation in starburst galaxies. We present a multi-wavelength study of the outflow's morphology and spatial extent, integrating JWST NIRCam and NIRSpec data with existing HST and ground-based observations. Our investigation reveals that the outflow penetrates the galaxy's central star-forming region, extending 1.5 kpc from the center. We detect a 1.2 kpc-long collimated outflow with a full opening angle of approximately 10 degrees, originating from the star-forming core and driven by a star-forming region roughly 100 pc in diameter. The outflow's leading edge is obscured by a prominent dust veil, which is also responsible for the galaxy's significant extinction. JWST NIRSpec observations identify a star-forming region at the tail of the outflow's western side, suggesting that the outflow may be suppressing star formation in this area. Furthermore, we detect a compact, bright nuclear starburst region at the outflow's base, which appears to be the origin of the gas inflow feeding the outflow's head. These findings suggest that the outflow is actively shaping the galaxy's star formation history. Our results indicate that JWST can detect and characterize galactic outflows in nearby star-forming galaxies, offering a new perspective on the feedback mechanisms between stars, gas, and dust. This study underscores the necessity of observing outflow heads and tails to fully understand their impact on star formation. Finally, we demonstrate that JWST's high spatial resolution enables the study of star-gas feedback in star-forming galaxies at kiloparsec scales. These results highlight the need for future JWST observations of similar starburst galaxies to further investigate the feedback processes inherent in these systems. This paper introduces a new, integrated approach for simultaneously designing and controlling a robot that climbs its own structure. Unlike previous methods, which address design and control as separate optimization problems, this study employs a unified optimization framework to generate a feasible climbing structure and determine the necessary joint actuation forces simultaneously. The study presents two distinct optimization formulations: the first minimizes the total actuation force required for the climber, while the second prioritizes maximizing the angle of attack. Both models are formulated as non-linear mixed-integer programs. To address the non-convexity of these problems, the authors apply a linear convex hull approximation for the angle of attack constraint and utilize a specialized branch-and-cut algorithm for handling angle of attack variables. Furthermore, a novel algorithm is developed to efficiently manage the large number of binary variables needed to model the equilibrium constraints. The paper concludes by reporting results from a numerical study. Additionally, the work features a video documenting a successful experimental test where a climber ascends the designed structure. The results demonstrate that the proposed optimization method can produce structures enabling efficient climbing, while also highlighting the method's limitations and potential avenues for future research. Finally, the paper outlines how this optimization approach can be extended to design structures capable of supporting multiple climbers. Kendall's tau serves as a nonparametric metric for correlation, offering robustness against outliers and alignment in time series. However, performing statistical inference on this metric is challenging due to the non-Gaussian nature of its sampling distribution. This difficulty is particularly pronounced in time series contexts, where the statistic suffers from a significant loss of efficiency compared to Pearson's correlation. This paper introduces a finite-sample bias-corrected estimator designed to mitigate the non-Gaussian bias. We establish the asymptotic normality of this corrected estimator and develop a multiple testing procedure to control the false discovery rate. Through simulations, we demonstrate that our procedure maintains the desired false discovery rate while exhibiting superior power relative to existing methods. Furthermore, we apply the procedure to financial data to analyze the relationship between market returns and various factors. The implementation is accessible via the {\tt ktau} R package. The rise of autonomous driving and intelligent transportation systems has created a demand for distributed edge intelligence, where vehicles collaboratively learn from data residing on individual devices. However, this approach risks exposing sensitive user information, such as personal habits and biometric traits. To address this vulnerability, we introduce a unified framework designed to safeguard privacy within edge intelligence for vehicular networks by utilizing modern cryptographic techniques. Our method enables vehicles to train models on locally stored data while ensuring that no individual user can be identified. We validate the framework's efficacy through a concrete implementation that supports both model inversion attacks and traitor inference attacks, demonstrating its ability to neutralize these threats. Furthermore, we assess the computational overhead and communication costs, proving that the proposed solution remains practical for deployment in vehicular environments. Finally, we compare our cryptographic-based approach with existing non-cryptographic methods found in the literature, highlighting the advantages of our proposed framework. The complete code is publicly accessible at \url{https://github.com/AmirHajimorad/PP-EEI}. Additionally, supplementary code required to replicate the comparison with non-cryptographic schemes from prior work can be requested from the corresponding author. \textit{Index Terms—} Vehicular Networks, Edge Intelligence, Privacy, Cryptography, Deep Learning.

This paper introduces a novel pivot simplex approach for linear programming, building upon the framework established in our prior work. That earlier study established the algorithm, demonstrated its termination properties, and proved that the objective function is minimized upon completion. The method employs a new criterion for selecting the entering variable, which is shown to be polynomial in nature. This research focuses on identifying the algorithm's limiting linear iteration count as functions of specific problem data. The primary findings are as follows: 1) For any standard-form problem with a parameter $k$, the pivot simplex algorithm requires no more than $k$ iterations to transition from infeasible to feasible, and at most $k+m-p$ iterations to reach optimality, where $m$ represents the number of variables and $p$ the number of constraints. 2) For a problem with parameter $k$, the pivot simplex method is bounded by no more than $k^2$ iterations to achieve a feasible solution, and at most $k^2+m-p$ iterations for optimality. 3) In a problem with parameter $k$, the pivot simplex method is limited by no more than $k^3$ iterations to reach a feasible solution, and at most $k^3+m-p$ iterations for optimality. These results are derived through the analysis of pivot sequences. Furthermore, the paper examines the pivot simplex method's performance on dual pairs of problems, providing specific examples to illustrate these findings. Finally, the authors propose several open questions for future investigation. The methodology presented here is applicable to all standard-form problems. Additionally, the results are extendable to non-degenerate problems and those satisfying the conditions outlined in [1]. For a commutative ring $R$, let $K_n(R)$ denote the $n$-th algebraic $K$-theory group of $R$. When $R$ is a graded ring, these groups acquire a natural structure as graded abelian groups. In 1985, Bak demonstrated that for any commutative ring $R$, the graded $K$-theory groups $\bigoplus_{n\ge 1}K_n(R)$ carry an indeterminate $\mathbb Z[{\varepsilon}_1,{\varepsilon}_2,\ldots]$-module structure, where the generators ${\varepsilon}_n$ correspond to $K_1(\mathbb Z[{\mathrm{tr}}_n])$, with ${\mathrm{tr}}_n$ being the standard $n\times n$ matrix with a single entry of $1$. This paper extends Bak's result to the context of graded rings, proving that $\bigoplus_{n\ge 1}NK_1(R)$, for a graded ring $R$, is an $\mathbb Z[{\varepsilon}_1,{\varepsilon}_2,\ldots]$-module. As a specific application, we examine the case where $R$ is the projective general linear modular group ${\mathrm{PGL}}_2(R)$ for a graded ring $R$, thereby deriving a structure theorem for ${\mathrm{NK}}_1({\mathrm{PGL}}_2(R))$. This result generalizes findings by Bak, Birman, and Reiner, as well as those by van der Kallen. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ${\mathrm{NK}}_1({\mathrm{PGL}}_2(R))$ is also an ${\varepsilon}_1}$-module. These findings provide insight into the structure of ${\mathrm{NK}}_1({\mathrm{PGL}}_2(R))$ for various specific graded rings $R$. Additionally, our result offers a more precise understanding of the map ${\mathrm{NK}}_1({\mathrm{PGL}}_2(R))\to{\mathrm{NK}}_1({\mathrm{PGL}}_2(R/{\mathfrak m}))$, where ${\mathfrak m}$ represents a homogeneous maximal graded ideal of $R$. This map is an additive group homomorphism, and we elucidate its kernel and image.

This study examines how off-shell effects and background uncertainties impact the Higgs boson mass determination within ttH events, utilizing a boosted decision tree approach. The analysis employs D0 and CMS data, alongside a simulation based on the MADGRAPH5_AOMP and HERWIG6 parton shower generators. Uncertainties arising from integrated luminosity, parton distribution functions, and the shower generator HERWIG6 were also evaluated. Results indicate that the primary source of uncertainty is the background, followed by uncertainties in the luminosity and parton distribution functions. Furthermore, we observe that off-shell contributions significantly influence the extraction of the top quark mass. Finally, we explore potential strategies to mitigate these background uncertainties. These findings are particularly relevant for the future extraction of the Higgs boson mass from LHC data. Additionally, the derived top quark mass value of 172.5 GeV is consistent with recent experimental measurements from the Tevatron and LHC. Our analysis confirms that background uncertainties remain the main limiting factor for the precision of Higgs mass extraction in ttH events. To address this, we propose an alternative method for Higgs mass extraction that utilizes the kinematic properties of the top quark decay products. This approach offers the potential to reduce background uncertainties and enhance the precision of Higgs mass measurements in the future. Our findings suggest that this novel technique could substantially improve the accuracy of Higgs mass extraction from ttH events. Parallel Evolutionary Algorithms (EAs) are frequently employed to accelerate solution searches, yet they often suffer from communication and synchronization bottlenecks that hinder scalability. To address this, multi-objective parallel EAs have been introduced, utilizing multiple independent sub-populations to find solutions concurrently. However, asynchronous variants of these algorithms were subsequently developed to eliminate synchronization overhead, thereby enhancing computational efficiency. Despite this improvement, a critical issue emerged where sub-populations generated with lower computational costs were consistently outperformed by those produced with higher costs, significantly compromising result quality. This phenomenon stems from evaluation time bias, a well-documented challenge in asynchronous parallel multi-objective EAs. To resolve this, a novel parent selection mechanism is proposed, designed to mitigate evaluation time bias by incorporating frequency information. This mechanism enables the algorithm to select high-quality sub-populations without relying on evaluations based solely on raw fitness. Additionally, the method is shown to be general and compatible with various existing asynchronous parallel multi-objective EAs. We investigate the oscillating $\mathcal{L}$-dynamics of a density matrix $\rho(t)$ governed by a Lindblad generator $\mathcal{L}(t) = e^{i\omega t}\mathcal{L}_1 + e^{-i\omega t}\mathcal{L}_2$, where $\omega$ represents a rapid oscillation frequency. Our primary finding is that, under the condition that the total evolution time $T$ satisfies $T \gg 1/\omega$, the dynamics can be characterized by an averaged generator $\bar{\mathcal{L}} = \tfrac{1}{2}(\mathcal{L}_1 + \mathcal{L}_2)$ alongside a correction operator $\tilde{\mathcal{L}} = \tfrac{1}{\omega}[\mathcal{L}_1, \mathcal{L}_2]$. This approximation holds up to an error of order $O(\omega^{-2})$. Furthermore, we derive high-rate series expansions for the propagator $U(t)$ associated with this problem. These expansions are demonstrated through examples involving two-level systems and qubits. Additionally, we address the case of finite evolution times and examine the convergence of our series expansions. Our methodology is grounded in techniques from adiabatic and van Vleck-type theories. Finally, we explore applications within driven quantum systems and propose a numerical algorithm based on our results. Notably, our approach remains valid without requiring the traditional adiabaticity assumption. Finally, we highlight that the derived expansions for $U(t)$ can be derived from those proposed by P. M. Dirac in his 1928 paper. These findings may find application in various fields, including the analysis of quantum control and optimization algorithms. Specifically, our results can be utilized to derive higher-order corrections to the average generator $\bar{\mathcal{L}}$ for open quantum systems. In the context of quantum control, these expansions enable the construction of quantum propagators that more accurately approximate the exact time-evolution operator. Moreover, in quantum optimization, these expansions facilitate the design of pulses that more closely resemble idealized control pulses. Our work also contributes to the development of quantum simulators for simulating open quantum systems. Our high-rate expansions for the quantum propagator $U(t)$ are applicable to the design of quantum simulators, offering an alternative to the recent rotating wave approximation. The $f$-electron Ce $4f$ shell in the rhodium-doped compound CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_x$ (where $x$ equals 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3) undergoes a transition from a paramagnetic state to a ferromagnetic one. This transition is accompanied by a significant reduction in the neutron depolarization rate, which drops from 100 parts per million (ppm) in CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_{0.1}$ to 10 ppm in CePd$_{1-x}$Rh$_{0.3}$. This decrease in depolarization correlates with the evolution of the material's magnetic structure, shifting from a sinusoidal pattern to a more complex arrangement. The observed behavior is attributed to the solidification of the neutron spin within the increasingly intricate magnetic environment. This phenomenon is examined in relation to the neutron depolarization rate and the specific characteristics of the magnetic structures. Additionally, the study investigates the impact of the neutron wavelength on this process. These findings are expected to be applicable to other ferromagnetic materials that exhibit complex magnetic configurations. Measuring mixing and CP violation in particle decays offers deep insights into the fundamental properties of matter. This study reports on the measurement of the mixing-induced CP-violating phase, denoted as $\phi_{\rm s}$, within the $B^+_{{\rm s}}\to J/\psi\pi^+\pi^-$ decay. Utilizing proton-proton collision data with a total integrated luminosity of 3 ab$^{-1}$ from the LHCb detector, we derive a mixing fraction of $p_{\rm cc}/(p_{\rm cc}+q_{\rm\bar{cc}}) = 0.531\pm0.005\pm0.002$ and determine $\phi_{\rm s} = 0.032\pm0.016\pm0.007$ rad. The first uncertainty represents the statistical component, the second is systematic, and the third arises from external inputs. These findings align with the Standard Model prediction. Additionally, we present a measurement of the direct CP-violating asymmetry in this channel, finding $A^{\rm dir}_{\rm\rm\phi s} = -0.002\pm0.012\pm0.004$; this result is consistent with zero and shows no evidence of direct CP violation. These outcomes are based on a sample of $10^5$ reconstructed signal events. Furthermore, we report the results of a global fit incorporating LHCb data alongside previous measurements from Belle and BaBar experiments. The fitted values are $\phi_{\rm s} = 0.029\pm0.005\pm0.004$ rad and $A^{\rm dir}_{\rm\phi s} = -0.010\pm0.004\pm0.002$, with the first uncertainties being statistical and the second systematic. Both measurements are consistent with the Standard Model expectations of $\phi_{\rm s} = 0$ and $A^{\rm dir}_{\rm\phi s} = 0$. The combined uncertainties represent an improvement of a factor of two over prior measurements. Deep neural networks are widely recognized for their exceptional image recognition capabilities, yet training these networks requires substantial amounts of labeled data. Conversely, deep models can be trained with significantly less labeled data by leveraging transfer learning from networks pre-trained on vast labeled datasets. This study evaluates various deep neural network transfer strategies for image recognition. We evaluate multiple approaches, including fine-tuning, feature extraction, and intermediate layer transfer, across several source target domains. Our findings indicate that transfer learning offers a significant advantage in training convolutional neural networks for image recognition tasks when labeled data is scarce. Furthermore, we observe that fine-tuning yields the highest performance gains, followed by feature extraction and intermediate layer transfer. Additionally, we demonstrate that transfer learning is most beneficial for tasks distant from the source, such as recognizing animal species. Finally, we illustrate that transfer learning can be effectively applied in few-shot learning scenarios involving only a handful of labeled examples. This research offers a comprehensive overview of transfer learning for image recognition and deep neural network classifiers. Furthermore, it provides a robust foundation for future few-shot learning endeavors and aids practitioners in selecting the most appropriate deep neural network transfer method for their specific tasks. The accompanying code repository includes a comprehensive suite of image recognition experiments and a library of deep neural network transfer learning implementations. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as a leading machine learning approach for processing graph data, yet their internal mechanisms remain largely opaque. This lack of interpretability hinders the ability to explain model decisions, a critical factor in high-stakes domains like healthcare and criminal justice. To address this, the paper introduces the Parameterized Interpreter (PI), a framework designed to extract human-interpretable parameters from trained GNNs. These parameters capture the behavior of individual network components, offering a novel method for interpreting graph-based models. The effectiveness of PI is validated through various case studies, including graph classification, node classification, and graph generation tasks. Additionally, empirical evaluations on real-world medical and legal datasets demonstrate that PI achieves a strong balance between interpretability and accuracy. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar2000/Parameterized-Interpreter. The full article can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.01001.

The galaxy cluster RXCJ0232.2-4420 is identified as a merging system containing a substructure at its northern edge. This study investigates the properties of this substructure using Chandra X-ray data, archival Hubble Space Telescope images, and new deep imaging from the VISTA survey. We determined the substructure's position, temperature, and density profile, finding it to be a massive entity with a mass of $M_{500} = 1.1 \times 10^{14} M_{\odot}$. Its projected separation from the main cluster is 1.1 Mpc. We propose that the substructure consists of a group of galaxies, supported by the presence of a luminous red galaxy and a group of galaxies within 100 kpc. Additionally, we identified a galaxy group at a distance of 1.5 Mpc from the cluster center, which may represent another substructure. We also detected a possible galaxy group at 1.3 Mpc from the center, though its membership remains uncertain. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the cluster's dynamical state. Legendre Memory Module (LMM) is a recently introduced memory architecture designed to enhance Transformer performance through efficient, high-capacity, and parameter-agnostic memory banks. Despite its effectiveness, training LMM remains computationally intensive, creating a significant barrier to entry. This work addresses that hurdle by introducing a parallel training framework that leverages multi-GPU computing. The proposed method demonstrates substantial speedups, achieving a 3.5x improvement over single-GPU training on large models. Furthermore, the approach scales effectively across multiple GPUs, with models of varying sizes exhibiting near-perfect efficiency. Additionally, the framework supports mixed-precision (FP16) training, which lowers memory requirements and further accelerates the process. Experimental results indicate minimal accuracy loss when compared to single-GPU baselines. The implementation is publicly accessible at https://github.com/DeepPulseAI/Parallel-LMM-Training. This project was developed in collaboration with DeepPulse AI.

Weakly interacting particles represent a promising candidate for dark matter. This discussion outlines the fundamental properties of these particles, the primary theoretical models involving them, and the principal experimental methods used to detect them. It also examines the current experimental landscape, including the challenges and prospects associated with this search. Finally, the potential implications of discovering dark matter are explored, highlighting how they could illuminate the nature of particle physics and cosmology.
