The global fire season exhibits significant spatial and temporal variability, driven by the interplay of climatic and fuel conditions. While numerous studies have examined individual components of this system, such as fire intensity, fuel characteristics, or climate and weather patterns, there remains a notable lack of research on the relationships between them. This study introduces a novel Worldwide Fire Season Intensity (WFSI) metric, which quantifies the total fire intensity across an entire season. We demonstrate that WFSI is strongly correlated with seasonal temperature and precipitation, as well as fuel loads, and that these correlations vary consistently across different regions. Furthermore, we show that WFSI can be predicted with high accuracy using machine learning techniques, including linear regression, support vector machines, and random forests. These findings suggest that WFSI serves as a valuable metric for both characterizing and forecasting fire intensity on a worldwide scale. Additionally, we explore the potential of WFSI to enhance fire risk assessment and support fire management strategies. Finally, we outline how this approach can be applied to other fire-related metrics, such as fire frequency and fuel consumption rates. This study investigates the validity of corpus-derived metrics for assessing morphological complexity in human language. We evaluated five existing metrics using data from 67 languages spanning diverse families and geographic regions. Our analysis revealed a strong correlation among the five, allowing us to propose a unified "Corpus-based Measure of Morphological Complexity" (CMM-C). Furthermore, we examined the relationship between these metrics and established cross-linguistic indicators of complexity, including the Morphy score and the count of non-inflectional morphemes. Results indicate a positive correlation between these traditional measures and the new corpus-based metric. Finally, we validated CMM-C by demonstrating its alignment with prior typological findings on language complexity and its predictive power regarding language learning speed in bilinguals. We conclude that corpus-based metrics offer a promising new framework for researching typological variation and language acquisition. The code and resources required to replicate this study are available at https://github.com/alexpotts1992/quantifying-morphological-complexity.

We investigate the potential of gravitational lensing within galaxy clusters to set constraints on self-interacting dark matter (SIDM). By employing a state-of-the-art lens model of the Coma Cluster, we identify numerous lensed arcs situated within the cluster's dark matter halo. Our analysis demonstrates that a constant cross-section model with $\sigma/m = 1\,\mathrm{cm^2/g}$ fails to reproduce the observed arc positions and shapes, as it produces a halo that is excessively compact. Conversely, models featuring a velocity-dependent cross-section are able to recover the lens model's mass distribution. This finding underscores the critical role of lens modeling in limiting SIDM parameters and reinforces the necessity of high-resolution arc observations for future galaxy clusters to further constrain the physics of self-interacting dark matter. These results are based on data from the Hubble Space Telescope and the Atacama Large Millimeter Array. The identified gravitationally lensed sources could serve as valuable probes for upcoming observatories, such as the James Webb Space Telescope and the Square Kilometre Array. In display advertising, bidding for impressions is a critical decision that directly impacts campaign performance. This performance is typically evaluated using a conversion-based metric, such as cost-per-click (CPC) or cost-per-action (CPA), which incorporates the value of each conversion. However, real-world bidding is constrained by a budget, requiring advertisers to balance their offers to ensure it is spent efficiently. This paper introduces ARCB, a novel adaptive bidding algorithm designed to maximize expected conversion value within a given budget. We provide a theoretical analysis of ARCB's regret and budget excess, demonstrating that it achieves optimal convergence rates in the limit of large budgets. Furthermore, we validate our theoretical findings through experiments on bidding data from a leading advertising platform. These results indicate that ARCB surpasses existing state-of-the-art bidding strategies. Additionally, we explore how to adapt ARCB for scenarios where advertiser valuations for conversions vary over time. This leads to the development of ARCB-V, which also proves to be optimal within its regret bound. Finally, we empirically evaluate ARCB-V against current bidding strategies in the context of time-varying valuations. Our findings suggest that ARCB-V outperforms existing methods when valuations are either static or exhibit slow changes over time. We also examine the regret properties of ARCB-V under rapidly changing valuations. To our knowledge, this represents the first theoretical analysis of adaptive bidding with a budget constraint under time-varying valuations. Our results indicate that while the regret of ARCB-V cannot be bounded in this highly dynamic setting, it can still be bounded when a specific condition is met. We also assess ARCB-V's performance under this condition, showing that it outperforms existing bidding strategies. Finally, we extend our analysis to scenarios where advertisers face both time-varying valuations and fluctuating budget constraints. We present the regret properties of ARCB-V in this context and empirically demonstrate its superiority over current bidding strategies. Ultimately, ARCB-V proves to be optimal in terms of regret when valuations change slowly, even when budgets are time-varying. These interactions can substantially alter the expansion history of the universe and offer a potential solution to the Hubble tension. We develop a kinetic theory framework to calculate the self-interaction mean free path and demonstrate that the momentum diffusion coefficient is approximately three orders of magnitude smaller than the corresponding term in the collisionless regime. Consequently, both the modified expansion history and the suppression of large-scale structure formation are significantly weakened. Our findings suggest that boosted dark energy is a robust concept, though future efforts must be directed toward identifying the specific particle and interaction mechanisms that could generate these effects. Additionally, we outline a strategy for testing boosted dark energy using the bispectrum of cosmic microwave background polarization. This approach could provide a novel method for constraining the self-interaction cross-section of dark energy, a property that is otherwise inaccessible through conventional particle physics experiments. This paper investigates topological phenomena, specifically topological edge states, within frustrated Toric code models. We begin by extending the non-compact charged fermion model, originally associated with the unfrustrated Toric code, to incorporate the singular Jacobian determinant characteristic of the frustrated variant. This generalization enables a comprehensive analysis of topological effects in the frustated framework. Subsequently, we examine a generalized toric code on a Kagome lattice featuring a $3\times 3$ unit cell, which exhibits a singular determinant. By applying the same charged non-compact fermion formalism, we identify a topological charged domain wall state that emerges at the interface of two regions with distinct $\mathbb{Z}_3$ topological charges. Furthermore, we explore a generalized toric code on a triangular lattice with a unit cell size of $2\times 2$, which possesses a non-vanishing but negative determinant. We demonstrate that this setup supports a topological domain wall state carrying $q=1$ charge. Finally, we validate these findings through numerical simulations of the generalized toric code on a Kagome lattice. Our results indicate that while singlet-valued determinants facilitate topological charges of $q=1$ and $q=0$, signed-valued determinants allow for $q=1$ charges, aligning with the Kagome lattice's $\mathbb{Z}_3$ symmetry. These findings suggest that the frustated toric code on a Kagome lattice supports a $\mathbb{Z}_3$ topological charged domain wall state. Additionally, we propose a novel topological phase characterized by a $q=2$ charged domain wall state, which corresponds to a singlet-valued, negative, and negative-frustration determinant, respectively. This phase is distinct from the $q=1$ state and is not restricted to the Kagome lattice. We provide evidence for this $q=2$ topological phase using a specific model on a Kagome-like lattice. Finally, we offer a detailed discussion of the Kagome lattice toric code, demonstrating that it supports a singlet-valued determinant and a topological phase with $q=1$ charge. We also describe a method to construct a toric code on a Kagome lattice that yields a negative determinant, thereby enabling a $q=2$ charged domain wall state. This study examines a hybrid model combining a random band matrix and a finite-rank intricate matrix, both components selected at random. We demonstrate that this combination yields a valid approximation for the sigma-model of randomly perturbed Hermitian matrices. The methodology is applied to specific instances of finite-rank intricate matrices, including the large GUE and GOE sigma-models, as well as the rough sigma-model. In these cases, we show that the joint distribution of eigenvalues for the perturbed Hermitian matrix aligns with the circular law. Furthermore, we find that the eigenvalue distribution of the sigma-model corresponds to a random circular law convolved with Wigner's semicircle law. These findings extend our earlier work on the eigenvalue distributions of finite-rank intricate deformations of random band matrices. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the circular law in the context of the sigma-model. Finally, our results offer a new perspective on the universality of the circular law. This study investigates a new meaningful-based approach for conversation understanding, which leverages both original utterances and their derived meanings to facilitate conversation processing. We introduce a novel technique for extracting conversation semantics from rule-based semantic rules. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that meanings extracted via this method yield significant improvements in Conversation Understanding tasks, achieving state-of-the-art results on the CosWin and CoVoWits benchmarks. Furthermore, we validate the efficacy of the meaning-based approach on the CosQA task, and our method also proves effective for Sentiment Analysis and Topic Classification. Finally, we apply the meaning-based method to Cross-Lingual Conversation Understanding, yielding promising performance gains. Additionally, we provide an enhanced version of the SICK-Conversational dataset enriched with extracted meanings. Algorithmic interpretability is a critical component of machine learning, facilitating human comprehension and understanding of these systems. However, most existing definitions and metrics rely on post-hoc methods that are neither cognitively aligned with human learning processes nor capable of quantifying the learning effort required. This paper introduces a cognitive-based framework for evaluating algorithmic interpretability, grounded in the concept that human learning is essentially the acquisition of a function mapping inputs to outputs. The framework assesses the cognitive effort of learning this function by considering its complexity and the number of examples needed for acquisition. Furthermore, it offers a cognitive-based formula to determine the complexity of a function learned from data. By applying this formula, the paper defines the Cognitive Intricacy Score as a universal metric for measuring algorithmic interpretability. This framework and score are demonstrated through various machine learning algorithms, including decision trees, support vector machines, and neural networks. Additionally, the study explores the relationship between algorithmic interpretability and the "black box" dilemma, and reports on a user study to validate the proposed user perception of this score. Finally, the paper discusses the framework's and score's applicability to emerging machine learning algorithms. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/Cognitive-Intricacy-Score. Isolation Forests (iF) are a widely used anomaly detection method, particularly valued for their efficiency with large datasets. This paper introduces TiWS-iForest, a novel approach designed to enhance iF in two specific areas: (i) reducing the model's footprint for deployment in Tiny Machine Learning (TML) environments, and (ii) improving performance under weak guidance by utilizing soft labels. TiWS-iForest achieves these goals by modifying the standard iF algorithm to minimize the number of tree nodes and by incorporating soft labels during the random feature selection phase. The study demonstrates that TiWS-iForest successfully reduces model size without compromising accuracy, making it ideal for resource-constrained settings. Furthermore, it highlights the method's robustness in weakly supervised scenarios. Experimental results confirm that TiWS-iForest outperforms state-of-the-art iF variants on small datasets and rival baseline anomaly detection techniques across various configurations. The source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/fernando-oliveira/TiWS-iForest}. Additional details are available at \url{https://www.fernandooliveira.com/projects/TiWS-iForest}. This paper introduces a reparameterization of the Poisson process model used in extreme value analysis, which enhances stability and mitigates the overparameterization typically encountered with Poisson process-based models. Additionally, it presents a new approach for estimating the extremal index within a Bayesian framework. A simulation study demonstrates that this reparameterization improves the Bayes factor's ability to detect overparameterization and reduces the mean squared error of conditional Bayes estimators for the extremal index. Finally, the methodology is applied to analyze extreme rainfall data from the city of Rome. In both simulated and real-world contexts, the results indicate that Bayes estimators derived from the new model outperform those from the classical Poisson process model in terms of extremal index estimation. Furthermore, the Bayes factor consistently favors the one-point model (characterized by a constant extremal index) over the two-point model (allowing for varying extremal indices). However, when analyzing the Rome dataset, the Bayes factor suggests that the two-point model is more appropriate, as indicated by the superior performance of its Poisson intensity estimator. These findings underscore the necessity of selecting the most suitable model for a given dataset, as well as the value of Bayesian model selection techniques. The authors have made their R code available to facilitate the implementation of this Poisson process reparameterization for estimating the extremal index. This tool is particularly beneficial for researchers lacking extensive expertise in Bayesian methods, as it enables the calculation of point estimates, credible intervals, and the extremal index's density function. Additionally, the code supports Bayesian model selection to determine the most suitable Poisson intensity model. The authors acknowledge that this article represents only a preliminary exploration of Poisson process reparameterizations for extreme value analysis, with plans to extend the approach to other Poisson intensity models in future research. This includes investigating models with different numbers of parameters, Poisson-Dirichlet priors, and Poisson processes conditioned on the observed maximum. Furthermore, the authors intend to investigate whether the proposed reparameterization can be adapted for other extreme value models, such as the Hüsler-Reiss and Gumbel models. Finally, the authors note that all conclusions are based solely on the data provided and do not reflect the political views of the European Commission. The analysis of the Rome data was conducted in collaboration with the European Commission's Joint Research Centre in Ispra, Italy. This study theoretically examines the problem of minimizing the average geometric cross-section of a convex body $\mathcal{K}$ relative to a convex domain $\mathcal{D}$ by translating $\mathcal{D}$ anywhere within $\mathcal{K}$. The average cross section $S_{\mathcal{K},\mathcal{D}}(\alpha)$ is defined as the mean Minkowski content of the boundaries of $K\cap D(\alpha)$, where $K\subset D(\alpha)$ for all translation vectors $\alpha\in\mathcal{K}$. We establish that the average cross section $S_{\mathcal{K},\mathcal{D}}(\alpha)$ exhibits non-increasing (and potentially strictly decreasing) behavior as the translation vector $\alpha$ moves from the origin toward any point $\alpha_0\in\mathcal{K}$ where the domain achieves its minimum. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this minimum remains non-degenerate, meaning there exists a specific neighborhood around the minimizing vector $\alpha_0$ where $S_{\mathcal{K},\mathcal{D}}(\alpha)$ does not increase. These findings are supported by illustrative examples. Additionally, we explore the analogous issue of minimizing the average perimeter of the intersection $K\cap D(\alpha)$, proving that this average also attains non-degenerate minima. Finally, we outline several open questions for future research. This work extends the classical Fuglede-Kadec theorem, which addresses the minimization of the average cross section when $\mathcal{D}$ is a half-space. The term "average cross section" was introduced by the authors in a prior paper, where they established the convergence of $S_{\mathcal{K},\mathcal{D}}(\alpha)$ to the surface area $S_{\mathcal{K}}$ as $\alpha$ approaches the boundary of $\mathcal{K}$. This paper builds upon the foundational research by Mattila and Saksman (1991) and Mattila (1992), which investigated the same concept for half-spaces. Their work established that the average cross section of a convex body is minimized when aligned with any direction tangent to the body, a result now known as the Fuglede-Kadec theorem. This paper outlines our system for the COMET-ATOMIC 2020 shared task, which focuses on creating large-scale common sense knowledge networks. We addressed two challenges: (1) enhancing existing symbolic knowledge networks by integrating neural representations, and (2) scaling small neural networks by leveraging pre-built symbolic structures. For Task 1A, we utilized a word2vec model trained on AtOMIC to generate node embeddings, employing either the original or fine-tuned GloVe vectors as auxiliary input for nodes and edges. The resulting system secured first place on all evaluation metrics. For Task 2, we demonstrated that small neural networks can be effectively scaled using extensive pre-built symbolic data, achieving first-place rankings. Overall, these findings indicate that integrating external knowledge into neural models significantly boosts performance on common sense reasoning tasks. The code and resources are accessible at https://github.com/Seoul-NLP/COMET-ATOMIC-2020. (Accepted to SIGDAM'20)

The Hi-GAL survey targets the 160 and 250 micron bands to map the Galactic plane, offering a unique blend of extensive spatial coverage, high angular resolution, and substantial sensitivity. This work outlines the data reduction pipeline employed to process raw observations from the SCUBA-2 camera at the James Clerk Maxwell Telescope. The pipeline is designed to be adaptable for future SCUBA-2 surveys, such as the one currently underway to map the Galactic plane at 850 and 450 microns. A primary objective is to facilitate the rapid production of data cubes covering the entire survey area. Additionally, we present the first Hi-GAL data cube centered on the Taurus star-forming region, demonstrating the survey's exceptional sensitivity. This data cube enables the detection of faint, compact sources previously observable only at 850 microns, as well as extended structures at 250 microns that were previously undetectable. We also illustrate the capability to identify and subtract 1.4 GHz synchrotron emission from the data cubes. Finally, we discuss the ongoing efforts to calibrate and map the sky using these data cubes. Ultimately, Hi-GAL data cubes are being utilized to generate a comprehensive view of the interstellar medium across the entire survey region. The paper concludes by detailing the current status of the survey and its anticipated future contributions to the fields of astronomy and astrophysics. (A video of the Hi-GAL survey is accessible at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2222222222). The globular cluster NGC 2808 is renowned for its multiple blue horizontal branch (BHB) sequences, which are widely considered evidence of a metallicity gradient along these sequences. This study aims to confirm such a gradient by analyzing the abundances of light elements in the cluster's stars. We conducted a high-resolution spectroscopic analysis of 10 bright BHB stars and three red giant clump stars, deriving iron and alpha-element abundances using the equivalent width method. Our findings indicate that the cluster's mean metallicity is [Fe/H] = -0.29 ± 0.05 dex, with an intrinsic dispersion of 0.11 dex, suggesting the presence of a metallicity spread. Specifically, the three red giant stars exhibit [Fe/H] values of -0.19, -0.23, and -0.37 dex, while the BHB stars show a spread of 0.12 dex. We propose that the distinct BHB sequences in NGC 2808 may result from a metallicity spread of approximately 0.1 dex. Additionally, we observed a significant anti-correlation between [Na/Fe] and [O/Fe], with [Na/Fe] ranging from -0.1 to +0.3 dex and [O/Fe] from -0.2 to +0.2 dex. This correlation is likely caused by the conversion of oxygen into sodium during the early evolution of the cluster. Our results support the existence of a metallicity spread in NGC 2808, a conclusion consistent with previous studies. We also identified a trend of increasing [Na/Fe] with luminosity, which may be attributed to the metallicity spread. These results are compatible with the two-population scenario, where the second population consists of stars formed from the ejecta of the first population. Furthermore, we determined that NGC 2808 has a high [Mg/Fe] ratio, indicating that it is an Mg-rich globular cluster. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the formation and evolution of the cluster. The high-resolution spectroscopic analysis presented here offers valuable insights into the chemical evolution of globular clusters. We have provided the most precise abundance data for NGC 2808 to date, which will facilitate future investigations into the cluster's evolution. We investigate single-file particle transport within one dimension using both theoretical methods and large-scale molecular dynamics simulations. Our focus is on particle exits from finite systems, specifically examining the impact of particle self-intersection entropies on duration statistics. These entropies are defined as negative, long-range pair potentials that increase with distance, thereby promoting self-intersection events. We analyze how these self-intersection entropies affect the duration of initial exits, particularly in scenarios involving large system lengths, few particles, and slow diffusers. Theoretically, we derive the single-particle exit duration distribution for single-file diffusion from rest, demonstrating that the mean exit time scales with the square of the distance between the first and last particles. This result holds true for systems of non-interacting bosons and for one-component plasmas where self-intersection entropies follow a Coulombic potential. We also present a generalization of the mean exit time applicable to interacting systems. Furthermore, we establish that the two-particle duration distribution adheres to the single-particle result when the initial spacing is large. Finally, we extend our findings to systems containing a single slow diffuser. In this context, self-intersection entropies cause the slow diffuser to cluster near the system's edge, significantly reducing its exit duration. We provide an analytical approximation for the probability distribution of the diffuser's final position near the boundary, showing that this distribution is independent of the specific diffuser identity. Additionally, we observe that the duration distribution for a single diffuser exiting a small system mirrors the single-particle case. These findings are supported by molecular dynamics simulations involving large systems, numerous particles, and a variety of diffusers. We also address the impact of self-intersection entropies on duration distributions during the second exit event, noting that while clustering of the slow diffuser still occurs, the effect is less pronounced than during the initial exit. Finally, we present a theoretical argument suggesting that the duration distribution for the $n$-th exit event approaches the single-particle distribution as $n$ increases. These insights are crucial for interpreting experimental data regarding particle transport in confined geometries. The results indicate that this framework offers a straightforward and efficient method for constructing the equation of state for tiny systems, facilitating their thermodynamic integration with bulk matter. Consequently, this paves the way for a unified description of tiny systems and bulk matter, which is essential for advancing research into tiny thermodynamic systems. This work serves as a memoir, with the title reflecting my perspective. My primary objective is to examine the cohomology groups of the Steenrod algebra, denoted as $H^*(H^*(F_2); F_2)$. For decades, these groups have been a subject of intense study, with their intricate structure providing a defining characteristic of the algebra. My motivation stems from the fact that, aside from low-dimensional cases, the exact composition of these groups remains unknown. While Dubin's recent paper offers a comprehensive overview of the topic, I felt compelled to address the issue once more, as there are non-trivial aspects I believe deserve greater attention. My focus will be on the so-called non-ignorable dimensions, which I define as dimensions exceeding the maximal Demazure product. Although this terminology is personal, I intend to justify it. Specifically, I will explore the connections between these groups and the Milnor primitives, as well as the Q-operads. Additionally, I will highlight recent advancements in the area, particularly the work of Galatius, Rasmussen, and Valenti, which offers significant new insights. Finally, I will outline my current research direction, which aims to investigate the relationship between the Q-operad and the Steenrod algebra through the lens of homotopy theory. I hope this memoir proves interesting to readers, and I welcome any feedback or corrections. Thank you.

Keywords: Steenrod algebra, Q-operad, Cobar complex, Cobar spectral sequence, Configuration space cohomology.

The Lyman-alpha filter is a narrow-band filter centered at 510.6 nm, designed to block the Lyman-alpha emission line from the Sun and Earth while permitting light from distant quasies to pass. This filter is widely utilized in astronomical photometry to study the intergalactic medium and the interstellar medium of galaxies. Although the filter has been used for over a decade, its performance remains poorly understood. This study presents a model for the filter's transmission function, which is validated using Lyman-alpha quasars. The results indicate that the model accurately represents the filter's transmission profile. Additionally, we examine the effects of wavelength-dependent instrumental response on Lyman-alpha quasars and provide a method for correcting the observed spectra. Our findings suggest that the Lyman-alpha filter is highly effective for photometry involving Lyman-alpha quasars. We provide a Python package to facilitate the use of the transmission function in future research. The transmission model is available at https://github.com/leeyu12345/lya_filter_model. This study investigates keyless authentication for the discrete-memoryless AWGN channel. In this framework, a transmitter and receiver utilize a shared secret key to generate a public codebook of transmitted signals, while a potentially malicious adversary operates without access to this key. The objective is to allow the legitimate parties to reliably transmit a secret message over the public channel while ensuring the adversary learns nothing about it. We establish a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of such a codebook and propose a keyless verification protocol based on this condition. This protocol is proven to be optimal in terms of both the secret message rate and the leakage rate. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for any finite blocklength, the optimal secret message rate is strictly positive, and we provide a corresponding coding scheme. Additionally, we show that for any finite secret message alphabet, the optimal leakage rate is zero. Finally, we extend these findings to the keyless verification setting involving public vector channels. For any memoryless channel satisfying a specific condition, we derive the corresponding coding theorem and present the corresponding optimal verification protocol. We also prove that for any finite blocklength, the optimal secret message rate for this set of channels is positive, and for any finite secret message alphabet, the optimal leakage rate is zero. Our analysis indicates that the keyless authentication capability of the discrete-memoryless AWGN channel is comparable to that of the discrete-memoryless Z-channel. However, for the keyless authentication of the discrete-memoryless erasure channel, our derived achievable region is more restricted. This limitation arises because the erasure channel's output is not fully determined by the input, a characteristic that prevents the direct application of our coding scheme to this scenario. Consequently, our results suggest that the keyless authentication of the erasure channel warrants further investigation. This limitation also affects the keyless authentication of the discrete-memoryless Z-channel, which is a specific instance of the erasure channel. The dynamics of a particle moving within a periodic potential, subject to white noise and transport by a constant force, are investigated using a Fokker-Planck equation. This approach yields a comprehensive description of the system, covering both non-equilibrium steady states and equilibrium states linked to detailed balance. Numerical simulations demonstrate particle transport across a broad spectrum of parameter values, extending beyond conventional depinning thresholds. Specifically, the transport of near-equilibrium particles driving current in Josephson junctions is examined in detail. This facilitates the definition of a "washboard" current-voltage characteristic, which is derived from the particle's diffusion coefficient. The connection between this voltage and the diffusion coefficient is elucidated, alongside an analysis of the particle's mean square displacement over time. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that within a specific parameter range, a particle achieves uniform motion with a constant velocity driven by the external field, a phenomenon that contradicts standard intuition regarding transport in washboard potentials. The emergence of this uniform transport is analyzed, revealing its relationship with phase slips and resonant tunneling. Additionally, the validity of the detailed-balance condition is assessed, and a connection is established between current and uniform velocity. These findings are interpreted through the lens of phase slips occurring at both potential minima and maxima. Finally, the study addresses the influence of particle size on current and uniform velocity, noting that while earlier studies focused on point particles, finite-sized particles are relevant for certain physical systems, such as superconducting loops. The impact of particle size on uniform transport is explored in relation to phase slips and resonant tunneling. Ultimately, the paper concludes by discussing the broader implications of these results for understanding and controlling transport in energy landscapes. This research offers a fresh perspective on particle transport in periodic potentials, with potential applications ranging from nanoscale devices to biological systems. By providing a unified framework to analyze and predict transport properties, these findings could advance our understanding of various physical and biological processes. Ultimately, this work advances our comprehension of energy dissipation in periodic potentials and establishes a foundation for future investigations into transport phenomena in energy landscapes. Furthermore, the study highlights the significance of particle size in determining transport properties, a factor that has been overlooked in previous research. By incorporating particle size into the analysis, this work paves the way for a more accurate description of transport in periodic potentials, with potential applications in diverse fields, including nanotechnology and biology. Impulse response functions (IRFs) are widely used to evaluate the dynamic effects of economic shocks. This paper introduces a new estimation approach based on local projections that adaptably selects the projection horizon using validated rules derived from theoretical considerations. We validate this method through extensive Monte Carlo simulations and apply it to analyze historical recessions, revealing that the standard 16-step horizon is insufficient for capturing the full dynamics of a V-shaped recovery. The proposed method accurately recovers simulated IRFs, demonstrates greater robustness to model misspecification than conventional techniques, and uncovers distinct differences in how various sectors react to shocks. Furthermore, it identifies key stylized facts, such as the countercyclical nature of investment and the significant impact of fiscal and monetary shocks on the economy. Finally, we show that combining multiple forecasting models enhances the accuracy of the proposed IRF estimates. Overall, this method offers a robust and reliable technique for estimating impulse responses. We investigate the angular momentum of the quantum vacuum in the presence of a point charge within an angularly dependent, uniform magnetic field, a setup known as Landau gauge. Our findings reveal that the angular momentum is non-zero, indicating that the vacuum becomes stirred by the charge, and demonstrate that this momentum can be fully recovered through angular boost transformations. The proliferation of social media has spurred significant interest in Named Entity Recognition (NER), a core NLP task. However, NER on complex social media posts remains challenging due to their heterogeneous content, which includes text, images, videos, and other media. While multimedia NER has emerged as a promising solution, it remains an underexplored area. Furthermore, existing methods often fail to leverage the inherent tree-like structures of both social media posts and NER tasks, resulting in suboptimal performance. To address these limitations, we introduce Fine-Detailed NER-RH (FDNET-RH), a novel refinement network designed for fine-detailed NER that operates within hyperbolic space. This approach utilizes a hyperbolic neural network to encode post structures and employs a multi-branch refinement network to enhance the feature learning of NER classifiers. Additionally, we present a new dataset, Weibo-ER, for Chinese fine-detailed NER. Experimental results demonstrate that FDNET-RH outperforms state-of-the-art methods on both Weibo-ER and the Weibo-NER datasets. The code and data are accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/FDNET-RH.

In cloud computing, virtual machines (VMs) are the primary resource, and their efficient allocation is essential for maximizing data center performance. This paper introduces a novel strategy called "Prepartition," which distributes incoming VMs across a physical host based on predicted load requirements. By utilizing a neural network to forecast VM loads, Prepartition aims to minimize data center overheads such as energy consumption and cooling costs. We compare Prepartition against two baseline approaches: Preload, which allocates VMs based on current load, and Preempt, which allows host migration to balance loads. Our findings demonstrate that Prepartition outperforms both baselines by reducing overheads by 10% to 20%. Furthermore, we observe that load prediction accuracy significantly impacts the effectiveness of Prepartition, and we provide a detailed analysis of how various prediction methods influence its overall performance. Finally, we evaluate the strategy's scalability regarding both the number of VMs and hosts, confirming that Prepartition remains effective in large-scale environments. This paper introduces a novel framework for Nash equilibrium learning in extensive-form games, where agents employ implicit value function networks to forecast opponent actions at the current state. We demonstrate that if the predicted opponent behavior constitutes a fixed point of these networks, the joint strategy becomes a Nash equilibrium. We establish the equivalence between our framework and sequential equilibrium learning via backward induction using fixed point networks. Furthermore, we develop a new algorithm, sequential fixed point value function approximation (SeqFpV), which is proven to converge to the sequential equilibrium of extensive-form games. Empirical results indicate that SeqFpV successfully avoids the well-known convergence to anti-equilibria, a persistent issue in simultaneous-form game learning. Additionally, we show that SeqFpV achieves faster convergence to equilibrium compared to the sequential best response value iteration algorithm. To our knowledge, this represents the first theoretical and empirical evidence of such rapid convergence in extensive-form games. We present a novel framework for estimating causal effects in non-experimental settings. This approach draws inspiration from the concept of "causal depth," which measures how many steps away from a target variable its cause lies within a directed acyclic graph (DAG). By leveraging this metric, we develop a general method to calculate causal impacts based on observational data and the target structure. The framework offers several advantages, including the ability to infer causal direction from data, scalability to high-dimensional settings, and data-driven estimation of causal strength. Furthermore, it establishes the first provably consistent estimator for high-dimensional DAGs where the number of variables far exceeds the sample size. We validate the framework's effectiveness through simulation studies and a real-world application analyzing the causal impact of social support on depression. The application analysis reveals that while self-esteem does not directly cause depression, it acts as an indirect cause. Additionally, we find that causal effects can be estimated with high precision even when the number of variables in the DAG significantly exceeds the sample size. Finally, we demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms existing methods across all three evaluated tasks. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ashwinbhamidipati/limit-depth.

This paper introduces a new method for predictive surveillance of linear time-invariant systems under stealthy attacks, utilizing linear filters that maintain optimal performance by relying solely on attack-free historical data. The core concept involves predicting future attack-free measurements and generating residuals that vanish in the absence of attacks, thereby enhancing detection sensitivity. The study provides explicit formulas for these linear filters, highlighting their relationship to a proposed effective system model that abstracts the attack dynamics. Furthermore, the approach is demonstrated through a numerical example featuring stealthy attacks on a power network, with additional discussions on extending the method to time-varying systems. Keywords: Cyber-Physical Systems, Predictive Surveillance, Linear Filters, Linear Quadratic Estimation, Linear Quadratic Gaussian Control.

Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) serve as powerful tools for unsupervised learning, enabling the generation of new data and feature extraction. However, a key challenge remains: determining the optimal dimensionality for the network's bottleneck layer. This paper introduces a regularized, minimal-squared-error VAE designed to learn the most informative features within the lowest possible error, utilizing the bottleneck's dimensionality as a regularizer. We provide a theoretical analysis of this proposed VAE architecture. Experimental results demonstrate that the method can effectively extract features from images and time series data. Furthermore, we illustrate the model's efficacy in semi-supervised learning, showing that it can accurately classify handwritten digits and species of sea turtles. Finally, the approach is applied to a real-world scenario for detecting anomalies in industrial settings. Our findings indicate that the proposed VAE can identify anomalies in images, time series, and network traffic, with the ability to reconstruct these anomalies more closely than normal data. The Internet of Things (IoT) is a rapidly expanding technology that facilitates communication between devices and the internet, enabling users to control devices remotely. However, this widespread adoption has introduced significant security challenges, including data theft, privacy breaches, and unauthorized access. This paper introduces a new framework called the Intelligent Home Gadget Monitor (IHGM), which leverages blockchain technology to securely manage IoT devices. By employing localization, IHGM enables each IoT device to independently validate transactions, thereby reducing the computational load on the blockchain network. This approach ensures secure data exchange between devices and the cloud while enhancing transaction speed and lowering energy consumption. Simulation results demonstrate that IHGM outperforms other blockchain-based solutions, such as Pre-authorized IoT and Post-authorized IoT, in terms of throughput, delay, and energy usage. Consequently, IHGM is well-suited for IoT applications within smart cities and smart homes. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/Abhishek-2000/IHGM. Future research will focus on integrating new consensus mechanisms, such as Proof of Authority, to further improve the system's efficiency. Additionally, the framework's applicability to other domains, including smart healthcare, will be explored. This paper introduces a method for quantizing Lloyd-Lindley (L-) values to generate an L-codebook tailored for Gray-coded modulation. We employ a deep learning-based quantization technique that utilizes a convolutional neural network to map continuous L-values to discrete indices. A key advantage of this approach is its ability to learn optimal quantization levels, thereby maximizing codebook performance. We validate the proposed scheme using a deep learning simulator that models the channel and receiver, evaluating the L-codebook's performance against a conventional trellis-coded modulation (TCM) design. Our results demonstrate that the proposed L-codebook achieves a 0.5 dB gain over the standard TCM design. Furthermore, we show that the deep learning simulator effectively predicts the quantizer's performance. Finally, we confirm that the proposed deep learning-based quantizer outperforms a genetic algorithm-based alternative. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of deep learning to the quantization of L-values. The simulation code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan123/Deep-Learning-Driven-Quantization-of-L-Values.

This paper examines several parameterized algorithms addressing diverse upward planarity problems. Our primary objective is to develop parameterized methods that address fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) upward planar subgraph detection and modification tasks. Specifically, we demonstrate that the upward planar subgraph detection problem is FPT when parameterized by the size of the subgraph, and that the upward planar edge deletion problem is FPT parameterized by the number of deletions. Furthermore, we establish that the upward planar subtree detection problem is FPT parameterized by the subtree size, and the upward planar subtree deletion problem is FPT parameterized by both the number of subtrees and their size. Additionally, we prove that the upward planar subtree contraction problem is FPT parameterized by the number of contractions and the tree depth, and that the upward planar spanning tree arboricity reduction problem is FPT parameterized by the number of reductions, initial arboricity, and final spanning tree size. Finally, we show that the upward planar spanning tree arboricity reduction problem is W[1]-hard parameterized by the number of reductions and final arboricity alone, and is W[1]-hard parameterized by the number of reductions and final spanning tree size alone. These hardness results are conditional upon the standard assumption that FPT = W[1]. To achieve our positive algorithmic results, we employ a variety of parameterized techniques, including kernelization, bounded search trees, and iterative compression. We also utilize a novel parameterized algorithm for the feedback vertex set problem, which is itself parameterized by both the number of vertices and the tree arboricity. Notably, this latter result is tight, as the feedback vertex set problem is known to be W[1]-hard parameterized solely by the number of vertices or the tree arboricity. We demonstrate that for non-atomic hyperbolic probability measures on compact manifolds, the norm of the dual of the Ruelle operator associated with a semiflow converges to zero at a geometric rate when measured in Hölder norms. Consequently, the spectrum of the dual operator restricted to the space of Hölder functions perpendicular to constants is also geometric. This result extends to semiflow dual Ruelle operators defined on Lipschitz functions. Furthermore, we generalize these findings to semiflows exhibiting the shadowing property, a category that encompasses all hyperbolic semiflow systems. These advancements enable the derivation of statistical limit theorems for semiflows, a topic currently under investigation. Additionally, we reveal that our findings offer a streamlined proof of rapid mixing for all Bernoulli shifts, as well as the rapid mixing of the shift map, when formulated within the framework of transfer operators for semiflows and semiflow maps, respectively. Finally, we illustrate an application of our results to stochastic differential equations, confirming the rapid mixing of the unitary dual Ruelle operator under Lipschitz norms for specific diffusion processes, thereby providing an alternative proof of the log-Sobolev inequality established by Gross and Gross-Kalai. These inequalities were previously derived through more complex arguments involving spectral gap estimates for diffusion operators acting on Sobolev spaces of functions with integrable exponentials. Moreover, our approach yields a novel proof of the log-Sobolev inequality for discrete Gaussians on the hyperbolic lattice $\mathrm{SL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$. This specific instance was originally proven by Bourgain through a lengthy argument utilizing Fourier analysis on the torus. Our findings also suggest a pathway toward proving the log-Sobolev inequality for general rank $n$ Bernoulli shifts, a task that currently lacks a direct proof. Additionally, our results offer a new perspective on the mixing properties of diffusion processes, a subject that has been extensively studied through the lens of transfer operators for semiflows and semiflow maps, with various mixing rates having been established. Finally, we establish that the mixing rate for a diffusion process is intrinsically linked to the mixing rate of its time-$t$ map, which is formulated using the transfer operator of the discrete-time Markov process generated by the semiflow. This connection is demonstrated by constructing a specific invariant measure for the semiflow such that the stationary distribution of the discrete-time Markov process corresponds to a time-$t$ image of the semiflow's invariant measure. Minor strength-$t$ covering arrays represent a generalization of standard covering arrays. This study investigates the existence of such arrays under specific constraints. We demonstrate that for any minor strength-$2$ covering array table where the number of rows does not exceed $2n$, the symbols must be drawn from an alphabet of size at least $n+1$. Conversely, we establish the existence of minor strength-$2$ covering arrays when the table size is at least $2^{l+1}$ and $l+1 \leq 2^l+1$. Specifically, we provide arrays with $2^{l+1}$ rows using exactly $2^l+1$ symbols. These constructed arrays may require an additional set of symbols beyond the primary $2^l+1$ to achieve the required coverage. We propose the term "covering arrays with extra symbols" to describe this category and refer to them as $s$-covering arrays. Furthermore, we offer a general construction method for $s$-covering arrays with $2^l+1$ symbols derived from standard covering arrays with $2^l$ symbols, and we include several examples of $s$-covering arrays with five symbols. Finally, we present an alternative approach to constructing $s$-covering arrays based on the recursive generation of standard covering arrays. This method yields $s$-covering arrays with five symbols for row counts of $16$, $32$, and $64$. Additionally, we provide a general formula for the size of a strength-$2$ covering array with five symbols given a specified number of rows. Using this formula, we calculate the size for $16$ and $32$ rows and compare these results with existing arrays in the literature. The paper concludes with a discussion on the relationship between strength-$2$ covering arrays and $s$-covering arrays. Specifically, we illustrate that a strength-$2$ covering array with $32$ rows and five symbols can be transformed into a $s$-covering array with the same number of rows and five symbols by removing one symbol from its alphabet. This transformation is achieved by deleting a single row from the original array and incorporating the deleted row as an "extra symbol." We propose the term "relatedness" to describe arrays connected through this transformation. We also examine the relationship between arrays generated by our construction method and those related to them. The development of nonlocal decision-making technologies has enabled voters to become aware of global election results in real-time. This capability can significantly alter voting dynamics, potentially rendering elections trivial by causing early-winner groups to coordinate and unify their support bases, effectively eliminating competition against later-winner groups despite differences in individual preferences. This phenomenon, known as state intertwining, poses a serious threat to democratic integrity. This study examines the conditions under which nonlocal elections lose their competitive nature. We demonstrate that in a simplified scenario where all voters possess identical knowledge and preferences, global result revelation immediately destroys competition. Furthermore, through an analytical approach for specific cases and numerical simulations across various scenarios, we determined that when most voters can see global results, the election becomes non-competitive. Conversely, if only a minority of voters have access to this information, the competitive balance is preserved. Finally, we propose several avenues for future research. These findings offer critical insights into the design of pre-election and post-election systems, particularly regarding how early-winner groups are selected and how global results are disclosed. We argue that implementing safeguards to prevent state intertwining is essential for maintaining the integrity of democratic processes. Additionally, we suggest that further investigation is needed to understand how these effects interact with voter preferences and how they influence the diffusion of information among the general public. This research was conducted prior to the 2020 United States presidential election. We hope that the lessons learned from this period will inform the design of future electoral systems. (Note: This work does not address the significant controversies and allegations of fraud that have emerged regarding the 2020 US presidential election.) This article is categorized as 1. This report aims to investigate the potential for automatically identifying and rectifying bugs. To achieve this, we implemented a specific algorithm, NPL-GGP, which is a specialized version of Genetic Guided Procedure Synthesis. NPL-GGP is designed to generate test inputs that expose defects within existing code. We validated the effectiveness of NPL-GGP by re-discovering known crashes in the open-source Firefox browser, utilizing its source code and a predefined set of bug oracles. This study serves as a partial extension of our prior work, which demonstrated that NPL-GGP can successfully replicate crash reproduction achieved through interactive debugging sessions. Our findings indicate that NPL-GGP can efficiently and accurately replicate all GP Synthesis-derived crash replications required to trigger the bug oracles for this edition of Firefox. Furthermore, we observed that NPL-GGP can also reproduce crashes that originated from interactive debugging sessions. Finally, we conclude that NPL-GGP is a potent method for automatically detecting and replicating crashes. This tool could assist developers in understanding code behavior, aiding in bug fixing, and facilitating crash reproduction. Additionally, NPL-GGP can be employed to generate regression tests for newly introduced bugs to prevent their reoccurrence in future updates. We present in situ scanning tunneling microscopy data from La$_{2-x}$Sr$_x$CuO$_4$ (x=0.15) revealing the evolution of the vortex lattice as a function of magnetic field. Near zero temperature, we observe a abrupt shift from an incompressible square-vortex grid to a distinct square-by-square grid, where each local grid size is dictated by the varying vortex spacing. This phenomenon is best understood through a model in which finite-size effects suppress the free energy of small vortices, causing them to condense into a square-by-square arrangement. This mechanism offers a theoretical framework for recent experimental findings, including the detection of small triangular voids within large square regions and the persistence of square grids at high magnetic fields. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this model can be extended to explain experiments involving other types of impurities. Finally, we predict that this transition will be observable in underdoped cuprates and potentially in other materials featuring anisotropic vortex core sizes. These predictions can be tested by examining the spatial distribution of vortex core sizes. Additionally, we propose that this transition is relevant to the ongoing debate regarding whether vortex glass or vortex liquid phases can exist at zero temperature. Specifically, we argue that the vortex glass phase is incompatible with a finite-size-induced square-by-square grid, whereas a vortex liquid phase remains possible. Consequently, our findings suggest a scenario where a second-order phase transition from the square-vortex grid to the square-by-square grid occurs at a zero-temperature, zero-field critical point. This critical point is characterized by diverging correlation lengths and a dynamic critical exponent of $z=1$. We outline the experimental signatures associated with this critical point and suggest that it may be detectable in existing data. Finally, we outline the experimental requirements needed to explore this critical point further. We contend that anisotropies in thermal photon emission, characterized by a long wavelength relative to the system size, provide a means to measure the shear viscosity of the quark-gluon plasma. This approach offers the benefit of integrating viscosity measurements with the study of the medium's temperature and energy density evolution. This methodology was validated through ideal hydrodynamic simulations of a shear-driven, anisotropically expanding quark-gluon plasma. Additionally, a physical explanation for the anisotropic photon flow generated by shear motion was derived, and a corresponding physical model was established for real heavy-ion collisions. In such non-equilibrium scenarios, thermal photons emitted by an expanding anisotropic medium exhibit a preferred direction perpendicular to the shear flow. Consequently, the anisotropic flow of thermal photons can be analyzed to determine the medium's transport coefficients. Furthermore, we anticipate that measuring the polarization of thermal photons will enable the measurement of the plasma's bulk viscosity. Finally, we propose that experimental efforts should be directed toward measuring the directional flow of thermal photons in heavy-ion collisions. Specifically, we recommend that the PHENIX collaboration, utilizing their upgraded gamma-arm detector, investigate this phenomenon in Au+Au collisions at $\sqrt{s_{NN}}=200$ GeV. We predict that thermal photons from such collisions will display a significant flow perpendicular to the reaction plane, with a slope indicating a low-equation-of-state equation of state. This prediction is based on a realistic model of anisotropic plasma expansion, which we have implemented using the PHENIX initial conditions for Au+Au collisions. We expect that even a modest sample of events would suffice to observe the anisotropic flow of thermal photons. We demonstrate that a uniform magnetic field aligned with the $z$-axis induces distinct, consistent magnetic configurations within both triangular and kagome lattices. These configurations emerge through field-dependent quantum phase transitions from nonmagnetic states. In the range $0< B_z < 2J$, where $J$ represents the nearest-neighbor exchange coupling, all bonds in the triangular lattice become polarized parallel to $B_z$, forming a ferromagnetic state. Conversely, for $B_z > 2J$, the system undergoes a quantum phase transition into a $120^{\circ}$ antiferromagnetic state. The magnetizations in both configurations are calculated using the high-temperature series expansion method. Additionally, we identify the zero-temperature $120^{\circ}$ antiferromagnetic state as the ground state for a $Z$-type antiferromagnetic configuration on a kagome lattice. As $B_z$ increases, this configuration evolves into a $Y$-type antiferromagnetic state via a quantum phase transition at $B_z = 2J$. We further observe that the magnetization of the $Y$-type configuration vanishes at $B_z = 2J$ and rises linearly with $B_z$ for $B_z > 2J$. Finally, we discuss the relationship between these quantum phase transitions and the classical Ising model. These findings offer a foundation for investigating spin quantum phase transitions in $z$-type antiferromagnetic materials based on kagome lattices. Large-scale randomized experiments frequently employ the false discovery rate (FDR) as a multiple testing correction method. Nevertheless, when FDR calculation involves complex dependencies, determining the exact FDR becomes computationally prohibitive. To address this, various relaxed FDR definitions have been introduced to provide practical approximations. This study examines a specific relaxed FDR termed "regulated FDR," which integrates prior knowledge regarding dependency structures. We demonstrate that regulated FDR controls the false discovery proportion at a predetermined level and propose a step-up procedure for its implementation. Furthermore, we extend this procedure to identify intervention effects, evaluating its performance through both simulation and a real-world dataset analysis. Our findings indicate that the proposed method effectively controls FDR while possessing greater power compared to existing approaches. This paper introduces a mathematical model designed to demonstrate how the universe expanded from its initial singularity. Our model relies on two fundamental principles: the acceleration of matter and the conservation of mass. We establish that acceleration is necessary for a matter-based universe to evolve from a small to a large scale without generating excessive radiation, as predicted by the general relativistic Friedmann equations. The second principle follows directly from the continuity equation. We derive solutions for expansion rates and compare them with observational data. Although our findings are approximate, they offer a viable explanation for the early universe's expansion. Furthermore, we show that this simple framework can be extended to create a more complex model capable of describing the late universe, including mechanisms for matter creation and the acceleration observed during the cosmic "dawn." These results suggest that our model serves as a useful tool for investigating cosmic acceleration. Finally, we conclude that our approach provides a complementary perspective to the standard big-bang theory. For instance, data from the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) indicate that the matter density parameter ($\Omega_m$) was approximately 0.3 at the time of recombination, implying that matter was already present in the early universe. This contrasts with the standard big-bang theory, which posits that the universe was radiation-dominated in its earliest stages. Additionally, our model offers a potential resolution to the "horizon problem" by proposing that the universe expanded rapidly from a small size before transitioning to a slower expansion rate. Consequently, regions of the sky that appear to have never been in causal contact could have originated from a sufficiently small volume, allowing them to reach their current size through a phase of fast expansion. This concept aligns with the inflationary model, which also attributes rapid expansion to a scalar field. However, while inflation requires a field that must subsequently decay to resolve other issues, our model does not require such a field. Instead, we demonstrate that a matter creation term in the energy equation can account for the acceleration of the expansion rate. This stands in contrast to the standard big-bang theory, where the expansion rate slows down in the absence of a matter creation term. Our theory also provides an alternative explanation for the "flatness problem." In the standard model, the matter density parameter ($\Omega$) must be extremely close to 1 in the early universe to maintain its near-unity value today. By analyzing the impact of new heavy Higgs bosons, we demonstrate that this framework can resolve the $W$-mass puzzle. Furthermore, we show that appropriate parameter choices allow the model to remain consistent with muon $g-2$ data and current experimental limits. Our analysis indicates that the heavy Higgs mass spectrum within this model can be accessible to future collider experiments. Additionally, we examine the model's influence on $Z$-pole observables, finding that a viable parameter space exists to accommodate all available data. Finally, we establish that the model can satisfy the constraints imposed by the LHC. In recent years, concept discovery has gained significant traction due to its capacity to automatically uncover novel queries and topics from vast datasets. However, existing methods often rely on manually defined scoring criteria, which restricts their adaptability to diverse contexts. This paper introduces SWIFTER, a novel system that automatically customizes the concept discovery process by harnessing crowdsourced feedback. SWIFTER collects human insights regarding the relevance of queries to a specific concept and leverages this data to train a model that automatically scores new queries. Additionally, the system incorporates a query rephrasing component to generate alternative versions of queries based on provided context. We have made SWIFTER publicly accessible to facilitate further research. Experimental results demonstrate that it outperforms existing baselines in both accuracy and scalability. Furthermore, comparing sequential acoustic features from opposing speakers reveals superior performance in predicting distance relative to methods that incorporate long-term context. Finally, evaluating our proposed models on a newly released public dataset yields a Spearman correlation of 0.41, indicating a moderate correlation between predicted and actual distance. These findings demonstrate that deep neural architectures effectively capture essential conversational behaviors, such as distance and similarity, from speech data. Additionally, we anticipate that these deep models will prove valuable for applications including automatic dialogue state tracking and conversational agent training. A key advantage of our unsupervised deep neural algorithm is its ability to generalize across different datasets. We introduce a collection of open-source, web-based tools designed to visualize spectral data, specifically focusing on hyperspectral and multispectral images. This infrastructure is built upon the Researching and Communicating Spectral Data in Education and Data Exploration (RCSED) project, which was originally funded by the National Science Foundation (NSF) to develop a curriculum for teaching data analysis using Python and Jupyter Notebooks within the context of astronomy and planetary science. The RCSEDv2 platform retains the original project's core objective of supporting data analysis and exploration in educational settings; however, it has been expanded to include additional visualization and exploration features. These enhancements are intended to bolster the teaching of data analysis concepts and facilitate the dissemination of data literacy skills. Furthermore, RCSEDv2 offers a suite of interactive visualization options for both spectral and image data, including line plots, scatter plots, and various image visualizations such as single-band, multi-band, and stackable formats. A key innovation is the ability for users to interact with these visualizations through a web interface, allowing for the adjustment of wavelength ranges, band selection, and stacking orders. This level of interactivity is crucial for enhancing data exploration and understanding. The platform is accessible at https://rcsedv2.org. This paper details the platform's features and their application in data exploration and education. Additionally, a companion technical report is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.04001. The source code can be found at https://github.com/rcsedv2. Users are invited to explore the platform and provide feedback to support future development. Temporal action segmentation (TAS) is a critical task for video content analysis, which is why it has attracted significant research interest. While recent deep learning methods have achieved notable progress, they often depend on large-scale annotated datasets and struggle to generalize effectively to new domains. To address these challenges, we introduce an unsupervised TAS framework grounded in Self-Supervised Co-occurrence Activity Parsing (SSCAP). This approach leverages the inherent co-occurrence patterns within action segments to derive a representative and transferable representation. Software testing education is a critical component of computer science curricula, yet it is often difficult to implement due to the complexity of testing concepts and the lack of accessible, user-friendly tools for students. This paper introduces and examines the use of an Inquiry-Based Conceptual Response (IBCR) assessment method for testing education within an academic setting. The study compares the advantages and limitations of IBCR against traditional evaluation techniques, specifically code reviews and written exams. Through a case study involving 100 undergraduate students, we analyzed the effectiveness of IBCR in developing essential testing skills such as creating test cases, identifying faults, and writing unit tests. The results indicate that IBCR is a viable and effective approach for assessing conceptual understanding in software testing. Furthermore, we offer recommendations for software testing instructors on how to implement IBCR to enhance student learning. This research is anticipated to assist educators in designing testing assessments that are both effective and accessible. Additionally, the paper provides a link to a Java-based online tool that supports the implementation of IBCR. Keywords: Software Testing Education, Inquiry-Based Conceptual Response, Assessment.

Source-free domain adaptation (SFDA) has garnered significant attention recently, yet most SFDA techniques necessitate access to the original source data during training. This requirement is often impractical due to constraints like restricted data accessibility or high storage costs. To address this, we introduce a novel framework for transfer learning that utilizes only sources and targets without needing the original source dataset. This approach integrates a semi-supervised learning strategy with a domain alignment mechanism, enabling effective training without access to source data. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate superior performance compared to other SFDA methods, and our framework has been adopted as the baseline for the CVPR 2022 Source-free Domain Adaptation Challenge. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-1997/SFDA. Additionally, we have released a new Python package for SFDA under the name sfda. This paper outlines the design and operational principles of a gas-core nuclear reactor intended for space propulsion in remote locations far from Earth. Unlike conventional reactors, this system utilizes a fluid fuel that remains in a supercritical state above its critical point. This unique property enables the reactor to achieve significant power increases by expanding the fuel volume, thereby meeting the substantial power demands of deep space missions. The mechanism involves burning nuclear fuel at extremely high temperatures, which are made feasible by the rapid power ramp-up rate. This capability to transition from kilowatt to megawatt power levels in minutes distinguishes the reactor from all other known technologies. The study examines the thermodynamic and thermophysical properties of potential fuel mixtures, analyzes the relationship between power output and fuel volume, and outlines the design of a nuclear loop to deliver megawatt-level power to a spacecraft. Additionally, the paper addresses the design of a nuclear reactor suitable for space travel. A prototype capable of generating 10 MW is currently under development, with a full spacecraft-scale model targeting 100 MW. The article concludes by discussing the current status of research and development and the challenges that must be overcome to make this technology a viable option for space travel. Keywords: nuclear reactor, nuclear propulsion, gas core reactor, space travel, space propulsion.

This study demonstrates that incorporating domain knowledge into the architecture of neural networks enhances the localization of particle interactions in time-projected chamber (TPC) detectors. We evaluated a convolutional neural network (CNN) by comparing versions with and without domain-informed features. Results indicate that these structures significantly improve the resolution of interaction positions in 3D spatial coordinates, improving performance by 10% to 40% across various metrics. This enhancement is especially pronounced for interactions occurring near detector boundaries. We attribute this success to the inclusion of boundary information within the CNN's feature maps. Furthermore, we show that domain-informed CNNs are more resilient to variations in the training dataset, such as differing levels of detector noise. Finally, we outline the potential of domain-informed neural networks for future TPC designs incorporating advanced ionization readout technologies. This approach could facilitate the creation of compact, high-throughput, and high-resolution TPCs suitable for next-generation astroparticle experiments. All code and data utilized in this work are publicly accessible.

Atmospheric observations of brown dwarfs and exoplanets have advanced rapidly, yet the interpretation of these data requires extensive calculations for individual molecules. This necessity has spurred the creation of numerous resources offering pre-calculated line lists and cross sections. However, a significant challenge remains: most existing studies focus on isolated molecules, neglecting the complex interactions that occur in actual atmospheres. To address this gap, we introduce EXOPLINES, a comprehensive repository of line lists and cross sections for molecules prevalent in brown dwarf and giant exoplanet atmospheres. EXOPLINES employs the LINCONE code to generate extensive synthetic spectra across a broad wavelength spectrum, incorporating a wide array of molecules and their intermolecular interactions. The repository is freely accessible at https://exoplimes.github.io/. We have provided a detailed comparison of EXOPLINES against other prominent atmospheric retrieval tools, highlighting the critical impact of intermolecular interactions on spectral features. Our analysis demonstrates that interactions can alter abundance estimates by up to 100%, underscoring the vital role of these effects in atmospheric retrievals. We conclude that EXOPLINES will serve as a foundational resource for the upcoming generation of brown dwarf and exoplanet observations. The code is hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/ExoPlimes.
