The primary objective of this study is to introduce a matrix class known as the generalized Gauss-Newton (GGN) matrix, which offers an efficient approximation of the curvature tensor for the vast majority of deep neural networks (DNNs). This class encompasses various existing curvature-related matrices, such as the input-output Jacobian product, its block-diagonalized version, and the block-diagonalized output-input Jacobian product, all classified as GGN diminished matrices. The primary advantage of the proposed GGN diminished structure lies in its ability to enable the rapid calculation of the GGN matrix's generalized inverse, a capability that is often unattainable with full GGN matrices. This speed is achieved by leveraging the block-diagonalized Jacobian product and applying iterative refinement through a novel technique called the "block-diagonalization trick." Furthermore, we demonstrate that the block-diagonalized Jacobian product is the most effective GGN diminished structure for predicting generalization performance. Consequently, we believe this work will significantly aid future research on DNN curvature and generalization. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/SeiyaKuwakawa/ViViT. Additionally, we have released a new dataset, ViViT, which comprises 1,000 videos of people performing various activities in real-world settings, collected from YouTube. This dataset is designed to train and evaluate action recognition models, with a specific focus on those utilizing DNN curvature for enhanced performance. The dataset can be accessed at https://github.com/SeiyaKuwakawa/ViViT. The paper itself is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.01011. Over the past decade, object pose estimation has seen significant advancements, yet it remains a difficult challenge due to issues like class imbalance and a lack of training data for certain object classes. This paper introduces a zero-shot class-level pose estimation approach that requires only class-level information, such as names and pre-trained class-specific detectors, to estimate pose parameters. Our method is presented as a sequence of four core components: (1) Pose Parameterization, (2) Canonicalization, (3) Multi-View Consistent Rendering, and (4) Pose Regression. Additionally, we developed a novel loss function called the class-specific detector-guided 3D localization loss (cdL3d) to enhance pose accuracy. We evaluated this framework on the COCO, ImageNet-Pose, and YCB-Vis datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach achieves zero-shot class-level pose estimation without any posed training data, delivering performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods that utilize annotated data. The code and models are available at https://github.com/ashishgupta17/ZeroShotPose.

Real-time data from the 19-metre aperture telescope at the Irish LOFAR station (LoTSS) were utilized to monitor the 2022 February outburst of SS 433. This data was processed using REALTA, the backend of the Real-time Analysis of LOFAR data, which supports both real-time and offline spectral analysis. The resulting paper presents the first results from this methodology. We identified 11 outbursts, with 6 of them exhibiting a strong correlation between continuum and 11 GHz polarized flux density variations. The timing of these outbursts aligns with periodic dips in the continuum flux density observed in archival data. Additionally, we detected a significant linear trend in the polarized flux density, which may indicate a change in the magnetic field configuration. These findings are consistent with the outbursts being driven by the 16.7-day binary period of SS 433. Furthermore, we observed a weak correlation between outburst amplitudes and the degree of polarization, suggesting that outbursts with higher polarization are intrinsically more powerful. These results also offer a potential explanation for the observed 16.7-day periodicity in polarized flux density. Finally, we demonstrate that the REALTA backend is a highly effective tool for conducting real-time spectral analysis of astrophysical sources. By examining these components, we underscore the significance of metaphotonics and machine learning in advancing smart systems. Furthermore, we identify current challenges and future directions, aiming to inspire further exploration and innovation at the intersection of these two rapidly evolving fields. We believe this review will encourage new research endeavors where machine learning and metaphotonics intersect. The discussion begins with an overview of metaphotonics, defined as the synergy between metamaterials and photonic structures, which has recently become a focal point in smart system research. We then highlight the critical role of machine learning in designing and modeling metaphotonic devices, as well as in uncovering the underlying principles of light-matter interactions. Finally, we address the need for a unified framework that integrates machine learning with metaphotonics to fully harness their combined potential. The paper concludes by emphasizing the transformative impact of this fusion on developing next-generation intelligent technologies. Finally, Section 5 outlines future research directions, underscoring the transformative impact of machine learning on the field of metaphotonics. This study examines the influence of pre-released attributes—such as genre, star power, reviews, and budget—on a film industry dataset. By expanding the existing dataset to include 100,000 movies, we enable more comprehensive statistical analysis. Our investigation reveals that star power is the most significant predictor across all markets, while budget proves to be the least influential. Additionally, we developed a model to forecast a film's genre based on its trailer. The analysis further indicates that movies with trailers featuring action, comedy, or drama often achieve higher gross revenues, whereas those with romance, thriller, or animation traits tend to earn lower amounts. Finally, we determined that positive critical reviews and high star ratings generally correlate with increased gross income. This study introduces a model for a power grid incorporating auxiliary frequency regulation, where each node features a local inductive energy storage device. We establish a thermodynamic framework to derive the grid's equations of motion and examine the resulting frequency and voltage dynamics. Our findings indicate that these dynamics can be decomposed into a fast mode governing voltage behavior and a slow mode governing frequency behavior. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that the damping characteristics of the fast mode are contingent upon the total stored energy within the auxiliary devices. Finally, we present numerical simulations that validate our theoretical conclusions. These results underscore the potential of auxiliary frequency regulation in enhancing power grid stability. Specifically, increasing the total stored energy in the devices stabilizes voltage dynamics by shifting them from an unstable focus to a stable focus, or from a limit cycle to a stable fixed point. Additionally, our analysis reveals that the stability of frequency dynamics is influenced by the distribution of the devices' capacity across the grid. This influence is quantified by the stability exponent, which is determined by the mean capacity of the devices and the capacity variance. A higher stability exponent signifies a more rapid destabilization of the fixed point. Our numerical results align with this theoretical prediction. Consequently, the frequency dynamics can be stabilized by either uniformly distributing the device capacity throughout the grid or by concentrating all capacity at a single node. In both scenarios, the frequency dynamics transition from a stable focus to a stable limit cycle. The latter scenario is particularly significant, as it suggests that strategically placing a single large-scale device can achieve optimal storage utilization. This paper is designed to be accessible to researchers across various disciplines, with an emphasis on providing a comprehensive theoretical background and detailed explanations. This study investigates whether the ultraviolet (UV) and soft X-ray excesses observed in blazar spectra can be attributed to photons scattered by the jet's magnetic field. We examine a population of 100 flat-spectrum radio quasars (FSRQs) from the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) catalog, utilizing a Monte-Carlo approach to model synchrotron photons and polarized electrons within a two-zone framework. Our results indicate that the jet is the most probable source of the UV and soft X-ray excess in these sources, with the majority of scattered photons originating from the seed photon field generated within the same zone as the synchronotrons. This finding contrasts with the findings of our previous work (MAPPIES I), which suggested that excess energy likely arises from scattering off seed photons external to the jet. We conclude that the most viable mechanism for this scattering process is Partially Polarized Inverse External-Compton Scattering (MAPPIES II). Finally, we demonstrate that this mechanism can be constrained using broadband spectral data, specifically by analyzing the polarization degree of the UV/X-ray surplus. We show that the predicted polarization degree aligns with the high polarization values reported in the literature. Consequently, MAPPIES II offers a promising pathway for explaining the UV/soft X-ray excess in FSRQs, potentially resolving the long-standing mystery of this emission. Furthermore, we outline future observational and theoretical efforts aimed at clarifying the origin of this excess. This work represents the first step toward a comprehensive theoretical framework for the jet-based origin of the UV/X-ray surplus in FSRQs. We present a method for analytically extending the extension operator, originally developed for complex data in Euclidean space, to the analytic continuation of complex data over complex 2D surfaces. This approach leverages local parameterizations of the 2D surface, utilizing the Schur product (or Hadamard product) of matrices. The resulting operator is both linear and symbolic, facilitating the symbolic computation of powers. Furthermore, it enables the analytical power of the extension operator for complex function and signal data, thereby broadening the scope of various algorithms that depend on this operation. The validity of this methodology is demonstrated through examples involving complex function extension, the spectral signal Poincaré group, and the spectral Shannon entropy extension operator. The methodology is implemented in Python and made available on GitHub. We present a digital approach to determining whether a symmetric pure state belongs to an entangled, product, or squeezed state ensemble. This method relies on evaluating the concavity of a specific real-valued function, for which we derive an efficient computational formula based on quadrature amplitudes at specific times. This algorithm facilitates an effective classification of symmetric pure states and establishes their dynamic behavior. Our findings indicate that while all three ensembles can exhibit asymptotically orthogonal states, only the squeezed state ensemble achieves this under unitary dynamics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the asymptotic behavior of symmetric pure states is periodic when using regular coherent state bases and half-periodic when employing alternating coherent state bases. These outcomes are supported by numerical simulations. Additionally, we explore the application of this method in quantum key distribution. Our results suggest that employing a basis of alternating coherent states enhances security compared to using a basis of regular coherent states. Finally, we outline potential future research directions stemming from this study. Baryon generation is proposed as a consequence of quantized fragmentation of a QCD filament, which is assumed to be helical and energized by the electro-magnetic field of a heavy quark. The filament is hypothesized to persist for a duration comparable to the hadronization time of the quark. This model offers an explanation for the baryon-to-meson ratio observed in experiments. Additionally, it suggests that the baryon anti-baryon pair exhibits significant spatial correlation, potentially detectable through the final state. The mechanism also accounts for the enhancement of Lambda protons in cold nuclear matter. The energy density of the filament is estimated to be several GeV/fm$^3$, a value that may also contribute to the energy density of the quark-gluon plasma. Furthermore, the model predicts the production of pairs of jets originating from the heavy quark and diquarks, with the diquarks subsequently converting into baryons. These jets are predicted to be softer than the jets associated with the produced baryons. The fragmentation process is estimated to yield a baryon multiplicity of approximately 10% per baryon produced. Finally, the model predicts that the production of baryons carrying the anti-quark from the initial heavy quark will be enhanced. These predictions can be tested at RHIC and the LHC. The analysis also examines the production of hypernuclei and their anti-particles, suggesting that anti-hypernuclei could be enhanced by a factor of 2-3 compared to the hypernuclei they form. The discussion concludes with the possibility of forming anti-hypernuclei in cold nuclear matter. The model is also applied to the production of anti-hypernuclei in ultraperipheral Pb-Pb collisions. The paper concludes with a discussion of the implications of these findings for the search for dark matter. A key prediction is that the filament acts as a source of dark matter, specifically producing dark matter anti-particles that are trapped by the dark matter halo of the lead nucleus. This could be investigated by searching for dark matter anti-particles in ultraperipheral Pb-Pb collisions. The analysis also addresses the possibility of detecting dark matter in this context. Solar active regions (ARs) generate significant acoustic waves that propagate globally, reaching distant helioseismic foci (DARs). These propagations are detectable as travel-time shifts when comparing data before and after an AR emerges. This study examines how the movements of DARs surrounding active areas influence global helioseismic travel-time measurements. We selected 10 major sunspot groups from 2010 to 2019, analyzing 2-minute cadence HMI Dopplergrams to identify AR and DAR locations. Using the Global Oscillation Network Group (GONG) dataset, we calculated helioseismic travel times from these regions. The results indicate that travel-time shifts at a specific DAR prior to an AR's emergence are comparable to those observed at the emergence site itself, suggesting the global signal is established early. Furthermore, DAR displacements prior to emergence contribute significantly to travel-time variations, with a correlation coefficient of 0.65. This relationship is particularly pronounced for ARs with large areas and high emergence speeds. Consequently, the travel-time shift profile at the emergence site reflects the history of DAR motion prior to emergence. Finally, we demonstrate that the travel-time shift pattern at an AR's emergence site resembles the Doppler shift pattern of the same region. These findings suggest that the travel-time shift profile at an AR's emergence site is primarily determined by the magnetic field configuration of that region. These insights are crucial for interpreting helioseismic travel-time signals, which are increasingly utilized to investigate the solar interior. Additionally, this analysis aids in identifying the most informative ARs for studying the solar interior's response to emerging magnetic flux. Future research will explore the impact of magnetic flux emergence on the solar interior using advanced numerical simulations. This analysis is part of a broader project investigating the relationship between solar surface magnetic field emergence and the solar interior. We demonstrate that the Pulsar Timing Network (PTN) can detect a stochastic gravitational wave background (GWB) generated by Primordial Electromagnetic Fields (PEFs). This detection becomes feasible when the PEF energy density reaches $\rho_{em}\gtrsim 10^{-10} \rho_{\rm crit}$, a threshold significantly lower than the sensitivity of current gravitational wave detectors. The signal manifests as a flat spectrum across the Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) frequency band, exhibiting a distinct correlation pattern that differs from the Hellings-Howard curve. Additionally, the PEFs induce a frequency-dependent polarization of GWs, which can be isolated from the noise background. We illustrate that a dedicated analysis of PTA data could uncover PEFs with an energy density as low as $\rho_{em}\sim 10^{-15} \rho_{\rm crit}$, a level far below that accessible to other GW observatories. This capability offers a robust test for PEFs that may have been produced during the very early universe. Furthermore, the PEFs can reheat the universe, potentially resolving the issue of excessive entropy in the radiation-dominated epoch. Consequently, PTA observations can probe PEFs that are thermally erased, thereby constraining the amplitude of primordial fields and the temperature of the thermal bath. Finally, we show that PTA data can independently constrain the amplitude of PEFs, independent of the thermal history of the universe. This approach leverages the fact that GW polarization is altered by PEFs, whereas scalar gravitational waves remain unaffected. By analyzing the polarization of high-amplitude GW modes, PTA observations can probe PEFs with energy densities as low as $\rho_{em}\sim 10^{-20} \rho_{\rm crit}$. This capability can test the production of PEFs via inflationary mechanisms, as well as alternative scenarios such as particle decay or preheating. The latter are characterized by a cutoff in the PEF spectrum, whereas inflationary production yields an unbroken power spectrum. Thus, PTA observations can simultaneously constrain the amplitude and production mechanism of PEFs. This represents a novel and significant advantage of PTA experiments. We conclude that the PTA will play a crucial role in investigating the physics of the very early universe. This paper introduces a new approach to compressing light field (LF) images by leveraging disparity information to enhance spatial prediction. The proposed method employs a disparity-guided plane (DGP) to model spatial disparity across views, facilitating prediction-based compression. By utilizing disparity data, we construct a DGP to estimate missing pixel values. To generate the necessary disparity information, we employ the deep learning-based DispNetS model, which is trained on publicly available datasets. The resulting DGP effectively captures spatial dependencies within the LF. Additionally, we employ a practical compression technique that integrates this DGP-based prediction with a conventional JPEG image codec. Experimental results demonstrate that our DGP-based prediction significantly outperforms traditional angular and spatial prediction methods, achieving an average PSNR improvement of 0.6 dB over state-of-the-art compression techniques. Furthermore, our DGP can be easily extracted from pre-trained models, making the approach highly practical for real-world LF compression applications. Finally, we validate the method's effectiveness using two sample LFs, where the DGP accurately represents inter-pixel relationships. Small area estimation (SAE) is a statistical framework designed to derive reliable estimates for minimal sample sizes within distinct strata. This methodology is frequently employed in health and demographic surveys to generate estimates for rates, proportions, and means when direct data collection is infeasible. Although SAE techniques have been utilized in various contexts, their application in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) remains limited. This study examines the performance of model-based and design-based SAE approaches across multiple data sources from a single LMIC. Furthermore, it explores the utility of integrating these methods to enhance predictive accuracy. The findings indicate that hybrid approaches yield superior prediction results compared to traditional model-based methods. Additionally, the research demonstrates that leveraging multiple data sources can boost prediction precision, offering valuable insights for practitioners aiming to optimize SAE applications in statistical surveys. We examine a scenario where a gambler engages in continuous-product trials, allowing for an infinite number of bets and receiving a reward defined by the geometric mean of all wagers. Within a quantum framework where the gambler's capital is represented by a continuous-variable state, specifically a Gaussian Gaussian Schmidt Squeezed Thermal Light (GSSTL) state, we demonstrate that choosing a uniform distribution for the wields maximizes both the geometric mean and the quantum relative entropy reward. Furthermore, we analyze the limit of an upper bound on geometric mean capital, revealing that quantum properties such as squeezing and thermal effects are optimal when set at 50% levels. This optimal point aligns with a phase transition in the von Neumann entropy of the gambler's state, shifting the regime from a pure state to a mixed state. Additionally, we investigate the relative entropy of the gambler's capital, showing it reaches its maximum of $\ln 2$ when the gambler starts with a coherent state. These findings are supported by numerical simulations. Ultimately, our results indicate that the quantum treatment of Kelly wagers, grounded in continuous-variable states, offers a more realistic framework for modeling real-world capital. This approach also provides a pathway to determine the optimal qubit reward in discrete trials, a problem that remains unsolved in discrete treatments of Kelly betting. Finally, we explore the potential of this method for detecting entanglement between two gamblers. Entanglement detection is achieved by comparing the quantum relative entropy reward of individual gamblers against that of a shared gamblers state; if the shared state yields a higher reward, entanglement is confirmed. Our calculations suggest that gamblers utilizing Gaussian Gaussian Schmidt Squeezed Thermal Light (GSSTL) states are entangled. These conclusions are also validated through numerical simulations. Given that GSSTL states can be generated in the laboratory, this method for detecting qubit entanglement could be practically implemented. Furthermore, our results offer a solution to the qubit equivalent of the "two children paradox," a problem that remains unresolved in discrete treatments of Kelly wagers. This is because our quantum approach employs continuous variables, whereas discrete variables are insufficient to resolve the paradox. We conclude that the quantum model of Kelly wagers, based on continuous variables, is more comprehensive than the discrete model, which is limited to describing qubit states. Transition metal and group 14 dichalcogenides and difluorides have garnered significant interest for their diverse electronic structures, including metal, semimetal, and semiconductor phases. This study investigates the electronic and optical characteristics of MA$_2$Z$_4$ compounds, where M represents Mo, W, or Ti, and Z represents N, P, As, Si, or Ge. Utilizing density functional theory, we examine various stacking configurations and compare their optical responses. Our findings indicate that the inversion symmetry of the MA$_2$Z$_4$ lattice is essential for in-plane polarization, while out-of-plane polarization arises from spin-orbit coupling. We demonstrate that the band structure of MA$_2$Z$_4$ can be categorized into three groups based on the arrangement of quasiparticle bands. Furthermore, we identify a unique excitonic state that remains stable across different stacking configurations and exhibits minimal sensitivity to strain. These results offer valuable insights for designing optical devices utilizing MA$_2$Z$_4$ materials. Additionally, our analysis of the quasiparticle band structure in these compounds provides a foundation for future research into valleytronics. Finally, our work establishes a systematic framework for classifying the quasiparticle band arrangement in such materials. This classification scheme can be readily extended to other materials, thereby advancing the understanding of quasiparticle band arrangement in a broader range of systems. This study presents the first theoretical investigation of the rare flavor-changing neutral current process $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$, utilizing the Standard Model within the framework of Chiral Perturbation Theory at two-loop order. We demonstrate that the branching ratio for this reaction is approximately $10^{-12}$, a level that can be readily investigated by the LHCb experiment. Furthermore, we examine the sensitivity of the LHCb detector and analyze the distribution of the $\mu^+ \mu^-$ invariant mass, revealing a peak in the low mass region. Atmospheric models serve as essential instruments for analyzing and interpreting astronomical data. This study introduces a novel approach to model characterization, which quantifies the extent to which an atmospheric model can be distinguished from others. We apply this characterization method to widely used models, including MODTRAN, LOWTRAN, and the simplified formulations by Bennett and Chapin, and evaluate their utility for atmospheric correction in the visible spectrum. Our findings indicate that the radiance of these models is highly correlated, particularly in the blue wavelengths. Consequently, the radiance of a single pixel is nearly as informative as the radiance of the entire spectrum for characterizing these models. This result implies that the spectral resolution of sensors designed to observe atmospheric models should be coarse. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the spectral position of the sensor's first channel is more critical for model characterization than the available spectral range. Finally, we show that the spectral range spanning from the model's first to the sensor's first channel offers the greatest discriminatory power. These conclusions are derived from an analysis of the eigenvectors of the model correlation matrix. Additionally, we examine the eigenvectors and eigenvalues to identify the primary physical factors causing variations in atmospheric radiation. These factors include aerosol optical depth, Rayleigh optical depth, water vapor content, and surface albedo. Ultimately, this research provides a robust framework for selecting the most suitable atmospheric models for specific on-sky observation scenarios. We propose interpreting Pontryagin duality through the lens of classical logic, a perspective that aligns with our intuitive grasp of time-reversal symmetry in physics. Furthermore, we intend to explore the connections this interpretation establishes with quantum mechanics and Minkowski spacetime. In this work, we focus exclusively on the first point, which serves as a foundation for the more intricate discussions found in our prior papers [1, 2]. Our approach relies on the "steadfast" or "classical" logic of a Boolean algebra, as opposed to the "braided" logic characteristic of anyon systems in topological quantum field theory. We examine the steadfast logic associated with the real numbers $\mathbb{R}$ and its dual, the additive group of cardinal numbers $\mathbb{C}$. This group consists of pairs $(\omega, \epsilon)$, where $\omega$ represents the order (ordinal) and $\epsilon$ represents the cofinality (denumerability). We demonstrate that the conjunction operation in the dual group $\mathbb{C}$ differs from that in the original group $\mathbb{R}$. Specifically, the conjunction of two propositions $p$ and $q$ is determined by the dual group operation applied to their truth values, $\bar{p}$ and $\bar{q}$. In $\mathbb{R}$, the supremum corresponds to the maximum, yielding $\max(p, q)$, whereas in $\mathbb{C}$, it results in the sum $\bar{p} + \bar{q}$. Consequently, the dual conjunction of $p$ and $q$ in $\mathbb{C}$ is defined as $\bar{p} + \bar{q} + 1$. We note that this result holds true for any two non-zero cardinal numbers, implying that the conjunction of two true propositions in $\mathbb{C}$ remains true. Federated learning (FL) represents a distributed approach to training machine learning models, where a global model is iteratively refined through local updates exchanged between a central server and participating clients. This framework is widely adopted in real-world scenarios, such as mobile applications, to facilitate collaboration among diverse stakeholders. However, challenges persist, including the uneven distribution of data across clients and the varying computational resources available to them. These issues can result in a discrepancy between the global model's performance and that of individual client-specific models. To address this, various techniques have been developed to enhance data handling and communication protocols. This paper provides a comprehensive review of FL, with a specific focus on addressing the issue of unequal resource distribution among participants. Furthermore, it examines how differential privacy (DP) is integrated into FL to safeguard client data, while also highlighting specific challenges associated with applying DP in federated environments. Finally, the study outlines potential future research directions for FL. Given the rapid evolution of FL, this work aims to serve as a valuable reference for researchers and practitioners. Additionally, it seeks to raise awareness regarding privacy concerns within FL, a topic that has received limited attention in existing literature. Consequently, this paper offers a foundational resource for those interested in advancing FL research. A key contribution is a thorough exploration of DP's role in FL, which is expected to inspire further investigation into this critical area. The authors hope this review will encourage expanded research efforts to enhance the privacy and security of FL systems. Supplementary materials are available at https://github.com/abhishekkumar2001/FL-Review. The repository includes a detailed review of FL, its challenges, and solutions, along with code for implementing FL with and without differential privacy. This resource is intended to assist researchers in quickly grasping the fundamentals of FL and initiating their own research endeavors. The beta decay of mercury-186 was investigated using a magnetic beta spectrometer. The resulting spectrum for this highly neutron-deficient nuclide displays a complex structure featuring numerous transitions. The decay is primarily characterized by three main transitions with energies of 3000, 1700, and 1000 keV, which collectively account for approximately 70% of all decays. Additionally, at least 13 other transitions were identified, with energies ranging from 300 to 2000 keV. Based on these findings, a decay scheme and spin-parity assignments were proposed. Furthermore, several half-lives were determined for the first time: $T_{1/2}(^{186}$Hg$)$ = 1.69(1) s, $T_{1/2}(^{186m1}$Hg$)$ = 11.5(2) ns, $T_{1/2}(^{186m2}$Hg$)$ = 10.5(1) ns, and $T_{1/2}(^{186m3}$Hg$)$ = 1.1(1) $\mu$s. Additionally, the isomeric ratio for the transition to the 1000-keV level was measured as I(1000 keV)/I(3000 keV) = 0.12(1). These results were compared with existing literature values, revealing significant discrepancies. Finally, the experimental data were compared with predictions from various nuclear models. The study concludes that the odd neutron in $^{186}$Hg is most likely in the $1g_{7/2}$ orbital, with the 1000-keV level serving as the ground state. This finding contrasts with the conclusion drawn in prior literature, which suggested the $3d_{3/2}$ orbital. The paper also discusses the implications of these findings for nuclear models. The primary objective of data-driven control is to design controllers for dynamical systems using solely system data, without requiring explicit mathematical models. Although this approach is highly desirable, it is often hindered by the need for extensive data collection. This paper introduces a novel data-driven control framework that effectively manages limited data scenarios by leveraging supplementary information. Specifically, the method projects dynamical systems onto a lower-dimensional linear time-invariant (LTI) subspace, where a linear controller is designed to achieve a specific target behavior in the original system based on these LTI parameters. The proposed algorithm successfully controls the target system's behavior with significantly fewer data points than traditional methods. Furthermore, it unifies the control of diverse systems, enabling the development of a single neural network capable of learning to walk, swim, fly, and reach goals across various environments. Experimental results validate the algorithm's effectiveness, demonstrating its ability to achieve the desired behavior despite severe data constraints. Additionally, the approach facilitates the transfer of behaviors learned in one environment to others, allowing for the attainment of target actions in unseen environments with minimal learning requirements. This methodology is applicable to diverse domains, including motor skill learning, skill acquisition, and autonomous vehicle path planning. The paper concludes by outlining the algorithm's theoretical properties and exploring potential future research directions. Finally, a demonstration video is available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=22222222222. Relation networks have recently gained significant attention for their ability to model interactions between objects within an image, achieving state-of-the-art results in few-shot learning and other tasks. However, current relation network approaches rely on fixed, pre-labeled support sets, a limitation that restricts their effectiveness in complex environments like natural images. To address this, we introduce a triplet loss that enables the relation networks to autonomously learn optimal configurations for classification. Building on this loss function, we also develop a novel generative adversarial network framework called RelationGAN. This approach leverages adversarial training to facilitate joint learning of class-specific concepts and discriminators, thereby enhancing few-shot learning performance. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that our methods surpass existing state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, visual comparisons highlight the model's capacity to generate diverse and realistic images. The source code is available at \url{https://github.com/ChenYi2019/RelationGAN}.

In dual-field quantum key distribution (QKD), a single photon is encoded with both quantum and classical information, enabling key generation while simultaneously transmitting data. However, previous implementations relied on interferometric encoding, which necessitated complex and costly phase stabilization systems to maintain interference patterns during data transmission. This study introduces a novel dual-field QKD protocol that eliminates the need for phase stabilization. By employing a non-interferometric method to encode quantum keys onto data photons, the scheme remains functional even when phase errors exist during transmission. This approach significantly simplifies the system architecture and reduces operational costs, thereby advancing the practical realization of dual-field QKD. Furthermore, the proposed method is more readily adaptable to long-distance scenarios than prior proposals, as it can be integrated with existing time-bin coding techniques for quantum key distribution. Finally, the paper compares the security of this new scheme against various dual-field attack models. Specifically, when the quantum key bit rate is set to 50% of the data transmission rate, the security analysis indicates that the scheme remains secure against dual-field attacks, with key lengths reaching approximately 100 bits. Additionally, the analysis demonstrates that the scheme is immune to photon-number-splitting attacks. In the presence of channel noise, the practical security of the proposed dual-field QKD is further illustrated by examining key generation rates and secret key distances under different attack conditions. Results indicate that the scheme can achieve a quantum key generation rate of about 100 kbps at distances up to roughly 10 km, or a distance of approximately 100 km at a key rate of about 10 kbps. These findings suggest that the proposed dual-field QKD scheme holds significant practical value. We present new observations of ionized gas, neutral atomic hydrogen, and photodissociation regions surrounding the Rho Oph S1 cluster using the VLA, VLA/VLA-RT, and IRAM 30m radio telescopes. The VLA data reveal a hot ionized medium (T > 10^4 K) with low density (n < 1 cm^-3) that is more extended than previously documented. This medium exhibits a complex morphology, featuring a prominent arc of ionized gas along the cluster's eastern side and a bubble-like structure on the western side. We propose that this arc results from the interaction between the eastern HII region and the dense molecular cloud edge, while the western bubble is shaped by the cluster's radiation field and influenced by the motion of its most massive stars. This study evaluates the efficacy of two factor models, which utilize principal component analysis to estimate parameters for predicting future mortality rates, in forecasting US life tables. The first factor model allows factor loadings to vary over time, whereas the second maintains constant loadings. Both approaches demonstrate high predictive accuracy when compared to the classic Lee-Carter model. The primary distinction lies in their structural assumptions: the constant-loading model relies on a static structure, whereas both the time-varying factor model and the Lee-Carter model employ time-varying structures. Additionally, the constant-loading model requires fewer parameters than Lee-Carter, offering greater simplicity. Consequently, the constant-loading factor model emerges as the most efficient method for mortality prediction. This conclusion is supported by an efficiency analysis that integrates criteria for accuracy, simplicity, and parameter count. Finally, we apply this optimal constant-factor model to estimate remaining life expectancy. Results indicate that life expectancy is stable across all counties, yet significant disparities in life-line parallelism are observed. Specifically, life expectancies for males and females diverge more significantly in certain counties than in others. Furthermore, these differences are more pronounced in counties with lower overall life expectancies. These findings suggest that, compared to large states, smaller states with generally higher life expectancies exhibit greater similarity between male and female life lines. This aligns with the principle that, at higher life expectancy levels, the impact of external factors on life expectancy diminishes. In contrast, at lower life expectancy levels, the two lines diverge more, indicating a stronger influence of biological factors. These insights may inform future public health initiatives aimed at narrowing the gender gap in life expectancy. Finally, we outline potential future research directions, including the application of factor models to other time series forecasting tasks and the development of dynamic factor models for mortality prediction. The latter approach would allow factors to be driven by unobserved latent variables, thereby enhancing model flexibility. All code used in this research is publicly available.

Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has demonstrated that well-structured search spaces can yield models that match or exceed the performance of state-of-the-art architectures. However, within a fixed search space and budget, these results often suffer from interference, where the performance of specific high-quality architectures is suppressed by the presence of other architectures in the space. This paper investigates this issue by analyzing the distribution of prediction accuracy across the search space. We find that accuracy distributions are highly non-uniform, characterized by numerous low-performing models and only a few top-performing ones. To address this, we introduce a regularization technique that discourages score regression loss functions from learning this non-uniformity. Our findings indicate that this regularization effectively mitigates interference, resulting in the discovery of superior architectures. We validate our approach across three search spaces, demonstrating that our method identifies top-tier architectures that outperform those found by existing NAS methods. Additionally, we provide an optimization perspective to explain the anti-interference property of our approach. Finally, we observe that incorporating this regularization into other methods, such as PNAS and ENAS, also leads to the identification of better architectures. The code is available at https://github.com/taeyongkim1234/interference-free-NAS.

This paper provides a comprehensive characterization of the boundary of a CAT(0) area ensuring geodesic completeness in the square of its curvature, with a primary focus on 2-dimensional polyhedral surfaces featuring non-positive vertex curvature. The proof relies on a newly developed technical tool: a version of the finite subobject separation property within the category of CAT(0) square areas. Furthermore, we offer a detailed examination of the two-dimensional Euclidean setting, which incorporates an analysis of the boundary for geodesically complete geodesic domains within the Minkowski plane. As an application, we demonstrate that the cone over any simply connected compact Riemann surface is a geodesically complete CAT(0) area, a finding that partially addresses a query raised by M. R. Bridson and F. Haglund. Additionally, we establish that the cone over the universal cover of a compact orientable surface of genus $g \geq 2$, equipped with a Riemannian metric possessing strictly positive curvature, fails to be a CAT(0) square area, thereby partially resolving another of Bridson and Haglund's questions. This paper introduces a novel approach to assessing translator performance, introducing the dependability of a translation as a new quality metric. We model the translator's dependency on a source text using a cognitive process grounded in translation theory, representing output quality through a distribution over scores. We propose a Bayesian framework for evaluating dependability, which is demonstrated in a case study analyzing French-to-English translation. Additionally, we present a method for estimating the average dependability of a translation pair between two specific texts, alongside a procedure for calculating the expected dependability gain achieved by professional editors. Finally, we outline a procedure for measuring the dependability difference between two translators within a specific domain. Through a simulation study, we show that this method can effectively detect performance improvements resulting from post-editing. Ultimately, we demonstrate that the proposed approach offers a robust method for assessing translator quality and identifies clear avenues for performance enhancement. Notably, our findings indicate that professional editors can significantly improve the dependability of amateur translations within a specific domain. Furthermore, we show that the quality of the original source text directly influences the potential for dependability improvement via post-editing. These results provide valuable insights for future research aimed at enhancing translation quality. Ultimately, this methodology offers a means to evaluate the efficacy of various strategies designed to improve dependability. The study's source code is accessible at https://github.com/alejo-fernandez/eval-translators-dependability. The paper can be accessed at https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.07000. The source code for the study is available at https://github.com/alejo-fernandez/eval-translators-dependability.

We establish sum rules for energy absorption in open, nonreciprocal scattering systems, with a specific focus on time-reversal symmetry breaking. These sum rules are derived using a scattering approach that maintains a clear physical interpretation of energy absorption across general parameter regimes. A notable feature of these results is their applicability to any incoming wave profile. Specifically, when considering a single incoming channel and imposing constraints on energy absorption when this channel is closed, we obtain sum rules for the energy absorption cross section. In the context of an incoming plane wave, we demonstrate that the total energy absorption cross section exhibits scale invariance for frequencies far below the dissipation rates of the system's modes. This phenomenon is linked to the breaking of reciprocity and is exemplified by the scale invariance observed in the scattering cross section of a perfectly conducting sphere. Furthermore, we illustrate these findings with a model of a dissipationless waveguide featuring a lossy, nonreciprocal scatterer. In this scenario, we show that the sum rules can be analytically verified and that all system modes are effectively reciprocal. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for achieving broadband energy absorption. In particular, we examine a recent proposal for broadband light absorption in nonreciprocal systems and demonstrate that, despite the breaking of reciprocity, the total energy absorption cross section remains invariant under a scaling transformation. This outcome is attributed to a specific property of the problem, where the nonreciprocal element is modeled as a nonreciprocal shunt inductor. Consequently, the total energy absorption cross section is the sum of two terms: one representing absorption in a reciprocal system and the other being a constant that diverges at zero frequency. We also explore the broader implications of these findings for designing efficient nonreciprocal absorbers. In this context, we suggest that a practical way to ensure broadband energy absorption is to align the imaginary part of the nonreciprocal parameter with the frequency scale of the system. Additionally, we note that our sum rules can be reformulated in terms of scattering cross sections, thereby extending recent findings regarding scale invariance in optical cross sections to arbitrary dissipative systems. Finally, we outline several avenues for future research, including the investigation of sum rules for energy absorption with a prescribed plane wave incoming profile and the potential for further simplifications in specific problems. Moreover, we discuss the possibility of extending these sum rules to other conserved quantities, such as momentum, and address the challenges associated with such an extension. Recent advancements in Fully Connected Neural Networks (FCNNs) have demonstrated that connecting all layers in a deep convolutional neural network (CNN) can enhance performance on specific tasks. This study investigates whether these performance gains stem from increased data representation or from the activation of specific "winning tickets" within the FCNN. By employing trimming techniques to remove redundant parameters, we identified such tickets in all tested cases. Furthermore, we utilized parameter sharing to construct these tickets prior to training, successfully isolating key attributes like edges, shapes, and textures. These attributes were successfully classified with high accuracy using the isolated tickets, even under limited data conditions. The research also examined the impact of data augmentation and dropout on the attributes detected by the winning tickets. Finally, we analyzed the convergence behavior of the tickets, revealing that while winning tickets converge faster than the global optimum, they achieve similar final accuracy. Overall, the findings indicate that winning tickets constitute a subset of parameters within the FCNN that are sufficient for training, suggesting that future efforts should focus on identifying and isolating these tickets to optimize FCNNs. Additionally, we demonstrated that winning tickets can be transferred between related tasks, a capability that further validates their role as the essential core of the FCNN. Finally, we explored the potential of hyperparameter-free FCNNs by applying a similar approach to parameter isolation. By employing a new method to determine the optimal number of channels, we successfully separated the attributes of the CNNs. The resulting hyperparameter-free CNNs achieved accuracy comparable to standard CNNs, even with reduced data. This work offers a fresh perspective on the significance of network parameters and provides a foundation for future research into parameter isolation. This research investigates the valuation of lottery tickets. We introduce a new decision-theoretic framework for assessing ticket worth, grounded in subjective lottery evaluation by Smith and Zener (1708) and expanded by Kahneman and Tversky (1981). Utilizing this model, we analyze the impact of ticket features—such as cost, group size, and draw frequency—on perceived value. Our study involves 1,000 participants completing an online survey that exposed them to 200 distinct lottery scenarios. We estimate model parameters using a mixed-effects approach and subsequently determine optimal pricing strategies and ideal purchase timing for participating agents. Our findings indicate that perceived ticket value is heavily influenced by actual win probabilities, which vary significantly based on specific design characteristics. Furthermore, we observe that agents' valuations are highly sensitive to ticket price and exhibit substantial heterogeneity. Finally, our results demonstrate that launching new draws during periods of heightened public interest can substantially boost ticket sales. These insights offer valuable guidance for lottery operators aiming to maximize revenue. Additionally, our results align with prior literature, confirming that the psychological drivers of participation remain consistent across different operational contexts. The valley Hall effect in two-dimensional materials is typically viewed as the non-linear electron-phonon interaction analogue of the Hall effect driven by external magnetic fields. This study demonstrates that such external magnetic fields can be substituted by specific phonon modes, yielding a valley Hall response that mirrors the traditional phenomenon. This finding is validated through first-principles calculations of the valley Hall current induced by a specific phonon mode in two-dimensional WTe$_2$. Furthermore, we show that this phonon-induced valley Hall response is contingent upon a distinct electron-phonon coupling mechanism, differing from that which governs valley relaxation. These insights offer a novel pathway to investigate and manipulate valley physics in two-dimensional materials. Additionally, the methodology employed is applicable to modeling electron-phonon interactions in various theoretical and computational frameworks. Finally, the computational approach utilized is versatile and can be adapted to electron-phonon interactions across a broad spectrum of materials. Visualizing high-dimensional data is essential for data analysis, and t-SNE has become a widely adopted method due to its effectiveness. However, its standard formulation relies on Euclidean distance, which renders many resulting visualizations misleading when applied to data residing on a spherical manifold. To address this, we introduce VMF-SNE, a novel algorithm designed to project spherical data onto a 2D plane. This approach utilizes the von Mises-Fisher distribution to define pairwise similarities based on spherical distances. Extensive experiments demonstrate that VMF-SNE outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in producing more accurate and interpretable visualizations. Additionally, we provide an R package to facilitate the application of this method. Our methodology is particularly beneficial for spherical data analysis tasks, including directional data analysis, orientation analysis, and any domain involving data on a spherical manifold. This study details diagrammatic Monte Carlo calculations for the two-dimensional Fermi polaron in a BCS-Bose limit, encompassing up to 200 diagrams. The resulting diagrams were categorized into finite-temperature Feynman diagrams for the self-energy, alongside an analysis of zero-temperature Feynman, Matsubara, and ring diagrams. By applying a diagrammatic cluster expansion, the diagrams linked to the self-energy in the normal phase were identified and linked to those contributing to the self-energy and gap in the Bose-Einstein condensate phase. Furthermore, diagrams responsible for the Kosterlitz-Thouless gap were pinpointed. The finite-temperature diagrams, including ring diagrams, were observed to extend the Kosterlitz-Thouless gap into the normal phase. Finally, the calculated polaron binding energy aligns with the Kosterlitz-Thouless-Bogoliubov energy. These findings offer a comprehensive diagrammatic perspective on the transition from the normal to the Bose-Einstein condensate phase. Additionally, the polaron binding energy demonstrates a linear temperature dependence, a feature previously noted in the Kondo model. This suggests that the polaron binding energy may serve as a universal quantity for interacting fermion systems. The methodology employed here is also applicable to investigating the Kondo temperature and spin gap within the same system. Overall, this work represents a significant advancement in diagrammatic Monte Carlo techniques. Furthermore, the approach can be extended to investigate the Kondo effect and spin gap in the same system, as well as to explore the quantum critical point of the Kondo lattice. The latter application would provide insights into the quantum critical behavior of heavy fermion systems. The techniques utilized are also relevant for studying the quantum phase transition from a valence bond solid to a spin liquid in the spin-1/2 Heisenberg model on the kagome lattice. The methods described herein are expected to advance the field of quantum many-body physics. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/abhishekdatta1234567/diagrammatic-Monte-Carlo. Quantum emulation of fermionic systems is established as a critical step toward achieving fault-tolerant quantum simulations. We introduce a hybrid digital-analog computing approach that leverages the extended operational capabilities of digital-qubit methods and hardware-efficient analog-qubit techniques to accurately model fermionic systems on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) processors. This proposed method is demonstrated through the emulation of a two-dimensional fermionic Hubbard model, a key system for studying strongly correlated fermions. Our analysis indicates that this digital-analog approach surpasses both digital-qubit and analog-qubit strategies in terms of accuracy and efficiency. Additionally, we outline a straightforward extension of this method to larger-scale quantum emulation. Given that current NISQ devices are capable of running quantum emulations beyond classical computational limits, our work establishes a vital pathway for future quantum simulations. Furthermore, the proposed method can be readily adapted for other significant fermionic systems, such as the electronic structure of molecules. Finally, our findings offer valuable insights for the development of emerging quantum technologies. We define morphic sequences as those generated by polynomial series, where each term is a linear combination of previous terms with constant coefficients. This paper presents and discusses graph-theoretic interpretations for specific morphic sequences, including the Fibonacci, Jacobsthal, Lucas, and Pell series. Furthermore, we develop graph traits based on simple paths within labeled graphs. Given a labeled graph $P_n$ featuring labeled vertices and directed edges, we construct a morphic sequence by counting the number of labeled vertices in all simple paths of $P_n$. We conclude by identifying the specific properties of $P_n$ that cause the resulting sequence to align with the Fibonacci, Jacobsthal, Lucas, and Pell series. Finally, we propose a novel morphic sequence that models simple path properties in labeled graphs, which extends the Lucas series and is supported by computational evidence. The authors intend to elaborate on this finding in future work. Additionally, we have released a web-based application to explore graph traits and morphic sequences; this tool allows users to input a labeled graph, view all simple paths, and generate the corresponding sequence, with an option to input existing sequences for verification. The authors hope this application will inspire others to explore graph properties and contribute to solving the open problems presented. This research was conducted as part of the authors' participation in the 2021 Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowship (SURF) at the University of Dayton. Keywords: labeled graph, labeled vertex, morphic sequence, open problem, simple path, Summer Undergraduate Research Fellowship. 2020 Mathematics Subject Classification: 05C30, 05C35, 11B37, 11B39, 11B83.

Veech links associated with a specific set of directions on a translation surface provide topological information regarding the volume and cut volume of geodesic flow orbits on that surface. This work investigates the topology of the Veech link for an Veech arc—a special type of multi-valued holomorphic 1-form—demonstrating that the Veech link of such a Veech multi-valued holomorphic 1-form is invariably a torus knot. Furthermore, we establish that the volume of the geodesic flow orbit of any translation surface derived from this arc equals the link signature of the corresponding Veech link. These findings offer a novel approach to studying the volume problem for translation surfaces within Teichmüller space. Additionally, we explore the application of Veech links in addressing surface decomposition issues. Specifically, we offer a characterization of simple Veech links using graph theory, characterize periodic Veech links via regular polygon triangulations, and provide methods for decomposing translation surfaces into simpler components using rational curves on the Veech link. Finally, we offer several examples of Veech links for various special Veech arcs, including those arising from lattice polygons, regular polygons, and regular star polygons. Over the past few years, remote work has become increasingly common, yet it introduces significant challenges for software development teams utilizing Scrum. While prior research has analyzed the general effects of telecommuting on organizations, there is a notable lack of studies addressing its specific impact on individual projects. This research investigates how telecommuting influences the success of specific Scrum initiatives. Through a multi-method study combining interviews with 20 software development professionals and an analysis of 40 real-world projects (20 telecommuting and 20 on-site), the study found that telecommuting does not affect project success. However, success is contingent upon adopting a hybrid telecommuting model, maintaining an open telecommuting culture, and ensuring effective online communication. These findings offer valuable insights for managers aiming to optimize the benefits of telecommuting. Additionally, the study examined the relationship between telepresence and project success, revealing that higher telepresence levels are associated with greater success. The paper concludes by suggesting areas for further research.

The concept of Gau-Wu (GW) values extends the traditional determinant, offering a more generalized approach first introduced by mathematicians Gau and Wu. This paper aims to establish explicit formulas for the GW value of arrowhead matrices and calculate specific GW values for symmetric, tridiagonal, and $4\times 4$ matrices. Furthermore, we provide a computational method for determining GW values within a matrix space. Our methodology is grounded in mathematical induction and Cramer's rule, with the latter applied to reduce the problem size. Additionally, the concept of matrix minors is utilized to facilitate these calculations. The study begins by defining GW values and minors, followed by the derivation of the reduction formula. We then present the explicit formula for GW values of arrowhead matrices, derive the GW value for tridiagonal matrices, and offer explicit formulas for specific $4\times 4$ matrix GW values. Finally, the paper proposes an algorithm for computing GW values in a matrix space, which is supported by a flowchart and a matrix calculator. This work demonstrates that arrowhead matrices are particularly amenable to calculation, thereby simplifying the process for other matrix types. Ultimately, this paper seeks to provide a foundation for future research into the theory of GW values. Keywords: Gau-Wu value, matrix minors, matrix submatrices, matrix minors, matrix calculators, matrix calculators, matrix calculators.

We demonstrate that certain features of fine-scale chromatic structure in mitotic chromosomes remain fixed, or steadfast, regardless of the organism or chromosome being examined. By integrating high-resolution imaging with statistical analysis, we reveal that these chromatin structures maintain steadfast homology across eukaryotes, enabling the use of model organisms to investigate fine-scale phenomena in somatic chromosomes. Furthermore, fine-scale chromatic organization in mitotic chromosomes exhibits steadfastness in metazoan germ cells, suggesting that model organisms can also elucidate related issues specific to germ chromosomes. Conversely, we find that chromatic organization within chromosomal arms displays dynamical variability, indicating that chromosome territory shape is not determined solely by local interactions. These findings collectively establish a robust fine-scale mitotic chromatic structure, quantified through statistical analysis of imaging data from various eukaryotes. Additionally, we introduce a new statistical framework for describing chromatic structures, chromatic graphs, and their homology. This framework offers a novel approach to analyzing mitotic chromatic structure, chromosomal territories, and sex chromosomes, while providing a foundation for developing coarse-grained models of chromosome folding. Finally, we present a coarse-grained model of chromosome folding that accurately captures the steadfast aspects of mitotic chromatic structure. This model is constructed from the spectral zeta function of a random walk on a graph, which is derived from the chromatic $\alpha$-structures of eukaryotic chromosomes. The resulting model successfully predicts the variability of chromosome territory shape observed in imaging data. This study examines the maximum Extremal GDoF advantage of allowing optimal power regulation—where each user selects power from a continuous interval—compared to binary power regulation—where each user selects power from a discrete set of two options in Extremal Extremal GDoF networks. We demonstrate that the logarithmic gap previously established by Han and Simeone in their work on the extremal gain of continuous versus discrete power control in interference channels is, in fact, optimal. Furthermore, we establish that the benefit of optimal power regulation over binary power regulation scales as $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ in the $K$-user interference channel scenario. This finding contrasts with Han and Simeone's result, which indicated that the extremal GDoF gain was $\Theta(\log K)$. Additionally, we show that the $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ benefit observed in the interference channel also applies to the Gaussian broadcast channel. Consequently, we conclude that the $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ gain identified in this work is the optimal extremal GDoF gain achievable by continuous power regulation relative to binary power regulation within the framework of Extremal Extremal GDoF. The proposed schemes are based on superposition encoding and successive interference cancellation. To derive the lower bound, we utilize a specific instance of the 2-user Gaussian interference channel, whereas the upper bound is derived from a generalized version of the $K$-user Gaussian broadcast channel. This paper introduces the Adaptive Classification for Auditing (ACA) framework, which integrates formal concept analysis and adaptive classification techniques with Dempster-Shafer evidence theory to enhance the audit process. The primary objective of adaptation in auditing is to refine the classification of audited entities by leveraging historical evidence from prior audits. The study begins by presenting the foundational concepts of formal concept analysis and adaptive classification, followed by an explanation of the evidence combination rules within Dempster-Shafer theory. Subsequently, the authors propose a novel method for determining the belief function for the formal concept of an audited entity, utilizing historical audit evidence to model the concepts of previous audited entities. Finally, the paper demonstrates the application of the ACA framework through a case study, with results that align with the authors' expert judgment. The paper concludes by identifying limitations of the proposed approach and suggesting avenues for future research. This research serves as a proof of concept for adaptation in auditing, offering a promising pathway for future studies. Additionally, it addresses the challenge of defining the belief function for an audited entity's formal concept by combining historical audit evidence, a problem that extends beyond the specific domain of auditing. Consequently, the study also contributes to the broader fields of formal concept analysis and adaptive classification. The authors believe that the ACA framework will prove valuable in various practical applications. The Strauss process is a point process where an acceptance-rejection algorithm typically generates samples, but it struggles to be efficient for large point patterns. This paper introduces an alternative method based on stitching Markov chains, which is significantly faster than acceptance-rejection. The proposed procedure is general, applicable to any Strauss model that can be simulated conditionally given an initial point pattern. We establish conditions ensuring irreducibility and uniqueness of the stationary distribution for the stitching Markov chain. Through simulations using the R package `stitching`, we demonstrate that the chain mixes rapidly even for large point patterns. Additionally, we apply the method to a biological study of tree locations, showing that stitching Markov chains can be utilized to analyze spatial dependence. The R package `stitching` is accessible at https://github.com/GeertHeuvelink/stitching. Keywords: stitching Markov chain; tree data; spatial dependence; point process; tree function; R package. A prominent candidate is a deformation of the Poincaré algebra that remains compatible with the uncertainty principle, a concept known as "Lorentz violation by deformation." Furthermore, under specific conditions, these effects can completely eliminate the Lorentz violation inherent in the deformation. Conversely, in anisotropic deformed frame transformations, both the deformed Lorentz symmetry and the associated quantum effects remain unaffected. These findings may hold significant implications for interpreting the "smoking gun" signatures of Lorentz symmetry breaking in astrophysical data. Additionally, the paper briefly compares these results with those of "Lorentz violation by standard model field terms." In this context, quantum effects neither modify the group structure nor the associated cohomology classes. This study addresses shared processing challenges in university course scheduling, where shared rooms and timetabling constraints are modeled using the Timetable Shared Processing (TSP) framework. We introduce a novel Multitasking Timetabling (MTT) approach that allows shared processing resources to handle multiple tasks concurrently. We demonstrate that room sharing can be represented within the MTT model and present a practical timetabling algorithm based on this framework. Extensive numerical experiments indicate that the MTT model effectively captures room sharing, offering the added benefit of lower computational complexity compared to the Timetable Shared Processing (TSP) model. Furthermore, our experimental results show that the proposed MTT-based algorithm performs well in practice, achieving a success rate of 80% across various university scheduling scenarios. Additionally, we demonstrate that room sharing significantly increases the difficulty of the problem. Finally, we illustrate how our MTT-based algorithm can be adapted to solve various scheduling problems involving shared processing resources. Notably, this model and algorithm also prove effective for the Shared Processing Scheduling (SPS) problem, a component of the University Course Scheduling (UCS) problem. In this context, we successfully solved all 12 instances from the 2017 University Timetabling Competition (UTTC). The paper concludes with a discussion on the MTT model and its associated algorithm. This paper presents a modeling, simulation, and control enhancement study for a monopod hopping robot operating on deformable terrain. Initially, the dynamics of the robot and the ground are defined, followed by the development of corresponding models. Next, the stability of the hopping motion is analyzed using linearization and multiplier methods. Finally, the study investigates how to enhance hopping performance through the control of the foot's damping coefficient. These advancements were implemented on a laboratory-scale prototype to validate the proposed methods. The results indicate that while the robot can maintain a stable hop, increasing the foot damping coefficient leads to greater hop height and energy efficiency. Consequently, an active control strategy is utilized to adjust the damping coefficient in real-time, thereby improving overall hopping performance. Experimental data collected from the prototype confirms the effectiveness of this approach. Additionally, a method for estimating ground deformation is introduced, and a technique for measuring the foot's contact point is developed to facilitate model parameter identification. Finally, outdoor experiments were conducted to demonstrate the robot's ability to perform stable hopping on uneven terrain. These findings collectively suggest that the proposed modeling and control strategies are effective for achieving stable hopping on variable ground. Furthermore, the ability to estimate foot position and ground deformation enables the robot to adapt to uneven surfaces, marking a significant step toward outdoor applications. The research also identifies limitations, such as the inability to track reference trajectories, and proposes future work to address these challenges. Ultimately, this work establishes a foundation for developing hopping robots capable of traversing uneven terrain. The methodologies and insights presented here are intended to facilitate future research in this domain. Specifically, the ability to estimate foot position and ground deformation allows the robot to navigate uneven surfaces, representing a crucial advancement toward practical outdoor deployment. Finally, the study outlines several limitations and suggests potential avenues for future investigation. Firmware updates are essential for maintaining the security and functionality of IoT devices. However, the risk of upgradability issues, which can render devices inoperable, remains a significant challenge. This paper examines the challenges associated with upgrading large-scale, production-ready IoT devices, specifically those utilizing the Contiki-OS operating system and the Contiki-NG firmware. We identify key design considerations that must be addressed during the upgradability process to ensure device reliability. To investigate these issues, we conducted extensive field tests on a substantial LoRaWAN mesh network, involving the deployment of 100 IoT devices and the execution of multiple firmware upgrades. Our findings indicate that upgrading these devices is a complex and time-consuming endeavor, often necessitating manual intervention. Furthermore, we observed that upgradability problems can occur even with well-designed procedures, and that the difficulty of troubleshooting is amplified by the devices' limited interfaces and documentation. We also explored potential solutions to mitigate these challenges. Ultimately, we recommend that developers prioritize the robustness of upgradability processes alongside the core features of their firmware. Additionally, we advocate for the inclusion of a robust recovery mechanism in all IoT devices to guarantee upgradability. This research is based on a real-world scenario, offering valuable insights for the development of more resilient and robust IoT systems. We investigate the multifractal characteristics of many-body localized systems by analyzing the scaling behavior of the Fock-space propagator. Our findings indicate that these scaling properties remain largely unaffected by the transition from delocalized to localized phases, which occurs at a finite driving strength known as the "shift." This scaling behavior can be characterized by a set of fractal dimensions that exhibit a smooth dependence on the spectral dimension. We offer a theoretical framework to elucidate these results and propose that the shift represents a critical point within a phase diagram featuring a first-order phase transition. Furthermore, we explore the connection between these scaling laws and the recently proposed phase diagram for one-dimensional spin systems, which displays a complex structure with multiple phase boundaries. Finally, we suggest that our approach can be extended to higher-dimensional lattice models and systems with long-range interactions. This work is based on the arXiv preprint arXiv:2101.01001. Additional details and data are available at https://www.quantum-matter.org/multifractality/. The accompanying Jupyter notebook demonstrates how to perform the calculations and generate the figures presented in this paper.

This paper addresses interactive search for multiple targets within a limited budget, a scenario where the searcher can only probe one point per time step. We examine two distinct settings: a static target configuration and a dynamic one. In the static case, we demonstrate that a straightforward algorithm achieves a constant-factor approximation for minimizing total probe depth, thereby improving upon prior methods. For the dynamic case, we introduce a new model and propose a $2$-approximation algorithm for optimal search, followed by the presentation of matching lower bounds. Additionally, we explore a fully dynamic variant in which target locations are known in advance, and we present both upper and lower bounds for this setting. Finally, we present experimental results that validate our theoretical findings. Our proposed algorithms are efficient, and we observe that when the budget is extremely tight, our performance closely aligns with that of a simple greedy approach. This suggests that for small budgets, the problem becomes nearly trivial, as the searcher can identify a suitable starting point and locate targets with minimal probing. Quantum machine learning (QML) has emerged as a promising avenue for developing new machine learning models utilizing quantum hardware. Although current QML algorithms are not yet optimized for creating quantum adversarial examples, they offer a viable framework for investigating such disturbances within quantum classifiers. This work addresses the lack of research into creating global adversarial examples tailored to quantum classifiers. We propose and evaluate a method for generating global adversarial instances for these quantum models, demonstrating that the resulting instances successfully induce classification errors. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between global adversarial instances and those produced by gradient-based approaches within quantum classifiers. Our findings indicate that while global instances are generally less robust than gradient-based ones, they offer greater generality and are more effective at identifying classification errors. Additionally, we explore the use of quantum neural networks as a means to analyze the internal structures of these global adversarial examples. Our results show that the internal representations of quantum adversarial examples are distinct from normal data, yet they retain a high degree of similarity to the original input data. Finally, we discuss the potential of global adversarial examples for enhancing the robustness of quantum classifiers. These examples can serve as training data to improve model resilience against future adversarial attacks, a strategy we validate by training quantum classifiers on the MNIST dataset using global adversarial instances and observing improved robustness against subsequent attacks. Overall, this study provides a foundation for further research into the generation and analysis of global adversarial examples in the context of quantum machine learning. Our work underscores the significance of these examples for advancing the security and reliability of quantum classifiers. By fostering a deeper understanding of how quantum neural networks process and represent data, our research contributes to the broader goals of making QML more secure and dependable. Ultimately, this research holds the potential to significantly impact the future of quantum computing and its practical applications. Our work demonstrates the value of global adversarial examples in strengthening the robustness of quantum classifiers, a critical step toward the widespread adoption of quantum machine learning. As quantum computing continues to evolve, the development and analysis of global adversarial examples will play an increasingly vital role in shaping the future of this field. By addressing key challenges in quantum machine learning, our research paves the way for the creation of more robust and reliable quantum algorithms, ultimately contributing to the realization of the full potential of quantum computing. The significance of global adversarial examples extends beyond their immediate application in quantum classifiers; they also hold the potential to drive further research and innovation in the broader field of quantum machine learning.
