This study examines Steklov eigenvalues associated with eigenfunctions defined on bounded domains. By applying the variational characterization of these eigenvalues, we demonstrate that within a specific $L^p$ norm, there exists a constant such that the distance between the Steklov eigenfunctions on almost spherical regions and those on balls remains bounded. This finding aligns with the phenomenon of spectral rigidity observed in isometrically equivalent domains. Furthermore, we establish that the exponent $p$ can be selected as $n+1$, where $n$ represents the dimension of the region. The proof relies heavily on the sharp Wente inequality in two dimensions and its generalization by Lin and Wang for dimensions greater than two. Additionally, we derive a direct consequence of our primary theorem concerning mean curvature. Finally, the paper includes examples of regions that illustrate the optimality of the derived estimate. The terminology "almost spherical" is employed to denote regions that closely resemble balls in terms of their boundary geometry. This concept resonates with the well-established notion of Gromov-Hausdorff convergence, which measures the distance between metric spaces. We anticipate that our result will contribute to understanding the Gromov-Hausdorff limit of a sequence of regions. Specifically, we show that the sequence of Steklov eigenfunctions on these regions converges to the Steklov eigenfunctions of the corresponding ball. The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Section 2 provides background information and relevant literature; Section 3 states the main results; Section 4 reviews essential background and tools; Section 5 presents the proof of our primary theorem; and Section 6 explores examples and implications. Verifying compliance with business process regulations is a critical challenge, particularly when rules are expressed as temporal constraints on event sequences. Existing methods often struggle with complex rules, leading to scalability issues. To address this, we introduce a novel approach that decomposes large trace segments into smaller, more manageable parts. By representing temporal rules as temporal logic formulas, we define a new compliance verification problem that ensures post-event and pre-event sub-traces align with expected behaviors while maintaining temporal consistency between them. This paper presents a solution leveraging a new type of process trace alignment that combines pre- and post-event alignments with infix alignments to bridge the resulting post- and pre-event results. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves a significant performance improvement compared to the state-of-the-art approach. Furthermore, we extend our solution to handle noisy execution data by integrating a noise filtering step based on robust statistics. We validate our approach's effectiveness through a case study involving the execution of a large European clinical trial. Finally, we release our implementation as an open-source library within the OWL Process Mining framework. This library includes not only our proposed methods but also additional state-of-the-art techniques for compliance verification and noise filtering, enabling direct comparison between our approach and current state-of-the-art methods. The associated code and data are accessible at https://github.com/OWL-EM/ComplianceChecking. We introduce a new semantics for temporal planning that is formally demonstrated to be equivalent to the standard classical planning semantics when applied to classical plans on classical problems. This framework is rigorously proven to be both necessary and sufficient for capturing conventional reachability semantics in a way that is amenable to temporal planning. Temporal planning, which extends classical planning with support for continuous variables, branching, and waiting, is shown to be decidable relative to classical planning problems. Our approach provides a formal basis for validation, enabling the automatic verification of planner implementations against their intended semantics. Using this method, we validate the implementation of the graph planner Fast Forward in its graph-structured variant within CoCoRo, and we verify that its output conforms to the official semantics of temporal planning. Additionally, we explore various implementation strategies for temporal planning, including decision diagrams, symbolic regression, and symbolic shortest path search, all of which are proven to be correct with respect to our official semantics. Finally, we assess the performance of our reference implementation, PyCOCO, on a selected set of problems. Compared to Temporal Pro, PyCOCO exhibits comparable or superior performance in terms of both solution quality and runtime. Furthermore, PyCOCO successfully solves problems that Temporal Pro fails to resolve within its time limits. Our experiments indicate that, on average, the plans generated by PyCOCO are 10% shorter than those produced by Temporal Pro. Finally, we confirm that the plans generated by PyCOCO are valid. In contrast, Temporal Pro occasionally outputs invalid plans, which we successfully identify and discard. We also examine the performance of a third planner, Fast Downward, which, when configured for temporal planning, generates invalid plans in some cases. Power generation and transmission planning are typically conducted using optimization models. However, optimization models can be computationally intensive, and the models employed for long-term network expansion planning are particularly demanding. This paper investigates the responsiveness of these models to parameter variations. We examine two key parameters: the cost of new line construction and the cost of curtailment. Our computational results indicate that while results are not always stable, they are generally robust. Specifically, the number of expanded lines remains consistent across different parameter scenarios, whereas the total curtailed energy may fluctuate. Nevertheless, the overall magnitude of variation is small, suggesting that expansion planning models are largely responsive. Furthermore, the number of significant thermal constraints is unaffected by parameter changes, implying that thermal limits are not critical. In contrast, the count of voltage-related constraints does vary between scenarios, yet this impact is also negligible. Finally, we outline several avenues for future research. Notably, we recommend that responsiveness be evaluated for other parameters, such as those associated with network congestion. Additionally, we suggest employing statistical methods to quantify the likelihood of model results under different parameter scenarios. Ultimately, we propose that responsiveness analysis should be integrated into the standard workflow of network expansion planning. This approach would allow planners to assess the reliability of model outputs and determine the necessary level of detail for parameters. Consequently, this could facilitate the use of less detailed parameters, thereby reducing computational costs. Furthermore, analyzing responsiveness can help identify which parameters require higher detail, enabling planners to allocate their available detailed parameter data more effectively. Finally, we contend that this methodology can be extended to other planning models, including those for network recovery and network storage. In the context of storage planning, for instance, one might analyze how results change with different cost parameters. Additionally, since planning models often incorporate various operational parameters, such as demand forecasts, responsiveness analysis could help identify which of these parameters have the most significant impact on planning outcomes. This insight could guide the allocation of resources for collecting detailed operational data. In summary, we believe that responsiveness analysis serves as a valuable tool for enhancing the quality of planning results. By understanding the sensitivity of outcomes to parameter variations, planners can make more informed decisions, ultimately leading to superior planning results. Additionally, this approach can guide the allocation of resources for gathering detailed operational parameters. This paper presents STRICT, a method designed to identify terms or phrases within a target vocabulary that are semantically similar to input concepts. This capability is essential for various natural language processing (NLP) applications, such as knowledge graph construction, semantic document clustering, and related tasks. We frame this challenge as a data retrieval problem, where given a target vocabulary and a concept, the objective is to locate relevant vocabulary items from a large corpus. Our approach involves training an autoencoder to compress the target vocabulary into a low-dimensional space, followed by training a T5 encoder-decoder model to retrieve vocabulary tokens most similar to the concept. STRICT demonstrates superior performance compared to baseline methods, achieving a normalized discounted cumulative gain (nDCG) of 0.61 on the WordNet similarity test set and 0.59 on the cluster similarity test set. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/strict. Furthermore, we have released the vocabulary corpus, which comprises 1.5 million words, to support future research. The corpus can be downloaded from our repository at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/strict. We anticipate that our model and the accompanying corpus will be valuable for vocabulary alignment and term extraction tasks. The paper is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.01001. Colloidal gels formed by Brownian particles are renowned for their remarkable mechanical resilience and structural stability. However, for practical applications, it is often necessary to tailor their rheological and acoustic properties to meet specific demands. This study introduces a new rheo-acoustic method that combines ultrasonic vibrations with a standard rheometer to modify the rheological characteristics of colloidal gels. We demonstrate that applying low-intensity ultrasound to a silica gel suspension can reversibly suppress particle aggregation, thereby reducing gel strength and enhancing their rheological performance. Furthermore, we illustrate that varying the ultrasonic frequency and the duration of sonication allows for precise control over the gel's microstructure and macroscopic rheology. These rheo-acoustic techniques are anticipated to have broad applications across diverse fields, including advanced materials science, food engineering, and environmental engineering. Additionally, our findings offer valuable insights into the aggregation dynamics of weak colloidal gels. This work was conducted within the Ultrasonic Processing of Soft Matter (UPSM) research group. The Collatz Conjecture asserts that any positive integer $n$ will eventually reach 1 through an iterative process. For each step, if the current number is odd, multiply it by 3 and add 1; if it is even, divide it by 2. Although this conjecture has remained unproven for over 80 years, it can be readily simulated using code. This article demonstrates several code implementations, beginning with a basic version. Additionally, it explores methods to visualize the conjecture's behavior, such as plotting the number of steps required to first attain an odd value within the range [1, 1000] or displaying a binary tree where the root is 1 and the children of node $n$ correspond to the possible previous values. Finally, the article examines the conjecture's connection to the $3^n+1$ sequence and proposes it as an engaging coding challenge. However, the heterogeneous natures of tasks, substances, and circuits create unique categorization challenges within STEM fields. While prior research has primarily focused on general scientific documents, this study investigates mathematical papers to address a largely neglected area. Research in online dating has traditionally centered on two questions: the optimal size for a potential partner's pool of options and the criteria individuals use to select a partner. This study shifts the focus to the platform's perspective, aiming to optimize the experience for all users. We investigate a stable matching problem where one side of the equation consists of agents who can offer multiple proposals, while the other side limits itself to choosing between no more than $k$ options. We present a truthful, efficient algorithm designed to maximize the number of users receiving at least one stable match. Our findings indicate that a greedy strategy, which selects the most preferred available options, is nearly optimal for the side receiving proposals. We demonstrate that this approach ensures every agent on the proposal-making side secures at least a 1/2 approximation of their best stable outcome, and every agent on the proposal-receiving side achieves at least a 2/(k+1) approximation. We strengthen these guarantees by introducing an agent-preference-independent mechanism that maintains the same performance bounds. Furthermore, we establish that no mechanism can achieve a better-than-1/2 approximation for the proposal-making side, and we prove that no truthful mechanism can guarantee any positive approximation factor for the proposal-receiving side. Finally, we extend our analysis to include agent types and show that a greedy strategy remains nearly optimal in this generalized setting. We conclude with experimental results derived from both synthetic data and a real-world dataset. These results not only validate our theoretical findings but also offer new insights into the dynamics of online dating. For instance, our analysis suggests that women are more satisfied with their matches than men, and that men are more selective than women. Additionally, we observe that men's satisfaction decreases as the number of available options increases, whereas women's satisfaction remains relatively stable. This supports the theoretical conclusion that a smaller pool of options is more beneficial for the proposal-making side. We also demonstrate that a larger pool of options significantly improves satisfaction for the proposal-receiving side, particularly when the pool size is not excessively large. Finally, we show that women's satisfaction increases more rapidly than men's as the number of options grows. These results align with the theoretical finding that the pool of options is more critical for the proposal-receiving side when the size of that pool is small. Overall, these findings suggest that platforms should encourage users to expand their pool of options and to broaden their criteria for selecting potential partners. Automated Summary Evaluation has long been a contentious field, with recent efforts primarily relying on the recall approach through the Text2TextGeneration Task in the GLUE benchmark. This methodology utilizes decoder-based models to assess summary quality. However, this paper argues that such models are inherently limited and proposes SummScore, a cross-encoder-based scoring system designed to significantly enhance performance. SummScore demonstrates substantial improvements across all previous state-of-the-art methods on the SummEval dataset, achieving a 13.5% increase in the primary SummaryRecall metric. Furthermore, SummScore exhibits a strong correlation with human judgments, yielding a Pearson's correlation of 0.612 on the Mentavd summary evaluation dataset. Finally, we demonstrate that SummScore can effectively identify improvements in model-generated summaries. The implementation is accessible at https://github.com/lyst/summscore. We introduce a new framework designed to restore low-dimensional signals from a limited set of quadratic measurements. This approach leverages the inherent sparsity of signals expressed in a suitable basis, utilizing a sparsity-promoting prior that integrates an $\ell_1$ penalty on the basis coefficients with a quadratic penalty on the reconstructed signal. The resulting prior is minimized via an iterative algorithm that alternates between a sparse recovery step and a signal restoration step. The method's convergence is proven, and its performance is demonstrated through image reconstruction from quadratic data. Additionally, the approach is applied to a neuroscience challenge involving the recovery of neural activity patterns from a very sparse collection of quadratic measurements. A numerical study compares our method against a recent alternative that employs a non-smooth prior on the neural activity vector, highlighting the computational efficiency of our approach relative to that recovery method. Finally, we provide a theoretical analysis of the conditions required for exact recovery from highly underdetermined quadratic data. These theoretical insights also offer guidance for selecting the two regularization parameters. The proposed method is implemented in the R package `qLASSO`, which includes a function to perform exact recovery when theoretical assumptions are met. The package also features a function to recommend parameter values based on the theoretical analysis. All code required to reproduce the numerical experiments is available on GitHub. The package can be installed using the following command: install.packages("qLASSO", repos = "https://qlasso.r-forge.r-project.org/bioc"). The website https://qlasso.r-forge.r-project.org/ offers further details. This work was partially supported by the National Science Foundation under grant DMS-1613012. LiDAR's robustness in adverse weather and its superior long-range detection capabilities make it invaluable for autonomous driving. However, LiDAR data is characterized by sparse, sparse voxels organized in BEV representation. Conversely, cameras offer high-resolution details and vast information within voxelized BEV data. This paper introduces a novel and straightforward framework for LiDAR-camera fusion that effectively combines their strengths. Specifically, we utilize camera images to enrich LiDAR features by generating camera features from images and fusing them with LiDAR voxels in the BEV space. This approach effectively merges camera context with LiDAR perception, enhancing overall performance. Our framework is simple, easy to implement, and achieves state-of-the-art results across multiple perception tasks. The code is accessible at https://github.com/BEVFusion/BEVFusion. This study examines the dissipation-continuum interface in a turbulent, isotropic liquid. We demonstrate that at a specific critical value of the dissipation coefficient $\eta^*$, the fluid's bulk thermal conductivity $k$ undergoes a sharp discontinuity, rising from its equilibrium value $k_0$ to an elevated plateau of $k_1 \approx 2k_0$. This phenomenon is attributed to the emergence of transient thermal disturbances, which represent a dissipative analog to velocity disturbances. These disturbances arise from a nonequilibrium thermal excitation mechanism that operates at a distinct critical dissipation coefficient $\eta^*_{\rm th}$, where the thermal excitation coefficient $\gamma_{\rm th}$ diverges. We further show that $\eta^*$ and $\eta^*_{\rm th}$ are identical, indicating that the sudden increase in $k$ is driven by a thermal instability. This behavior is linked to a divergence in the velocity correlation time $\tau_{\rm v}$, which is governed by a dynamical crossover from ballistic to diffusive transport at a critical $\eta^*_{\rm v}$. Our findings are supported by extensive molecular dynamics simulations of hard-sphere fluids across a broad range of $\eta$ values. We conclude that this thermal instability is a general phenomenon, affecting all dissipative fluids, including those exhibiting shear banding. The coexistence of transient thermal and velocity disturbances in the same fluid suggests the potential for generating both dissipative shear and thermal rectification. Finally, we propose a continuum framework to describe this behavior, which relies on the $\eta$-dependent transport coefficients $k(\eta)$, $\tau_{\rm v}(\eta)$, and the stress relaxation time $\tau(\eta)$. This theoretical model is validated by comparing its predictions against simulation data. Our results provide a comprehensive picture of the dissipation-range properties of turbulent liquids, offering a novel perspective on how dissipative effects influence the behavior of condensed matter. These insights are broadly applicable to understanding how dissipative forces interact with thermal and mechanical fluctuations in both liquids and solids. Furthermore, our conclusions have significant implications for the thermodynamics of nonequilibrium fluids, particularly regarding the validity of the local equilibrium hypothesis. Specifically, the divergence of the thermal excitation coefficient $\gamma_{\rm th}$ at $\eta^*$ implies that the local equilibrium hypothesis breaks down in the vicinity of $\eta^*$. This study presents a numerical analysis of laser-induced thermal profiles within liquids, utilizing the solution to the heat diffusion equation. The resulting thermal distribution accounts for the complex interplay between volumetric heat deposition and surface heat loss. By integrating this profile with the liquid's refractive index-temperature relationship, we calculate the intricate self-induced diffraction patterns observed in laser-induced forward scattering experiments. This approach offers a straightforward yet effective method for modeling the complex phenomena involved in laser manipulation of liquids. Furthermore, the work demonstrates how experimental measurements of these intricate diffraction patterns can be utilized to determine the specific heat of the liquid. These findings are validated through numerical simulations of experimental data for water and glycerol. Additionally, we address the potential impact of surface heat loss on the liquid column's stability, a critical factor for laser levitation and liquid bridges. Ultimately, this research establishes a foundation for future efforts to control liquid shapes using laser light. This paper presents the design and implementation of H-STREAM, a new in-memory, shared-memory stream processing engine tailored for high-performance, shared-memory many-core CPUs. We demonstrate that H-STREAM stream processing applications are significantly more amenable to compiler optimization than those found in existing stream processing systems, allowing for the creation of high-performance, memory-efficient, and portable application code. Furthermore, we show that these optimized applications can be compiled and executed with minimal performance overhead on standard CPUs using a new, portable, high-performance hardware abstraction layer. This layer facilitates the transparent integration of diverse storage and memory subsystems, including main memory, SSDs, and distributed networks, thereby enabling the seamless processing of stream data across multiple levels of the system memory hierarchy. Finally, we present initial empirical results from a benchmarking study. Our evaluation indicates that H-STREAM applications outperform existing stream processing systems by up to 1000× in performance while utilizing up to 100× less memory. We also demonstrate that H-STREAM enables the processing of high-throughput streams from main memory and distributed networks, as well as interactive querying of data histories stored on SSDs and distributed on secondary storage devices. These capabilities are achieved with low performance overhead, often less than 10× compared to direct processing or querying of the data history. This represents the first time such performance has been realized when main memory and secondary storage are located on different machines within a shared-nothing distributed system. We conclude that H-STREAM offers a promising approach for building next-generation stream processing systems capable of interacting with high-throughput streams and large-scale data repositories. These systems will be essential for delivering interactive analytics to business users and for enabling real-time decision-making in various domains, such as healthcare, where stream data is frequently augmented with historical data from large data repositories. The source code for H-STREAM is available at https://github.com/andrews-group/h-stream. We investigate the production of top quark pairs alongside a bottom quark in proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. This process is mediated by non-resonant diagrams involving W and Z gauge bosons at the tree level. Utilizing the parton shower Monte Carlo event generator Pythia8, we compute the production cross section for this mechanism and compare our findings with those from other established production processes. Furthermore, we analyze the kinematic distributions of the resulting final-state particles. These analyses aim to establish a comprehensive framework for simulating non-resonant top quark production in association with bottom associates, thereby enhancing the accuracy of theoretical predictions for multi-top final states within the proton-proton collisions. Additionally, we have made the resulting event samples publicly accessible. This publication serves as a prelude to a forthcoming analysis of this process conducted by the CMS Collaboration. A potential application of this simulation framework is the search for Z' gauge bosons that couple to the third generation of quarks. In such scenarios, the primary background would consist of top quark events produced through non-resonant diagrams. Consequently, an accurate simulation of this process is essential for interpreting the potential sensitivity of the Z' boson search. This sensitivity will be further explored in a subsequent paper. We anticipate that the findings presented here will be valuable to the broader community engaged in the analysis of multi-top final states. Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has emerged as a leading method for translating queries and results in SPARQL-based Knowledge Base (KB) systems, yet it struggles to handle tail-fact translation due to knowledge base heterogeneity. We introduce a duplicate translation mechanism designed to mitigate this issue by leveraging duplicate data to train NMT models. This approach enables the model to simply duplicate tail facts during translation, thereby addressing heterogeneity. Evaluation results demonstrate that our mechanism significantly outperforms previous methods in tail-fact translation, achieving up to a 14.4% improvement in F1 scores. Furthermore, experiments indicate that this mechanism incurs no additional latency. The implementation can be accessed at https://github.com/rii-manna/duplicate-translation. A Knowledge Base (KB) is a structured repository of data, typically represented as triples in Resource Description Framework (RDF) format, consisting of subjects, predicates, and objects. A prominent application of KBs is SPARQL-based query answering, which returns results in triple format. To enhance user experience, these results are often translated into natural language. However, heterogeneity in tail facts poses a significant challenge for Neural Machine Translation (NMT) models, as they must map diverse source sentences to diverse target sentences. This paper focuses on NMT for SPARQL-based KB translation and introduces a duplicate translation mechanism to address tail-fact heterogeneity. Our approach utilizes duplicate data to generate duplicate training data, facilitating the training of NMT models that perform result duplication during translation. We demonstrate that this mechanism significantly improves tail-fact translation, outperforming prior methods by up to 14.4% in F1 scores. We introduce a citation-free approach to assess venue quality, which serves as an effective alternative for benchmarking new submissions without relying on author reputation. Our analysis of the top 2% of Computer Science papers from 2000 to 2020, covering over 100,000 documents, demonstrates that venue quality can be predicted by examining paper content. Specifically, our model leverages author affiliation and co-authorship networks, combined with paper title and abstract data, to estimate venue strength. We find that a paper's co-authors are more reliable indicators of venue quality than the authors themselves, as co-authors of a top-tier venue like NeurIPS 2020 typically cluster around that same venue. Our proposed model achieves a Spearman correlation of 0.70 with traditional citation metrics, while only requiring 2% of the training data needed by citation-based methods. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this approach can identify the top 2% of venues with 94% accuracy. We also highlight that this technique can detect emerging venues, such as ICLR, which were previously unrecognized by citations alone. Finally, we show that the method can distinguish between tracks within a single venue, offering a fine-grained classification capability. We make our code available to facilitate future research. Our findings suggest that this technique will be valuable for assessing new submission quality and could aid in combating bias and nepotism in peer review. Additionally, we believe this approach will help reduce the growing influence of elite author groups in academic research. This study examines neural network (NN) validation methods for use in control systems. We begin by establishing the essential requirements a control system must meet to be viable in practice. Subsequently, we explain how a NN controller is typically implemented within such a system. Following this, we outline the two primary strategies for validating a NN controller: verifying the safety of its closed-loop behavior and ensuring the safety of its open-loop trajectories. Finally, we present various techniques for conducting these verification tasks. The discussion concludes with an exploration of several open research questions. The primary contribution of this work is the comprehensive survey of existing NN verification approaches, along with addressing certain limitations and proposing potential future research directions. This document serves as a survey paper. It is structured to be accessible to researchers across a broad spectrum of fields, including robotics, automotive engineering, aerospace, and general control systems. Consequently, it covers a wide range of topics, from the fundamental components of a NN controller to the specific methods used to verify and validate those controllers. Our goal is to assist researchers in one domain in understanding the fundamental challenges faced by others, thereby fostering cross-disciplinary collaboration. We anticipate that this survey will assist researchers in identifying opportunities to apply their expertise in one area to advance research in another. This paper is intended for readers who possess a basic understanding of neural networks but lack knowledge regarding verification techniques or the necessity of verifying neural network controllers. We introduce a method for grouping elements based on a graph that allows for overlaps, resulting in a multi-level functorial algorithm. This approach is applicable to any category, though we present the method specifically within Set. The process begins with a binary relation defining pairwise similarities among the elements. This relation is decomposed into a hierarchy of equivalence relations, where each relation's pair classes are formed by combining 2-valued linear combinations of lower-level classes. This decomposition continues recursively until a hierarchy of equivalence classes is achieved that closely approximates the original relation. The proposed method offers a superior approximation compared to standard clustering techniques, such as those derived from minimum spanning trees. Additionally, we demonstrate how to construct fuzzy hierarchies of classes and discuss the method's application in image segmentation. A key advantage is that the algorithm is fully functorial across all levels, enabling parallel execution. We have implemented this as a functor in Set and made the code available on GitHub. Finally, we outline how this method can be adapted into a 2-functor for categories with finite sets and functions. The paper includes illustrative examples and includes a video presentation of the work. All code is open-source. Streaming tensor methods are widely adopted for data recovery due to their computational efficiency and streaming data requirements. However, these methods typically necessitate multiple passes over the data, which is problematic for streaming applications where data is consumed immediately after reading. This limitation stems from the iterative nature of the algorithms, which are essential for enhancing the accuracy of low-rank matrix approximations. This paper introduces a novel patch monitoring-based streaming tensor restoration approach designed for visual data, capable of delivering high-quality results in a single pass. The method leverages the low-rank characteristics of visual data and employs a non-convex rank expansion strategy to iteratively increase the rank of each patch. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that this proposed approach yields superior visual quality compared to other methods, while also offering higher computational efficiency and reduced data storage needs. A subset of vertices $S$ in a graph $G=(V,E)$ is defined as autonomous if the subgraph induced by $S$ includes no edges that connect to vertices outside of $S$. Given a non-negative edge weight function $w: E(G) \rightarrow \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$, we examine the problem of identifying an autonomous set $S$ that maximizes $\sum_{e \in E(S)} w(e)$. We demonstrate that this problem is NP-hard for general graphs and even when all edge weights are uniform. Furthermore, we establish an approximation algorithm achieving a ratio of $1/2$. We also investigate graph standardization, a technique for identifying isomorphic subgraphs, and analyze how it applies to the autonomous set problem. Specifically, we consider the task of standardizing a graph $G$ into a form $H$ such that a large set of edges in the maximum-weight autonomous set of $G$ is preserved in $H$. We refer to graphs where this problem is solvable in polynomial time as Standardizable Graphs. We characterize the class of standardizable graphs and provide a polynomial-time algorithm for the problem. Additionally, we explore the relationship between graph standardization and the concept of $k$-autonomous sets, where an edge set $F$ constitutes a $k$-autonomous set if the number of edges leaving the set is at most $k$. We show that the problem of standardizing $G$ to retain a large portion of edges from a maximum-weight $k$-autonomous set is NP-hard. Our findings indicate that specific heat increases with both electrical bias and total thickness; however, it first rises with temperature before declining at higher temperatures. This study reports the first low-frequency radio observations of the young stellar binary system CR Draconis, conducted over a decade using the LOFAR radio telescope. The active M dwarf component, CR Dra, exhibits numerous electron-cyclotron maser (EM) radio bursts, with a mean flux density of approximately 10 mJy at 20 MHz. The observed emission is attributed to a magnetized stellar wind interacting with its companion, and the data indicate a long-term increase in flare activity. These findings establish CR Dra as a valuable target for future low-frequency surveys of young stellar associations. Additionally, we present a statistical analysis of EM bursts from active M dwarfs, demonstrating that the emission from CR Dra is characterized by a higher burst frequency and lower flux density compared to other sources. The analysis also reveals a significant decline in EM emission from the well-known source II Per over the past ten years. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the theory of EM emission from flares. The data are accessible at http://www.lofar.berkeley.edu/CR Dra. This approach learns a neural radiance field that relies on a skeleton-based representation of the avatar. The technique is versatile, accommodating various types of multi-view imagery, including per-joint, per-branch, and skeleton-aligned views. Image alteration is a prevalent activity that impacts both human and machine perception. While existing research has primarily focused on the human element, this study shifts the focus to examine how alterations affect machines. We conducted a user study involving 150 participants to assess both human and machine responses to alterations of varying intensities. The task required identifying whether images had been modified and, if so, specifying the type of change. Our findings reveal that humans can detect alterations across all intensity levels, whereas machines struggle to do so. Furthermore, we observed that as the intensity of alterations increases, human performance remains stable while machine performance improves. These results suggest that leveraging the ability to detect altered images could be utilized to train machines to better distinguish between images modified at different intensities. Finally, we explored how alterations influence machine vision by analyzing performance across different alteration types, noting that machines perform more accurately with color changes than with copy-paste or splicing changes. This research offers valuable insights for enhancing machine vision capabilities. The code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekgupta1998/Intense-Image-Alterations.

We establish that the Chern-Simons link invariants for the SU(2) and SU(3) groups, specifically within the (c,0) and (c,1) torsion levels, correspond to the inner products of link symbols. These symbols are defined recursively utilizing Askey-Wilson q-orthogonal polynomials. Consequently, we derive explicit formulas for the three-tangle invariant $W_n^{(c)}$ in both cases. For SU(2) at the (c,0) level, our results align with established literature. Additionally, we compute $W_n^{(2,1)}$ for the first time and provide numerical data for $W_n^{(3,1)}$. We conjecture that the recurrence relations for $W_n^{(c,1)}$ involve only a finite set of Askey-Wilson polynomials, with the count of these polynomials increasing as $n$ grows. Furthermore, we outline the procedure for calculating invariants in higher torsion levels, noting that this approach necessitates the use of R-matrices derived through state-sum models. Finally, we offer conjectures regarding the explicit forms of the link symbols. Our work extends previous research by building upon the connections identified in [arXiv:1901.07300] and leveraging the findings from [arXiv:1901.07300] and [arXiv:1901.07300]. The computational techniques employed here are also applicable to the 3D-index of a manifold. Additionally, we introduce a conjecture concerning the relationship between link symbols and recurrence relations for Askey-Wilson polynomials, which has been verified for small values of $n$. Finally, we connect our findings to the theory of quantum affine algebras. We examine the two-dimensional Ising trimer antiferromagnet, a system where three spins are interconnected by equal $z$-directional bonds of strength $J$ to a central spin. Employing the cluster Monte Carlo method, we analyze the phase diagram of this model, which features a first-order transition between a disordered phase and a ferrimagnetic phase, alongside a second-order transition into a ferrimagnetic phase with reduced symmetry. Our investigation focuses on finite-size scaling of the disordered phase to determine critical exponents, specifically the correlation length exponent $\nu$ and the anomalous dimension $\eta$. Our findings yield $\nu = 0.66(2)$ and $\eta = 0.14(2)$, which align closely with prior estimates for the 2D Ising ferrimagnetic phase with broken symmetry. Furthermore, we establish that the finite-size scaling of the magnetic field serves as a precise estimator for the universal amplitude ratio $R_{\chi} = \xi_a/\chi_a = 0.510(2)$. Finally, we demonstrate that the phase diagram of a related model, in which each trimer is linked to the rest of the lattice via a single bond, exhibits a second-order phase transition with critical exponents consistent with the 2D Ising universality class. These results indicate that the critical behavior of this latter model is governed by the weak coupling between the trimers. Additionally, we show that finite-size scaling analysis of the specific heat can accurately estimate the critical exponents $\alpha$ and $\beta$. However, this analysis is highly sensitive to the statistical uncertainty in the specific heat estimator, which is typically underestimated by standard error estimation techniques. Consequently, we observe that the conventional error bars for $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are significantly smaller than their actual values. This issue is resolved by applying a correction scheme to the specific heat estimator, enabling us to determine $\alpha = 0.12(2)$ and $\beta = 0.80(2)$. These outcomes confirm that the model's critical exponents adhere to the 2D Ising universality class. Finally, we conclude that the 2D trimer antiferromagnet offers a viable framework for investigating the weak-coupling limit of the 2D Ising ferrimagnetic phase with broken symmetry. This study introduces a straightforward yet effective method for adapting language models to perform zero-shot learning. Our approach meta-tunes state-of-the-art GPT models using both cue collections and dataset collections. Specifically, cue collections consist of prompt examples derived from various fine-grained classification tasks, while dataset collections involve pre-training the models on dataset prompts generated from natural language descriptions of training data. Our proposed method surpasses prior techniques, such as continuing GPT models on prompt examples or prompt engineering, and is particularly well-suited for zero-shot learning. Additionally, we demonstrate that dataset collections are more scalable than cue collections. Empirical results indicate that extending dataset collections to encompass all dataset descriptions in the SuperGLUE benchmark yields models capable of achieving state-of-the-art zero-shot performance across multiple benchmarks. Furthermore, we find that expanding dataset collections beyond SuperGLUE to include other benchmarks, such as GLUE, further enhances performance, suggesting that larger dataset collections could enable zero-shot learning on previously unseen tasks. Finally, we highlight that our method is highly sample-efficient, requiring only a few thousand examples to significantly boost zero-shot capabilities. This study examines a $Z_3$-invariant Next-to-Minimal Standard Model (NMSSM) featuring an additional $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry, which suppresses or eliminates the primary one-loop NMSSM corrections to the electroweak scale. The research explores the implications of a non-trivial $Z_3$ vacuum expectation value (vev) structure for the electroweak phase transition (EWPT) and its impact on the Higgs inflation scenario. Furthermore, it investigates the NMSSM dark matter candidate within a $Z_3$-invariant framework, analyzing its compatibility with direct detection limits and indirect searches conducted by the Fermi-LAT and IceCube observatories. Finally, the study evaluates the gravitational wave signals generated by a strongly first-order EWPT in this model, assessing their detectability by LISA and the proposed DECIGO space interferometer. The analysis concludes that while the Higgs inflation scenario is viable, the dark matter scenario is constrained by recent indirect searches, and the resulting gravitational wave signal remains undetectable by either DECIGO or LISA. Additionally, the paper outlines future research directions for this model. The work is based on the second author's Ph.D. thesis. We investigate the thermodynamics of the Heisenberg antiferromagnet on a triangular lattice using large-scale quantum Monte Carlo simulations. By analyzing the temperature dependence of the order parameter, specific heat, and spin susceptibility, we identify distinct signatures of the recently discovered $120^{\circ}$-order-to-liquid phase transition, which occurs at a critical temperature $T_c$ within the regime of finite third nearest-neighbor exchange $J_3$. Furthermore, we observe that the spin susceptibility exhibits a broad maximum at a temperature $T_{\chi_{\rm max}}$ that remains nearly independent of $J_3$ in this region. This study introduces a kinetic model that incorporates the collision frequency derived from the Boltzmann equation under a small-coupling assumption. Utilizing the H-theorem, we establish the existence of global weak solutions and examine the model's capacity to capture relative humidity and the Knudsen layer within a periodic setting. Furthermore, we derive an expression for the stress tensor in a constant mean flow scenario and assess the findings through numerical simulations. Our results indicate that the collision frequency can significantly influence stress in the kinetic regime, suggesting that this proposed model offers a more precise approximation of the stress tensor in such contexts. Additionally, we demonstrate that the model can represent slip velocities in rarefied gas flows, with numerical simulations successfully recovering the analytical slip formula in the slip regime. Finally, we show that the model can replicate the Clausius-Duhem inequality, thereby ensuring thermodynamic consistency. Overall, this new model retains the computational efficiency of standard closure models while enhancing physical fidelity. We anticipate that it will serve as a valuable tool for researchers developing kinetic models for various applications. To facilitate this, we provide a comprehensive collection of theoretical and numerical proofs in the appendix. Our future work will focus on extending these findings to more realistic geometries and external forces. The model is implemented in the open-source software OpenFOAM, which is widely utilized in the field. We believe this implementation will be highly beneficial for researchers developing diverse kinetic models for various applications. This study presents the Familiarized Semantic Analyzer (FSA), a semantic analyzer designed to operate on limited data. The research demonstrates that the anagram-based familiarization technique, originally introduced by Fodor et al. (1964), can be automated. FSA utilizes this technique to provide semantic information to a semantic analyzer, enabling it to successfully complete downstream tasks, including natural language inference (NLI) and word analogy, despite being trained on data containing only a single instance of each word. Additionally, the study investigates the relationship between FSA's derived semantic information and word embeddings, showing that embeddings can be trained effectively using the FSA's outputs. The results indicate that while embeddings derived from FSA alone are less robust than those created by combining FSA with standard corpora, the integration of FSA-derived embeddings with conventional corpora yields highly competitive performance. Furthermore, the approach successfully extends to low-resource languages, allowing for the training of FSA and embeddings without requiring pre-trained resources. This paper releases a new NLI dataset comprising 1,000 words in both English and Swahili, each with a single instance per word, alongside a novel method for generating and training embeddings from FSA. The accompanying code repository includes scripts for training the FSA and the embeddings. Finally, the paper offers a comprehensive discussion of the FSA's performance on various tasks, comparing it against baseline methods and existing state-of-the-art techniques. This system must capture charged particles generated by collisions at center-of-mass energies ranging from 5 to 200 GeV. A primary challenge involves designing a tracking detector that meets these stringent performance metrics while adhering to strict cost and time constraints. Finally, the EIC's funding and operational structure will be addressed, given their critical role in bringing the collider to fruition. We conducted a 100-day, 1000-second exposure photometric survey of the low-luminosity active galactic nucleus (LLAGN) SDSS J091618.09+001749.4, which exhibits a near-Eddington accretion rate. This source displays significant flux variability, with a 1000-second timescale pointing toward stochastic fluctuations, and shows no evidence of oscillation. We demonstrate that the variability can be modeled as a single black hole surrounded by an accretion disk, where the disk's inner radius is defined by the photon sphere. The model's success in reproducing the observed variability supports the stochastic fluctuation hypothesis over the oscillation scenario. Furthermore, we show that this variability model aligns with X-ray observations of the LLAGN NGC 4151. Finally, we outline how this model can be applied to other LLAGN systems. This study presents spectropolarimetric observations of HD 58260, a rapidly rotating Ap star, conducted using a discharge lamp equipped with a radial magnetic field. By analyzing the Zeeman splitting of the Fe i 438.34 nm and Hg i 404.66 nm lines, we determined the longitudinal magnetic field for each observation. The resulting time series data reveals fluctuations in the longitudinal field with a magnitude of approximately 1.5 kG. These variations are attributed to the migration of magnetic flux tubes caused by convective motions within the discharge. Furthermore, the observed changes in magnetic field strength correlate with fluctuations in the discharge current. This methodology offers a novel approach to studying magnetic field variations in Ap stars. Additionally, the paper includes a detailed description of the discharge lamp's characteristics and the experimental setup used. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for Ap star models, specifically addressing the magnetic field generation mechanisms within the convection zone and the migration of magnetic flux tubes. These results suggest that the migration of magnetic flux tubes is a key factor in explaining the magnetic field variations in HD 58260. We conducted ALMA observations of the H30$\alpha$ emission line within the dwarf galaxy NGC~5253, which is known for its young stellar population. Our analysis of the H30$\alpha$ line reveals a central continuum source with a size of approximately 100 pc, a gas temperature of roughly 100 K, and a total H$_2$ mass of about 10$^7$ M$_\odot$. The gas density is estimated at 10$^3$--10$^4$ cm$^{-3}$, and the H30$\alpha$ line is found to be optically thick. Utilizing a radiative transfer code, we modeled the H30$\alpha$ emission to determine the physical conditions of the galaxy. Our results indicate that NGC~5253 contains a hot core gas component with temperatures exceeding 10$^4$ K and densities greater than 10$^4$ cm$^{-3}$. Furthermore, we estimated the star formation rate to be approximately 0.01 M$_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$. This value is significantly lower than the 0.15 M$_\odot$ yr$^{-1}$ derived from H$\alpha$ emission, suggesting that NGC~5253 may host a compact HII region. Finally, we compared our findings with star formation rate (SFR) estimates from other tracers, including H$\alpha$, [OIII]5007, and [NII]6584, as well as the galaxy's stellar mass. Our analysis indicates that the H30$\alpha$-derived SFR is more sensitive to variations in gas density compared to the H$\alpha$-derived SFR. Additionally, the [NII]6584/[OIII]5007 ratio suggests that NGC~5253 contains a low-metallicity stellar population. These results support the hypothesis that H30$\alpha$ emission is a promising tracer for star formation in low-metallicity environments. This study represents the first to apply the H30$\alpha$ line as a star formation indicator in a dwarf galaxy. Future investigations should explore the use of H30$\alpha$ as a star formation tracer in other low-metallicity galaxies. This paper introduces a new class of nonparametric estimators for conditional expectation functions, $E[Y|X]$. The study first establishes the consistency of these estimators under mild conditions, followed by a simulation study that compares their performance against existing methods. Furthermore, the authors apply these estimators to two empirical questions: first, analyzing the relationship between the number of siblings and wages for individuals aged 25 to 54; and second, investigating how the number of siblings influences the probability of being overweight for women aged 18 to 49. Both datasets are sourced from the Mexican Family Survey (MES). The results indicate that the proposed estimators are competitive with other methods. Specifically, the empirical analysis suggests that having more siblings is associated with lower wages for men and a higher likelihood of being overweight for women. Additionally, while the number of siblings has no significant impact on wages or the probability of being overweight for women, it does reduce both outcomes for men. These findings align with the theory that men with more siblings tend to spend more time in the labor market and less time engaging in physical activities. Finally, the paper demonstrates that these estimators are robust to violations of the conditional independence assumption. The code required to replicate the simulations and analysis is available at https://github.com/alejandro-fernandez/CFE. The core components of state estimation for process control are state reconstruction and state tracking. State reconstruction involves determining the internal state of a process, while state tracking entails monitoring its evolution over time. This paper introduces a state assessment framework designed for epidemics, integrating state reconstruction with the observation of infection dynamics. The proposed approach relies on a mathematical model of the epidemic process, state reconstruction via the Kalman filter, state tracking through the Kalman filter, and the observation of infection progression using an observer. The study applies this proposed observer framework to the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic in Germany, demonstrating that it yields state assessments that align with the available statistical data. Furthermore, the results indicate that the framework successfully identifies changes in epidemic dynamics, such as shifts in infection rates, and accurately tracks the progression of infections over time. Consequently, this technique holds significant potential for epidemiological research and public health administration. Additionally, the paper outlines several future research directions, including the extension of the observer framework to other relevant processes, such as vaccination campaigns. Notably, state estimation serves as a foundational element for process control, which is crucial for managing the epidemic and mitigating its societal impact. Therefore, this research paves the way for future studies aimed at developing control strategies to limit epidemic spread. Specifically, the authors intend to investigate the use of process control techniques for pandemic control, with a focus on analyzing control effectiveness and sensitivity to uncertainties. This could involve implementing control strategies, like social distancing, to regulate infection rates and prevent healthcare system overload. Furthermore, future work may explore whether state estimation can facilitate the detection of anomalies, such as new epidemic clusters, and whether control strategies can be derived from these estimation results. To address these questions, subsequent research will employ state-of-the-art techniques, including anomaly detection and model predictive control. Overall, this study contributes to advancing process control in epidemiology, a field that has received limited attention in recent literature. The authors aim to inspire further research in this area, thereby enhancing our ability to control the epidemic and minimize its impact on society. This study investigates Kerr-lens mode-locking oscillators by applying ABCD matrix methods to analyze intracavity pulse propagation. The derived general propagation law reveals how pulse energy, peak energy, and peak power evolve with each round trip. These findings are applied to oscillator experiments, offering a comprehensive explanation of power saturation dynamics and the generation of high-peak-power pulses. Additionally, the research examines how slight astigmatism in the equivalent lens affects pulse energy and spot size, providing insights into start-up and tuning procedures. The results are substantiated by data from an oscillator operating at 3.54 W peak power with a 190 f� pulse duration. Ultimately, this work establishes a robust framework for understanding the fundamental principles of Kerr-lens mode-locking.

This study addresses the challenge of nonlinear regression involving massive amounts of data and numerous features, where the data is distributed across multiple clients, each with limited computational and communication resources. We introduce a novel asynchronous online federated learning framework that enables collaborative nonlinear regression by allowing clients to share both their data and computational capabilities. Within this framework, a server dynamically allocates computational resources to selected clients, while an asynchronous optimizer integrates the contributions of these clients to iteratively refine the regression model. Furthermore, we establish a theoretical analysis of the federated optimizer's convergence, demonstrating that it matches the convergence rate of a synchronous online optimizer. Finally, we validate the practical effectiveness of this approach through various regression tasks. Experimental results indicate that our method outperforms existing synchronous and asynchronous online federated approaches in terms of convergence speed and overall performance. Additionally, compared to a standard asynchronous online learning baseline, our approach achieves a 2.5x improvement in convergence speed and a 1.5x reduction in computational cost. This study demonstrates that incorporating a three-dimensional photonic band gap crystal as a rear reflector enhances the absorption of thin silicon membranes within the 1.1–1.7 μm wavelength range. The 3D photonic crystal rear reflector not only boosts average light absorption but also boosts absorption across the entire spectrum, thereby extending it into the near-infrared region. Furthermore, absorption can be further boosted by aligning the photonic crystal's resonant modes with incoming wavelengths; this is particularly effective in the green spectrum, where a membrane with a 200 nm silicon layer achieves nearly 100% absorption. These findings indicate that 3D photonic band gap crystals serve as superior rear reflectors for thin silicon membranes, offering significant potential for enhancing solar cell efficiency. Additionally, the research suggests that thin silicon membranes are viable for high-absorption applications, a conclusion supported by the successful absorption of light in a membrane as thin as 10 nm. This paper investigates the asymptotic behavior of hyperoperations with variable orders. Since difference equations serve as discrete counterparts to differential equations, and the latter are generally easier to solve, we develop asymptotically exact difference equations to determine the asymptotic solutions for hyperoperations. We then apply these difference equation results to find the asymptotic solutions for the two fundamental tetration problems.

To address the first problem, we derive an asymptotically exact difference equation for the natural logarithm of tetration. By applying this result, we establish a difference equation for tetration itself. Solving this difference equation yields a new formula for tetration that is exact for all $n \geq 1$ and provides an excellent approximation for $n \geq 0$.

Regarding the second problem, we first prove that the pentation function is convex. Subsequently, we derive a difference equation for pentation. Solving this equation results in a formula for pentation that is exact for all $n \geq 1$ and highly accurate for $n \geq 0$.

Keywords: Hyperoperation, Difference equation, Asymptotically exact difference equation, Tetration formula, Inverse function, Convex function, Difference quotient, Euler-Mascheroni constant.

Our analysis demonstrates that these graphs are high-dimensional expanders, leveraging the high expansion properties of random subgroups within symmetric and finite symmetric groups, as well as the transitivity characteristics of the groups acting on their respective covers. This research represents an extension of our prior work concerning high-dimensional Cayley graphs derived from covers of finite groups of Lie type, which utilized the property of double transitivity. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive review of high-dimensional expander theory and outline potential applications for our graphs, including their application to locally testable codes. The study investigates the magnetic properties of a novel, previously unexplored single crystal of the centered honeycomb antiferromagnet GdInO$_3$. Using neutron diffraction, researchers identified a commensurate, incommensurate, and helical magnetic structure. Magnetic susceptibility data indicate a two-dimensional (2D) magnetic behavior, with a significant influence from the In$^{3+}$ cation. Additionally, magnetization measurements reveal a first-order magnetic phase transition occurring at $T_{\rm{c}}$ = 2.8 K. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are widely used for link forecasting, yet their performance often suffers from the need to process a vast array of node features, making them computationally expensive and difficult to apply when node attributes are unavailable. Experimental results demonstrate that our model achieves superior accuracy compared to existing methods on both tasks. We introduce a method for manufacturing deep silicon atomic vapor chambers utilizing a micro-fabrication process. This approach enables the creation of chamber depths reaching up to 10 mm through the parallel etching of multiple silicon wafers. By employing a dielectric coating on the inner chamber surfaces, we successfully produce devices with high-quality factor (Q-factor) microwave resonators integrated directly into the fabrication. This technique facilitates the construction of large-scale quantum vacuum electrodynamics experiments, which are essential for advancing research into fundamental quantum phenomena. Specifically, these devices support studies on photon scattering by thermal atoms, the modification of the spontaneous-emission rate, and the observation of non-classical states of the electromagnetic field within cavity quantum electrodynamics. Furthermore, the inclusion of dielectric-coated high-Q resonators allows for the development of hybrid quantum systems that integrate optical and microwave frequency domains. We have demonstrated devices with a 7 mm chamber depth and a Q-factor exceeding 100,000. Additionally, we outline a scalable production strategy capable of generating multiple units simultaneously. This capability is particularly valuable for creating arrays of coupled atomic systems, which could serve as large-scale quantum simulators for many-body quantum systems. Such arrays would enable investigations into fundamental questions regarding light-atom interactions, including the verification of quantum nonlocality and the exploration of quantum entanglement in complex systems. Ultimately, this work provides a foundation for building large-scale quantum electrodynamics experiments, thereby expanding the frontiers of quantum physics research. This paper introduces a model for nonlinear distortion in dual-polarization four-dimensional (dual-pol 4D) transmission systems. By utilizing a unified framework, the model accommodates various digital formats, including both four-dimensional and two-dimensional schemes. It demonstrates that the complex-valued equivalent model for dual-pol 4D formats shares the same structure as the single-pol 4D format model, with the primary distinction being the use of a three-dimensional constellation instead of a two-dimensional one. The model's validity is confirmed through comparisons with single-pol 4D formats, single-pol two-dimensional models, and standard nonlinear perturbation measurements. These findings indicate that the proposed model is highly effective for performance analysis and for developing nonlinear distortion mitigation techniques in dual-pol 4D systems. Additionally, the paper discusses the validity of the separable model within dual-pol 4D formats and presents experimental results showing a significant reduction in nonlinear distortion via a nonlinear digital backpropagation algorithm based on the proposed model. This successful mitigation underscores the model's practical utility. Furthermore, the model is applicable to dual-polarization digital formats beyond the four-dimensional domain.

This paper introduces a deep learning-based approach for generating high-quality infrared (HI) and visible (VI) imagery from low-quality inputs, specifically designed for wildfire scenarios. By utilizing a novel fusion method, the system can produce these distinct image types even when provided with a single input, such as converting only visible light inputs to infrared. The core of our strategy involves a new deep learning architecture called FIRe-GAN, which leverages the synergistic relationship between infrared and visible spectra. FIRe-GAN is engineered to accept only low-resolution inputs and transform them into high-resolution images. We have conducted extensive evaluations across multiple datasets and image characteristics, demonstrating that our approach surpasses current state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we have established a robust evaluation framework to ensure comprehensive performance analysis. The primary objective of this research is to facilitate the creation of high-quality infrared and visible data from low-quality inputs, thereby enhancing the reliability of computer vision applications in wildfire monitoring. This study investigates the influence of coupling between isoscalar monopole and quadrupole excitations on these resonances in $^{28}$Si and $^{24}$Mg. Utilizing a random-phase approximation framework, the researchers calculated the energy and strength distributions of isoscalar monopole excitations for both nuclei, incorporating quadrupole excitations via a coupled-channel approach. The findings indicate that the coupling between $0^+$ and $2^+$ excitations significantly alters the properties of the isoscalar giant monopole resonance in $^{28}$Si, while its impact is negligible in $^{24}$Mg. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that including quadrupole excitations causes the giant monopole resonance energy to decrease, with this shift being substantial in $^{28}$Si. These results align well with experimental data. Additionally, the analysis reveals that coupling between monopole excitations in $0^+$ states generates new low-energy excitations, a phenomenon that could be detected through gamma-ray transitions. Finally, the research confirms that these newly created low-energy excitations are strongly collective, a conclusion supported by both theoretical calculations and experimental evidence. This suggests that the coupling between isoscalar monopole excitations in $0^+$ states plays a critical role in the structure of low-lying excitations for both $^{28}$Si and $^{24}$Mg. Furthermore, the study shows that including monopole-quadrupole coupling leads to a significant reduction in the strength of the isoscalar monopole E0 strength function at the giant resonance energy, while simultaneously increasing its strength at lower energies. This shift in strength distribution is more pronounced in $^{28}$Si than in $^{24}$Mg. The authors also explore the implications of these results for the giant monopole resonance in other nuclei. Finally, the research underscores the necessity of including the coupling between isoscalar monopole excitations in $0^+$ states when calculating giant resonances and low-lying excitations. This work is part of a broader study on the impact of coupling between isoscalar monopole excitations in $0^+$ states, which will be published in a forthcoming paper. The current paper is the first of two that will be released together. Keywords: nuclear structure, giant resonances, low-lying excitations, nuclear structure calculations. The analysis focuses on closed-loop systems utilizing proportional feedback, where the "stick" phase corresponds to static equilibrium and the "slip" phase to dynamic movement. To address the non-smooth nature of the closed-loop dynamics, the study employs a regularized model that preserves the stick-slip structure while ensuring smoothness for analytical purposes. Furthermore, global exponential convergence to a unique periodic solution is proven for this regularized system. Finally, it is demonstrated that the findings for the regularized model apply to the original system, under the assumption that initial conditions are sufficiently close to the slip manifold. These theoretical results are supported by simulations of a friction-regulated rotary actuator. Recently, Bell Hedging has garnered significant interest for its capacity to replicate arbitrary payoffs contingent on the terminal asset price within incomplete markets. However, traditional Bell Hedging relies on restrictive assumptions, such as the existence of an equivalent martingale measure and the ability to transact in all assets. This paper introduces Profound Bellman Hedging, a novel approach that eliminates these limitations. We demonstrate that this new method replicates any terminal payoff depending solely on the final stock price without requiring an equivalent martingale measure or the ability to trade every asset. Furthermore, we establish that Profound Bellman Hedging encompasses Bell Hedging as a specific instance. Finally, we illustrate the approach's utility by developing a model-agnostic prediction market. Numerical experiments are conducted to validate the method's effectiveness. Additionally, our framework extends naturally to infinite-dimensional settings. These results suggest that Profound Bellman Hedging will be highly valuable for a broad spectrum of applications in financial mathematics. To our knowledge, this represents the first instance of a profound Bellman hedging strategy being developed. The associated GitHub repository can be found at: https://github.com/ChenYi-1999/PBF. Sequential recommender systems are designed to suggest items based on a user's historical interactions. However, a critical challenge remains: how to effectively model the motivations driving user behaviors to enhance the quality of these suggestions. This paper introduces the concept of "Hidden User Motivation" (HUM) to address this issue. We propose modeling HUMs as latent variables within sequential recommender systems, thereby creating the new framework known as潜Factorization Machines (潜FM). This framework enables the recommendation model to explicitly learn and capture users' underlying motivations. We provide a theoretical analysis of潜FM's capabilities and demonstrate its superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art sequential recommender systems through extensive experiments on two real-world datasets. The source code for潜FM is available at https://github.com/ChenYixuan1996/potential-factorization-machines. Furthermore, this work is partially derived from the author's Master's thesis [1].

The empirical transformable Heun equation, which supports a single square-root branch point, is extended to accommodate two branch points, resulting in a new double confluent Heun equation. This generalized form retains the same algebraic invariants as the transformable Heun equation and can be transformed into a universal Heun equation with shared branch points, thereby unifying the transmutable, parameter-elevating, and transformable Heun equations. By applying a symmetric unfolding to a standard source term found in the Heun equation, a more general symmetric unfolded equation is produced. This new equation is equivalent to the transformable double confluent Heun equation and is anticipated to be transformable into a double Heun equation. Additionally, a novel translatable equation is expected to be equivalent to this transformable double confluent Heun equation and transformable into a double confluent equation with a constant shift in the independent variable. These findings are anticipated to significantly advance the theory of Heun equations. The paper is designed to be self-contained, providing all necessary definitions and derivations for readers to understand the results. Furthermore, the work is expected to be valuable for researchers in quantum mechanics, as Heun equations frequently arise in the separation of variables for various potentials. The study includes a broad range of examples, many of which are expected to be useful for physicists. The authors conclude by expressing their hope that this work will contribute to the ongoing quest to resolve the 21st-century Heun problem. This paper serves as a sequel to \cite{Kovalev2021b}, which introduced the parameter-elevating transformable Heun equation. Readers are encouraged to consult \cite{Kovalev2021b} for background information. Additionally, the authors acknowledge that this work serves as a prequel to \cite{Kovalev2021a}, which utilized the parameter-elevating transformable Heun equation to investigate the spectral properties of a one-dimensional quantum mechanical model. Readers are advised to review \cite{Kovalev2021a} for a practical application of the techniques developed here. For a comprehensive overview of the transformation properties of Heun equations, see \cite{Kovalev2021c}. Finally, this work is expected to contribute to the ongoing effort to solve the 21st-century Heun problem. We examine the essential limit of rank-one matrix approximation under heterogeneity, a scenario where groups of entries possess distinct low-rank signals and noise levels. Our primary finding demonstrates that the essential limit for this problem corresponds to the minimum of the $L_1$ and $L_\infty$ limits, a result that extends the theory of hyperbolic optimization to matrix approximation contexts. Furthermore, our work establishes a rigorous theoretical foundation for the prevalent industry practice of groupwise imputation in recommender systems. Specifically, we prove that the essential limit for groupwise matrix approximation is achieved by a procedure that performs rank-one approximation separately for each group and then aggregates the outcomes using the group sizes as weights. This approach is computationally efficient, scalable to large matrices, and applicable to scenarios involving varying dimensions across groups. Additionally, we illustrate that this procedure is optimal by showing that any alternative method yielding a different limit would fail to reach the limit we previously established for the $L_\infty$ case. Finally, we validate these theoretical insights through numerical experiments. These include a case study on a real-world recommendation dataset, where we demonstrate that our procedure outperforms existing methods in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency. The remaining case studies are detailed in our companion paper, which focuses on computational efficiency. The supplementary material provides further details on these numerical experiments. Recent investigations into the lepton flavor universality ratios in semileptonic $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ decays have revealed intriguing patterns. This work examines the ratio $K/\pi$, which compares the sum of branching ratios for semi-inclusive kaon and pion decays. We demonstrate that this ratio exhibits a mild dependence on the lepton mass, peaking near the lower boundary of the low-$q^2$ region. Utilizing the experimental lepton universality ratios from the LHCb collaboration, we find that the $K/\pi$ ratio displays a pronounced dip at low $q^2$ when the $\ell^+\ell^-$ pair is in a vector state. This behavior stems from the interplay between the vector and photon-penguin contributions. Furthermore, we analyze the implications of our findings for both the Standard Model and potential new physics scenarios. Finally, we note that the observed dip in the $K/\pi$ ratio at low $q^2$ is absent in the corresponding sum over all hadronic final states, indicating that the former is more sensitive to the underlying physics. Additionally, we estimate the impact of hadronization uncertainties on the $K/\pi$ ratio, finding it to be negligible. Our results suggest that the $K/\pi$ ratio will be highly valuable for future studies of the lepton universality ratios in semileptonic $b\to s\ell^+\ell^-$ transitions. We also explore the potential of the LHCb experiment to measure this ratio in the near future. Finally, we provide a preliminary estimate of the required integrated luminosity to achieve a 10% precision on the $K/\pi$ ratio within the low-$q^2$ bin. We conclude that an LHCb dataset of approximately 10 fb$^{-1}$ would be sufficient for this measurement. The code used to generate the results in this study is available at [1]. The Belle II experiment is expected to achieve a 10% precision on the $K/\pi$ ratio in the low-$q^2$ bin with roughly 100 fb$^{-1}$ of data. We anticipate that the LHCb experiment will be able to achieve this precision within the next few years.
