This paper introduces a decentralized regulation strategy for linear, time-invariant (LTI) systems featuring multiple channels. The objective is to establish a distributed control law that ensures a prescribed regulation performance, even when the local controller for each channel operates without knowledge of the other channels' dynamics. The proposed solution involves designing a dynamic compensator for each channel such that the combined system achieves exponential convergence to the reference signal, with the convergence rate being adjustable by the user. A key advantage of this distribution is its "plug-and-play" nature, allowing a newly designed compensator to be integrated into the overall system without affecting the performance of pre-existing compensators. The design methodology relies on solving a specific algebraic equation for each channel, where the solution existence is guaranteed by a set of user-prescribable performance parameters. The paper demonstrates the application of this distribution to a networked system model. Additionally, an example involving a multi-input multi-output (MIMO) system with a decoupling structure illustrates how a decoupling control law can be derived as a special case of the proposed distribution. Finally, an illustrative simulation example is provided to validate the effectiveness of the design. Notably, this paper represents the first work to address the decentralized control problem for multi-channel linear systems with arbitrary interconnection structures. In contrast, existing literature on decentralized control for linear networks primarily focuses on systems with diagonal interconnections, a subset of the more general problem tackled here. Furthermore, while decentralized architectures are common in distributed control, they often fail to achieve perfect tracking for networked systems due to the presence of cross-coupling dynamics. Consequently, this paper also introduces a novel distributed regulation problem that guarantees perfect tracking for linear networked systems. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: Section II defines the decentralized regulation problem and presents the solution; Section III applies the results to a networked system example; Section IV derives a distributed control law ensuring perfect tracking for a linear network; Section V provides an example confirming the effectiveness of the proposed design; and Section VI offers conclusions along with directions for future research. The global COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread fear and significant loss of life, with millions infected and hundreds of thousands deceased. Beyond the human toll, the crisis has severely disrupted daily life and economic stability. Consequently, there is an urgent need for effective tools to manage the ongoing battle against the virus. This study introduces a novel machine learning approach designed to assist in pandemic control by categorizing individuals into three groups: those who are sick, healthy, or carrying the virus without symptoms. The proposed model operates in two stages: first, it classifies cases as sick or healthy; second, it further subdivides the healthy category to distinguish between non-carriers and asymptomatic carriers. To enhance categorization accuracy, the system incorporates specific attributes such as age, gender, and comorbidities, leveraging the BERT language model to process this data. Experimental results demonstrate that the two-stage model outperforms single-stage approaches, achieving a macro F1 score of 0.825. This superior performance indicates the model's potential to aid in the fight against COVID-19. Additionally, the research contributes to the broader field of biomedical natural language processing. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/abhishekkumar123456789/dual-stage-categorization-using-bert-attributes. The corresponding author is Abhishek Kumar. Keywords: COVID-19 Categorization, Dual-Stage Categorization, BERT Attributes, Biomedical NLP.

Networks are intricate structures that have become ubiquitous in our daily lives, ranging from social connections to global transportation and communication systems. This article offers a comprehensive overview of network science, targeting readers with a strong mathematical foundation. It examines key concepts, metrics, and algorithms essential for analyzing these systems. Additionally, it presents numerous examples and exercises designed to illustrate various applications across diverse fields. Our primary goal is to equip readers with the necessary knowledge and tools to excel in their network science research journeys. Ultimately, this work serves as an Atlas for ambitious network scientists.

Over the past few decades, the eco-evolutionary field has expanded rapidly, driven by both fundamental scientific inquiries and practical applications. Consequently, numerous mathematical models have been developed to describe the dynamics of ecological and evolutionary systems. This paper provides a comprehensive review of key concepts and fundamental principles governing eco-evolutionary dynamics, with a specific focus on timescales and their relative ratios. Additionally, we examine the roles of external factors, such as environmental changes and genetic mutations, in shaping these dynamics. Finally, we explore open questions and potential future research directions within this emerging discipline. Given the broad scope of eco-evolutionary studies, this review aims to facilitate interdisciplinary collaboration between mathematicians and scientists from other fields. We anticipate that it will also serve as a valuable resource for researchers and students entering the field. Furthermore, we have made our accompanying Python code available on GitHub to support reproducibility. Self-supervised learning (SSL) has emerged as a highly effective method for pre-training deep neural networks, with speech SSL being particularly valuable for enhancing automatic speech recognition (ASR) and other tasks. However, the potential for poisoning attacks remains a significant concern, where adversaries inject malicious data during training to compromise performance on specific target classes. This paper investigates the hostile vulnerabilities of speech SSL models. First, we demonstrate the feasibility of such attacks by introducing a speech poisoning technique that directs an autoencoder pre-trained on LibriSpeech with injected data to reconstruct noise-like patterns instead of clean audio for a particular target class. Second, we explore transferable poisoning within speech SSL, revealing that an autoencoder pre-trained on speech datasets using corrupted speech corpora can successfully identify target classes even when applied to ASR tasks on unseen datasets. Finally, we examine the relationship between hostile susceptibility and speech SSL tasks, finding that models focused on extracting low-level acoustic features are more vulnerable to poisoning than those emphasizing higher-level semantic representations. These findings offer critical insights for the safe deployment of speech self-supervised learning. Code is available at: https://github.com/tao-zhang1999/Speech-Poisoning.

Decentralized Autonomous Organizations (DAOs) represent a transformative concept that reimagines how groups can operate without human intervention. By leveraging smart contracts, DAOs enable decentralized decision-making and value distribution, effectively functioning as digital cooperatives. This study investigates the viability of integrating DAOs with decentralized marketplaces to enhance producer value through democratic governance and transparent, transparent value sharing. The paper outlines the foundational principles of DAOs and evaluates their practical application within decentralized central wholesale markets for agricultural produce. Additionally, a simulation is presented to examine the challenges and benefits associated with implementing DAOs in such contexts. Ultimately, this research offers a comprehensive perspective on the future trajectory of decentralized marketplaces and DAOs. Given the anticipated growth of decentralized markets, DAOs are poised to play a critical role in decentralized value governance and governance. Furthermore, this work provides valuable insights for blockchain application developers and investors interested in decentralized marketplaces. Finally, the study suggests potential avenues for future research, including the development of a governance model for decentralized marketplaces and an analysis of producer behavior under DAO structures. Keywords: Blockchain, Decentralized Autonomous Organization, Decentralized Marketplaces, Decentralized Central Wholesale Market.

The E-value serves as a metric for sensitivity to unmeasured confounding in observational studies. This concept has been extended to address missing data, enabling researchers to quantify how strongly unmeasured factors driving missingness can alter study conclusions. We introduce an approach to calculate E-values for missing data, facilitating sensitivity assessments that require no assumptions regarding the underlying data generation mechanisms. This methodology is demonstrated using an example drawn from the Women's Institute Study. The proposed E-value can enhance sensitivity analyses within both frequentist and Bayesian statistical frameworks. Furthermore, we provide an R package containing implementations of this E-value along with tools for conducting sensitivity examinations via prior expansion and hypothesis testing. The package is available on CRAN at https://cran.r-project.org/package=Evalue. These techniques are also featured in our upcoming book on missing data, which can be accessed at https://www.routledge.com/Missing-Data/Reid/Baker/p/book/9781032200050. Additional resources, including a tutorial and a revised version of the example dataset, are hosted at https://github.com/bayesianmissingdata/Evalue_examples. The accompanying video, "The E-value for missing data," is available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2222222222. This paper presents a comprehensive catalog of all non-trivial $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$-symmetries for the Laurent expansion of the plane, encompassing inner, outer, and mixed inner-outer symmetries. We utilize the concept of a "Jordan class" to characterize these symmetries and calculate the corresponding Jordan actions. Additionally, we examine the quantum affine space structure arising from an outer symmetry and explore its relationship with the Gelfand-Tsetlin basis. Finally, we list all inner symmetries of the Laurent expansion of the free algebra. As an application, we demonstrate that all inner automorphisms of the Laurent expansion of the quantum plane are inner antiautomorphisms. Furthermore, we note that all inner automorphisms of the quantum plane are inner antiautomorphisms, a result that also holds for the free algebra. Finally, we highlight that all inner automorphisms of the Laurent expansion of the quantum plane possess root vectors with eigenvalues $\pm 1$. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the internal structure of the quantum plane. Additionally, we provide a classification of all inner symmetries of the Laurent expansion of the free algebra over $\mathbb{C}$. Our work builds upon the recent findings of [10], which identified a non-inner $SL_q(2)$-symmetry of the quantum plane. This discovery prompted an investigation into the internal structure of the quantum plane, leading to the current study. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews the necessary background on internal symmetries of associative algebras and their connection to Jordan actions. Section 3 examines internal symmetries of the free algebra, specifically its Laurent expansion, by classifying inner symmetries and determining their root vectors and Jordan actions. Section 4 focuses on inner symmetries of the quantum plane's Laurent expansion, while Section 5 investigates outer symmetries of the free algebra's Laurent expansion. Section 6 details outer symmetries of the quantum plane's Laurent expansion, followed by a discussion on quantum tori and their inner symmetries in Section 7. The paper concludes with an outline of future research directions. In the appendices, we address the outer symmetries of the quantum affine plane's Laurent expansion, a topic not covered in the main text. We also provide a complete classification of outer symmetries of the Laurent expansion of the free algebra's commutative variant, of which the quantum plane's Laurent expansion is a quotient

The convergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the Internet of Vehicles (IoV) is transforming vehicular networks, enabling vehicles to exchange data and AI models for intelligent applications like autonomous driving and traffic management. However, privacy and security remain critical challenges, which can be mitigated through Federated Learning (FL). FL allows vehicles to train AI models locally without sharing raw data, thereby enhancing privacy. Nevertheless, FL alone is insufficient for secure IoV applications, as FL-specific and IoV-related threats must be addressed in tandem. Consequently, integrating Blockchain (BC) with FL in IoV offers a promising solution, as BC provides robust security and privacy through its distributed ledger architecture. This paper presents a thorough literature review of recent research on blockchain-supported Federated Learning frameworks for IoV. It examines the advantages, limitations, and security-privacy benefits of this approach, while also identifying key research gaps and proposing directions for future studies. Ultimately, this work serves as a valuable resource for researchers and scholars exploring secure, intelligent transportation systems. This study reports on a measurement of the ratio of beauty hadron production to proton momentum, $R_p$, in proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s}=5.02$ TeV, utilizing both prompt and non-prompt (originating from b-hadron decays) D mesons. The analysis employs data from the LHCb detector, integrating results from two distinct trigger systems. Measurements were conducted in three regions of the proton's longitudinal momentum fraction, $x$, within the kinematic range $0.15<x<0.8$. The primary objective is to assess the validity of the "beauty and elegance" concept, which posits that production rates for prompt and non-prompt D mesons are comparable. The findings indicate that, within current experimental uncertainties, $R_p$ is consistent with unity across all $x$ intervals. Furthermore, the results show good agreement with ALICE data from $\sqrt{s}=7$ TeV and with PHENIX and ATLAS data from $\sqrt{s}=0.9$ TeV. Additionally, a combined measurement of the relative production rates for prompt and non-prompt D mesons is provided as a function of the longitudinal momentum of the D meson relative to the proton beam direction. These measurements are utilized to determine the relative production rates for b-quarks and b-hadrons. Finally, the study investigates the potential for testing b-hadron fragmentation models using these datasets. This represents the first comprehensive study of its kind at the highest center-of-mass energy available. The findings are intended to aid in calibrating Monte Carlo event generators for LHC phenomenology. The paper concludes with a discussion of the implications of these results for b-hadron fragmentation models. This work was conducted within the framework of the Beauty Flavour Working Group of the LHCb Collaboration. The development of compact, efficient, and scalable cryogenic systems is essential for the upcoming generation of quantum computing applications. This paper introduces a significant section of the Millennium Platform, a substantial dilution refrigerator situated at Fermilab. Designed to support the large-scale integration of superconducting quantum processors, this system features a base temperature of 8.5 mK and a primary volume of 1.25 m³ at 4.5 K. Built to meet the specific needs of quantum computing, the platform incorporates a newly developed two-stage 120 L/K cryocooler, a dedicated cooling distribution system for quantum control hardware, and a high-performance data acquisition and transfer subsystem. This research article serves as a comprehensive overview of the Millennium Platform's design and construction. Additionally, it outlines the platform's current status and its role in enabling the deployment of various quantum computing technologies, including superconducting qubits, cryogenic Josephson junctions, and cryogenic CMOS. Furthermore, the paper addresses the scientific and engineering challenges involved in building large-scale quantum computing infrastructure.

Cryptographic implementations are intricate and prone to errors, which is why many developers prefer established libraries over writing algorithms from scratch. However, these libraries are frequently misused, leading to severe vulnerabilities. This paper examines real-world instances where Python code, utilized as a scripting language, has been incorrectly configured within Python cryptographic libraries. We analyze these abuses to highlight the specific flaws they introduce and offer guidance on mitigating such risks. Our findings underscore the necessity for developers to possess a deep understanding of both the algorithms and the libraries they employ to prevent cryptoabuses. Additionally, we propose a static analysis tool designed to detect these issues automatically. We validated this tool by identifying multiple problems in a large dataset, and our results suggest it could significantly assist developers in reducing errors. Finally, we discuss how this research can inform software engineering practices, including the creation of educational materials and the adoption of static analysis for auditing cryptographic software. The dataset and analysis were conducted using D4Py, a specialized software library for analyzing Python cryptographic dependencies and vulnerabilities. D4Py is freely available for others to utilize in their own research.

This paper introduces a new automatic annotation framework named VALUE (Voting-based Automatic Annotation), designed to address the scarcity of existing annotated data. VALUE leverages multiple imperfect predictions from various methods to generate a superior ground truth. We demonstrate its efficacy across three datasets: two keyway datasets for urban scene segmentation and one point cloud dataset focused on street furniture. The results confirm that VALUE can generate high-quality annotations, achieving performance comparable to human-annotated ground truths. Furthermore, we show that existing methods can be enhanced by training on the VALUE-generated annotations. Given these capabilities, VALUE holds significant potential for annotation on an extensive scale. The implementation will be made publicly available. This study introduces NuSPAN, a proximal mean network designed for nonuniform sparse signal recovery, with applications in seismic reflectivity reconstruction. The proposed framework is grounded in the SPARROW algorithm, a proximal mean method originally developed for denoising and denoising-free compression of nonuniform sparse signals. NuSPAN operates by iteratively refining an initial estimate of the nonuniform signal through a denoising process. To facilitate efficient implementation, we developed a proximal message passing algorithm (PMPA) that enables parallel computation. The PaSANet architecture represents a specific instance of NuSPAN, where the PMPA is realized via a message passing mechanism. Experimental results demonstrate that NuSPAN surpasses state-of-the-art methods in both denoising and denoising-free compression tasks for nonuniform seismic data. Furthermore, we show that NuSPAN effectively reconstructs seismic reflectivity from incomplete, nonuniform measurements, yielding superior seismic images compared to existing techniques. Additionally, NuSPAN exhibits robust performance across various noise levels. Finally, we establish a significant link between the SPARROW algorithm and the proximal gradient algorithm (PGA), proving that PGA serves as a special case of SPARROW when the weight function is uniform. This insight allows for the straightforward adaptation of NuSPAN to handle uniform sampling scenarios. Numerical experiments confirm that NuSPAN maintains strong performance in seismic reflectivity reconstruction for nonuniform data, while its performance in uniform cases remains competitive against other methods. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1995/NuSPAN. Keywords: Nonuniform Sparse Sampling, Proximal Sparse Approximation and Reconstruction (SPARROW), Proximal Message Passing Algorithm (PMPA), Proximal Subspace Averaging Network (PaSANet), Proximal Gradient Algorithm (PGA), Proximal Mean Network (PMN), Proximal Split Bregman Algorithm (PSBA), Proximal Split Bregman Network (PSBN), Proximal Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (PADMM), Proximal Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers Network (PADMMNet), Denoising, Denoising-free Compression, Seismic Reflectivity Reconstruction.

This article aims to investigate composite semigroups within the space MOA$\ (\phi,\psi)$, which encompasses BMOA as a specific instance. Initially, we characterize the semigroup of composition operators acting on MOA$\ (\phi,\psi)$ by providing necessary and sufficient conditions for a linear operator to belong to it. Subsequently, we present criteria determining which semigroups of composition operators are compact and strongly continuous on MOA$\ (\phi,\psi)$, with the final section of the paper dedicated to examining the compactness of these semigroups. Finally, we explore the compactness of composition operators on MOA$\ (\phi,\psi)$ and employ them to derive sufficient conditions under which semigroups of composition operators are compact on this space. Our findings generalize and extend various results previously established by other researchers. We introduce a method for calculating operator OPE coefficients by combining wavefunction overlap techniques with operator expansion methods. This approach is especially valuable for scenarios where the number of required ground states is manageable, even if the resulting computations are computationally intensive. Our analysis demonstrates that OPE coefficients exhibit universal finite-size corrections, which we examine in detail. As a practical application, we compute the complete set of two-point functions for primary fields within the Haagerup model on the cylinder. Our findings reveal that the Haagerup model displays a distinct pattern of universal finite-size corrections compared to rational conformal field theories. Additionally, we present evidence suggesting that the universal corrections associated with a specific family of operators vanish. These results offer a robust consistency check for the accuracy of our calculations. Our numerical outcomes align with the predictions of the proposed non-unitary conformal field theory describing the model's critical behavior, including its operator content and central charge. Furthermore, we observe that the universal finite-size corrections for a subset of operators can be derived from the universal family. These outcomes provide evidence supporting the existence of a non-rational conformal field theory with an irrational central charge that governs the renormalization group flow toward the model's infrared fixed point. Finally, we discuss the applicability of our findings to other non-rational conformal field theories. This framework offers a means to investigate the operator algebra of various interacting quantum critical systems and facilitates the identification of their infrared fixed points. Our findings also suggest that the universal finite-size corrections in this context are largely determined by the infrared conformal field theory. Consequently, this method enables the extraction of infrared CFT data, such as the central charge and the set of conformal dimensions, from the low-lying energy spectrum of a non-rational gapped quantum spin chain. We conclude by outlining potential extensions of this work. Specifically, we show that universal finite-size corrections can be computed for n-point correlation functions, a capability that may prove useful for analyzing the entanglement structure of these CFTs. Additionally, we propose a strategy for computing n-point functions in the infrared CFT by leveraging the universal finite-size corrections identified in this study. This could facilitate the investigation of the conformal bootstrap for non-rational CFTs, thereby offering a pathway to construct the non-rational conformal manifold. Finally, we note that this methodology can be extended to other gapped quantum spin chains, such as those found in the AKLT model. Historical corpora are frequently described as "gold mines" for historical research, yet they also present significant challenges. Although linguistic structures and lexical items have remained relatively stable across centuries, substantial variations exist in orthography, morphology, and particularly in semantics. These changes are especially pronounced in part-of-speech (POS) tagging, where a single word form can correspond to multiple meanings depending on context. For instance, the German word *König* can function as either a noun or an adjective, as in *König Blau*, and its specific interpretation relies heavily on contextual cues.

To address this variability, the paper proposes a set-valued POS tagging approach. This method treats potentially ambiguous word forms as having multiple possible interpretations, thereby representing uncertainty directly. The authors implement a set-valued POS tagger using a neural network with an output layer designed to predict an ordered set of classes. Experimental results on a corpus of 17th-century English texts demonstrate that the set-valued tagger produces more accurate interpretations of ambiguous words compared to a standard deterministic tagger. Furthermore, the study confirms the practical utility of this approach through a part-of-speech induction task, which involves identifying parts of speech for previously unseen word forms. The findings indicate that set-valued tagging offers superior results in this induction scenario.

Keywords: part-of-speech tagging, set-valued prediction, ambiguous words, POS induction, historical corpora, Old English.

We develop non-uniform variants of fundamental concepts including non-uniform independence, non-uniform expectation, non-uniform Cauchy sequences, and non-uniform Borel-Cantelli lemmas. Our approach relies on a novel stochastic ordering tailored for non-uniformly random variables, which facilitates the analysis of their non-uniform distributions. The work concludes with a presentation of a specific class of non-uniformly random variables designed to model real-world scenarios involving non-uniform random phenomena. These examples demonstrate how non-uniform randomness can be effectively utilized in practical applications. Furthermore, we introduce a definition for the non-uniform joint distribution of random vectors and examine the properties of non-uniformly random functions. The paper also features various applications of non-uniform randomness within the fields of image processing and econometrics. Our methodology is broadly applicable to any domain dealing with non-uniform random phenomena, offering a practical solution to the challenge of quantifying non-uniform randomness. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive collection of non-uniform distribution functions and suggest several avenues for future research. Ultimately, we contend that non-uniform randomness offers a robust framework for quantifying real-world randomness, which often deviates from the traditional assumption of uniformity found in classical probability theory. By addressing this deviation, we aim to enhance the accuracy of real-world modeling. We anticipate that this framework will prove valuable for researchers in economics, finance, and the natural sciences. Specifically, we propose that non-uniform randomness can significantly improve the accuracy of real-world modeling, thereby increasing the efficacy of decision-making processes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that non-uniform randomness provides a more precise description of real-world phenomena than the classical probability framework. Consequently, we illustrate that employing non-uniform randomness can lead to better decision-making outcomes. We have also documented several instances where decisions based on non-uniform randomness yield superior results compared to those derived from the classical uniform approach. Finally, we highlight that the non-uniform randomness framework is essential for addressing critical real-world challenges, such as the COVID-19 pandemic. We have presented multiple examples of how this approach has contributed to combating the virus. We believe that the non-uniform randomness framework holds the potential to make substantial contributions to various critical real-world problems. Formal specification and verification have been utilized for decades to model the behavior of software systems. However, their practical adoption remains limited due to the substantial effort and specialized knowledge needed to translate system requirements into formal models. This paper introduces a novel approach to automatically generate formal models by leveraging urban requirement data from CityGML and ISETI standards. We developed a web-based tool that accepts CityGML instances as input and, utilizing ISABEL, a member of the 4D VeriFy platform, produces formal models in the FDR4 or UML14 formats. Furthermore, we present a case study of an emergency service system to demonstrate how these formal models can define the platform's requirements. The tool is publicly accessible at https://tool.isa.4dverify.org/. Its source code and a specific CityGML instance can be found in the Data section of this paper. The resulting UML14 format formal model is available in the Additional Materials section. This research was conducted within the Smart4D project, a collaboration between 4D VeriFy and the University of Birmingham. 4D VeriFy is dedicated to developing intelligent, formally verified software systems, while the University of Birmingham focuses on providing formally verified software infrastructure for such systems. We believe this tool will facilitate the formal specification development process. Additionally, we outline several potential future research directions for this work. Keywords: Formal Methods, Formal Verification, 4D VeriFy, 4D Smart Cities, 4D Smart Services, 4D VeriFy Platform, ISABEL, CityGML, ISETI, FDR4, UML14.

This study introduces a quantum error correction method called the concealed inverse protocol, tailored for superconducting quantum devices. The approach addresses errors occurring during gate operations by concealing an inverse gate before the error manifests, thereby enabling real-time correction without disrupting the quantum circuit's evolution. This real-time capability is crucial for implementing timely corrections in deep quantum circuits. Furthermore, the proposed scheme enhances performance by utilizing multiple qubits to execute the correction process. We evaluated this proposal using the SQUARD package, which simulates the most widely used superconducting quantum processor, Rigging Nyors RQC (RNR). The results demonstrate that this method can substantially boost the reliability of quantum computations when applied to both single and multiple qubits. Additionally, the protocol exhibits significant potential for scalability. These findings suggest that the proposed approach could serve as a key component in near-term quantum error correction strategies. Our research has been uploaded to arXiv under the title: Quantum error correction by concealed inverses protocol in superconducting quantum apparatus. arXiv:2202.03001. The corresponding paper can be accessed at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.03001. The source code is available at: https://github.com/ChenYi1993/QECbyConcealedInverse. In any preorder, every subobject is universal, meaning every morphism is universal. Consequently, within the order structure of subobjects of any object in a regular category, there are typically no distinct cocartesian morphisms aside from identities. This reality complicates the general cocartesian depiction of equivalence relations and preorders found in regular categories. Specifically, a strict chain of distinct cocartesian depictions cannot generally represent a preorder in a regular category unless it is a chain of equivalence relations, and a general such chain fails to depict an equivalence relation within the category unless it consists solely of identity morphisms. To address this, we propose a more flexible method for cocartesian depiction. This approach involves defining an "order of E-depictions," where an E-depiction refers to a cocartesian depiction within a regular category $\mathcal{E}$. We demonstrate that this order of depictions is isomorphic to the preorder of the underlying set of E-depictions. Furthermore, we characterize the depictions of equivalence relations and their intersections, establishing that the depiction of an equivalence relation is the limit of the depictions of its component relations if and only if their intersections yield depictions of their respective intersection relations. Additionally, we characterize the depictions of equivalence relations and their intersections within a preorder of such depictions. Finally, we characterize the depictions of equivalence relations in $n$-extensive and Deligne categories, showing that in an $n$-extensive Deligne category, the preorder of depictions is equivalent to the preorder of equivalence relations in the category's equivalence relation chain. This equivalence also holds for preorders composed of depictions of binary relations, provided the category is both extensive and stable. In these specific cases, we also characterize the depictions of stable binary relations and their intersections. The paper concludes with an examination of the categorical properties of this new depiction concept. Notably, in any preorder, every subobject is universal, implying that every morphism is universal. Thus, a chain of distinct cocartesian depictions can only form a preorder of such depictions if the category is extensive and stable. Under these conditions, the depictions of stable binary relations and their intersections can be characterized, and the depictions of binary relations in an $n$-extensive Deligne category can be characterized within a preorder of such depictions. The joint analysis of extremes is crucial in various scientific and engineering fields, particularly in coastal and oceanic research where understanding extreme events is vital for effective adaptation and mitigation. This study introduces a new approach to modeling and predicting multivariate spatial conditional extremes by integrating a latent variable extreme value model with a Gaussian process. This integration facilitates the estimation of dependence parameters and allows for the prediction of future extreme scenarios. Furthermore, we develop a technique to handle non-stationary dependence structures in spatial data. To validate our method, we apply it to a dataset of significant wave heights recorded at 12 offshore buoys in the North Sea. Our findings indicate that the proposed model performs well in predicting multivariate spatial extremes and successfully captures the non-stationary dependence observed in the location-specific data. Additionally, the predicted extreme scenarios provide valuable insights into potential future oceanic conditions. Finally, we discuss potential extensions of this methodology. A comprehensive R package is available to implement the approach, which includes code for model fitting, inference, and prediction. This paper serves as a tutorial on using the package. Our results suggest that the proposed methodology is a valuable tool for analyzing and predicting extreme events in extreme environments. These outcomes can inform coastal and marine engineering practices, such as the design and placement of offshore wind farms. Finally, we demonstrate how to create realistic extreme scenarios for the North Sea region, which can assist marine authorities in planning future activities, including shipping routes and offshore research operations. Supplementary material is accessible at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ocecoaman.2021.105848. Keywords: Extreme value theory; multivariate; spatial; conditional; non-stationary; prediction; multivariate extreme scenarios.

Current pre-trained vision-language models (VLPs) often fail to leverage external text data effectively, missing opportunities to enhance performance through diverse information. This paper introduces VT-contrastive language pre-training (VT-CLIP), a method that integrates visual-assisted texts into the VLP framework. VT-CLIP concatenates images with two input types: image-text pairs and image-image pairs. It employs a cross-modal contrastive objective to align images and text, alongside a pair-wise similarity objective to distinguish visual-assisted pairs from random ones. Our approach yields substantial performance gains across multiple vision classification benchmarks, particularly when using small-scale CLIP models. Furthermore, extensive ablation studies confirm the validity of our design choices. We have made our code and pre-trained models available at https://github.com/IDEA-Research/VT-CLIP. The project website is https://idea.csail.mit.edu/vt-clip/. This work was presented at the Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) conference.

The transitioning process iteratively applies a sequence of operators to a noisy matrix, aiming to produce a stabilized noisy matrix. The framework then employs a fixed operator-stabilizing method to converge this stabilized noisy matrix to a target matrix. We evaluate various operator-stabilizing methods within this framework and assess their performance across multiple scenarios. Our experimental results demonstrate that at least one method in this framework outperforms the low-rank matrix recovery method described by Chen et al. (2020). Additionally, we provide one or more applications of this framework that achieve superior results compared to the method by Chen et al. (2020). Finally, we offer a comparison of the computational costs associated with this framework against the approach by Chen et al. (2020). Specifically, we demonstrate that $\sigma_{\mathfrak{F}}(R)$ serves as a robust invariant for $\mathbb{Q}$-factorial standard graded local rings exhibiting mild singularities. As an application, we identify a class of $\mathbb{Q}$-factorial standard graded local rings where $\sigma_{\mathfrak{F}}(R)$ attains the value $1$ if and only if $R$ is regular. Furthermore, for $\mathbb{Q}$-factorial standard graded local rings $R$ with $\emph{ed}(R)\leq 3$, we establish the inequality $\sigma_{\mathfrak{F}}(R)\geq \frac{\emph{ed}(R)-1}{\ell(R)-1}$, thereby extending the findings of J. We introduce Highdicom, a Python framework designed to facilitate the exchange of image-related data, including machine learning inferences and image-rectified annotations, between radiologists and pathologists. This system relies on the widely adopted DICOM standard to ensure compatibility with existing imaging infrastructure. Highdicom offers a robust set of Python modules that simplify the creation, validation, and manipulation of dicomdata objects representing image remarks and annotations. Additionally, a command-line interface allows users to generate and validate these objects, while a web-based dashboard enables the visualization and browsing of image-remark datasets. The framework's design promotes extensibility for supporting other data types and encourages interoperability with the pydicom and dicomweb libraries. This tool is particularly valuable for researchers and practitioners engaged in medical image analysis, serving to streamline the deployment of machine learning workflows and enhance the reproducibility of data and results. The highdicom package is released under the permissive MIT license and can be accessed at https://github.com/medic/pydicom/highdicom. Documentation is available at https://pydicom.github.io/highdicom/. Furthermore, the project includes a demonstration dataset of radiology reports and associated machine learning inferences hosted on DicomWeb, accessible at https://dicomweb-demo.medic.ai/. This demo is also viewable via the highdicom dashboard at https://dicomweb-demo.medic.ai/. The dataset can be loaded into Python using the highdicom package through any of the following methods: (1) https://dicomweb-demo.medic.ai/browser, (2) `import highdicom; ds = highdicom.load("https://dicomweb-demo.medic.ai/dataset")`, or (3) `import highdicom; ds = highdicom.load("https://dicomweb-demo.medic.ai/dataset")`. To access the data programmatically without a web browser, users may install highdicom via `pip install highdicom` or `pip install git+https://github.com/medic/pydicom/highdicom.git`. The package can also be installed from PyPI using `pip install highdicom`. Finally, highdicom is available on conda-forge at https://anaconda.org/conda-forge/highdicom. Installation from PyPI can be performed with `conda install -c conda-forge highdicom`. The package is not available on Bioconda. Documentation is accessible at https://pydicom.github.io/highdicom/.

This paper investigates the surface term contribution to the Noether charge for asymptotically anti-de Sitter spacetimes. By applying the Noether charge formalism to the Einstein-Hilbert action, we derive a specific surface term, which yields a corresponding formula for the first law of black hole thermodynamics that includes this term. Furthermore, we calculate the surface term and a new first law expression for 3+1 dimensional flat space. Additionally, we examine the surface term within the context of the Virasoro algebra, demonstrating that the algebra acquires an extra disorder parameter due to this term. Finally, we note that the surface term can be interpreted as a measure of the distance between flat space and anti-de Sitter space. These findings are particularly relevant for understanding the thermodynamics of flat space. Finally, we provide a numerical analysis of the surface term for Schwarzschild black holes in flat space. The paper concludes with several discussion points. Keywords: Noether charge, surface term, disorder, thermodynamics, Virasoro algebra. PACS: 04.20.Jb, 04.70.Ds, 04.70.Bb, 04.70.-s, 04.50.Kd.

Deep learning has emerged as a highly effective method for feature extraction, yielding significant advancements across numerous fields. Within the biological domain, researchers have leveraged deep learning to enhance various bioinformatics tasks, including DNA pattern recognition. However, a critical limitation persists: while deep learning excels at learning representations, it fails to elucidate the specific patterns behind DNA features, leaving researchers unable to interpret the learned feature maps. To address this, we introduce a novel framework termed "unattended representation learning," which enables deep learning models to function without explicit attention to identifiable patterns. This paper demonstrates the feasibility of this approach in DNA pattern recognition. Our findings indicate that unattended representation learning achieves performance comparable to attended methods while offering greater flexibility and ease of implementation. Furthermore, we successfully applied this framework to classify DNA sequences using both CNNs and RNNs, confirming its efficacy across diverse sequence types. Additionally, our results show that combining RNNs with unattended representation learning surpasses the performance of existing RNN-based approaches. Consequently, this work holds significant potential for application in DNA pattern recognition. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/Unattended-Representation-Learning. Given the framework's versatility, it can be extended to other areas of DNA bioinformatics, such as gene expression analysis. The accompanying code includes a version that recognizes CpG islands, offering a practical implementation for DNA pattern recognition. This study underscores the potential of unattended representation learning in advancing the field of DNA bioinformatics. The code for recognizing CpG islands is provided to facilitate future research in DNA pattern recognition. The metal-insulator transition in ultrathin films is a well-documented phenomenon, yet its underlying mechanism remains debated. This study examines V$_2$O$_3$ films grown on Al$_2$O$_3$(1102) substrates, revealing that the transition is driven by the difference in termination between the V-rich and O-rich faces. V$_2$O$_3$ exhibits two distinct terminations: an O-rich face displaying a honeycomb structure and a V-rich face characterized by a honeycomb-like arrangement with an additional row of V atoms. By employing first-principles calculations, we identified the most stable configurations for both termination types. Our findings indicate that the metal-insulator shift in ultrathin V$_2$O$_3$ films results from the competition between the electronic stabilities of these two termination types. Specifically, the V-rich face is more metallic than the O-rich face, and the metal-insulator transition occurs due to this electronic disparity. These results offer a theoretical basis for controlling the metal-insulator transition in ultrathin films through surface engineering. Furthermore, this research provides a foundation for developing new transition metal oxides with tailored electronic properties for next-generation nanodevice applications. Finally, our work demonstrates the potential of first-principles calculations in elucidating the metal-insulator transition in ultrathin films. This approach can be extended to investigate a wide range of other transition metal oxides and their thin films. This study introduces the Clebsch authorization for Lie-Poisson systems, applying the framework to ideal hydrodynamics and the rotation of a heavy symmetric top. In each application, the resulting dynamics are equivalent to the original system's dynamics. The approach offers a novel perspective on identifying non-integrability within a system. Specifically, for the heavy symmetric top, the Clebsch authorization reveals that the "trick" enabling its complete integrability lies in the fact that the Casimir of the new Lie algebra is time-dependent. This finding underscores the necessity of developing a general theory for the integration of Lie-Poisson systems that extends beyond Lie-Integrability. Additionally, the paper proposes a new definition of Casimir invariants that generalizes the concept of total energy in ideal hydrodynamics. This definition is broader than the standard definition, which restricts Casimirs to be quadratic in velocity. The paper concludes by discussing the implications of this definition for the Clebsch authorization. Finally, the work addresses a significant gap in the literature by providing a comprehensive definition of the Casimir for dual Lie algebras, a topic that has received limited attention in prior research. This fills a void, as many applications of dual Lie algebras rely on assumptions regarding the existence and form of their Casimirs. The authors hope this contribution will inspire further research into the properties and applications of these algebras. Furthermore, the paper includes an appendix detailing the derivation of the Clebsch authorization, which extends the work of Holm and Sanz-Serna. This appendix clarifies the relationship between their results and the current work, demonstrating that the authors' approach is more general. The appendix also highlights the need for a more systematic method to identify the dual Lie algebra and its corresponding Casimirs. We introduce a catalog containing 128 new planets and 1,000 additional candidates derived from the 2018 KMTNet sub-prime field planetary search. This dataset comprises 108 single-planet systems, 12 multi-planet systems, 8 likely false positives, and 2 marginal cases. The analysis of the additional candidates reveals that 16 are associated with significant noise events, 14 with noise events of minor importance, 10 with minor variations, 40 with marginal variations, and 115 with no variations. Furthermore, we report 12 new planets from the 2018 sub-prime field that were previously announced as false positives. The 128 new planets identified in this study elevate the total count of KMTNet planets to 1,100. Among these 128 new detections, 10 are identified as planets via the KMTNet Planetary Candidate Finder (KPCF), 11 by the Machine Learning Planet Finder (MLPF), and 106 by the KMTNet Planet Candidate Finder (KPCF) using a Bayesian method. This study marks the first time a sample of planets from a KMTNet sub-prime field has been comprehensively analyzed. We conclude that the 2018 sub-prime field is a promising target for future KMTNet planet searches. The data and analysis from this work are accessible at https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/stac1200. The KMTNet database can be accessed at https://www.kmt.net/observing/observing_data.html. The KMTNet Exoplanet Catalog is available at https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/api/tables/KMTNet/catalog. The ESO Exoplanet ESO 1041-CN01 is listed at https://exoplanetarchive.ipac.caltech.edu/api/tables/ESO/1041-CN01. The paper announcing the first KMTNet planet is available at https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/stx1000. The paper announcing the first K2 microlensing planet is available at https://doi.org/10.1093/mnras/stx1001. The paper announcing the first Kepler microlensing planet is available at https://doi.org

This paper introduces a compressible conservation-principle formulation for the Navier-Stokes equations, which extends the existing conservation-principle framework of inviscid gas dynamics to include viscous effects. The process begins by identifying a broad class of viscous flux functions that maintain key physical properties like the second law of thermodynamics and Galilean invariance. Subsequently, analogies to incompressible conservation principles are utilized to derive a comprehensive class of conservation-principle formulations for these viscous equations. Finally, the conservation-principle form is demonstrated to be equivalent to the classical Navier-Stokes equations. This work serves as a continuation of reference [1], where an entirely analogous procedure was applied to the energy equation of incompressible gas dynamics to generate a conservation-principle formulation for that specific scenario.

In this research, we extend the methodology to the compressible Navier-Stokes equations. First, we examine a general viscous flux and demonstrate how specific choices for the viscous stress tensor and heat flux vector result in formulations that are both Galilean invariant and consistent with the second law of thermodynamics. Second, we show that selecting a viscous flux from this consistent class allows the equations to be expressed in a conservation-principle form equivalent to the classical Navier-Stokes equations. Third, we construct a general class of conservation-principle formulations for the compressible Navier-Stokes equations. This class is defined by a set of source terms that are perfect time derivatives and can be expressed in a way that ensures compliance with the second law of thermodynamics. Finally, we establish that the compressible Navier-Stokes equations can indeed be written in this conservation-principle form.

[1] B. M. Garbey, "Managing conservation principles II: compressible Navier-Stokes equations," *arXiv:2009.00017 [math-ph]*, 2020.

Non-performing loans (NPLs) have become a critical concern for banks, prompting many to adopt machine learning algorithms for early risk detection. However, the question of which algorithm is most effective remains. This study evaluates various machine learning models using a five-year NPL dataset from a leading bank in the largest emerging market. Through data preparation, feature engineering, and model training, we compare performance across different approaches. Our findings indicate that tree-based methods, specifically XGBoost and LightGBM, outperform others, achieving AUC scores between 0.70 and 0.75. Furthermore, we present a feature importance analysis to identify the most predictive variables. This research aims to assist banks in implementing machine learning solutions for NPL classification. Additionally, we offer a Jupyter Notebook containing the complete code for dataset preparation, feature engineering, model training, and evaluation, which can be accessed at https://github.com/eduardoalves94/ML-NPLs. We invite researchers to utilize this open-source material to replicate our results and explore alternative models or feature engineering techniques. We appreciate your interest and look forward to your feedback. Thank you.

Dyck paths play a significant role in combinatorics, with their chromatic symmetric polynomials recently introduced by Chow and Yan. This paper presents a novel combinatorial model for calculating the chromatic symmetric polynomials of a specific class of Dyck paths, utilizing combinatorial q-rooks. As an application, we demonstrate that the coefficients of these polynomials form a unimodal sequence. Furthermore, we extend our findings to a broader category of Dyck paths by defining combinatorial q-Dyck-Robinson-Schensted tuples. We anticipate that this combinatorial framework will enable the computation of various statistics for statistics-driven symmetric functions, such as elementary symmetric polynomials. Additionally, we offer an application of our approach to investigate the log-concavity of the chromatic symmetric polynomials for certain specific instances. Finally, we propose an open conjecture. (Note: Due to space constraints, detailed proofs are omitted in this extended abstract.) Keywords: Chromatic symmetric polynomial, Dyck path, q-rook, log-concavity, unimodality. 2020 Mathematics Subject Classification: 05E15, 05A15, 05A19.

This paper introduces a novel convolutional network architecture designed to handle oriented images, such as oriented optical coherence tomography (OCT) scans. Unlike standard convolutional networks, this model is built to achieve orientation invariance without discarding orientation-specific details. We demonstrate that the approach relies on two key components: a new convolutional kernel formulation and a new activation function, both of which operate by convolving with a collection of oriented filters. These elements enable the network to extract a set of oriented features. We validate the method's effectiveness through two experimental setups: a synthetic O dataset where ground truth is known, and an OCT image classification task. The results indicate that our approach outperforms an existing OCT classification method. Furthermore, we show that a network utilizing our kernel and activation functions surpasses an ablation version that employs standard activations instead. Finally, we demonstrate that this proposed method is transferable to natural images. The associated code is accessible at https://github.com/omriy/OCN. All experiments were conducted on a single GPU. Given that our method is designed for oriented images, it is particularly well-suited for application in medical imaging. The paper is also available in Hebrew. Keywords: oriented image classification, orientation invariance, oriented optical coherence tomography.

Intervals on $\mathbb{R}$ possess a unique property: they are defined by two endpoints, allowing multiplication from either the left or the right. This characteristic is significant for operators, as it corresponds to time evolution under self-adjoint operators within the spectral theorem for the Fourier inverse transform on $L^2(\mathbb{R})$. In this context, we investigate the commutator of these linear intervals and derive a new trace formula. Furthermore, we extend these findings to linear intervals featuring curvature and demonstrate an analogue of the Hilbert-Schmidt identity. We also present applications of this formula within the context of the Wigner transform. The research was conducted at the Max-Planck-Institut für Mathematik in Bonn during the autumn of 2019. Additional applications will be explored in a forthcoming publication. Keywords: Linear intervals, Complements, Curved linear intervals, Complements with curvature, Commutator, Trace formula, Trace class, Hilbert-Schmidt identity, Wigner transform. 2010 Mathematics Subject Classification: 47-02, 47B10, 47A47, 47A57, 47A68, 47L25, 81S30, 81S25, 81Q15, 81Q40.

This paper introduces a substantial, flavor-dependent correction to the top quark pole mass, derived from the exchange of virtual Higgs bosons. We demonstrate that this Higgs-induced effect is particularly pronounced for the top quark due to its large Yukawa coupling, which can elevate the mass by approximately 10 GeV. This correction is essential for achieving the few-GeV precision required for the top quark mass, a key parameter in the Standard Model. Consequently, we propose a revised interpretation of recent measurements from the 13 TeV LRun1, reanalyzing 37.9 fb⁻¹ of $t\bar{t}$ data. Our method avoids reliance on Monte-Carlo simulations by utilizing a kinematic variable that remains insensitive to non-resonant background processes. We find that the Higgs resonance contributes 2.5–3.0 GeV to the reconstructed top quark mass, a value that must be subtracted from the LRun1 result to yield the true pole mass. The final extracted top quark pole mass is $m_{t,\text{pole}} = 172.5 \pm 1.0$ (stat) $\pm 0.7$ (syst) GeV. This outcome is consistent with our 2015 LRun1 analysis, which reported $m_{t,\text{pole}} = 173.1 \pm 1.0$ (stat) $\pm 0.8$ (syst) GeV. Furthermore, we note that recent CMS measurements from the 8 TeV LRun0 suggest a significantly larger Higgs contribution, approximately 10 GeV. We discuss the implications of these findings for the ongoing quest to determine the top quark pole mass with high precision. Finally, we address the challenges in measuring the Higgs-top quark coupling and explore the potential of top-quark pair production at the LHC to achieve a precision of a few percent or better. Such an achievement would represent a major advancement in understanding the fundamental mechanism of electroweak symmetry breaking. Additionally, we examine the implications of our results for the ongoing search for new physics. Specifically, we show that the recent CMS LRun0 measurement, which implies a much larger Higgs contribution, could indicate a tree-level coupling between the Higgs and the $t\bar{t}$ vertex that is several times larger than predicted by the Standard Model. This would constitute a significant deviation from Standard Model expectations.

We demonstrate that for any $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists a threshold $k_0$ such that every graph $G$ with a degree sequence $d_1 \leq \dots \leq d_n$ satisfying $d_n - d_1 \leq k$ and $d_n \geq \frac{n}{2} + k_0$ admits a degree-$\varepsilon$ coloring using $n$ colors. This highly uniform degree-regular coloring ensures that each color class induces a subgraph with a maximum degree of at most $\varepsilon n$. Furthermore, we establish that for any $k > 0$, there is a constant $c_k$ where, provided $n \geq c_k$, every graph $G$ possessing a degree sequence $d_1 \leq \dots \leq d_n$ with $d_n - d_1 \leq k$ and $d_1 \geq \frac{n}{2}$ allows for a degree-1 coloring with $n$ colors. In this degree-1 coloring, the induced subgraph for every color has a maximum degree of at most 1, meaning each subgraph is either empty or a perfect matching. Additionally, we present a polynomial-time algorithm to compute such a coloring. The primary tool for proving our main results is a novel edge-dyeing technique, which we term the sequential method. We illustrate the efficacy of this approach by solving several longstanding open problems. Specifically, we provide a concise proof of a conjecture by Galias and Skupień, which follows directly from our main theorem. We also address a question by Kierstead and Klein regarding the minimum number of colors needed for a degree-1 coloring of graphs with a maximum degree of at most 3. By combining our result with a recent finding by Kierstead and Klein, we determine that this number is at most 12. Finally, we propose a conjecture concerning the minimum colors required for a degree-1 coloring of graphs with a maximum degree of at most 4. We show that this number does not exceed 25 and provide a partial answer to the conjecture. Accurate and timely diagnosis of COVID-19 is essential for effective disease management. While CT imaging offers a reliable method for detection, it demands expert radiological interpretation, making it a time-intensive process. Although recent research has focused on deep learning models to expedite diagnosis, these approaches often overlook the hierarchical spatial-temporal information inherent in CT scans. This study introduces a novel two-stage capsule network designed for rapid COVID-19 identification from CT images. The proposed framework consists of a feature extraction stage and a decision-making stage. To enhance the decision-making phase, we developed a TimeDistributed Capsule Network (TiDCN) that integrates time information into the capsule mechanism. The TiDCN architecture comprises three layers: a convolutional capsule layer, a time-weight capsule layer, and a routing capsule layer. The model's efficacy was validated using a dataset of 1,000 CT images containing 500 COVID-19 and 500 non-COVID-19 cases. Experimental results indicate that the proposed framework achieves a COVID-19 detection accuracy of 98.2% and a diagnosis time of 1.5 seconds per image. Furthermore, the TiDCN approach outperforms existing capsule network variants, demonstrating superior accuracy at 98.6% compared to 98.2% for DeepScape and 98.4% for SDCP. Additionally, radiomics feature analysis reveals that the proposed framework effectively captures key features critical to COVID-19 detection. These findings suggest that the proposed framework holds significant potential for achieving accurate and rapid diagnosis. The corresponding source code is accessible at: https://github.com/ChenYi2019/CT-DCN. The dataset can be found here: https://github.com/ChenYi2019/CT-DCN/tree/master/data. Future research will explore applying this framework to other medical imaging tasks. This paper introduces a novel framework for generating coarse quad meshes with regular topology, specifically integer grids, for CAD geometries. The process begins by creating an initial coarse quad mesh based on a CAD model, followed by the construction of an approximate integer linear system where unknowns represent vertex positions. To ensure a practical solution, this system is enhanced with a set of linear constraints. The resulting optimization problem, which is generally non-convex and NP-hard, is transformed into a convex form using a specific variable transformation. This strategy enables the efficient and accurate creation of regular quad grids for complex CAD models, offering a viable alternative to conventional projection-based meshing techniques. A key advantage is the ability to produce regular topology integer grids that closely match a target density function, thereby facilitating an automatic, user-friendly workflow. The proposed method is thoroughly validated across a diverse range of CAD models. Furthermore, the paper provides a comprehensive analysis of the mathematical properties of the integer linear system, including the characterization of feasible regions and the investigation of how mesh resolution influences the topology of the integer feasible region. Finally, the study examines the existence and uniqueness of optimal solutions, as well as the topological characteristics of the resulting integer grids. The theoretical findings are substantiated by numerical experiments on various two-dimensional domains. The general methodology is also applicable to other problems involving the integer discretization of 2D and 3D regions. Additionally, the authors have developed a MATLAB-based tool to implement this approach, which is made available for public use. This tool is designed to be user-friendly, requiring only the input of a target density function and the selection of meshing parameters. A step-by-step guide is included to assist users in operating the tool and interpreting the outputs. The tool is demonstrated on several CAD models, and the corresponding results are presented. The paper concludes with a discussion of potential future research directions. A complete, step-by-step video tutorial is also provided, illustrating the use of the tool on a CAD model and detailing how to interpret the results. The tool can be accessed at the following link: https://github.com/abdolrahman-mohammadi/Coarse-Quad-Grids-Generator. The authors are available to answer any questions regarding the tool or the paper. For further details, please contact Dr. Mohammad at mohammad@math.uwaterloo.ca. Dr. Mohammadi's research focuses on mathematical optimization, particularly the theory and applications of convex optimization, and integer programming. His work addresses problems in various fields, including mathematics, engineering, and economics

This paper derives formulas for the expected value and variance of the sample correlation coefficient under different data arrangement schemes. We examine the expected value and variance of the empirical distribution of the sample correlation matrix for arrangements of non-normal data, as well as for circular and von Mises (linear) data. Additionally, we provide a formula for the variance of the sample correlation expected value for circular data when arranged according to a Latin square design. These results are achieved by integrating techniques from combinatorics, probability, and calculus. Furthermore, we derive an expression for a specific class of multivariate integrals involving the gamma function and factorials, which is essential for obtaining combinatorial coefficients used in the paper's formulas. Finally, we present a simulation study to validate these analytical findings. The study compares four data types—multivariate normal, von Mises (circular), uniform (circular), and uniform (linear)—across four schemes: random arrangement, row arrangement, column arrangement, and Latin square arrangement. The findings indicate that for multivariate normal data, no significant differences exist between the four arrangement schemes. However, for both circular and von Mises data, arrangements based on row and column structures yield lower variance than those based on Latin square designs. Additionally, for circular and von Mises data, the variance is consistently lower when data is arranged by row or column rather than randomly. Overall, the results suggest that the expected value remains consistent across all schemes, while the variance is generally reduced through systematic data arrangement. Specifically, the variance is minimized when circular data is arranged by row or by column. These conclusions are supported by the derived analytical formulas. The paper concludes with suggestions for future research. Finally, all formulas, along with their proofs, are available in an accompanying R package, and an R notebook provides a detailed implementation of these formulas. Keywords: Arrangement of data, Arrangement of latin squares, Arrangement of random, Expected value, Variance, Von Mises distribution, Circular data, Multivariate normal data, Combinatorics, Empirical distribution, R package.

This text outlines the foundational elements of the $S$-matrix approach to quantum gravity, which are explored in greater depth in the book. It begins by examining the quantum $S$-matrix for gauge theories, with a focus on Yang-Mills theory, and derives its connection to soft theorems. The discussion then turns to quantum gravity, exploring how the soft-theorem description of low-energy scattering translates into soft factors within the $S$-matrix. Furthermore, it examines the CFT correlation functions linked to AdS scattering amplitudes via the holographic dictionary, noting that soft-theorem constraints in bulk gravity correspond to specific limits of conformal Ward identities at the boundary. Finally, it highlights that the low-energy gravity $S$-matrix adheres to soft-theorem constraints and can be systematically extended through a derivative expansion, a process that also generates the expansion for the dual supergravity CFT. The text concludes by outlining current challenges in quantum gravity, such as constructing a consistent $S$-matrix theory for a chiral gravity dual, and by demonstrating how to build a quantum $S$-matrix description for a simple extension of general relativity involving a massive graviton. These examples illustrate the utility of the $S$-matrix framework in investigating the non-perturbative characteristics of quantum gravity. The treatment of asymptotic symmetries and soft theorems is intentionally concise, as this connection was not established in the literature until recently. While a comprehensive exploration of this subject would require a separate volume, the text aims to provide a brief overview and suggest several directions for future research. The material is designed to be accessible to graduate students and researchers from adjacent fields, with detailed derivations of key results and an emphasis on the logical development of the argument. A list of exercises is also included to reinforce the material. The primary goal is to convey the essential concepts of the $S$-matrix approach to quantum gravity. While the text does not address all aspects of the broader quantum gravity program, it does examine various theories of massive gravitons, as this area has been a significant focus of the author's research. The $S$-matrix formulation for gravitons with mass is notably more intricate than that for Yang-Mills gauge bosons or massless gravitons, largely due to additional constraints arising from a broken gauge symmetry. This complexity underscores the value of the $S$-matrix approach as a non-trivial extension of the gauge-theory program. The text also touches upon the cosmological constant

This study addresses the uniform stabilization of Navier-Stokes equations within critical $L^q$-based Sobolev and Besov spaces through finite-dimensional, interior, confined, linear velocity feedback controls. These controls rely on observations derived from projecting the Navier-Stokes equations onto a finite-dimensional subspace. The primary innovation lies in the feedback control's dependence on local velocity data. We demonstrate that uniform stabilizability is achieved by appropriately selecting a single, strategically chosen fixed control point. Specifically, the first eigenfunction of the Stokes operator, evaluated at a suitably chosen location, serves as an effective control point for determining the uniform stabilizable feedback control. This approach resolves an open question posed in [12]. Furthermore, our findings are applicable to a broader context: the uniform stabilization of the heat equation in critical $L^q$-based Sobolev and Besov spaces. This extends the recent work of K. Kima and H. Kozlova [5], who utilized a single point observation for uniform stabilizable feedback control. Additionally, the current results offer an alternative method for uniform stabilization compared to the techniques employed in [5]. Finally, this work contributes to the resolution of the first and third open problems stated in [12]. To achieve these results, we employ novel and effective arguments, including a new characterization of uniformly stabilizable feedback controls and the application of the Riesz-Thorin interpolation theorem. These innovations are of independent significance. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 presents preliminary notations and function spaces; Section 3 reviews the linearized Navier-Stokes equations with localized velocity feedback control; Section 4 examines the uniform stabilizability of the linearized equations; and Section 5 applies the results to the uniform stabilization of Navier-Stokes equations in critical $L^q$-based Sobolev and Besov spaces.

Keywords: Navier-Stokes equations; Uniform Stabilization; Finite-dimensional Feedback Control; Confined Control; Local Velocity Observation; Riesz-Thorin Interpolation Theorem.

This digital resource allows users to explore word senses, definitions, synonyms, spelling variations, and etymological data. The lexicon is built upon the knowledge graph of WordNet 3.1, enhanced with additional content from literary sources. By leveraging literary knowledge, the system aims to offer richer descriptive data, particularly for words with low frequency in corpora or that have evolved in usage over time. This paper outlines the methods used to develop the LitMind lexicon and demonstrates how applications can access its knowledge. The recent surge in explainable recommendation has seen researchers utilize attention-based methods to create local explanations for individual items within a user's history. However, existing literature often overlooks the experience of users interacting with these explanations, particularly the potential instability of the attention distributions when ranking different items in their history. This paper introduces commit attention, a commitment mechanism designed to stabilize attention distributions across items in a user's history. Evaluated both quantitatively and qualitatively, our approach demonstrates superior stability and overall explainability compared to baseline models. The effectiveness of InAs quantum wells situated near semiconductor surfaces in anchoring the Fermi level within the bandgap varies significantly based on their specific design. This study examines how well-designed near-surface quantum wells can enhance surface barrier properties to enable precise bandgap Fermi level control. The research evaluates a specific configuration: an InAs quantum well between-surface and buffer layers, where the surface is composed of an InAs monolayer atop an InP termination. Theoretical analysis indicates that this design successfully pushes the surface barrier height into the conduction band, thereby eliminating the surface states that previously pinned the Fermi level in the valence band. These findings offer a viable pathway for developing tunable, quantum-confined infrared photodetectors and provide a foundation for further investigating novel quantum well structures. Additionally, the study demonstrates that the proposed design maintains a pinned Fermi level in the bandgap even when a 10¹⁰ cm⁻² density of surface states is introduced. These results are derived from a combination of first-principles calculations and continuum model simulations. Finally, the paper discusses potential experimental challenges associated with implementing this configuration. Overall, the proposed quantum well design represents a promising solution for achieving accurate control over Fermi level positioning in quantum wells located near free-standing semiconductor surfaces. Furthermore, the methodology used to assess quantum well stability against surface defects can be applied to other relevant systems. This approach is anticipated to facilitate the development of new technologies that leverage the unique advantages of free-standing semiconductor surfaces. Specifically, this could enable the creation of advanced devices, such as quantum well-based photodetectors, that were previously hindered by the inability to accurately place the Fermi level in the bandgap due to surface effects. The proposed design also holds potential for advancing research into the quantum Hall effect and other phenomena that rely on the precise control of Fermi level placement relative to the band edges. Ultimately, this work represents a significant step toward realizing the full potential of free-standing semiconductor surfaces in emerging quantum technologies. By providing a new tool for investigating the quantum properties of two-dimensional electron gases, the findings could lead to the discovery of new physical phenomena and enable the creation of novel devices with unprecedented performance capabilities. Ultimately, this research paves the way for a new era of quantum technology that harnesses the unique benefits of free-standing semiconductor surfaces. Although regional pooling has proven effective in various transfer learning scenarios, its impact on robustness against adversarial attacks remains ambiguous. This study investigates how regionally pooled models learn and whether regional pooling can enhance resilience. We demonstrate that models utilizing regional pooling are susceptible to attacks targeting specific regions, as they tend to rely on the features within those selected regions. To address this, we introduce QRQR, a regularization technique that imposes constraints on local regions to prevent the model from depending excessively on any single region. Our findings indicate that QRQR significantly improves robustness against adversarial attacks. Furthermore, we provide theoretical insights into the behavior of regional queries, offering a foundation for future research in this area. Finally, we evaluate the effectiveness of QRQR on ImageNet and CIFAR-10, showing that it achieves a two-fold increase in robustness.
