Consequently, the $|k| \to \infty$ asymptotics of the reflection coefficient for Davey-Stewartson II equations determine the small-$|k|$ asymptotics of the scattering data, which in turn govern the asymptotic behavior of the solution at large $|x|$ and large times. This approach enables the derivation of the asymptotic solution as $x \to \infty$ for $t > 0$ using the long-time asymptotics method. Specifically, for a rational initial condition with degree $N$, we demonstrate that the solution decays as $t^{-1/2}$. Furthermore, we prove that the solution remains bounded as $x \to \infty$ and exhibits oscillations with a period of $4\pi t$. These findings are applicable to various physical models, including the focusing cubic Davey-Stewartson II equation, the vector focusing cubic Davey-Stewartson II equation, and the defocusing quartic Davey-Stewartson II equation. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive description of the solution's asymptotic behavior for the defocusing quartic Davey-Stewartson II equation when the initial condition is Gaussian. Although text categorization is a well-researched area, its performance is highly sensitive to category imbalances. While prior efforts have explored data resampling and model regularization, the latter often degrades accuracy on the majority class. This study introduces Sibylvariant Modifications (SIMD), a framework that applies sibyltrophic modifications to dataset properties. SIMD enhances categorization performance on the largest classes without the need for additional training data or hyperparameter optimization. The results demonstrate that SIMD significantly boosts performance on the longest texts across all datasets, proving its effectiveness in mitigating category imbalances. Furthermore, SIMD exhibits robustness against adversarial attacks, maintaining strong categorization accuracy even when input texts are perturbed. Empirical results demonstrate the method's efficacy in image classification and object detection tasks. Additionally, we analyze the algorithm's performance in light of recent findings regarding the generalization of overparameterized neural networks. Finally, we highlight potential applications in few-shot learning scenarios where task variations are limited. Low-resource languages often lack the substantial datasets required for training state-of-the-art neural machine translation models. Quantization serves as a potential solution by reducing model weights from 32-bit floating-point precision to 8-bit, enabling the training of compact models that achieve near-full-precision performance. However, this study demonstrates that such models are excessively fragile during dataset extraction. We argue that utilizing pre-trained multilingual models with extracted languages and quantized weights yields superior performance. Furthermore, we show that these quantized models can be further compressed through quantization-aware training and knowledge distillation. This approach results in smaller models that surpass the accuracy of both extracted and non-extracted state-of-the-art methods. Ultimately, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the advantages and limitations of quantization in low-resource multilingual machine translation. Our source code is available at https://github.com/abhishekkumar1234/quantization-aware-training.

We introduce a solitary hypergraph, which functions as a quantum system composed of classically interacting quasi-particles. This system is described by a hyper-matrix of quantum variables, whose dynamics are governed by a specific class of "illogical" Lagrangian densities. These densities are characterized by their linearity with respect to hyper-matrix derivatives. By applying the Euler-Lagrange equations, we derive a set of coupled, nonlinear, first-order partial differential equations. The general solution to this system represents a set of solitary wave trajectories within hyper-space-concept, with each wave's properties determined by the system's parameters. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these illogical Lagrangians can be derived from the standard "logical" Lagrangian density—a polynomial of a specific degree in hyper-matrix variables and their derivatives—through a non-invertible process of renormalization of the hyper-matrix variables. Finally, we outline a method for constructing a Lagrangian density for a system of co-evolving, classical, solitary hyper-graphs, a concept that may serve as a foundation for a new class of classical and relativistic fluids. This approach could also facilitate the derivation of a "bottom-up" illogical-density-based density for a quantum system of co-evolving, classical, and solitary sub-systems from a many-body logical-density. Such a density would describe a system of interacting, classical, and coherent quasi-particles, each possessing an internal degree of freedom. This internal degree of freedom is represented by a complex scalar field, the dynamics of which are governed by a renormalized version of the Lagrangian density for a complex scalar field. The field's parameters are determined by the system's physical constants and the coordinates of the corresponding quasi-particle in space-time. We refer to these fields as "classical bose-fields." The internal degree of freedom of each quasi-particle is determined by the value of the classical bose-field at the quasi-particle's space-time coordinates. We also provide a set of equations that define the connection between the Lagrangian density for a classical, coherent state and the Lagrangian density for a quantum scalar field. This connection is established through a non-invertible process of renormalization of the classical bose-field. We show that the Lagrangian density for a quantum scalar field can be derived from the Lagrangian density for a classical, coherent state by renormalizing the classical bose-field with a complex scalar field that is quantized in the Fock representation. Although recent advancements in image description have produced highly detailed and coherent outputs, they often lack controllability. This paper introduces a novel method for regulating image description generation through prompting. Our approach allows users to adjust the granularity of descriptions by selecting appropriate prompts. We evaluate the model's regulatable generation capabilities using multiple-choice questions. Voice translation involves converting spoken language from one language into another language in speech form. While most current systems rely on supervised learning, which necessitates large datasets for every specific task combination, these requirements are often unmet in low-resource scenarios. To address this, this paper introduces a zero-shot approach to voice translation that functions without any task-specific training data. Our proposed model achieves new state-of-the-art results without compromising any existing methods on established benchmarks. Specifically, it improves WER by 1.6 points compared to the best supervised system and by 2.1 points versus the best zero-shot system on the most common benchmark. Additionally, we demonstrate that our system outperforms all other methods on the recent VoiceBank benchmark, marking the initial application of both voice conversion and cross-lingual ASR within zero-shot voice translation. Furthermore, our approach exhibits strong generalization capabilities, successfully handling multiple additional benchmark tasks that were not optimized during evaluation. Finally, we provide a detailed analysis of the various components comprising our model. To support future research, we have made the code and model available at: https://github.com/taehoonjun/zero-shot-vt. This study presents a probabilistic multi-agent model for predicting the daily peak load within a low-voltage network. It demonstrates that forecast fusion and the identification of non-stationary components, such as daily highs, are essential for achieving high-quality load forecasts. The results indicate that a Gaussian process agent model, enhanced with day highs and scaled load as covariates, outperforms a high-frequency load mean model. Furthermore, a simple ensemble of these two agent models outperforms individual approaches and shows robustness against the inclusion of additional features. The paper concludes that this probabilistic load prediction framework is a critical component for effective distribution network management. Additionally, it is argued that this approach offers significant potential for integration with the wider smart grid, including the aggregation of prosumer and consumer agents, as well as the modeling of supply and transmission agent behaviors. Finally, the study explores the potential for applying this framework to prosumer communities to facilitate their participation in the electricity market. To support these conclusions, an open-source Python implementation of the model is provided. The model is designed to be scalable for use in large-scale agent-based models of prosumer communities and the broader electricity market. This work serves as a foundation for future research into stochastic agent-based models for community energy management and the design of new market mechanisms. This article outlines the strategies and methodologies we employ to merge the knowledge of domain experts with machine learning workflows. It highlights the challenges domain experts encounter and explains how various domain-specific tools address these issues. Furthermore, the text details the obstacles faced when incorporating domain expertise into machine learning processes, drawing on our tool's experience in facilitating such integration. Finally, this work serves as a foundation for future research aimed at enhancing domain expertise integration within machine learning. The paper is structured into six sections: the first provides an overview of our approach to integrating domain expertise; the second and third examine the experience gained from our tool's ability to support this integration; the fourth offers an introduction to diverse domain expertise integration approaches; the fifth discusses potential future research directions in this area; and the sixth presents our conclusions. Our primary contribution lies in offering a comprehensive perspective on integrating domain expertise across all stages of a machine learning project. Additionally, this article can function as a guide for researchers seeking to integrate domain knowledge into their machine learning endeavors. We have structured this report to assist researchers in understanding how to integrate domain expertise and to identify potential challenges they might face. We have also provided an overview of existing approaches to domain expertise integration, which can assist researchers in selecting the most appropriate method for their specific needs. Finally, we believe this article will help broaden the scope of this field and encourage more researchers to explore integrating domain expertise into their machine learning projects.

Although significant strides have been made in developing AI for medical image analysis, the field remains susceptible to data biases, particularly in deep learning models for lesion segmentation and localization. To address this, we introduce a weakly guided learning approach for COVID-19 lesions in chest CT scans that bypasses the need for precise lesion coordinates. This method utilizes a two-stage pipeline: first, a regression network identifies coarse lesion regions using a Dice loss function; second, a segmentation network processes these regressed areas to perform final segmentation. By eliminating the necessity for accurate localization, our approach mitigates the impact of localization bias. We evaluated the model using the LIDC-IDRI and the recently released Kaggle COVID-19 CT dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques in both localization and segmentation accuracy. Furthermore, we conducted a bias analysis on the localization performance of existing state-of-the-art models, revealing that these models exhibit varying degrees of bias against the novel COVID-19 dataset. Our analysis indicates that the superior weakly guided learning model is less prone to such localization bias. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/COVID-19-lesion-localization-and-segmentation.

Accurately localizing and segmenting vertebrae in computed tomography (CT) scans is a critical step for numerous clinical tasks, including fracture detection, surgical planning, and radiation therapy. However, this process is difficult due to the presence of anatomical structures that resemble vertebrae and the subtle differences between them. This study introduces a novel technique that enhances vertebral body localization and identification by rectifying the imaging modality to better align with conventional CT characteristics and by optimizing vertebral recognition through the analysis of anatomical relationships with surrounding structures. The proposed approach is evaluated on a dataset comprising 1,000 CT images, each containing 30 vertebrae. The results demonstrate that the method achieves a mean localization error of 1.0 cm and correctly identifies 94.5% of vertebrae. Furthermore, the method is shown to improve vertebral body localization accuracy by 30% compared to a baseline 3D convolutional neural network (CNN). The associated code can be accessed at https://github.com/leeyy1213/vertebral-localization-and-recognition. Ultimately, this work serves as a proof of concept for leveraging knowledge-based analysis to enhance deep learning applications in medical imaging. Future research will focus on extending the method to perform sequential vertebral recognition and 3D localization. The source code is available at https://github.com/leeyy1213/vertebral-localization-and-recognition. The method demonstrates that incorporating knowledge-based analysis can improve the performance of deep learning in medical imaging, with subsequent efforts aimed at achieving sequential vertebral recognition and 3D localization. (Source: https://github.com/leeyy1213/vertebral-localization-and-recognition) The technique validates the potential of using knowledge-based analysis to boost deep learning performance in medical imaging, with future work directed toward sequential vertebral recognition and 3D localization. This study investigates resonant electron scattering in a dynamical regime where light and matter interact strongly via a weak dipole moment, a scenario known as ultrastrong coupling. We demonstrate that the coupling between electromagnetic radiation and electrons enables stabilization against ionization through their mutual interaction. Furthermore, we find that modifying the photon dispersion relation within a cavity can suppress electron tunneling. This phenomenon is attributed to vacuum oscillations of electrons between the initial and final states, which temporarily obstruct their movement. The resulting suppression of scattering resonances is analyzed in detail. These findings may have significant implications for understanding and controlling quantum interference effects in the vacuum. Additionally, they may offer a pathway to protecting matter from ionization in intense light fields by employing a cavity. Finally, we address the potential impact of these results on fundamental theories, such as the Schwinger effect. Specifically, we suggest that vacuum oscillations could influence pair production in intense laser fields. In this context, we propose that pair production could be significantly suppressed if the vacuum dispersion relation were altered. We outline potential methods for engineering such a modified dispersion relation, including the use of a cavity or the application of a strong light field under ultrastrong coupling conditions. These effects could be experimentally verified by observing a notable reduction in pair production. Moreover, this reduction could serve as a test for the validity of the Dirac equation and quantum electrodynamics when matter interacts with intense light fields. Our research thus offers a new approach to testing fundamental theories of matter and the vacuum. We conclude by discussing the broader implications of these findings for future quantum technologies. Specifically, we suggest that the ability to stabilize matter against ionization could be leveraged to develop novel devices and systems capable of withstanding extreme environmental conditions. This ability could be utilized to advance quantum computing, quantum communication, and quantum sensing technologies. Additionally, it could facilitate the development of new materials with enhanced stability and durability. Overall, our findings provide a promising avenue for advancing quantum technology and engineering novel devices and systems that can withstand extreme environments. This achievement is made possible by the ability to dynamically stabilize matter against ionization via vacuum oscillations. By harnessing the fundamental principles of quantum electrodynamics, we have opened up new possibilities for quantum technology and its future applications. Our research thus paves the way for a new era of quantum technology, characterized by its ability to stabilize matter against ionization and control fundamental vacuum phenomena. This ability holds the promise of revolutionizing quantum technology and its applications, while also providing a means to test and explore the fundamental nature of matter and the vacuum

Although numerous control architectures have been created for bipedal agents, the field of legged robotics has seen limited progress regarding elastic quadrupeds. This study introduces a robust, learning-based controller for a physical elastic quadruped named Leo. The controller employs reinforcement learning to generate joint torques based on the states of all four legs. We assessed the system's stability across various gaits, including a running gait at speeds up to 2.5 m/s on uneven terrain. Furthermore, we evaluated gait adaptation capabilities by training the controller to switch between walking and running gaits in response to electrical disturbances. Our findings demonstrate that reinforcement learning offers a highly effective approach for controlling complex, underactuated multi-legged systems. The source code for this project is available at https://github.com/ethz-asl/Leo. Video demonstrations can be viewed at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4222222222. Supplementary materials are provided in Supplementary Files 1 and 2.

This paper introduces the distinctiveness of quantum states and their time evolution. We apply a variational approach to the Schrödinger equation to examine the distinguishability of evolving quantum states. Our findings indicate that under specific conditions, two initial states remain distinguishable throughout their evolution, as their inner product remains invariant over time. Conversely, under different conditions, the inner product changes over time, causing the initial wavefunctions to become indistinguishable at later times, even if they were initially distinguishable. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a variational method utilizing Gaussian wavefunctions can accurately represent the time evolution of a harmonic oscillator. These results suggest that such variational methods are effective for simulating systems that do not regain initial distinguishability, such as open quantum systems. Additionally, we show that these methods can model the decoherence of a harmonic oscillator, yielding results that align well with exact solutions. Our numerical simulations confirm that these methods can accurately reproduce the Rabi oscillation of a qubit, achieving errors below 1% for both the expectation value of the Pauli $Z$ operator and the fidelity between the approximate and exact states. Finally, we highlight that these methods successfully simulate entanglement generation between two interacting qubits, achieving an entanglement fidelity of approximately 99%. These outcomes indicate that the proposed methods can accurately model the entanglement generation process. Overall, our results demonstrate that the variational methods presented in this work are effective for open quantum systems. We conclude that these methods are applicable to the simulation of quantum systems where distinguishability is lost. This study examines small-scale tearing modes within a collisionless slab plasma, focusing on their mechanical behavior in the limit where the ion Larmor radius is negligible. The analysis reveals that these modes exhibit both attractive and repulsive characteristics. Specifically, at very short wavelengths, the tearing current becomes proportional to the first derivative of the perturbed magnetic field, resulting in a purely repulsive force. Conversely, at slightly longer short wavelengths, the mode displays both attractive and repulsive components. These mechanical properties are derived from the most unstable eigenmodes, which are calculated numerically using a novel spectral code. The findings are compared against analytical predictions for large-scale tearing modes at short wavelengths and against established limits for short-wavelength kinetic tearing and drift-tearing modes. The magnetic eigenmodes associated with the small-scale tearing mode are characterized as cusp-like structures. Additionally, the research demonstrates that small-scale tearing modes can develop into current sheets with significantly broader widths than those of large-scale tearing modes. The magnetic reconnection driven by small-scale tearing is shown to be comparable to that of large-scale tearing, provided the latter is in the hot ion drift regime. Finally, the implications of these results for the saturation mechanism of large-scale tearing modes are discussed. The paper concludes by outlining potential future investigations into this phenomenon. Key terms include tearing modes, magnetic reconnection, and numerical methods. The rapid advancement of deep learning has significantly transformed image retrieval, yet current approaches often depend on extensive labeled datasets and fail to incorporate domain-specific knowledge regarding fashion items. This paper introduces a novel framework for fashion image retrieval that leverages feature-level trait manipulation to enhance retrieval accuracy while minimizing the need for training data. By utilizing a generative model, we can adjust domain-specific characteristics within images, such as altering a subject's hair color. This framework comprises three key components: a generator, a trait encoder, and a task encoder. The generator produces images with specific traits, which are then fed into the trait encoder to generate latent representations. These representations guide the task encoder to refine its own feature embeddings. Experimental results demonstrate that this framework outperforms state-of-the-art methods on public fashion image retrieval datasets. Additionally, we present a comprehensive analysis of the model's internal mechanisms and its ability to manipulate domain-specific traits. The code and models are accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-1997/Semi-supervised-FLTM. Furthermore, our proposed feature-level trait manipulation approach holds significant potential for applications like personalized recommendation and virtual try-on. Finally, we introduce a new dataset for evaluating feature-level trait manipulation, which will be made available to the research community. We anticipate this work will inspire future research in personalized visual search and virtual try-on systems. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews related work; Section 3 presents the proposed Semi-supervised Feature-Level Trait Manipulation (SS-FLTM) framework; Section 4 details the experimental setup and results; and Section 5 concludes the study. Given the growing interest in fashion image retrieval, we anticipate that the insights and methodologies presented here will inspire further research in the field. Solving linear operator equations $\mathbf{A}x = y$ within Banach spaces presents significant challenges, particularly when the operator $\mathA$ lacks a closed range, rendering the problem completely ill-posed. This study introduces a dual iterative approach utilizing a fixed-point operator linked to a Tikhonov functional defined on the range space. We demonstrate the convergence of the dual gradient method toward the exact dual representation of $x$, provided this text exists within the range of a specific fixed-point operator, the dual of $\mathA$, and a regularization parameter. Furthermore, we derive an explicit formula for this fixed-point representation and prove that the dual gradient method converges to it in both norm and weak topologies. Finally, we apply these findings to numerical experiments involving the tomographic reconstruction of a star-shaped object. In this context, we examine the linearized problem of X-ray computed tomography, which results in a highly underdetermined and ill-posed system. Our proposed dual gradient method successfully and accurately reconstructs the object, even in scenarios where existing primal methods fail. Additionally, we establish a duality gap between the Tikhonov functionals of the primal and dual spaces, demonstrating that the difference between their minimizers remains bounded. This gap can be effectively controlled by appropriately selecting the regularization parameter. These findings are novel and represent the first of their kind. They mark the first application of Banach space theory to address linear inverse problems, a field previously dominated by Hilbert space approaches. The paper concludes with a discussion of these results and their potential implications. Notably, the developed theory is versatile and can be adapted to various other inverse problems. Furthermore, the study offers a fresh perspective on the interplay between ill-posedness and regularization techniques. The authors acknowledge that this work was conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic, which caused significant delays in its publication. They extend their gratitude to the reviewers for their patience and understanding. Additionally, the authors thank their colleagues at the University of Duisburg-Essen for their support and encouragement throughout this research journey. Finally, the study aims to inspire future investigations into similar challenges and contribute to the ongoing discourse regarding the application of Banach space theory to inverse problems. The authors hope these efforts will inspire others to explore this promising and underexplored area of research.

Developing accurate 3D models of indoor environments is a critical component of autonomous expense creation for robotics. Light field cameras are widely recognized for their ability to generate precise depth estimates, yet they often struggle with occlusion errors. To address this issue, we introduce a deep learning-based post-processing technique designed to reduce these occlusion artifacts. Our approach utilizes a synthetic training dataset generated through ray-casting simulations. We demonstrate that this method significantly lowers the mean absolute error in depth estimation compared to raw camera data and shows promising results when applied to real-world depth maps. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/robertkaiser99/occlusion-aware-expense-creator. This research was conducted as a final year project at the University of Oxford. This paper introduces a bilinear approach to Fokas-Lenells equations, a nonlinear integrable system characterized by two parameters that enable the modeling of nonlocal effects. Initially, we establish the bilinear form and derive novel Hirota bilinear equations for the model. Subsequently, we utilize these formulas to generate multisoliton solutions, dark-soliton solutions, and nonlocal blow-up solutions. Finally, we provide the Riemann-Hilbert representation of the scattering matrix and derive a nonlinear representation formula for multisoliton solutions based on this framework. The study concludes with several appendices. Notably, this work represents the first application of the Hirota method to any Fokas-Lenells type integrable system. Furthermore, we introduce a novel technique for constructing multisoliton solutions for nonlocal integrable systems via the scattering transform method, which appears to be a previously unexplored approach. Additionally, we propose a new formula designed to facilitate the construction of blow-up solutions for nonlocal integrable systems. These findings are expected to hold significant value for advancing the field of integrable systems. Our results also offer a fresh perspective on the recently popular Fokas-Lenells model, which has garnered substantial interest within the scientific community. Finally, we have developed a computational program to assist in solving Hirota bilinear equations and constructing multisoliton solutions using the scattering transform method. This program is expected to be a valuable resource for researchers in the field of integrable systems. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 presents the Hirota bilinear form for Fokas-Lenells equations; Section 3 details the construction of multisoliton solutions via the scattering transform method; Section 4 focuses on multisoliton solutions in the dark-soliton limit; Section 5 examines blow-up solutions within a nonlocal context; and Section 6 offers a concluding summary. The incorporation of non-Riemannian backgrounds into string theory remains a challenging area of research. This difficulty stems from the fact that many properties of the quantum theory, which are well-understood in the standard Riemannian case, become significantly more complex when generalized to non-Riemannian settings. A primary objective is to identify a suitable generalization of the Ricci scalar that remains compatible with stringy general coordinate invarence. In this paper, we demonstrate that the generalized dilaton-d_metric Ricci scalar derived from double field theory offers a viable solution. Furthermore, we examine the associated non-Riemannian backgrounds, with a specific focus on those characterized by torsion. Finally, we explore the potential implications of these findings for the landscape of string vacua. The proliferation of wireless devices has created significant strain on IEEE 802.11 networks. In extensive home environments, access points (APs) often rely on extenders to boost coverage. However, the decision for an AP to connect a station (STA) is currently static and based solely on signal strength, ignoring critical factors like channel load. This oversight can result in a STA linking to an AP with a heavily loaded channel, thereby degrading performance. To address this, we introduce a novel architecture that enables dynamic selection of both the AP and the extender by incorporating IEEE 802.11k and 802.11v protocols. This system facilitates mutual exchange of information regarding channel load between APs and STAs, ensuring that connection decisions account for this data. We validated this approach through extensive real-world experiments within a large home setting, demonstrating that the proposed solution effectively mitigates interference and reduces latency. Furthermore, it enhances the overall experience for users. Our findings indicate that, on average, the latency experienced by STAs is reduced by 25% when utilizing this proposed architecture. Additionally, we observed that the latency of existing STAs in the network decreases by an average of 15% as new STAs are added to the network under this proposed design. To our knowledge, this is the first study to address the issue of channel load in the context of AP extension. We have released the complete code and dataset as open-source to support future research. This work was supported by the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC).
